notes: The World Bank announced a USD 13.5 million Mangrove Blue Carbon Pilot Program in Ghana under the Blue Economy for Resilient Africa Program and the West Africa Coastal Areas Management Program. The financing package combined IDA and PROBLUE resources with private funding and was intended to support planting, technical assistance and maintenance of approximately 3,000 hectares of mangroves over a twenty-year period. The programme is an implementation and blended-finance initiative rather than a general policy statement. The announcement does not by itself establish a national carbon-credit methodology, confirm project registration or report issued credits. Long-term climate benefits depend on restoration survival, maintenance, community participation, land and carbon rights, environmental safeguards and credible monitoring of additional and durable carbon gains.
source: World Bank
status_note: Announced in November 2022 as a financed long-term mangrove pilot under the World Bank's African blue-economy programme.

document_title: Costa Rica Marine Payment for Environmental Services Pilot for Mangrove Conservation
notes: Costa Rica launched its first marine Payment for Environmental Services pilot for mangrove conservation in the Gulf of Nicoya with World Bank support and Earthshot Prize funding. The arrangement involves national environmental, conservation, fisheries and finance institutions and community associations representing mollusk gatherers. Participants receive recurring payments tied to verified compliance with conservation, monitoring, surveillance, restocking and sustainable-use activities under approved management plans. The pilot extends results-based environmental finance from terrestrial forests to marine-coastal ecosystems and covers more than 6,000 hectares of mangroves. It is an ecological-compensation mechanism, not automatically a tradable carbon-credit programme. The official description does not state that offsets are issued, transferred or usable for compliance, and payments reward verified stewardship rather than a quantified volume of additional carbon removal.
source: Government of Costa Rica / World Bank
status_note: Active pilot formalized through an inter-institutional cooperation arrangement and supported by a national executive decree.

document_title: Thailand Blue Economy Financing and Blue Carbon Credit Readiness Assistance
notes: The World Bank technical-assistance package supports Thailand's development of blue-economy finance, coastal protection and sustainable ocean planning. It includes work toward a sovereign blue bond, integrated seascape management and financing structures under which mangrove restoration may be organized to generate blue-carbon credits and attract private capital. The initiative is relevant to policy readiness, finance design and possible market integration rather than evidence that a functioning blue-carbon credit programme already exists. The official announcement does not identify an approved mangrove methodology, registered project, issued credit volume or compliance-market recognition. Any future credits would still require clear project boundaries, additionality, carbon rights, safeguards, monitoring, verification and consistency with Thailand's broader carbon-market and sustainable-finance rules.
source: World Bank / Government of Thailand
status_note: Active World Bank technical-assistance and financing-readiness initiative announced in September 2025.

document_title: Yale Blue Carbon Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement Initiative
notes: The Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture launched a Blue Carbon Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement initiative to investigate whether alkalinity generated through mangrove and other blue-carbon ecosystem processes can provide a durable, measurable carbon-removal benefit and a new source of restoration finance. The programme combines field monitoring at restoration sites, mechanistic research, method development, stakeholder workshops and engagement with carbon registries. Planned outputs include best-practice guidance, MRV approaches and protocol-development field trials. The initiative is explicitly at the research and methodology-development stage. It has not established an approved crediting protocol, demonstrated that all measured alkalinity represents additional atmospheric carbon removal, authorized deliberate alkalinity deployment or reported issued credits. Ecological safeguards, attribution, transport, durability and double-counting remain central research questions.
source: Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture (YCNCC)
status_note: Active research initiative launched in 2025, with MRV and protocol-development work continuing in 2026.

document_title: Salt Marsh Ecology in an Era of Sea Level Rise
notes: This long-term NOAA research project examined whether North Carolina salt marshes can maintain elevation and carbon-storage functions as sea level rises. Field surveys, experimental studies, surface-elevation tables and simulation models were used to connect tidal inundation, sediment accretion, above- and below-ground plant growth, root decay and the persistence of carbon in marsh soils. The project generated evidence on the conditions under which marshes may continue to accumulate blue carbon while remaining physically sustainable. It was an ecological research and monitoring programme rather than a restoration authorization or carbon-market instrument. The work did not establish a mandatory accounting method, validate a project baseline, determine additionality or permanence for crediting purposes, or issue carbon credits.
source: National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science (NCCOS), NOAA
status_note: Completed NOAA research project conducted from January 2004 through December 2018.

document_title: Establishing a Blue Carbon Network for the Gulf Coast
notes: This NOAA-funded science-transfer project established a Gulf Coast blue-carbon network for reserve staff, local governments, researchers, restoration practitioners, nonprofit organizations and resource managers. The network was designed to share scientific information, coordinate regional activities, support locally relevant tools and projects, and test ways of using the recognized value of coastal carbon to attract funding for wetland conservation and restoration. The project therefore addressed capacity, coordination and early-stage finance readiness rather than directly restoring a specified site. It did not create a regional carbon registry, approve a crediting methodology, establish ownership of carbon benefits, register an offset project or issue credits. Any subsequent restoration or market activity required independent project design, permitting, accounting, safeguards and verification.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed science-transfer project implemented from September 2015 through August 2017.

document_title: Is macroalgal carbon sequestration the 'elephant in the Blue Carbon room'?
notes: This NERC studentship investigates the contribution of exported macroalgal carbon to long-term burial and benthic food webs in the deep Arctic fjord of Kongsfjorden. The project uses an existing digital landscape model, sediment-carbon information and field observations to build a geographically constrained inventory of macroalgae-derived blue carbon and to distinguish sequestration from biological consumption and remineralization. Its purpose is to reduce major uncertainty surrounding the fate of carbon exported from macroalgal source habitats and to support translation of evidence into United Kingdom blue-carbon policy discussions. The project studies natural carbon pathways and does not authorize macroalgae cultivation, deliberate biomass sinking or commercial deployment. It has not established a crediting protocol, verified removals or issued carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Active NERC studentship with a funded study period from September 2020 through August 2027.

document_title: The Significance of Macroalgal Detritus for Marine Food Webs and Blue-Carbon Sequestration
notes: This NERC studentship quantified how macroalgal detritus contributes to carbon burial and marine food webs in Scottish fjords. The project combined seabed-camera surveys, sediment coring, stable-isotope analysis, isotope-tracing experiments, food-web modeling and geographic information systems to develop a first-order assessment of the carbon subsidy transferred from macroalgal habitats into deeper sea-loch sediments. It addressed uncertainty over whether exported macroalgal material is durably sequestered, consumed or remineralized and was connected to the Scottish Blue Carbon Forum to support policy relevance. The research did not constitute a macroalgae farming or biomass-sinking project, did not authorize intervention in marine ecosystems, and did not establish project-level additionality, permanence, ownership or an approved carbon-credit methodology.
source: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Completed NERC studentship with a study period from September 2020 through January 2026.

document_title: Migration of CO2 through North Sea Geological Carbon Storage Sites: Impact of Faults, Geological Heterogeneities and Dissolution
notes: This NERC research grant examined the security of offshore geological carbon storage by quantifying CO2 migration, dissolution and capillary trapping in faults and heterogeneous strata representative of North Sea reservoir overburden. Work associated with the Goldeneye field combined geological characterization, core experiments, geochemical analysis, analogue flow experiments and seismic assessment to improve predictions of leakage pathways and the detectability of CO2 above a storage reservoir. The project generated scientific tools relevant to operators and regulators evaluating offshore storage integrity. It was a risk-reduction research programme, not a storage permit or injection authorization. It did not approve the Goldeneye site, establish a legally binding monitoring plan, certify stored volumes or demonstrate that any carbon credits or compliance units had been issued.
source: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Completed NERC research grant implemented from April 2016 through April 2021.

subnational_area: North Sea and Ardmucknish Bay, Scotland
document_title: Quantifying and Monitoring Potential Ecosystem Impacts of Geological Carbon Storage
notes: The QICS research project conducted a controlled, small-scale sub-seabed CO2 release experiment to quantify how leakage from geological storage could affect marine sediments, water chemistry, microorganisms and benthic communities. The programme measured the movement and fate of released CO2, evaluated ecosystem response and recovery, tested geophysical and biogeochemical monitoring techniques, and developed models and recommendations for early leakage detection and environmental risk assessment. Its results became an evidence base for planning and monitoring offshore carbon-storage demonstrations. The experiment was scientific research under controlled conditions and did not authorize commercial storage or routine marine release. The project did not issue a storage permit, establish a binding regulatory standard, certify stored quantities or create carbon credits, although its monitoring findings may inform later regulatory and verification systems.
source: British Geological Survey / UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Completed NERC research grant conducted from April 2010 through April 2015.

document_title: Characterization of Major Overburden Leakage Pathways above Sub-seafloor CO2 Storage Reservoirs in the North Sea (CHIMNEY)
notes: The CHIMNEY project investigated near-vertical geological structures that could provide leakage pathways above sub-seafloor CO2 storage reservoirs in the North Sea. Researchers combined marine seismic imaging, ocean-bottom instruments, drilling and core analysis, rock-physics experiments, fluid chemistry and three-dimensional modeling to estimate pathway continuity, permeability and potential leakage scenarios. Outputs were intended to improve overburden characterization, storage-site monitoring and regulatory confidence under offshore carbon-storage rules and international marine agreements. This record represents the transferred continuation award shown by UKRI rather than a separate commercial storage operation. The project did not authorize CO2 injection, approve a storage complex, establish a binding site-monitoring plan, quantify creditable removals or issue carbon credits. Its contribution was scientific methodology and risk evidence.
source: National Oceanography Centre / UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Completed transferred NERC research award implemented from November 2019 through October 2021; it continued an earlier grant that began in 2016.

document_title: Empowering Coastal Communities through Seagrass Restoration and Fisheries Sustainability Project
notes: This Gulf of Gabes initiative was selected as one of six flagship carbon projects supported by the IUCN-managed WALD Innovation Facility, which provides early-stage grants of up to EUR 1.5 million per project. The Tunisia project combines marine ecosystem restoration with sustainable fishing practices to improve climate resilience, ecosystem condition and coastal livelihoods. The wider facility is intended to move high-integrity nature-based projects toward investment readiness while applying biodiversity, community, transparency and benefit-sharing safeguards. The announcement confirms project selection but provides no detailed restoration area, implementation schedule, approved methodology, registry status or quantified removal volume for the Tunisia activity. It therefore represents funded project preparation and prospective restoration, not evidence that carbon credits have been registered, verified or issued.
source: International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) / WALD Innovation Facility
status_note: Selected for WALD Innovation Facility grant support in October 2025; detailed implementation and credit-registration status were not stated in the official announcement.

document_title: Estimating Global Carbon Storage of Mangrove Ecosystems
notes: This World Bank technical report developed global estimates of mangrove biomass and soil-organic-carbon stocks using harmonized spatial datasets. It reports carbon stocks and changes for 122 countries with mangrove extent and provides comparisons by region and income group for multiple observation years between 1996 and 2020. The work was designed to strengthen natural-capital evidence, national and regional planning, restoration prioritization and understanding of uncertainty in global mangrove carbon estimates. It is an analytical report rather than a regulatory inventory rule or project-level methodology. The estimates do not establish additionality, permanence, leakage, ownership or a verified baseline for individual carbon projects, and the report does not authorize restoration, certify national greenhouse-gas submissions, register offsets or issue carbon credits.
source: World Bank
status_note: Published World Bank technical report issued in 2024 and available as an active evidence resource.

document_title: Just How 'Green' Is the Grass on the Other Side? Particulate Carbon and Microplastic Capture Potential by Seagrass Meadows in Wales
notes: This active NERC studentship studies how the structure, condition and environmental setting of temperate seagrass meadows influence the capture of particulate carbon and microplastics in Wales. Broad-scale surveys and manipulative field and laboratory experiments examine factors such as meadow density, biomass, rhizome depth, epiphyte load, sediment grain size, nutrient input, physical disturbance and surrounding macroalgae. The project is intended to improve management of seagrass ecosystem services and address uncertainty about the relationship between habitat condition and carbon capture. It is scientific research rather than a restoration programme or crediting system. The study does not establish that all captured particulate carbon is durably sequestered, approve a monitoring standard, authorize seagrass intervention or generate verified carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Active NERC studentship with a study period from September 2024 through March 2028.

document_title: Effects of Ozone on Carbon Sequestration by Mangroves
notes: This active NERC studentship investigates whether ozone pollution reduces the carbon-sequestration capacity of mangrove ecosystems. The project combines international field studies, controlled ozone-exposure experiments and predictive modeling to assess present-day impacts, identify ecological characteristics associated with ozone sensitivity, and map where vulnerable mangroves overlap with global ozone-pollution hotspots. Its expected contribution is an improved evidence base for mangrove conservation and climate policy, particularly where atmospheric pollution may weaken anticipated carbon benefits. The work does not directly restore or expand mangroves, establish a carbon-credit project, define a national inventory method or authorize deployment. It also does not assume that standing carbon stocks equal additional removals; the magnitude, persistence and policy implications of ozone-related effects remain research questions.
source: UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Active NERC studentship with a study period from September 2024 through March 2028.

document_title: Recovery of Seagrass for Ocean Wealth UK (ReSOW UK)
notes: ReSOW UK was a national research programme designed to build the scientific, spatial, economic and governance evidence needed for large-scale seagrass recovery. The consortium combined field measurements, Earth observation, habitat-suitability analysis, social science, natural-capital accounting and stakeholder engagement to map existing and potential seagrass, quantify carbon and fisheries benefits, identify barriers to restoration, and develop a Coastal Ecosystem Enhancement Decision Support Tool. The programme supported restoration planning and financing discussions with public agencies and practitioners, but the grant itself did not authorize restoration at specific sites or establish a national seagrass carbon-credit methodology. It did not register projects or issue credits, and any future intervention still requires site-specific ecological assessment, permissions, additionality analysis, safeguards and long-term monitoring.
source: National Oceanography Centre / UK Research and Innovation (UKRI)
status_note: Completed research grant implemented from November 2021 through December 2025.

document_title: Carbon Storage in Intertidal Environments (C-SIDE)
notes: C-SIDE produced a national-scale assessment of carbon storage and burial in British salt marshes. Research across contrasting coastal regions combined sediment cores, radioisotope dating, vegetation and soil measurements, source attribution, citizen science, historical mapping, three-dimensional habitat mapping and statistical modeling to identify controls on carbon stocks and accumulation rates. The project generated extensive datasets and evidence intended to support coastal management, natural-capital assessment, greenhouse-gas inventory development and evaluation of managed realignment or salt-marsh creation. It was a completed research programme rather than a restoration authorization or formal accounting standard. The outputs do not independently establish project additionality, permanence, leakage or ownership, and the grant did not register carbon projects, certify national inventory values or issue credits.
source: University of St Andrews / UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) / Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)
status_note: Completed NERC research grant implemented from May 2018 through May 2023.

document_title: Scalable, Multiparameter Chip-Size Carbon Sensors
notes: This ARPA-E SEA-CO2 project funds Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution to develop a system-on-a-chip for ocean carbon-flux monitoring. The proposed miniature device integrates measurements such as pH, oxygen and particulate organic carbon while reducing power demand, instrument size and manufacturing cost for use on gliders and profiling floats. Semiconductor fabrication and scalable calibration are intended to replace hand-built, small-batch sensor production and support broader marine carbon dioxide removal monitoring. The award is a research and technology-development activity, not an approved MRV standard, commercial verification service or field-deployment authorization. The official description does not state that the sensor has completed operational validation, certified removals or supported issuance of carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023; the official project description presents an active research and sensor-development award without reporting commercial deployment or credit issuance.

document_title: Acoustic Methods for mCDR Based on Blue Carbon Burial in Seagrass Meadows
notes: The University of Texas at Austin SEA-CO2 project develops an acoustic sensor network to estimate biological activity and carbon burial in shallow seagrass meadows. The system is designed to detect oxygen bubbles released during photosynthesis and use sound refraction through the seabed to estimate carbon stored in roots and sediments. ARPA-E presents the technology as a lower-cost monitoring approach for large-scale seagrass remediation and marine carbon dioxide removal assessment. The award supports measurement development and validation rather than the restoration of a specified meadow. It does not establish an approved blue-carbon methodology, determine project additionality or permanence, authorize habitat intervention, register a carbon project or confirm that credits have been issued.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023 as an active acoustic MRV research project; no restoration permit, registry approval or issued credits are reported.

document_title: SLEUTH: Spectroscopy of Oceanic Liquid Environments Using Towed Optical Sensor Heads
notes: The University of Colorado Boulder SEA-CO2 project develops an optical underwater sensing system for dissolved carbon compounds. A sensor head using dual-frequency-comb laser-stimulated Raman spectroscopy is intended to be towed beneath an autonomous wave-energy-harvesting surface vehicle through an optical-fiber cable. The objective is to transfer laboratory spectroscopy into persistent, mobile and in-situ ocean observations that can improve spatial coverage for marine carbon dioxide removal measurement. The project is an early-stage instrumentation award rather than an operational monitoring network. The official description does not report completed marine deployment, a legally required MRV protocol, quantified atmospheric carbon removal, third-party verification or carbon-credit issuance, and it does not authorize any particular mCDR intervention.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023; the official material describes ongoing instrument development and does not report operational certification or verified removals.

document_title: SEAfloor Self-Sustaining CO2 Assessment Probe Edge (SEASCAPE)
notes: The University of Utah SEA-CO2 project develops low-power micro-optical and micro-electronic probes for long-duration measurement of carbon accumulation in marine sediments. Groups of probes are intended to be inserted across broad seafloor areas and operate for more than one year while measuring carbon dioxide and pH through a novel bubble-based mechanism. The project aims to address calibration, energy-consumption and sensor-degradation constraints that limit persistent seafloor carbon monitoring. It is an instrumentation-development award and not a marine geological storage permit or approved verification protocol. The official description does not demonstrate operational deployment at a commercial storage site, establish project additionality or permanence, certify stored carbon or report issuance of carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023 as an active seafloor-sensor development project; commercial validation and regulatory acceptance are not reported.

document_title: Spatially Resolved Multi-Parameter Sensing of Ocean Carbon Dynamics Using Fiber-Optic Time-of-Flight Sensors
notes: GE Research's SEA-CO2 award develops a fiber-optic sensor cable intended to measure multiple chemical ocean-carbon parameters across kilometer-scale transects while being towed from marine vessels. Chemically responsive polymer coatings distribute sensing capability along a continuous optical fiber, potentially expanding the volume observed and reducing costs relative to stationary or slowly lowered point sensors. The project supports spatially resolved marine carbon dioxide removal monitoring and the development of scalable observation technology. It remains an R&D project rather than an operational MRV service or mandatory standard. The official description does not report completed field qualification, accepted uncertainty thresholds, quantified removals, regulatory approval or issuance of carbon credits based on the sensing system.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023; the project remains technology development and the official description does not report completed certification or credit use.

document_title: Computational Systems for Tracking Ocean Carbon (C-Star)
notes: The C-Star SEA-CO2 project led by [C]Worthy develops a community framework for marine carbon accounting, model construction and data assimilation. The proposed system combines observational and forcing datasets, an ocean general-circulation model, biogeochemistry, tracers, marine carbon dioxide removal modules and ecosystem components to estimate ocean state and treatment effects. Its purpose is to improve transparency, reproducibility and accuracy in model-based MRV across mCDR approaches. The award builds research infrastructure and does not itself establish a legally binding accounting methodology or carbon-credit registry. The official description does not specify that the framework has completed independent validation, achieved an accepted error threshold, verified a commercial removal project or supported issuance of tradable credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023 as an active modeling and data-assimilation project; formal methodology approval and credit use are not reported.

document_title: Hybrid Distributed pH, CO2, Temperature and Acoustic Sensing for Monitoring and Verification of Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal
notes: The University of Pittsburgh SEA-CO2 project develops buoy-mounted optical-fiber sensors for continuous measurement of pH, carbon dioxide, temperature and acoustic conditions from the ocean surface to the seafloor. Chemically selective coatings are integrated into low-cost commercial fibers using a reel-to-reel manufacturing approach intended to support large-scale production. The technology is designed for nearshore mCDR applications including ecosystem recovery, ocean alkalinity enhancement and electrochemical processes that require persistent monitoring. This is a funded sensor-development project, not an approved environmental monitoring requirement or operational verification service. The official description does not report completed field validation, a standardized uncertainty framework, authorization of an mCDR intervention, certified removal quantities or carbon-credit issuance.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023; the official project description reports technology development but no completed regulatory qualification or verified removals.

document_title: Integrated Experimental and Modeling Assessment of Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement for Scalable Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal
notes: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's SEA-CO2 project combines numerical modeling with mesocosm experiments to evaluate ocean alkalinity enhancement effectiveness and ecological impacts in three major United States coastal settings. Tank experiments provide ground-truth data for models intended to estimate how treatment size, location, frequency and duration influence carbon removal and ocean-acidification mitigation. The award supports technology assessment, model validation and environmental evidence needed before responsible scale-up. It does not authorize alkalinity addition in open waters, define a binding national OAE methodology or establish a carbon-credit programme. The official project description does not report a completed field deployment, independently verified net removal, accepted durability calculation or issuance of carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: Selected for SEA-CO2 funding in October 2023 as an active model and mesocosm assessment; no open-water deployment authorization or issued credits are reported.

document_title: Development of Thin-Film Composite Hollow-Fiber Membranes for Direct Ocean Capture
notes: ARPA-E funded Captura to develop low-cost thin-film composite hollow-fiber membranes for stripping carbon dioxide from ocean water. The project modifies inexpensive water-filtration fibers with highly CO2-permeable coatings and uses computationally assisted contactor design to improve counterflow and cross-flow gas transfer. Its stated objective is to reduce the capital cost of the CO2 stripping stage and validate a direct ocean capture component at laboratory scale. The project page identifies a September 2022 start and March 2026 end date and lists the award as Alumni. It was a technology-development project rather than a commercial deployment permit, ocean discharge authorization or carbon-credit methodology, and the official page does not report issued credits or independently verified net removals.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: ARPA-E lists the project as Alumni, with a funded period from 6 September 2022 through 5 March 2026.

document_title: Electrochemically Modulated CO2 Removal from Ocean Waters
notes: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology ARPA-E project develops a battery-like electro-swing process that releases dissolved CO2 from seawater through electrochemical proton-gradient control and then alkalizes the treated water before its return. The approach is designed to avoid chemical additives and costly membranes while allowing compact systems to operate on platforms or ships using renewable electricity. ARPA-E lists the project as Active with a funded period from February 2021 through September 2026. The award supports engineering research and prototype development, not commercial offshore operation or a discharge permit. The official page does not report full-system field validation, independently verified atmospheric removal, storage certification, an approved crediting methodology or issuance of carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: ARPA-E lists the project as Active, with a funded period from 24 February 2021 through 30 September 2026.

document_title: Hydrolytic Softening of Ocean Water for Carbon Dioxide Removal
notes: The University of North Dakota Energy and Environmental Research Center received ARPA-E support to develop hydrolytic softening for direct ocean carbon dioxide removal. The process adapts conventional water-softening chemistry by precipitating dissolved inorganic carbon as calcium carbonate, decomposing the precipitate to release a concentrated CO2 stream, and regenerating lime for repeated use. ARPA-E describes a potential energy-cost reduction relative to sodium-chloride splitting with bipolar membrane electrodialysis. The project ran from May 2021 to November 2022 and is listed as Alumni. It was a completed early-stage research award and did not authorize offshore operation, establish a storage pathway, verify lifecycle net removal, create a carbon-credit methodology or issue credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: ARPA-E lists the project as Alumni, with a funded period from 21 May 2021 through 20 November 2022.

document_title: Incorporating Record-Breaking Catalysts in Electrospun Bipolar Membranes
notes: The National Renewable Energy Laboratory ARPA-E project develops high-performance bipolar membranes for lower-cost acid and base production used in direct air and direct ocean capture regeneration cycles. Three-dimensional interfaces, advanced water-dissociation catalysts and roll-to-roll electrospinning are intended to improve current density, energy efficiency, durability and manufacturability of electrodialysis stacks. The project is an enabling technology for environmental CO2 capture rather than a complete marine carbon removal system. The official page lists the project as Active and gives a scheduled end date of 2 July 2026, but final administrative closure is not independently confirmed. It does not constitute a marine deployment permit, establish net-removal accounting or report carbon-credit issuance.
source: U.S. Department of Energy / Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E)
status_note: The official ARPA-E page lists the project as Active and gives a funded period from 30 September 2022 through 2 July 2026; final closure is not reported.

document_title: DeCarbonHIX Seawater-Regenerated Metal-Polymer Hybrid Sorbent for Ocean Carbon Capture and Alkalinity Improvement
notes: Advanced Cooling Technologies was selected under DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 to develop DeCarbonHIX, an abiotic ocean-based system using a seawater-regenerated metal-polymer hybrid sorbent. The project covers full-scale offshore design and modeling, air-side pressure-drop and capture testing, assessment of weak-acid regeneration efficiency and electrical demand, benchmarking against alternative carbon dioxide removal technologies, and preparation of a pilot-scale system design. The concept is intended to capture and store CO2 while reducing seawater acidification. The selection represents funded feasibility and engineering development, not an offshore construction permit or operational deployment. DOE does not report a completed pilot, independently verified net removals, an approved MRV methodology or issued carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy — Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management
status_note: Selected in DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 on 9 August 2023; the official page does not provide a project-level closure date or report completed deployment.

document_title: Atmospheric CO2 Removal via Direct Ocean Capture on an Offshore Platform
notes: Captura Corporation was selected under DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 for conceptual design and feasibility studies of a direct ocean capture system located on an offshore oil or gas platform to be provided by Equinor. The proposed design targets approximately 1,000 tonnes of CO2 removal per year and examines how existing offshore infrastructure could host marine carbon capture equipment and associated operations. The award is intended to lay technical and commercial groundwork for future deployment and coastal employment. It is a distinct feasibility project from Captura's membrane-development work. The selection does not authorize offshore construction or discharge, confirm a storage destination, verify lifecycle net removal, establish a crediting method or report issued carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy — Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management
status_note: Selected in DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 on 9 August 2023 for conceptual design and feasibility work; no project-level closure or deployment authorization is reported.

subnational_area: California; coastal aquaculture and brine-outfall settings
document_title: Integrating Aquaculture and Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement for Low-Cost Carbon Removal and Ecosystem Benefit
notes: Ebb Carbon was selected under DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 to study integration of ocean alkalinity enhancement with aquaculture and coastal brine outfalls. The project uses clean aqueous alkalinity intended to reduce local acidification and increase atmospheric CO2 uptake into ocean bicarbonate, while examining opportunities to support shellfish production. DOE describes the concept as a combined carbon-removal and regional ecosystem-benefit pathway. The selection funds technology and integration studies rather than unrestricted alkalinity discharge or commercial operation. The official page does not identify a completed field trial, permitted treatment volume, approved environmental monitoring plan, independently verified removal quantity, accepted carbon-credit methodology or issued credits. Additionality, durability, secondary precipitation and ecological response remain project-level questions.
source: U.S. Department of Energy — Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management
status_note: Selected in DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 on 9 August 2023; the official selection page does not report project completion, deployment authorization or issued credits.

document_title: Ocean Energy Carbon Removal
notes: Ocean Energy USA was selected under DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 to integrate renewable wave energy with direct ocean capture. The conceptual design combines an Ocean Energy Buoy wave-energy converter with the Naval Research Laboratory's Electrolytic Cation Exchange Module for removing carbon dioxide from seawater. The project is intended to examine field-validation architecture for a combined offshore energy and carbon-removal platform. It is an engineering feasibility award and does not represent construction, operation or environmental authorization for an offshore system. DOE does not report a completed integrated prototype, storage arrangement, energy and lifecycle balance, independently verified removal quantity, approved MRV protocol or carbon-credit issuance. Marine safety and ecological impacts would require separate evaluation before deployment.
source: U.S. Department of Energy — Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management
status_note: Selected in DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 on 9 August 2023 for conceptual design; the official page does not provide a closure date or field-deployment approval.

document_title: Development of Modular Electrochemical Tubes to Remove Dissolved Inorganic Carbon from Ocean Water
notes: The University of Houston was selected under DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 to develop modular electrochemical tubes for removing dissolved inorganic carbon from seawater. The concept seeks to avoid costly ion-exchange membranes, regulate pH with lower-cost electrode materials, and enable installation at onshore desalination facilities or offshore infrastructure. The project includes theoretical modeling of controlling parameters followed by laboratory validation using synthetic seawater. This is an early-stage research and prototype award, not an authorization to process or discharge ocean water at a commercial site. DOE does not report field deployment, a storage or utilization pathway for recovered carbon, independently verified net atmospheric removal, an accepted accounting methodology or issuance of carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy — Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management
status_note: Selected in DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 on 9 August 2023 for modeling and laboratory validation; no project-level completion date is reported.

subnational_area: Kentucky; prospective Rhode Island offshore wind setting
document_title: Depolarized Electrochemical Reactor for Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement and High-Purity Carbon Recovery
notes: The University of Kentucky Research Foundation was selected under DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 to develop a depolarized electrochemical reactor for direct ocean capture and ocean alkalinity enhancement. The concept would use power near a proposed offshore wind farm off Rhode Island, recover a high-purity CO2 stream from ocean water, and increase alkalinity-driven abiotic carbon capture while targeting reduced energy consumption. The award supports engineering design and validation rather than offshore construction or operation. DOE does not report a completed reactor, permitted intake or discharge, confirmed carbon-storage destination, independently verified atmospheric removal, ecological monitoring results, an approved carbon-credit methodology or issued credits. Lifecycle energy use, alkalinity fate and marine impacts remain necessary assessment areas.
source: U.S. Department of Energy — Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management
status_note: Selected in DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 on 9 August 2023; the official page does not report project completion or offshore deployment authorization.

subnational_area: North Dakota; prospective offshore field-validation setting
document_title: Hydrolytic Softening for Ocean Carbon Dioxide Removal — Field Validation Design
notes: The University of North Dakota Energy and Environmental Research Center received a separate DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 selection for conceptual design of a hydrolytic-softening field-validation unit capable of removing up to ten tonnes of CO2 per year from ocean water. This record represents a follow-on project decision distinct from the earlier ARPA-E laboratory award. The work focuses on translating the process toward an offshore validation unit and assessing practical scale-up. The selection does not authorize installation or marine operation and does not report that the proposed unit was built or tested. DOE also does not identify verified net removal, a permanent storage arrangement, an approved methodology, commercial registration or issued carbon credits.
source: U.S. Department of Energy — Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management
status_note: Selected in DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 on 9 August 2023 as a follow-on field-validation design project; no project-level closure or completed field trial is reported.

document_title: TRACER: Electrochemical Removal of Carbon Dioxide from Ocean Water — Field Validation
notes: The University of Texas at Arlington was selected under DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 for TRACER, a field-validation project using continuous electrochemical treatment of seawater. The approach exploits ocean-atmosphere CO2 equilibrium and abundant alkaline cations to store carbon in stable carbonates, hydroxides and aqueous bicarbonate or carbonate forms. DOE presents the concept as a potentially scalable pathway with durable mineral or dissolved storage. The selection funds development and validation and is distinct from other electrochemical ocean-removal awards. It does not establish that a field system has received environmental authorization, demonstrate lifecycle net removal, define a verified project boundary, provide independent permanence confirmation, approve a crediting method or report carbon-credit issuance.
source: U.S. Department of Energy — Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management
status_note: Selected in DOE FOA 2614 Round 2 on 9 August 2023 for field-validation development; the official page does not report completion or issued credits.

document_title: Land to Sea: Assessing Urban Impacts on Coastal Water Quality in Charleston, South Carolina
notes: This active NCCOS project evaluates how urban land-use change, flooding, extreme precipitation and sea-level rise influence water quality, nutrient transport, microbial communities and blue-carbon fluxes in Charleston Harbor. The programme combines uncrewed aerial vehicles, Landsat and Sentinel observations, hyperspectral remote sensing, weekly field sampling and analysis of dissolved organic matter, chlorophyll, carbon dynamics and phytoplankton biomass. Results are intended to support coastal planning and open-source monitoring capacity. The project is funded through a Congressionally Directed Spending award under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024. It is a research and observation programme, not a carbon-removal deployment, restoration permit, accounting methodology, carbon registry or credit-issuance mechanism.
source: National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science (NCCOS), NOAA
status_note: Active NCCOS project running from March 2025 through February 2030.

subnational_area: United States ocean, coastal and Great Lakes observing domains
document_title: NOAA Oceanic and Atmospheric Research Ocean Carbon Observing Science Plan FY25 to FY35
notes: This ten-year NOAA Oceanic and Atmospheric Research science plan establishes priorities for sustained ocean, coastal and Great Lakes carbon observations, carbon-cycle science, data management, modeling, product development and user engagement. It organizes the programme around observing changes in the ocean carbon cycle, improving carbon data and services, and expanding community participation and technical capacity. The plan is intended to guide coordination across NOAA laboratories and programmes and with interagency and international partners. It supports the evidence infrastructure required for climate projections, mitigation planning and future marine carbon dioxide removal assessment. It is a research strategy rather than a deployment authorization, carbon-accounting methodology or crediting mechanism, and it does not certify removals or issue carbon credits.
source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Oceanic and Atmospheric Research
status_note: Published as a NOAA Special Report in 2025 and designed to guide ocean carbon observing priorities across fiscal years 2025 to 2035.

document_title: Climate Protection Measures in Coastal Ecosystems: Reporting, Accounting and Financing of Blue Carbon Measures
notes: This German Environment Agency report assesses how protection and restoration of mangroves, seagrasses and tidal marshes can be reflected in climate reporting, carbon accounting and financing arrangements. It reviews scientific criteria for credible blue carbon measures, existing projects, IPCC reporting opportunities, voluntary carbon-market approaches, public and private finance, additionality, permanence, monitoring needs and biodiversity and social safeguards. The report emphasizes that credible measures require demonstrable human influence on carbon uptake or storage, appropriate carbon-flux monitoring and alignment with nature-based-solution principles. It is an analytical federal research publication and does not create a German crediting programme, mandate inventory treatment, approve an individual project or authorize marine intervention. Its recommendations provide evidence for later policy and financing decisions.
source: German Environment Agency (Umweltbundesamt)
status_note: Published in June 2026 as Climate Change report 37/2026 and available as an active federal evidence and policy-analysis resource.

document_title: Blue Carbon Ecosystems in Indonesia Roadmap and Action Guide
notes: Indonesia's Roadmap and Action Guide provides a coordinated national framework for protecting, restoring and sustainably managing mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes. Jointly developed by the responsible Indonesian ministries with technical support from the Global Green Growth Institute, it sets policy directions for ecosystem management, monitoring, institutional coordination, climate-plan integration, financing and participation in carbon-market frameworks. The guide aligns blue carbon action with Indonesia's national climate commitments, carbon economic value framework and land-sector mitigation goals. It is a strategic reference rather than a project permit or a complete national crediting methodology. The document does not by itself register projects, establish site-level additionality or permanence, quantify verified removals or authorize issuance and transfer of carbon credits.
source: Government of Indonesia / Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI)
status_note: Officially launched at COP30 in November 2025 and published as an active national roadmap and action guide.

subnational_area: North Sumatra — Pulau Kampai, Pangkalan Siata, Halaban and Salahaji
document_title: Gold Standard Design Certification and Registration of the Global Mangrove Trust Blue Carbon Restoration Project
notes: Gold Standard completed design certification and registration for the Global Mangrove Trust Blue Carbon Restoration Project in North Sumatra under its Sustainable Management of Mangroves methodology. The registered programme and first voluntary project activity cover 146 hectares of validated restoration areas and use project identifiers GS23179 and GS23180. Independent validation reviewed additionality, permanence, safeguards, baseline setting, carbon accounting and the monitoring framework. The project announcement estimates 203,672 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over a thirty-year crediting period. This milestone is design certification and registration, not verification of delivered removals. Restoration and monitoring must continue, Indonesian registry coordination remains relevant, and the official materials do not report completion of first verification or issuance of carbon credits.
source: Gold Standard for the Global Goals / Global Mangrove Trust
status_note: Design certification documents were uploaded in January 2026 and registration was announced in February 2026; first verification and credit issuance were not reported.

subnational_area: Sine Saloum Delta and Casamance Estuary
document_title: Verra VCS and CCB Registration of the Senegal Blue Carbon Mangrove Project
notes: The Senegal Blue Carbon Mangrove Project achieved registration under the Verra Verified Carbon Standard and Climate, Community and Biodiversity Standards using VM0033 for tidal-wetland and seagrass restoration. The project covers approximately 7,500 hectares in the Sine Saloum Delta and Casamance Estuary and combines mangrove reforestation, ecosystem recovery, community participation and biodiversity objectives. The developer estimates approximately 2.2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over a forty-year crediting period extending through 2062. Registration followed technical assessment, environmental studies, stakeholder engagement, field implementation, independent validation and regulatory review. Registration establishes eligibility for future monitoring and verification; it is not equivalent to issuance. The official announcement does not state that verified carbon units had already been issued.
source: Verra VCS and CCB Standards / Karbon-X
status_note: Project registration was announced on 16 June 2026; future monitoring and verification remain necessary before any credit issuance.

document_title: M0167 Revision to VM0033 Methodology for Tidal Wetland and Seagrass Restoration, v2.0
notes: Verra's M0167 development process is preparing a revised methodology for quantifying greenhouse-gas emission reductions and removals from restoration of blue carbon ecosystems, including tidal wetlands. The revision is intended to update procedures for eligible activities, baselines, biomass and soil-organic-carbon accounting, leakage, additionality and other methodological requirements. Verra identifies the work as Step 3, Draft Methodology Development, and is seeking funding, general stakeholder interest and independent expert reviewers. The proposed revision is globally applicable but has not completed expert review, public consultation, validation or final approval. It therefore cannot yet replace the active VM0033 methodology or be treated as an operational crediting rule, and no project can claim issuance solely on the basis of this draft development record.
source: Verra
status_note: Under development at Step 3 as of August 2026; Verra requested independent expert-review proposals by 24 August 2026.

document_title: CM-LU-CW-001 Blue Carbon Methodology for Mitigation of Climate Change in Coastal Wetlands, Version 1.1
notes: Cercarbono's methodology establishes eligibility and greenhouse-gas accounting procedures for restoration and revegetation of mangroves, seagrass meadows and tidal marshes. It defines project boundaries, baseline and project scenarios, eligible areas, carbon pools, greenhouse-gas sources, additionality, leakage, uncertainty, non-permanence, buffer provisions, monitoring, reporting, validation and verification. The methodology draws on IPCC wetland guidance and includes requirements for environmental and social safeguards within the voluntary certification programme. Version 1.1 is an active programme methodology that can support project preparation and certification, but it does not itself approve any specific project or guarantee credit issuance. Projects must separately satisfy programme registration, monitoring and independent verification requirements before quantified mitigation outcomes can be issued or used.
source: Cercarbono
status_note: Version 1.1 was published in 2026 as an active methodology within the Cercarbono voluntary certification programme.

document_title: Isometric Direct Ocean Capture and Storage Protocol, Version 1.1
notes: This Isometric protocol specifies requirements for calculating net atmospheric carbon dioxide removal through direct ocean capture followed by durable storage. It covers eligible electrochemical, chemical-looping and photochemical separation systems, project baselines, cradle-to-grave greenhouse-gas accounting, air-sea carbon uptake modeling, uncertainty, ownership, additionality, independent validation and verification, environmental and social safeguards, permitting, monitoring and long-duration storage. Eligible projects must be officially permitted, demonstrate net-negative impact and provide storage on at least a thousand-year timescale. The protocol creates a voluntary certification pathway rather than a government deployment permit. Publication of the protocol does not mean that every direct ocean capture project qualifies, and credit issuance requires project-specific validation, measured performance, verification and compliance with all referenced modules.
source: Isometric
status_note: Current Version 1.1 is active on the Isometric registry in 2026; project-level permitting, validation and verification remain mandatory before credit issuance.

document_title: Isometric Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement from Coastal Outfalls Protocol, Version 1.1
notes: This Isometric protocol defines a voluntary carbon-removal certification pathway for ocean alkalinity enhancement delivered through stationary coastal outfalls. It specifies applicability conditions, baselines, lifecycle greenhouse-gas accounting, alkalinity measurement, plume and air-sea uptake modeling, uncertainty, additionality, independent validation and verification, environmental and socio-economic safeguards, stakeholder engagement, official permitting and long-term ocean monitoring. Project proponents must quantify net atmospheric removal rather than merely report alkalinity discharged, and must monitor biological and ecological indicators around the deployment area. The protocol is not an environmental permit or blanket authorization for alkalinity discharge. Publication does not demonstrate that a particular project is safe or creditable; project-specific data, regulatory approvals, model validation, verification and compliance with all referenced Isometric modules are required before credits may be issued.
source: Isometric
status_note: Current Version 1.1 is active on the Isometric registry in 2026; official permits and independent project validation and verification are required before issuance.

document_title: Isometric Air-Sea CO2 Uptake Module, Version 1.1
notes: The Isometric Air-Sea CO2 Uptake Module standardizes how additional atmospheric carbon uptake caused by a marine carbon dioxide removal intervention must be quantified. It applies to approaches that create a surface-ocean carbon-dioxide partial-pressure deficit, including coastal-outfall ocean alkalinity enhancement and direct ocean capture and storage. The module defines model-domain, physics, biogeochemistry, simulation, output, validation, uncertainty, documentation and crediting-timeline requirements and permits calculation through air-sea flux or dissolved-inorganic-carbon approaches with cross-checks. It relies on extensively validated ocean biogeochemical models because direct observations generally cannot isolate project-induced uptake across the necessary spatial and temporal scales. The module is a supporting accounting rule, not a deployment permit, standalone project approval or evidence that any removal has already occurred.
source: Isometric
status_note: Version 1.1 is an active Isometric accounting module in 2026 and is referenced by the current OAE and direct ocean capture protocols.

document_title: Isometric Dissolved Inorganic Carbon Storage in Oceans Module, Version 1.0
notes: This Isometric module defines durability, reversal-risk and buffer requirements for atmospheric carbon stored as dissolved inorganic carbon in the ocean. It is designed for use with approved Isometric protocols after net removal has been quantified and environmental and social safeguards have been satisfied. The module describes the ocean dissolved-inorganic-carbon reservoir, relevant bicarbonate and carbonate storage forms, expected long storage times, mechanisms that could reverse or shorten storage, and risk treatment for pathways including ocean alkalinity enhancement and direct ocean capture. It does not independently calculate total project removals or authorize discharge into marine waters. A project must still comply with the relevant protocol, quantify lifecycle emissions and air-sea uptake, obtain permits, complete independent validation and verification, and satisfy issuance requirements before storage claims can support credits.
source: Isometric
status_note: Version 1.0 is an active Isometric storage module in 2026 and is referenced by multiple marine carbon-removal protocols.

document_title: Isometric Electrolytic Seawater Mineralization Protocol, Version 1.1
notes: This Isometric protocol defines requirements for quantifying net atmospheric carbon dioxide removal through electrolytic seawater mineralization. The pathway uses seawater electrolysis in a controlled facility to store carbon as dissolved bicarbonate and carbonate ions and as solid carbonate minerals, while potentially producing hydrogen as a co-product. The protocol covers applicability, lifecycle greenhouse-gas accounting, additionality, uncertainty, independent validation and verification, feedstock characterization, process measurements, environmental and social safeguards, official permitting and storage durability. It limits crediting to carbon removal occurring within the engineered system and does not automatically credit later open-ocean uptake. The protocol is a voluntary certification framework rather than a marine operating permit, and project-specific verification is required before any credit issuance.
source: Isometric
status_note: Version 1.1 is active on the Isometric registry in 2026; individual facilities must still obtain permits and complete validation and verification before credits may be issued.

document_title: Isometric Wastewater Alkalinity Enhancement Protocol, Version 1.2
notes: This Isometric protocol establishes a voluntary carbon-removal accounting framework for adding qualified alkaline rock or mineral feedstock to biological wastewater-treatment processes. The intervention converts carbonic acid produced during organic-matter degradation into bicarbonate that is discharged to a river or ocean and stored over long timescales. The protocol specifies eligible treatment plants, project boundaries, baselines, feedstock characterization, greenhouse-gas accounting, river and ocean losses, additionality, uncertainty, monitoring, verification, permitting, environmental safeguards and proof of partnership with the wastewater facility. It applies to retrofits of eligible municipal and industrial biological treatment systems rather than every wastewater discharge. Publication does not authorize a retrofit or discharge, and independently verified net removal is required before credits can be issued.
source: Isometric
status_note: Version 1.2 is active on the Isometric registry in 2026 and requires project-specific permitting, validation, monitoring and verification.

document_title: Isometric Mangrove Restoration Protocol, Version 1.1
notes: This Isometric protocol provides procedures for calculating net carbon dioxide removal from restoration of historically present mangrove habitat. Eligible activities may include replanting native mangrove species, restoring hydrological conditions and active management that enables ecosystem recovery. The protocol covers ecological screening, project baselines, biomass and soil-organic-carbon accumulation, lifecycle emissions, additionality, leakage, durability, monitoring, uncertainty, independent validation and verification, community engagement, biodiversity protection and environmental and social safeguards. It requires project proponents to document restoration activities, land and carbon rights, species selection and long-term management. The protocol is a voluntary crediting standard rather than a government restoration permit. Project registration and credit issuance remain conditional on site-specific validation, measured performance, verification and compliance with applicable national rules.
source: Isometric
status_note: Version 1.1 is active on the Isometric registry in 2026; project-level land rights, permits, validation and verification remain necessary before credit issuance.

document_title: Blue NDC Challenge
notes: Brazil and France launched the Blue NDC Challenge at the 2025 United Nations Ocean Conference to encourage governments to integrate ocean-based climate action into updated Nationally Determined Contributions. The inaugural participants also included Australia, Fiji, Kenya, Mexico, Palau and Seychelles. Depending on national circumstances, participating governments may strengthen conservation and restoration of coastal and marine ecosystems, marine spatial planning, integrated coastal management and other ocean-related mitigation and adaptation measures. The initiative provides international political coordination and access to supporting partner networks rather than a uniform regulatory programme. Joining the Challenge does not automatically amend a national NDC, authorize a blue-carbon project, establish a carbon-credit methodology, quantify additional removals or create a binding financing obligation.
source: Governments of Brazil and France / World Resources Institute and supporting partners
status_note: International political initiative launched on 9 June 2025 and active as a platform for integrating ocean action into national climate commitments.

document_title: Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue Plenary Statement 2025
notes: This formal submission to the 2025 UNFCCC Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue explains how mangrove-positive Nationally Determined Contributions can advance mitigation, adaptation, coastal resilience and biodiversity objectives. The Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force recommends science-based, measurable and actionable mangrove targets, use of relevant IPCC wetland guidance, stronger baseline mapping and carbon-stock assessment, and alignment between NDCs, the Global Goal on Adaptation and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. It also presents technical guidance developed for governments preparing NDC updates. The statement is an expert policy submission rather than a negotiated UNFCCC decision. It does not bind Parties, approve national targets, allocate finance, establish a carbon-credit methodology or authorize restoration activities.
source: Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force / United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)
status_note: Submitted to the co-facilitators of the SBSTA 62 Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue on 10 June 2025 as a non-binding stakeholder statement.

document_title: Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force SB64 Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue Plenary Statement 2026
notes: The 2026 Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force statement updates the Task Force's recommendations for the UNFCCC Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue. It reports that twelve endorsing governments had incorporated mangrove-specific targets into their NDCs and shifts attention from target formulation toward implementation, investment planning, finance, technical capacity, monitoring and international cooperation. The statement encourages measurable targets for governments still preparing NDC 3.0 documents and proposes stronger alignment of mangrove action with biodiversity, adaptation and climate-finance processes. It is a distinct annual submission reflecting later implementation priorities, not a revision of the 2025 statement. It remains non-binding and does not release funds, approve projects, verify carbon outcomes or issue carbon credits.
source: Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force / United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)
status_note: Submitted to the SBSTA 64 Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue co-facilitators on 5 June 2026 as a non-binding implementation-focused statement.

document_title: Examples of Mangroves in Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)
notes: This Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force policy brief compiles examples of mangrove-related targets previously submitted by governments in Nationally Determined Contributions. It organizes examples around baseline data, management, conservation, restoration, finance and halting ecosystem loss and explains the characteristics of a mangrove-positive NDC target. The brief encourages ambitious, measurable, time-bound and area-based commitments, use of IPCC wetland guidance for mitigation accounting, field verification of mangrove extent and carbon stocks, and specification of financing and technical-support needs. It is a reference resource assembled from existing national commitments rather than a new international standard. The examples do not automatically apply to other countries, create project eligibility, replace national approval or demonstrate verified carbon removals.
source: Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force / Global Mangrove Alliance
status_note: Policy brief published in May 2025 and available as an active reference for governments preparing or revising NDCs.

document_title: Reasons for Governments to Include Mangroves in Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)
notes: This policy guidance brief presents the case for including measurable mangrove-positive targets in Nationally Determined Contributions. It summarizes the adaptation, mitigation, loss-and-damage and climate-finance relevance of mangrove conservation, restoration and sustainable management. The document highlights coastal protection, carbon storage, community and biodiversity benefits and the potential for NDC recognition to improve policy coordination and access to implementation support. It is intended to help public authorities justify stronger mangrove commitments during preparation of NDC 3.0 documents. The brief does not prescribe a mandatory national target, supply a project-level carbon-accounting method, establish eligibility for Article 6 or voluntary markets, allocate finance or prove that conservation and restoration activities will deliver additional and permanent removals.
source: Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force / Global Mangrove Alliance
status_note: Policy guidance published in 2025 and retained as a non-binding resource for national climate-policy development.

document_title: Template Language for Including Mangroves in Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)
notes: This Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force document provides adaptable wording for governments seeking to recognize mangrove conservation, restoration and sustainable management in revised Nationally Determined Contributions. The templates cover policy framing, measurable targets, implementation actions, monitoring, financing, adaptation and mitigation and can be adjusted to national ecosystems, data availability, institutional capacity and policy priorities. The resource is designed to make mangrove-positive commitments clearer and more actionable while maintaining alignment with wider climate and biodiversity strategies. It is model language rather than a negotiated decision or approved national submission. Using the template does not make a target legally binding, determine a greenhouse-gas baseline, satisfy project additionality and permanence requirements, authorize restoration or establish a carbon-credit mechanism.
source: Mangrove Breakthrough NDC Task Force / Global Mangrove Alliance
status_note: Template guidance published in 2025 and available for voluntary adaptation by governments preparing NDC updates.

document_title: Integrating Mangrove Ecosystems into NDCs with Global Mangrove Watch
notes: This policy brief explains how governments can use Global Mangrove Watch data and tools when integrating mangrove ecosystems into Nationally Determined Contributions. It links remote-sensing information, global monitoring, policy dashboards, mangrove-extent tracking and carbon-stock datasets with national climate reporting, restoration planning, emissions-reduction strategies and investment decisions. The resource emphasizes mangroves as nature-based solutions that store carbon, strengthen coastal resilience and support livelihoods. Its principal contribution is improved access to evidence and decision-support infrastructure. It does not replace national field validation, greenhouse-gas inventory procedures or project-level monitoring, and it does not certify carbon stocks, establish additionality or permanence, approve restoration sites, create tradable credits or guarantee that Global Mangrove Watch estimates are sufficient for regulatory compliance.
source: The Nature Conservancy / Global Mangrove Watch
status_note: Global policy brief published on 1 January 2025 and available as an active data and policy-integration resource.

document_title: Mangrove Breakthrough 2025 Impact Report
notes: The Mangrove Breakthrough 2025 Impact Report reviews progress across finance, policy, project pipelines, communications and international convening. It records twelve new government endorsements, continued work toward mobilizing USD 4 billion for protection and restoration of 15 million hectares of mangroves by 2030, development of a catalytic facility and transition-bond concept, publication of investment guidance, NDC technical support and mapping of community-led projects. The report also notes that eleven endorsing governments had included mangroves in their NDCs. It is a programme progress report rather than an independently audited carbon account. Reported endorsements, pipeline development and proposed finance do not demonstrate that all funds have been committed, restoration completed, removals verified or carbon credits issued.
source: Mangrove Breakthrough Hub
status_note: Impact report published on 30 January 2026 covering Mangrove Breakthrough activities and progress during 2025.

document_title: Government of Mexico Endorsement of the Mangrove Breakthrough
notes: Mexico's federal government formally endorsed the Mangrove Breakthrough in January 2025, supporting the international objective of mobilizing USD 4 billion by 2030 to protect and restore 15 million hectares of mangroves globally. The endorsement was accompanied by a national workshop involving government representatives, researchers, civil-society organizations, financial institutions and the private sector to strengthen a pipeline of mangrove-positive initiatives and financing opportunities. The commitment reinforces mangrove conservation and restoration as national priorities and connects Mexico with the initiative's NDC and investment-support work. It is a political endorsement rather than a new binding Mexican law, quantified domestic restoration target, project approval, budget appropriation, carbon-accounting methodology or evidence that credits have been issued.
source: Government of Mexico / Mangrove Breakthrough Hub
status_note: Federal endorsement announced on 29 January 2025 and active as an international mangrove-policy commitment.

document_title: Carbon Markets, Blue Carbon and Blue Bonds in the Caribbean
notes: This UNFCCC Regional Collaboration Centre Caribbean and GIZ capacity-building session examined international carbon markets, Article 6 implementation, blue-carbon projects, blue bonds and debt-for-climate finance in Caribbean countries. The programme discussed voluntary and compliance markets, emerging regional cooperation, examples of mangrove-related project finance and practical risks involving asset ownership, hurricane exposure, project resilience and carbon-credit permanence. It also identified technical-support channels for carbon-pricing strategies and participation in international markets. The session was an informational and coordination activity rather than a Caribbean carbon-market agreement or approved methodology. It did not establish a regional registry, authorize a project, determine ownership rights, guarantee blue-bond issuance, validate carbon removals or create credits eligible for national or international compliance.
source: UNFCCC Regional Collaboration Centre Caribbean / Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ)
status_note: Completed regional capacity-building session held in Grenada on 1 April 2025; its materials remain available as a policy and market-development resource.

document_title: IMPACT-Ghana: Integrated Mangrove Restoration and People-Centered Action for Coastal Thriving Resilience
notes: IMPACT-Ghana is a submitted project concept for integrated mangrove restoration and community-led nature-based solutions in Ghana's eastern and western coastal zones. The proposal targets restoration and sustainable management of 500 hectares of mangroves and 200 hectares of coastal wetlands by 2030, strengthened local governance, baseline assessment, climate information, livelihood support and increased participation of women in mangrove decision-making. It explicitly links ecosystem recovery with carbon sequestration, adaptation and Ghana's national climate commitments. The document is a project submission and implementation proposal, not evidence of completed financing or delivery. It does not itself constitute environmental approval, land authorization, an operational carbon-credit programme, verified removal results or confirmation that all restoration targets have been funded.
source: IMPACT-Ghana project proponents / United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) submission portal
status_note: Project concept submitted to the UNFCCC platform on 2 October 2025; the source does not confirm full financing, permitting or completed implementation.

subnational_area: Keta Lagoon Complex Ramsar Site and selected coastal regions
document_title: Support to Government of Ghana Access to Green Climate Fund (GCF) — TCP/GHA/3901
notes: This FAO Technical Cooperation Programme project strengthened Ghanaian institutional, technical and community capacity for coastal and blue-carbon ecosystem management. After the original Green Climate Fund proposal-development pathway encountered administrative constraints, activities were redirected toward training on an Environmental Sensitivity Map, mangrove establishment and sustainable management, digital equipment for national environmental institutions, community engagement and restoration at the Keta Lagoon Complex Ramsar Site. FAO reports that mangrove-restoration targets under the revised work plan were achieved and that monitoring and planning capacity improved. The project ran from September 2023 through December 2025 and is complete. It did not itself secure approval of a full GCF investment proposal, establish a crediting methodology or report verified carbon-credit issuance.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
status_note: Completed FAO Technical Cooperation Programme project implemented from 1 September 2023 to 31 December 2025, with the terminal factsheet published in 2026.

subnational_area: Case studies in the Dominican Republic, Grenada, Haiti and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
document_title: Remote Sensing Techniques for Mapping and Monitoring Mangroves at Fine Scales
notes: This FAO and The Nature Conservancy manual provides practical technical guidance for mapping mangrove extent, structure, condition and change at spatial resolutions finer than five metres. It covers high-resolution satellite imagery, historical aerial photography, uncrewed aerial systems, photogrammetry, open-source software, field validation and use of the Blue Carbon Explorer. The manual responds to gaps in local monitoring capacity and the growing need for reliable information to support restoration planning, coastal management and blue-carbon market development. It is a capacity-building and measurement guide rather than a mandatory MRV standard. Applying its methods does not independently establish carbon stocks, project baselines, additionality, permanence or credit eligibility, and local ecological conditions and quality-control procedures remain necessary.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) / The Nature Conservancy
status_note: Technical manual published in 2024 and available as an active international capacity-building resource for fine-scale mangrove monitoring.

document_title: Optimizing Global Observations of Carbon Dioxide in the Surface Ocean Using Machine Learning
notes: This NOAA-funded project uses machine learning to improve the design and value assessment of global surface-ocean carbon-dioxide observations. Researchers evaluate individual measurements in the Surface Ocean CO2 Atlas, compare interpolation methods and use a model testbed to identify how ships, buoys and autonomous platforms can be deployed more efficiently. The work aims to reduce spatial bias and uncertainty in estimates of air-sea CO2 exchange and the integrated ocean carbon sink. Funding was provided across fiscal years 2023, 2024 and 2025 under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law.
