status_note: Funded from August 2022 to August 2024; the research award has ended.

document_title: Constraining Respiration Rates of Mesopelagic Fishes
notes: The NERC award developed and applied a method for estimating field respiration rates of vertically migrating mesopelagic fishes across contrasting Atlantic temperature regions. The project addresses an important but poorly constrained component of the biological carbon pump because fishes consume carbon near the surface and respire part of it at depth. Results are intended to improve estimates of fish-mediated carbon transport and its representation in ocean biogeochemical models. This is fundamental carbon-cycle research and does not constitute an engineered sink-enhancement project, deployment approval, accounting methodology or carbon-credit programme.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of Southampton
status_note: Funded from August 2022 to August 2024; the research award has ended.

document_title: C-QWIZ — Future Global Ocean Carbon Storage: Quantifying Warming Impacts on Zooplankton
notes: The C-QWIZ project investigated how zooplankton physiology and body size respond to warming and food availability and translated the resulting understanding into global ocean-ecosystem models. Its purpose was to reduce uncertainty in projections of zooplankton-mediated carbon export and deep-ocean storage during the twenty-first century. The project therefore strengthens understanding and modelling of the biological carbon pump but does not intervene in the ocean, enhance a sink directly, approve a deployment activity or create a carbon-accounting or crediting system.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre and University of Exeter
status_note: Recorded by UKRI as an August–September 2022 research award; the funded activity has ended.

document_title: IDAPro — Integrating Drivers of Atlantic Productivity
notes: The NERC-funded IDAPro project combines ship-based experiments, autonomous platforms and satellite observations to determine how light, nutrients, grazing, viral mortality and other interacting processes control North Atlantic net primary production and net community production. The project is designed to reduce uncertainty in estimates of biological carbon uptake and storage and to provide stronger observational constraints for numerical climate and carbon-cycle models. It is an active research programme rather than a negative-emissions deployment project and does not itself authorise field manipulation, quantify additional removals for crediting or establish a project MRV standard.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of Southampton and National Oceanography Centre
status_note: Funded from November 2023 to October 2026; active as of August 2026.

document_title: Blue Carbon Assessment for Mangrove Systems in Seychelles
notes: The government-commissioned assessment used local field measurements of mangrove structure, biomass and soil organic carbon to establish a national baseline for Seychelles. It estimated that the country's mangroves store approximately 688,000 tonnes of organic carbon, equivalent to about 2.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide, with most of the stock held in soils, and it identified major spatial differences including the importance of Aldabra. The estimates describe ecosystem stocks and sequestration potential and support conservation, restoration and NDC planning. They are not verified project-level additional removals, a crediting methodology or an authorisation to sell offsets.
source: Seychelles Ministry of Agriculture, Climate Change and Environment / SWIOFish3 / World Bank
status_note: Prepared as a 2022 government assessment and subsequently published through the official ministry project portal.

document_title: New Insights on the Age and Climate Mitigation Significance of Shelf Sea Sedimentary Organic Carbon Stores
notes: The NERC-funded study examined the age, persistence and climate-mitigation significance of organic carbon stored in shelf-sea sediments. Its purpose was to improve interpretation of seabed carbon stores and the evidence available for marine management and mitigation decisions, including the distinction between long-lived stocks and carbon that may be vulnerable to disturbance or remineralisation. The completed award was a research activity and did not create a statutory seabed-carbon accounting method, restrict fishing or other activities, authorise restoration, or certify carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of St Andrews
status_note: Funded from 1 November 2022 to 31 October 2023; officially listed as finished.

document_title: ReBELS — Resolving Biological Carbon Export in the Labrador Sea
notes: The NERC-funded ReBELS project investigates biological carbon export in the Labrador Sea, combining observations and process understanding to resolve how organic carbon is transferred from surface waters into the ocean interior. Its results are intended to reduce uncertainty in the magnitude, controls and climate sensitivity of biological-pump carbon storage and to improve predictive models. The project is a multi-institutional research award with field and modelling components; it does not deliberately enhance carbon export, authorise marine carbon dioxide removal, establish a commercial MRV method or generate carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre and partners
status_note: Funded from July 2023 to July 2027; active as of August 2026.

document_title: Second Basic Plan for the Sustainable Management and Restoration of Tidal Flats and Adjacent Areas (2026–2030)
notes: The statutory five-year plan restructures Korea's tidal-flat management and restoration system for 2026–2030. It introduces evaluation of restoration feasibility and performance, enables private participation, prepares ecosystem-service payment guidance and strengthens local monitoring. For blue carbon, it continues R&D on carbon-removal calculation standards for tidal flats and macroalgae, establishes the Blue Carbon Demonstration Research Center under a 2023–2029 programme with KRW 38.1 billion, and integrates tidal-flat information through the Marine Environment Information System. The plan also supports international cooperation on recognition of new blue-carbon sinks. These measures establish research, accounting and governance infrastructure, but the plan does not itself issue carbon credits or verify a quantified volume of additional removals.
source: Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, Republic of Korea
status_note: Finalized and officially announced as the statutory 2026–2030 basic plan

document_title: Fourth Basic Plan for Fisheries Resource Management (2026–2030)
notes: The statutory fisheries-resource plan applies from 2026 through 2030 and combines climate-responsive stock assessment, ecosystem-based habitat recovery and a staged sea-forest carbon market pathway. It directs integration and standardization of climate, ocean and fisheries data, development of AI-based assessment systems, and climate-adaptive habitat-restoration technologies. For sea forests, the plan provides for a carbon-trading system based on seaweed transplantation and cultivation, with pilot operation in 2026, related legislative amendments planned for 2028–2029 and emissions-trading implementation targeted for 2030. It also expands a Blue Credits pilot intended to recognize carbon absorbed by seaweed. The plan therefore creates a formal policy pathway toward crediting and compliance-market use, although the trading system and legal amendments are not yet fully operational.
source: Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, Republic of Korea
status_note: Officially adopted statutory plan; sea-forest crediting and trading measures remain staged for pilot and later implementation

document_title: Our Ocean Conference 2025 Commitment — National Blue Carbon Rapid Assessment, Network and Database
notes: Indonesia committed at the 2025 Our Ocean Conference to conduct a rapid assessment of seagrass blue carbon in twenty marine protected areas, initiate a national Blue Carbon Network and Blue Carbon Database, formulate supporting policies and technical guidance, and strengthen international cooperation. The package is primarily an evidence and governance programme: it is intended to improve spatial coverage, data availability and institutional coordination for seagrass-related blue carbon. The commitment does not disclose a carbon-crediting methodology, verified removal quantity, project-level authorization or a completed national inventory. It should therefore be read as an active government work programme for assessment, database development and policy preparation rather than as proof that carbon credits or deployable removal projects have already been approved.
source: Government of Indonesia — Our Ocean Conference 2025 commitment
status_note: Formally announced international commitment with assessment, database and policy-development actions underway or scheduled

document_title: Our Ocean Conference 2025 Commitment — Indonesia Blue Carbon Science, Policy Integration and Restoration Programme to 2030
notes: Konservasi Indonesia committed to a programme through 2030 that links blue-carbon science, national policy integration and field implementation. The commitment covers mapping and data development, preparation of emission factors and activity data, incorporation of blue-carbon measures into policy and the nationally determined contribution, and conservation or rehabilitation activities across eleven provinces. Because the commitment combines accounting inputs, governance integration and ecosystem action, it is recorded as a multi-component programme rather than as separate duplicate records for each workstream. The official commitment does not establish a completed crediting standard, identify issued credits or provide verified net-removal totals. Reported mapping, emission factors and restoration activities will still require site-specific baselines, additionality, permanence and leakage assessment before they can support carbon-credit claims.
source: Konservasi Indonesia — Our Ocean Conference 2025 commitment
status_note: Multi-year commitment announced for implementation through 2030

subnational_area: Washington — Port of Seattle, Smith Cove
document_title: Our Ocean Conference 2025 Commitment — Smith Cove Blue Carbon Pilot Phase 2
notes: The Port of Seattle committed to a second phase of the Smith Cove blue-carbon pilot, building on earlier restoration and evaluation work involving kelp, eelgrass and shellfish habitat near the Seattle waterfront. The programme combines ecological restoration with monitoring intended to test whether working waterfronts can improve habitat and contribute to carbon sequestration. It is treated as an independently identifiable subnational pilot because it has a defined site, implementing port authority and phased programme structure. The commitment does not demonstrate that the site has generated certified carbon credits or a verified quantity of durable net carbon dioxide removal. Carbon benefits remain subject to continued measurement, attribution, lifecycle analysis and permanence assessment, while the habitat and water-quality objectives are broader than carbon removal alone.
source: Port of Seattle — Our Ocean Conference 2025 commitment
status_note: Phase 2 commitment announced; pilot restoration and evaluation activities continue

document_title: Our Ocean Conference 2025 Commitment — Blue-Carbon-Based Coastal Restoration Technology Development
notes: The Republic of Korea reported a USD 29.4 million commitment to develop blue-carbon-based coastal restoration technology through 2026. The measure is classified primarily as research and technology development because the official commitment emphasizes development of restoration technology rather than a completed nationwide deployment programme or a legally established carbon-crediting system. It may support later restoration of tidal flats, vegetated coastal habitats or other nationally recognized blue-carbon ecosystems, but the short commitment description does not identify a single ecosystem pathway, project site, accounting protocol or quantified removal outcome. The funding therefore strengthens the technical evidence and demonstration base while leaving deployment scale, ecological safeguards, permanence and eligibility for national greenhouse-gas accounting or carbon markets to subsequent decisions.
source: Government of the Republic of Korea — Our Ocean Conference 2025 commitment
status_note: Funded technology-development commitment reported as continuing through 2026

country_or_region: Republic of Korea and Viet Nam
document_title: Our Ocean Conference 2025 Commitment — Mangrove Restoration Technical Capacity for Vietnamese Aquaculture
notes: The Republic of Korea committed approximately USD 2.1 million through 2026 to strengthen technical capacity for Vietnamese aquaculture through mangrove-ecosystem restoration. The programme links restoration of coastal carbon-storing habitat with aquaculture resilience and capacity building, making it an international implementation and knowledge-transfer project rather than a general diplomatic statement. Its principal policy function is to support restoration and field capability; the commitment does not disclose a carbon-accounting methodology, credit registry, verified removal volume or authorization for offset sales. Any climate benefit must therefore be distinguished from broader livelihood, habitat and aquaculture outcomes, and future carbon claims would require site-specific baselines, monitoring of biomass and soil carbon, permanence safeguards and treatment of displacement or leakage.
source: Government of the Republic of Korea — Our Ocean Conference 2025 commitment
status_note: International capacity-building and mangrove-restoration commitment reported as continuing through 2026

document_title: Our Ocean Conference 2025 Commitment — Innovative Marine Protected Area Guidelines for Blue Carbon
notes: Konservasi Indonesia committed to complete innovative marine protected area guidance by 2026 with a focus on sustainable fisheries, blue carbon and charismatic marine species. The commitment is included because it is a formal programme to produce governance guidance that explicitly integrates blue carbon into protected-area design and management. Its principal function is standard and policy development, not direct carbon removal. The official description does not specify a carbon-accounting formula, mandatory legal status, eligible ecosystem list, crediting rules or quantified sequestration target. Until the guidance is completed and adopted by competent authorities, it should be treated as an active guidance-development initiative. Mention of blue carbon does not by itself authorize restoration projects, generate tradable credits or demonstrate additional and permanent carbon storage.
source: Konservasi Indonesia — Our Ocean Conference 2025 commitment
status_note: Guidance-development commitment scheduled for completion by 2026

document_title: Our Ocean Conference 2025 Commitment — Climate Smart Shrimp and Mangrove Protection Programme
notes: Konservasi Indonesia committed to improve approximately 491 hectares of shrimp ponds and protect about 293 hectares of mangroves by 2027 through its Climate Smart Shrimp programme. The approach combines improved pond and wastewater management with mangrove protection or restoration, seeking livelihood, water-quality, resilience and blue-carbon benefits. This record represents the national programme commitment rather than duplicating every project update or harvest announcement. The area figures are implementation targets, not verified carbon-removal quantities. The commitment does not establish an approved offset methodology, registry or permanence guarantee, and improved aquaculture production must not be counted as carbon removal. Carbon outcomes require separate monitoring of mangrove biomass and soils, comparison with credible baselines, and safeguards against pond expansion or ecological displacement.
source: Konservasi Indonesia — Our Ocean Conference 2025 commitment
status_note: Implementation commitment active through 2027; area targets are not verified carbon-removal results

document_title: Our Ocean Conference 2025 Commitment — Enhancement of Coastal Blue Carbon Storage
notes: Taiwan announced a formal commitment at the 2025 Our Ocean Conference to enhance coastal blue-carbon storage. The commitment is relevant because it states an intended government direction toward increasing carbon retained in coastal ecosystems. However, the published commitment list provides little operational detail: it does not identify the ecosystems, sites, area target, budget, implementation agency, accounting method, timetable for verified outcomes or relationship to a carbon market. The record is therefore classified as a planned enabling commitment rather than an implemented restoration project or approved crediting mechanism. Subsequent official plans, funding decisions, permits or monitoring reports would be required to establish the precise engineering pathway and determine whether any additional, durable and measurable carbon removal has occurred.
source: Taiwan authorities — Our Ocean Conference 2025 commitment
status_note: Formally announced commitment; detailed implementation measures and verified outcomes were not disclosed in the commitment list

document_title: Our Ocean Conference 2025 Commitment — Carbon Lock Marine and Ocean-Based Carbon Dioxide Removal
notes: Australia listed Carbon Lock as a marine- or ocean-based carbon dioxide removal commitment at the 2025 Our Ocean Conference. The official commitment list identifies the initiative and its mCDR orientation but supplies insufficient detail to assign a specific technical pathway such as ocean alkalinity enhancement, direct ocean capture, biomass sinking or ecological restoration. No project site, budget, permitting decision, environmental assessment, removal quantity, monitoring protocol or deployment schedule is disclosed in the published entry. It is therefore recorded conservatively as a planned research and programme commitment covering ocean negative-emissions engineering in general. Inclusion in the conference list does not constitute regulatory authorization, demonstrate safe and durable removal, or establish eligibility for Australian greenhouse-gas accounting or carbon credits.
source: Government of Australia — Our Ocean Conference 2025 commitment
status_note: Formally listed mCDR commitment with the specific technology, deployment status and regulatory pathway not publicly defined in the commitment entry

document_title: Our Ocean Conference 2025 Commitment — BOSI Beach-Cast Seaweed Biochar and Biofertilizer Valorisation
notes: The BOSI commitment proposes to valorise beach-cast seaweed in Mauritius and the wider Indian Ocean region by converting collected biomass into biochar and biofertilizer products. It is included as an ocean-linked negative-emissions demonstration concept because it seeks to manage marine-derived biomass while potentially stabilizing part of its carbon in biochar. The brief commitment does not report a full lifecycle assessment, feedstock additionality rules, avoided decomposition emissions, pyrolysis energy balance, biochar durability, application safeguards, budget or verified net carbon-removal volume. Collection of stranded seaweed may also affect beach ecology and nutrient cycling and therefore requires environmental assessment. The record represents a planned programme concept, not an operating carbon-credit methodology or evidence that durable net removals have already been delivered.
source: BOSI — Our Ocean Conference 2025 commitment
status_note: Programme concept announced; no verified removal, operating crediting method or complete lifecycle assessment was disclosed

document_title: Mediterranean Blue Natural Capital Facility
notes: IUCN announced development of the Mediterranean Blue Natural Capital Facility to channel investment into economically viable and scalable protection and restoration projects for Posidonia oceanica meadows, saltmarshes and coastal wetlands. The facility is designed to provide structured support from feasibility analysis and project incubation through financial design and policy integration, addressing gaps in governance, technical capacity, finance and monitoring. It therefore functions primarily as a blue-natural-capital finance and project-development mechanism with secondary restoration and evidence-building roles. At announcement, IUCN stated that operations would begin shortly; the page did not identify approved investee projects, issued carbon credits, a mandatory accounting methodology or quantified verified removals. Financing readiness and ecosystem recovery should not be treated as equivalent to certified carbon removal.
source: International Union for Conservation of Nature — Centre for Mediterranean Cooperation
status_note: Facility announced in October 2025 and described as preparing to begin operations

country_or_region: Southeast Asia and Pacific eligible countries
document_title: SEAP FIT Coalition 2026 Call-for-Projects — Blue Carbon Forestry
notes: The first SEAP Forest Investment and Technical Partners Coalition call for projects accepts proposals from ten eligible Southeast Asian and Pacific countries and expressly lists Blue Carbon Forestry among eligible activities. The call is intended to shape investment-ready nature-based-solution pipelines, connect proponents with technical and financial partners and consider projects for possible grant support. It is a competitive funding and project-incubation mechanism, not an award to every applicant and not a carbon-crediting standard. As of the database update date, submissions were open until 21 August 2026, with evaluation scheduled for 22 August–30 September and selection notification in October. No blue-carbon project had yet been selected through this cohort, and inclusion as an eligible category does not prove additionality, permanence, quantified removals or regulatory approval.
source: International Union for Conservation of Nature — SEAP FIT Coalition
status_note: 2026 call open for submissions; projects had not yet been evaluated or selected

document_title: GEF Project 5398 — Implementing a Ridge-to-Reef Approach to Preserve Ecosystem Services, Sequester Carbon, Improve Climate Resilience and Sustain Livelihoods in Fiji
notes: The GEF-supported Fiji Ridge-to-Reef project applied integrated watershed, land, forest and coastal management in priority areas on Fiji's two main islands. Its formal objective explicitly included sequestering carbon alongside biodiversity protection, ecosystem services, climate resilience and livelihoods. The project used planning, capacity building and local demonstrations rather than a stand-alone marine carbon-credit programme. Because carbon outcomes were embedded across connected terrestrial-to-coastal landscapes, the record uses the land–sea coordinated negative-emissions pathway and does not infer a specific natural carbon pump. GEF records list the project as completed. The programme did not establish that all reported ecosystem improvements represented additional, permanent and independently verified atmospheric carbon removal, and its carbon contribution should be interpreted within a broader multi-benefit ridge-to-reef framework.
source: Global Environment Facility and United Nations Development Programme
status_note: GEF project completed and closed

document_title: GEF Project 5404 — Testing Integrated Ridge-to-Reef Management to Store Carbon in Pacific Island Countries
notes: The regional Pacific Ridge-to-Reef project tested integration of water, land, forest and coastal management across participating Pacific island countries through strategic planning, capacity building and pilot local actions. Its official title expressly includes storing carbon, while the wider programme also addresses ecosystem services, climate resilience and livelihoods. The project is classified as a cross-border implementation and evidence-building programme using land–sea coordinated management rather than a single blue-carbon ecosystem or engineered mCDR technology. GEF records list the project as completed. The official project description does not establish a regional carbon-crediting mechanism or provide a single verified net-removal total attributable only to coastal interventions. Carbon storage is therefore treated as one programme objective among several, requiring location-specific monitoring and counterfactual assessment for any stronger removal claim.
source: Global Environment Facility and United Nations Development Programme
status_note: Regional GEF project completed and closed

document_title: GEF Project 514 — The Role of the Coastal Ocean in Disturbed and Undisturbed Nutrient and Carbon Cycles
notes: This UNEP/GEF research project under the Land–Ocean Interactions in the Coastal Zone framework investigated how coastal seas function in nutrient and carbon cycles and how eutrophication changes carbon sequestration. It supported empirical estimation, modelling, synthesis, workshops and capacity building intended to improve understanding of whether different coastal systems act as carbon sources or sinks under disturbed and less disturbed conditions. The project is included as foundational theory and research directly addressing coastal-ocean carbon processes, not as a restoration or deployment programme. GEF records list it as completed. Its outputs improve scientific evidence but do not constitute a carbon-accounting standard, regulatory authorization, carbon-credit issuance or proof of a durable quantity of additional atmospheric carbon removal.
source: Global Environment Facility, United Nations Environment Programme and LOICZ
status_note: Research project completed and closed

document_title: GEF Project 9766 — Mainstreaming Conservation of Coastal Wetlands through Adaptive Management in South-Central Chile
notes: The GEF project strengthens adaptive management of coastal wetlands in south-central Chile through policy and regulatory mainstreaming, institutional capacity, improved management and pilot landscape action. Official project materials include a guide and supporting appendix for carbon calculation in Chilean coastal landscapes, providing a direct carbon-accounting and evidence component within a broader biodiversity and land-degradation programme. The project is therefore included for its coastal-wetland carbon assessment and restoration relevance, while recognizing that its primary formal objective is conservation rather than issuance of carbon credits. GEF records list the project as approved and provide continuing implementation reports. The existence of a calculation guide does not by itself verify additional removals, establish a national crediting methodology or authorize trading.
source: Global Environment Facility and United Nations Environment Programme
status_note: GEF project approved with implementation and reporting materials available

document_title: Policy Recommendations for Sustainable Blue Carbon Ecosystem Management and Shrimp-Farm Expansion in Saleh Bay
notes: The policy-recommendation document applies an ocean-accounting approach and spatial feasibility analysis to the linked questions of blue-carbon ecosystem management and shrimp-farm expansion in Saleh Bay. It is included because it provides formal evidence and policy advice intended to guide spatial decisions where aquaculture development may affect carbon-storing coastal ecosystems. The document's function is analytical and advisory: it does not itself amend zoning, issue an aquaculture permit, approve habitat conversion, establish a carbon-credit methodology or demonstrate verified removals. Its recommendations should be interpreted as inputs for government planning and safeguards. Any later development or restoration decision would still require competent legal approval, environmental assessment, transparent treatment of ecosystem carbon stocks and protection against leakage or displacement.
source: Konservasi Indonesia
status_note: Published policy-recommendation and spatial-feasibility document; implementation depends on later government decisions

document_title: Feasibility Study Synthesis Report of the Seagrass Ecosystem Blue Carbon Project in East Bintan
notes: The feasibility study assesses a reported 2,416.10 hectares of seagrass meadow in East Bintan and examines a prospective restoration area of approximately 800 hectares. It develops preliminary scenarios and carbon estimates over ten- and thirty-year periods to evaluate whether a seagrass blue-carbon project could be technically and environmentally feasible. The study is an evidence-building and project-design document, not a project permit, completed restoration action or verified credit issuance. Proposed areas and modelled carbon benefits remain subject to field validation, baseline selection, additionality, leakage, permanence, ecological-risk assessment, tenure and community safeguards, and approval by relevant authorities. The record therefore captures a formal feasibility stage and does not treat prospective or modelled carbon values as achieved removals.
source: Konservasi Indonesia
status_note: Feasibility study published; proposed restoration and carbon outcomes remain subject to validation and approval

document_title: Seagrass Monitoring Pocket Book
notes: The pocket book provides practical field guidance for community surveillance groups completing seagrass-monitoring sheets, supported by examples and photographs. It was developed from initial use in Bintan and is intended to be adaptable for seagrass monitoring elsewhere in Indonesia. The document contributes to blue-carbon evidence by improving consistent observation of the ecosystem that stores and accumulates carbon, but it is not a complete greenhouse-gas or carbon-credit MRV methodology. It does not prescribe project baselines, additionality tests, carbon-stock equations, uncertainty deductions, permanence requirements, verification procedures or credit issuance. The guide is therefore classified as active monitoring guidance with a research-support role, and monitoring data produced under it would need additional scientific and methodological steps before supporting quantified carbon-removal claims.
source: Konservasi Indonesia
status_note: Published field-monitoring guide available for community and programme use

document_title: GEF Project 10696 — Inclusive Conservation of Sea Turtles and Seagrass Habitats in Northern Madagascar
notes: The GEF project supports inclusive conservation and improved management of sea-turtle and seagrass habitats in northern and north-western Madagascar, including policy and planning frameworks, local implementation, community participation and sustainable finance. GEF communications identify seagrass meadows as important carbon-sequestration and storage ecosystems, providing a direct blue-carbon co-benefit rationale for inclusion. Nevertheless, the project's formal objective is biodiversity conservation rather than delivery of a specified quantity of carbon dioxide removal. The official project page does not establish a carbon-crediting methodology, report issued credits or provide a verified additional-removal total. Seagrass protection preserves existing carbon stocks and may avoid emissions, while any claim of new sequestration from restoration would require separate baseline, additionality, permanence and monitoring evidence.
source: Global Environment Facility and United Nations Environment Programme
status_note: GEF project approved and under implementation; carbon is a stated ecosystem co-benefit rather than a verified crediting output

subnational_area: Central Sulawesi — Lalombi Village, South Banawa
document_title: Lalombi Climate Smart Shrimp Pilot and Mangrove Restoration Project
notes: The Lalombi Climate Smart Shrimp pilot integrates improved shrimp-pond water and waste management with restoration of approximately 3.5 hectares of mangroves and monitoring conducted with research partners. The project reached a first harvest in 2025 and is treated as an independently identifiable local demonstration because it has a defined site, field interventions and implementation milestones. Reported shrimp production is an aquaculture yield and must not be interpreted as carbon removal. Carbon-stock or sequestration estimates associated with restored mangroves remain preliminary unless supported by repeated field measurements, a defensible baseline, additionality and permanence assessment and independent verification. The project does not itself establish a carbon-crediting methodology or prove that tradable credits have been issued.
source: Konservasi Indonesia and project partners
status_note: Local demonstration operating with first harvest reported in 2025; carbon outcomes remain preliminary and unverified

subnational_area: East Java — Wringinputih Village, Banyuwangi Regency
document_title: Banyuwangi Climate Smart Shrimp Aquaculture Programme (2024–2027)
notes: The Climate Smart Shrimp Aquaculture programme has supported farmer groups in Wringinputih Village since January 2024 and is scheduled to continue through 2027. It combines clean-water management, communal wastewater treatment and mangrove restoration within an aquaculture production system. The programme reported construction of treatment capacity serving multiple farmers and restoration of approximately 4.1 hectares of mangroves, while government and partners also proposed integrating farm carbon-reduction assessment into sustainability improvements. This is a distinct local implementation programme rather than a duplicate of Indonesia's broader national Climate Smart Shrimp commitment. The restored area is not a verified carbon-removal quantity, and the programme page does not establish a crediting methodology, baseline, permanence requirement or issued credits.
source: Konservasi Indonesia, Banyuwangi Regency Government and programme partners
status_note: Local implementation programme active from 2024 through 2027

document_title: ESA Coastal Blue Carbon Earth Observation Project
notes: The European Space Agency-funded Coastal Blue Carbon project develops Earth-observation products, indicators and methods for monitoring mangroves, tidal saltmarshes and seagrass ecosystems. Launched in March 2024, it combines Sentinel imagery, very-high-resolution satellite data, ground validation and modelling to prototype ecosystem-extent maps, biomass estimates, change detection, health assessments and carbon-stock products. The project is designed to support restoration and conservation decisions and potential inclusion of blue-carbon ecosystems in national inventories and nationally determined contributions. Its main role is measurement and evidence infrastructure rather than direct restoration or carbon removal. Prototype maps and stock estimates are not equivalent to verified project credits, and country-level use still requires transparent uncertainty treatment, local validation, accounting boundaries and official adoption.
source: European Space Agency — Earth Observation Science for Society
status_note: ESA-funded research and demonstration project launched in March 2024 with products and stakeholder consultation continuing through 2026

document_title: Earth Observation Blue Carbon Baseline for the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden
notes: The European Space Agency and World Bank collaboration integrates Earth-observation information into a Marine and Coastal Ecosystem Assessment for the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. It provides a harmonized regional evidence base on the extent, condition and carbon stocks of mangroves and seagrasses for countries including Egypt, Djibouti, Yemen and Jordan, addressing previously fragmented spatial data. The programme supports planning, assessment and future investment by making comparable blue-carbon information available across national boundaries. It is an assessment and monitoring initiative, not a restoration authorization or carbon-credit standard. The regional baseline does not by itself demonstrate additional sequestration, avoided loss, permanence or ownership of carbon benefits, and any project or national inventory use requires country validation, uncertainty analysis and consistency with domestic reporting rules.
source: European Space Agency Global Development Assistance and the World Bank
status_note: Regional Earth-observation assessment and baseline programme reported in May 2026

document_title: Earth Observation for Coastal Carbon and Fisheries Assessment in Madagascar and Comoros
notes: The ESA Global Development Assistance Fast EO Co-Financing Facility, working with the World Bank and national stakeholders, delivered satellite-derived information for coastal planning in Madagascar and Comoros. The Madagascar component maps mangroves and saltmarshes through time, estimates blue-carbon stocks and identifies areas of ecosystem loss or restoration; the Comoros component focuses mainly on ocean conditions and fish-habitat suitability. The combined initiative demonstrates how Earth observation can support coastal policy and investment, but only the Madagascar workstream provides a direct blue-carbon assessment. The outputs are evidence products rather than carbon credits, project permits or verified additional removals. Use in inventories or restoration finance requires local field validation, accounting rules and clear treatment of uncertainty and ecosystem change.
source: European Space Agency Global Development Assistance and the World Bank
status_note: Earth-observation assessment outputs reported in March 2026 and used to support ongoing coastal planning

subnational_area: Shenzhen, Guangdong — Nan'ao Sub-district, Dapeng New District
document_title: AI-Enabled Community for Ocean Literacy (AI-ECO)
notes: The UN Ocean Decade-endorsed AI-ECO project establishes a locally operated digital monitoring and public-engagement system for marine carbon-sink ecosystems in Shenzhen's Nan'ao area. The project deploys drones equipped with nutrient and carbon-dioxide sensors to observe carbon-sink dynamics associated with corals, mangroves and coastal wetlands, links observations through an integrated air-sea-land network, and feeds the information into the Nan'ao Smart Platform for visual ecological balance sheets and conservation management. A community application is intended to record individual participation, provide multilingual learning materials and operate a carbon-sink points exchange. These points are an engagement mechanism rather than verified carbon credits. The project builds monitoring capacity and traceable ecological data but the official description does not provide an approved carbon-accounting methodology, quantified additional removals, permanence rules or authorization for an engineered marine carbon-dioxide-removal deployment.
source: UNESCO-IOC Ocean Decade / Dapeng New District Nan'ao Sub-district Office, Shenzhen
status_note: Ocean Decade project running from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2030; active as of August 2026.

document_title: Sustainable Total Value Chain of Cockle Industry
notes: This Ocean Decade project, led by Malaysia's Fisheries Research Institute and hosted under Global ONCE, supported a more sustainable cockle-industry value chain. Its official scope covered responsible cockle culture and harvesting, animal-welfare practices, food-safety improvement, community and traditional-knowledge participation, stakeholder collaboration and the repurposing of discarded shells for wastewater treatment. Because cockles produce calcium-carbonate shells, the project is relevant to fishery carbon-sink research and carbonate-cycle management. However, the official project description does not demonstrate that shell formation was counted as net atmospheric carbon removal, does not account for respiration, processing or lifecycle emissions, and does not establish permanence, additionality, monitoring or credit issuance rules. The record therefore identifies an applied shellfish programme with research and demonstration value rather than a certified negative-emissions or carbon-credit project.
source: UNESCO-IOC Ocean Decade / Fisheries Research Institute Malaysia
status_note: Ocean Decade project period: 1 November 2021 to 31 December 2025; the recorded project period has ended.

document_title: BushBank Traditional Owner Project — Blue Carbon Opportunities for Western Port Bay
notes: The Victorian Government's BushBank programme lists Blue Carbon Opportunities for Western Port Bay as a Traditional Owner-led project delivered through the Bunurong Land Council Aboriginal Corporation. BushBank allocates long-term public funding to biodiversity restoration, climate action and Traditional Owner participation and includes opportunities connected with restoration and carbon markets. The named Western Port Bay project is sufficiently identifiable as an independent place-based blue-carbon opportunity assessment, but the public project list does not specify an approved methodology, funded amount for this individual project, target hectares, implementation schedule, ecosystem-specific intervention, expected tonnes of carbon dioxide removed or arrangements for credit ownership. It is therefore classified as an active evidence-building and project-development activity. The record does not imply that restoration has already occurred, that removal quantities have been verified or that a crediting mechanism has been established.
source: Government of Victoria — Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action
status_note: Listed as a current BushBank Traditional Owner project on the Victorian Government programme page updated in July 2026; no separate completion date is published.

document_title: Marine Environment and Fisheries Fund 2025/26 — Blue Carbon Restoration Support
notes: Northern Ireland's Marine Environment and Fisheries Fund for the 2025/26 financial year provided a public funding route for marine and fisheries activities aligned with the Joint Fisheries Statement, Green Growth and net-zero objectives. Eligible environmental work included the restoration of blue-carbon habitats alongside broader marine-conservation, fisheries, innovation and community measures. The scheme could therefore finance practical coastal blue-carbon restoration, related research and demonstration activity, but the programme page does not identify a single blue-carbon award, prescribe a carbon-accounting method, quantify expected removals, create tradable credits or guarantee that every funded project concerned carbon sinks. Applications closed during the financial year and supported projects were required to complete work and submit final claims by 31 March 2026. This record captures the annual funding instrument rather than duplicating the separate 2026/27 fund or treating individual publicity updates as new policies.
source: Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland
status_note: The 2025/26 application period closed and funded activity was required to be completed with final claims submitted by 31 March 2026.

document_title: SARDINE — Southern Ocean Carbon Indices and Metrics
notes: The NERC-funded SARDINE project examined how Southern Ocean circulation and water-mass formation regulate the global ocean carbon cycle. It investigated the competing effects of surface waters that leave the Southern Ocean and draw atmospheric carbon dioxide into the ocean interior, and carbon-rich deep waters that return to the surface and may release carbon dioxide. The research evaluated changes in mode-water volume and overturning under different emissions scenarios, developed carbon indices and metrics, and used observations and Earth-system modelling to improve the interpretation of Southern Ocean carbon uptake and storage. The work was directed at scientific diagnosis and climate-model assessment, not deliberate ocean manipulation. It did not authorize a marine carbon-dioxide-removal activity, establish project-level MRV or additionality rules, or claim verified removal tonnes. The funded research ended in 2024.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of Liverpool
status_note: Funded from January 2020 to July 2024; UKRI records the award as closed.

document_title: Marine Frontiers — Frontiers of Instability in Marine Ecosystems and Carbon Export
notes: Marine Frontiers is a NERC-funded modelling and process-research programme investigating thresholds and instability in marine ecosystems and the resulting consequences for biological carbon export. The project represents processes such as viral infection, organism mortality, early life-cycle dynamics, food-web interactions and microplastic stress, and examines how multiple pressures may change the amount and form of organic carbon transferred from surface waters to the ocean interior. Its purpose is to identify nonlinear ecosystem responses and improve projections of the biological carbon pump under environmental change. The programme produces knowledge, numerical tools and risk-relevant evidence; it does not intentionally increase carbon export, conduct a commercial sinking operation or provide authorization for marine carbon-dioxide removal. No project-level carbon-credit methodology, permanence claim or verified removal quantity is established by the award.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of East Anglia
status_note: Funded from March 2021 to September 2026; active as of 6 August 2026.

document_title: CUSTARD — Carbon Uptake and Seasonal Traits in Antarctic Remineralisation Depth
notes: CUSTARD was a multi-institution NERC research programme focused on the depth at which sinking organic material is remineralised in the Southern Ocean and the implications of that depth for long-term carbon storage. The programme combined Antarctic field observations, autonomous measurements, particle-flux research and modelling to determine how seasonal ecosystem traits control the transfer of biologically fixed carbon below the surface and whether it remains isolated from the atmosphere. UKRI records linked initial and continuation awards, reflecting one continuous scientific programme rather than separate policies. CUSTARD strengthened understanding of the biological carbon pump and informed climate-model representation, but it did not deliberately enhance export, authorize biomass sinking, define creditable additionality or verify engineered removals. The research programme and its continuation funding have ended.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre and partners
status_note: Initial funding ran from April 2018 to October 2019 and continuation funding from November 2019 to December 2023; the programme has ended.

document_title: Understanding the Role of Antarctic Sea Ice in Dense-Water Formation and Heat and Carbon Sequestration
notes: This NERC-funded doctoral research project investigates how Antarctic sea ice influences dense-water formation, ocean circulation and the sequestration of heat and carbon. It combines satellite-altimetry products from missions including CryoSat-2 and ICESat-2 with large climate-model datasets, including CMIP6, and applies data-intensive and machine-learning methods to connect sea-ice production and change with the formation and export of dense water. The resulting evidence is intended to improve understanding of physical ocean carbon uptake and the representation of Antarctic processes in climate projections. The award supports observation, analysis and modelling only. It does not manipulate sea ice or circulation, deploy an artificial-downwelling intervention, establish a carbon-accounting standard or provide a basis for issuing removal credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of Leeds, National Oceanography Centre and British Antarctic Survey
status_note: Studentship funded from September 2021 to February 2027; active as of August 2026.

document_title: ORCHESTRA — Ocean Regulation of Climate by Heat and Carbon Sequestration and Transports
notes: ORCHESTRA was a five-year NERC Long Term Science programme involving the National Oceanography Centre, British Antarctic Survey and other research centres. It combined ship and autonomous observations, historical-data analysis and numerical simulations to improve understanding of Southern Ocean circulation and of the ocean's absorption, transport and storage of heat and carbon. The programme addressed the physical pathways through which carbon-rich and carbon-poor water masses are formed and redistributed, while also supporting better climate prediction and coordination across United Kingdom polar and ocean-science institutions. ORCHESTRA was a national research programme with international scientific relevance, not an intervention designed to enhance the ocean sink. It did not authorize artificial circulation, establish a project MRV or crediting system, or report additional removal tonnes attributable to engineered activity.
source: Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre and British Antarctic Survey
status_note: The five-year programme began in spring 2016 and ended in March 2021.

document_title: ENCORE — Extension of the ORCHESTRA Southern Ocean Research Programme
notes: ENCORE provided a separately funded extension to the ORCHESTRA Southern Ocean research programme. It preserved research capability and enabled additional analysis, coordination and completion of work on Southern Ocean circulation, heat uptake, carbon transport and carbon storage after the original five-year programme. The extension is recorded separately because it had its own formal UKRI award and implementation period, while its notes make clear that it continued an existing scientific programme rather than creating a new deployment activity. ENCORE supported observations, synthesis and modelling intended to reduce uncertainty in climate and carbon-cycle projections. It did not engineer an increase in carbon uptake, authorize field manipulation, create monitoring rules for commercial marine carbon dioxide removal or issue verified removal credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre and partners
status_note: One-year ORCHESTRA extension funded during 2021–2022; ORCHESTRA and ENCORE were reported as completed in March 2022.

document_title: COMICS — Controls over Ocean Mesopelagic Interior Carbon Storage
notes: COMICS was a NERC Discovery Science programme designed to quantify the flow and transformation of organic carbon through the ocean's mesopelagic or twilight zone. It combined research cruises, particle and respiration measurements, ecological process studies and modelling in the tropical Atlantic and Southern Ocean to determine how much surface-produced material reaches depth and how rapidly it is consumed or remineralised. The programme generated evidence needed to improve the representation of biological carbon export and interior-ocean storage in climate models. Although its subject is carbon transfer into the deep ocean, COMICS observed natural processes and did not deliberately sink biomass, enhance productivity or operate a negative-emissions demonstration. It established neither a deployment authorization nor a commercial carbon-accounting, permanence or crediting methodology.
source: Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre and partner institutions
status_note: The NOC programme ran from April 2017 to March 2021; associated research awards are closed.

document_title: Fish Carbonates — Dissolution Potential under Elevated Hydrostatic Pressure
notes: This NERC research grant investigated whether calcium-carbonate particles produced by marine bony fish dissolve differently as they sink under elevated hydrostatic pressure. Laboratory experiments were designed to test pressure and fluid-flow effects and to assess whether fish-derived carbonate could help explain observed increases in ocean alkalinity within the upper approximately one thousand metres. The project contributed to fundamental understanding of the marine inorganic carbon budget, carbonate production and dissolution, and the carbonate pump. It did not cultivate fish as a carbon-removal intervention, alter ocean alkalinity in the field or claim that fish carbonate formation automatically represents net atmospheric carbon sequestration. No deployment permit, project MRV framework, additionality test, permanence assessment or carbon credits resulted from the grant.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of Exeter
status_note: Funded from March 2012 to September 2014; UKRI records the research grant as closed.

document_title: CaNDyFloSS — Carbon and Nutrient Dynamics and Fluxes over Shelf Systems
notes: CaNDyFloSS was a coordinated NERC programme examining carbon and nutrient dynamics across continental-shelf systems. Linked institutional awards supported observations, experiments and modelling of production, respiration, particle processing, benthic-pelagic exchange and the transfer of carbon and nutrients between shelf waters and the open ocean. The programme improved understanding of whether shelf seas retain, remineralise or export organic carbon and how those functions vary with physical mixing and ecosystem activity. Multiple grants listed under the same programme title are consolidated here because they formed one collaborative research effort rather than separate policies. CaNDyFloSS did not deliberately increase shelf-sea carbon uptake, implement land-sea negative-emissions engineering, authorize a removal project or establish project-level carbon credits or MRV rules.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre, Plymouth Marine Laboratory, University of East Anglia and partners
status_note: Collaborative awards began in 2013 and the longest linked award ended in 2018; the programme has ended.

document_title: DINOTROPHY — Deuterium in Organic Biomarkers and Marine Mixotrophy in the Global Carbon Cycle
notes: DINOTROPHY was a BBSRC-funded research programme developing deuterium measurements in organic biomarkers as a tool for investigating marine mixotrophy and its role in the global carbon cycle. Mixotrophic plankton combine photosynthesis with the consumption of other organisms, so their activity can change carbon fixation, food-web transfer, respiration and export in ways that are poorly represented in conventional ecosystem models. The project linked laboratory and analytical-method development with ocean-carbon interpretation to provide evidence on how these organisms influence biologically mediated carbon storage. It was a fundamental research award rather than an intervention in plankton communities. The project did not authorize fertilization or cultivation, quantify additional engineered removals, establish permanence requirements or create a monitoring and crediting standard.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council / University of Oxford and National Oceanography Centre
status_note: Linked awards ran from April or May 2021 to October or November 2025; the funded programme has ended.

document_title: BATMAN — Biological Carbon Pump Assessment Using the Transport Matrix Method and Global Nutrient Distributions
notes: BATMAN was a NERC research project assessing the biological carbon pump through a transport-matrix modelling method combined with global nutrient and carbon distributions. The project used inverse and numerical approaches to evaluate how biological production, remineralisation and ocean circulation determine the amount and residence time of carbon transferred from surface waters into the ocean interior. Its outputs were intended to constrain natural carbon storage and improve interpretation of present and past ocean carbon-cycle behaviour. BATMAN was entirely an assessment and modelling activity. It did not stimulate primary production, sink biomass, change ocean circulation or otherwise deploy a negative-emissions pathway, and it did not establish a project monitoring protocol, additionality baseline, permanence rule or carbon-credit issuance mechanism.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre
status_note: NERC award period: August 2013 to December 2016; the project is closed.

document_title: BIARRITZ — Bridging International Activity and Related Research Into the Twilight Zone
notes: BIARRITZ was a NERC-funded coordination and synthesis project concerned with the ocean twilight zone, approximately 100 to 1,000 metres below the surface. It brought together international activity and related research on the processes that determine whether organic material produced by plankton sinks into the ocean interior, is consumed and respired at intermediate depth, or remains stored away from the atmosphere for decades to centuries. The project helped connect United Kingdom research with the wider international twilight-zone community, identify common scientific priorities and support future observations and modelling. It was a networking and research-integration award rather than a biomass-sinking or ocean-fertilization project. BIARRITZ did not authorize intervention, verify removals or establish carbon-accounting and crediting requirements.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre
status_note: Funded from September 2018 to October 2019; UKRI records the award as closed.

document_title: PUCCA — Photosynthetic Underpinnings of Coccolithophore Calcification
notes: PUCCA is a NERC-funded research programme investigating the physiological connection between photosynthesis and calcification in coccolithophores. These plankton fix organic carbon while also producing calcium-carbonate plates, so changes in their metabolism affect both the biological and carbonate pumps and the capacity of seawater to absorb carbon dioxide. The programme uses laboratory, physiological, geochemical and modelling approaches to determine how calcification responds to environmental change and how those responses should be represented in ocean-carbon projections. PUCCA studies natural organisms and processes; it is not an ocean-alkalinity-enhancement or microalgal deployment project. The award does not authorize releases, claim additional removals, prescribe a commercial MRV method or create carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of Oxford and partner institutions
status_note: Linked programme awards began in 2021 and include funding extending into 2027; active as of August 2026.

document_title: AtlantiS — Atlantic Climate and Environment Strategic Science
notes: AtlantiS is a large NERC national-capability programme led by the National Oceanography Centre to observe, understand and predict the Atlantic Ocean's role in climate and environmental change. The programme explicitly addresses the ocean's absorption of anthropogenic carbon and heat, changes in circulation and biogeochemistry, ecosystem productivity, shelf and coastal processes and the consequences of multiple stressors. It integrates sustained observations, research expeditions, autonomous systems, data services and modelling across a wide international partnership. AtlantiS supplies strategic evidence and infrastructure for climate mitigation and adaptation decisions, but it is not a marine carbon-dioxide-removal deployment programme. It does not deliberately increase ocean uptake, authorize a project, establish additionality or permanence requirements, or issue carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre
status_note: National-capability award funded from March 2024 to March 2029; active as of August 2026.

document_title: Building the UK Biogeochemical Argo Array
notes: This NERC infrastructure and research award established the United Kingdom contribution to the international Biogeochemical Argo observing network. It supported autonomous profiling floats equipped to measure biological and chemical variables relevant to ocean productivity, oxygen, carbon cycling and particle export, together with data processing, quality control and integration into the global network. The project expanded sustained open-ocean observations needed to assess natural carbon uptake, biological-pump variability, deoxygenation and ecosystem change and to constrain ocean and climate models. Although the observing system can support future evaluation of marine carbon dioxide removal, the award itself did not conduct a removal intervention, define a project-specific carbon-accounting methodology, determine additionality or permanence, or verify carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre
status_note: Award period: January 2021 to March 2024; the funded project has ended, while the wider observing network continues.

document_title: Arctic PrIZE — Arctic Productivity in the Seasonal Ice Zone
notes: Arctic PrIZE was a NERC research programme examining how seasonal sea-ice change affects Arctic Ocean primary productivity, food-web processes and carbon cycling. The work combined field observations, biological and chemical measurements, remote sensing and modelling to identify the environmental controls on phytoplankton growth and the transfer of newly fixed organic carbon through the seasonal ice zone. Its results were intended to improve projections of ecological change and the role of polar marine ecosystems in climate regulation as sea-ice conditions shift. The programme observed natural productivity and did not undertake iron fertilization, algal cultivation or another engineered sink-enhancement measure. It did not establish deployment authorization, quantify additional removal for a carbon market or create permanence and MRV rules.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of Oxford and partners
status_note: Linked award recorded from February 2017 to September 2021; the programme has ended.

document_title: PHYCASO — Phytoplankton Evolution and Carbonate Dynamics during Past Southern Ocean Regimes
notes: PHYCASO used material and records associated with IODP Expedition 392 to investigate coccolithophore evolution and carbonate dynamics during past Southern Ocean climate regimes. Coccolithophores produce calcium-carbonate plates and contribute to organic production, carbonate export and carbon-rich marine sediments; understanding their historical response provides evidence about the sensitivity of the biological and carbonate pumps to environmental change. The project analysed geological and biological records rather than altering present-day ecosystems. It therefore supports fundamental carbon-cycle reconstruction and model development but does not represent ocean alkalinity enhancement, plankton cultivation or another deployed negative-emissions pathway. No additional atmospheric removal, project permanence, MRV method or carbon-credit entitlement was established.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of Oxford
status_note: Award period: January 2022 to September 2024; the research project has ended.

document_title: REMAIN — Remineralisation of Organic Carbon by Marine Bacterioplankton
notes: REMAIN was a NERC-funded programme investigating how marine bacterioplankton remineralise organic carbon and return it to dissolved inorganic forms. The project addressed a major uncertainty in estimates of ocean carbon storage: the rates, controls and variability of microbial respiration that determine whether organic material persists, is transported to depth or is converted back to carbon dioxide. Laboratory and field measurements were combined with process understanding and modelling to improve representation of microbial carbon cycling in ocean and climate models. REMAIN studied natural microbial respiration and did not seek to engineer microbial mineralisation, increase refractory dissolved organic carbon or deploy a marine removal technology. It created no deployment permission, project-level MRV protocol, additionality test, permanence rule or carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of East Anglia and partners
status_note: Lead award funded from December 2017 to November 2022; the programme has ended.

document_title: PICCOLO — Processes Influencing Carbon Cycling: Observations of the Lower Limb of the Antarctic Overturning
notes: PICCOLO is a long-running NERC programme investigating carbon cycling associated with the lower limb of the Antarctic overturning circulation. Its linked awards support oceanographic observations, biogeochemical measurements and modelling of dense-water formation, the movement of carbon between surface, deep and abyssal waters, biological particle processes and exchanges relevant to Southern Ocean carbon storage. The programme integrates contributions from the University of East Anglia, Plymouth Marine Laboratory, the British Antarctic Survey and other partners. It improves evidence on natural physical and biological sequestration but does not operate an artificial-downwelling or biomass-sinking intervention. PICCOLO does not itself authorize marine carbon dioxide removal, determine additionality or permanence for credits, or report verified engineered removal tonnes.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / University of East Anglia, Plymouth Marine Laboratory and British Antarctic Survey
status_note: Linked programme awards began in July 2017 and include funding through December 2027; active as of August 2026.

document_title: LOCATE — Land Ocean Carbon Transfer
notes: LOCATE was a major NERC programme designed to quantify the transfer, transformation and fate of carbon moving from land through rivers, estuaries, shelf seas and the open ocean. It combined coordinated field sampling, autonomous and conventional observations, laboratory analysis and modelling to determine how much terrestrially derived carbon reaches coastal waters, how much is respired or buried, and how land management and hydrological change affect downstream carbon budgets. The programme directly strengthened evidence on land-ocean coupling and shelf-sea carbon cycling. It did not constitute land-sea coordinated negative-emissions engineering: no nutrient or carbon inputs were deliberately manipulated to increase marine uptake, and no removal project, permanence requirement, accounting standard or crediting mechanism was established.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre and partners
status_note: Main programme funded from March 2016 to November 2019; the original award has ended.

document_title: Land Ocean Carbon Transfer — One-Year Extension
notes: This formally funded one-year extension continued the LOCATE Land Ocean Carbon Transfer programme after the original award. The extension preserved the collaborative observation and synthesis effort needed to complete analysis of carbon moving through catchments, rivers, estuaries and shelf seas, integrate datasets and models, and translate findings on carbon and nutrient biogeochemistry. It is recorded separately because UKRI assigned a distinct award reference and implementation period, not because it represents a second deployment project. The extension remained an evidence-building research activity. It did not deliberately modify land-derived inputs to enhance a marine sink, authorize a land-sea negative-emissions intervention, establish project additionality or permanence rules, or generate verified carbon credits.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre, Plymouth Marine Laboratory and partners
status_note: Separate extension award funded from March 2021 to March 2022; the extension has ended.

document_title: FOCUS — Future States of the Global Coastal Ocean: Understanding for Solutions
notes: FOCUS was a large NERC research programme addressing the global coastal ocean through modelling, satellite remote sensing, field surveys, laboratory work, data synthesis and international collaboration. Its carbon-related work included coastal carbon and nutrient biogeochemistry, trends in productivity, land-management effects on coastal waters, climate-driven carbon change and the potential for healthy seagrass, mangrove and seaweed systems to draw carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The programme assessed how protection and restoration could improve carbon uptake while also considering pollution, ocean acidification, ecosystem resilience and social exposure. FOCUS generated evidence, datasets and policy-relevant analysis but did not itself restore a specified area, authorize marine carbon dioxide removal, quantify additional and durable project removals, or establish a crediting methodology. Its references to restoration potential must not be treated as proof of deployed or verified removal.
source: UK Research and Innovation — Natural Environment Research Council / National Oceanography Centre and Plymouth Marine Laboratory
status_note: Funded from June 2022 to March 2026; UKRI records the research grant as closed.

document_title: ENEOS Large-Scale Seaweed Cultivation Demonstration for Blue-Carbon Sink Expansion in Okushiri
notes: Japan's Ministry of the Environment selected ENEOS Holdings Co., Ltd. as one of five independent recipients under the 2026 subsidy programme for launching large-scale demonstrations of blue-carbon and other greenhouse-gas sink measures. The project will conduct open-sea cultivation trials around Okushiri, Hokkaido, to develop a new seaweed-cultivation system whose primary stated purpose is greenhouse-gas absorption and to test whether the approach can support implementation at a substantially larger scale. This project-level record is separate from the database's programme-level selection record because it has its own awardee, location and technical objective. The award establishes public financial support for development and demonstration, but the official selection notice does not report measured net atmospheric carbon removal, permanence, leakage, lifecycle emissions, ecological impacts or additionality. It does not issue carbon credits, approve an accounting methodology, or provide a general commercial deployment permit. Any future claim of removals would therefore require project-specific monitoring, transparent system boundaries, independent verification and safeguards beyond the selection decision itself.
source: Ministry of the Environment, Government of Japan
status_note: Selected as an active 2026 national demonstration project; implementation results have not yet been reported.

subnational_area: Japanese coastal waters; multi-depth cultivation site not specified in the notice
document_title: Okabe Multi-Stage Deep Seaweed Cultivation Demonstration for Enhanced Carbon Fixation
notes: Japan's Ministry of the Environment selected Okabe Co., Ltd. for a distinct three-year blue-carbon demonstration using a multi-stage cultivation facility that extends seaweed production vertically from shallow water to approximately 18 metres depth. Multiple arame and kajime seedling types are to be attached at several depth levels, while harvesting and regrowth management will be tested to reduce repeated seedling supply, lower operational effort and strengthen carbon fixation. The project is recorded independently from the umbrella award announcement because its cultivation architecture, species group, duration and management experiment are specific to this recipient. The selection supports technical development and field demonstration; it is not evidence that the cultivation system has already achieved net, durable atmospheric carbon removal at scale. The official notice does not provide a baseline, counterfactual, full lifecycle balance, treatment of harvested biomass, durability rule, ecological carrying-capacity assessment or approved crediting protocol. No carbon units are issued by the award, and the record should not be interpreted as a blanket authorization for deployment outside the approved demonstration context.
source: Ministry of the Environment, Government of Japan
status_note: Selected in June 2026 for a three-year demonstration; quantified outcomes and credit eligibility remain unverified.

document_title: Green Coop Large-Scale Sargassum horneri Bed Expansion and Blue-Carbon Methodology Demonstration
notes: Japan's Ministry of the Environment selected the Green Coop Association for an independent large-scale demonstration in the Buzen Sea. The project is intended to expand Sargassum horneri beds, measure and compare biomass increases, quantify carbon uptake and fixation attributed to the intervention, and establish a methodology that could support future carbon-credit creation. The recipient also proposes later replication through sixteen Green Coop consumer cooperatives in western Japan. A separate project record is warranted because the initiative has a defined ecosystem, implementation area, measurement objective and prospective methodology pathway that differ from the other awards listed in the same national decision. The selection itself does not constitute an approved crediting methodology, a registry decision or issuance of tradable units. The official notice does not yet demonstrate additionality, permanence, treatment of detached or harvested biomass, leakage, complete lifecycle emissions, ecological side effects or independent verification. Credit creation is an intended future outcome rather than an accomplished policy result, and any expansion remains contingent on field performance, safeguards and subsequent methodological acceptance.
source: Ministry of the Environment, Government of Japan
status_note: Selected as a 2026 demonstration; carbon quantification and a prospective credit methodology are under development, not approved.

document_title: Nippon Steel–Hokkaido University–Matsumae Kelp-Bed Restoration and Cultivation Demonstration
notes: Japan's Ministry of the Environment selected a consortium led by Nippon Steel Corporation, with Hokkaido University's Muroran Marine Station and Matsumae Town, for a distinct blue-carbon demonstration in Matsumae. The project will combine restoration of natural seaweed beds and makonbu kelp cultivation with marine fertilizing material derived from steel slag, testing whether the intervention can stabilize and expand biomass and support a locally adapted model for social implementation. The project is entered separately from the national selection summary because it has a named consortium, defined municipality, specific material input and combined restoration–cultivation design. Public selection confirms eligibility for demonstration support but does not prove that the material produces net climate benefit or that restored biomass results in durable carbon storage. The notice provides no complete lifecycle assessment of material production and transport, no quantified baseline, no permanence or leakage rules, no final ecological-risk findings and no approved crediting method. It therefore should be treated as an active technical and governance demonstration rather than verified removal, credit issuance or unrestricted authorization to apply steel-slag-derived inputs in other marine areas.
source: Ministry of the Environment, Government of Japan
status_note: Selected as an active 2026 consortium demonstration in Matsumae; climate performance and ecological safeguards remain to be demonstrated.

subnational_area: Japanese wakame and kelp aquaculture grounds; exact sites not specified in the notice
document_title: Riken Food Consortium Seaweed Production Optimization and Underwater Biomass-Monitoring Demonstration
notes: Japan's Ministry of the Environment selected a consortium led by Riken Food Co., Ltd., with Sumitomo Osaka Cement Co., Ltd. and Nichimo Co., Ltd., for an independent blue-carbon scale-up demonstration. The consortium will optimize nutrient, aquaculture and propagation materials used in seaweed seedling production and cultivation, and will combine existing underwater drones with underwater cameras to establish a broadly usable method for estimating standing biomass in wakame and kelp farms. Its stated objective is to maximize production and evaluate the blue-carbon effect of seaweed aquaculture through an integrated cultivation and monitoring system. The record is distinct from the umbrella selection entry because the consortium, production inputs and observation technology are project-specific. The award does not establish that increased farm biomass equals net, durable atmospheric carbon removal, and the official notice does not resolve harvested-product fate, dissolved and particulate carbon export, additionality, lifecycle emissions, permanence or ecological carrying capacity. It neither approves a carbon-credit methodology nor issues units; those outcomes would require later evidence, independent verification and appropriate environmental safeguards.
source: Ministry of the Environment, Government of Japan
status_note: Selected as an active 2026 demonstration; the cultivation system and biomass-estimation method are still being developed and validated.

document_title: Second 2026 Call for Large-Scale Demonstration Projects for Blue Carbon and Other Greenhouse-Gas Sink Measures
notes: Japan's Ministry of the Environment opened a second 2026 call under the subsidy programme for launching large-scale demonstrations of blue carbon and other greenhouse-gas sink measures. Supported by the fiscal 2025 supplementary budget and fiscal 2026 initial budget, the call finances technology development and demonstration, collection and organization of evidence, public understanding and preparation for earlier social implementation in conjunction with a national institutional foundation. Applications opened on 10 July 2026 and remain due by 17 August 2026 at 17:00, so no second-round recipients had been announced as of 6 August 2026. The programme can cover several sink categories, including blue carbon, biochar and carbon-absorbing concrete; this database record concerns only the explicitly eligible marine blue-carbon component and does not imply that every future award will be ONCE-related. The call is a funding opportunity, not a project approval, deployment permit, crediting methodology or verification decision. It does not itself demonstrate carbon removal, permanence, additionality or ecological safety, and future proposals must be assessed individually before being treated as operational marine negative-emissions projects.
