source: Ministry of the Environment, Government of Japan
status_note: Open for applications from 10 July to 17 August 2026; second-round awards had not been announced as of 6 August 2026.

document_title: Ocean Decade Call for Decade Actions No. 10/2025 — Global ONCE and GO-BC Endorsement Window
notes: The Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO opened Call for Decade Actions No. 10/2025 to invite partners to request Ocean Decade endorsement for programmes, projects and contributions. The call explicitly listed the Global Ocean Negative Carbon Emission programme (Global ONCE) and the Global Ocean Decade Programme for Blue Carbon (GO-BC) among the host programmes to which eligible project proposals could attach, creating a formal international route for new research, observation, capacity-building and solution-oriented actions to enter the Decade network. The window opened in October 2025 and closed in early 2026, so this record captures a completed coordination and endorsement procedure rather than an active funding round. Ocean Decade endorsement is a recognition and alignment mechanism; the call itself did not award research money, approve marine intervention sites, establish legal permission, certify carbon-accounting methods or issue carbon credits. Inclusion of Global ONCE and GO-BC indicates thematic eligibility, not evidence that every submitted or endorsed action removes carbon. Each resulting action requires separate project-level evidence and classification before it can be recorded as research, engineering deployment or a standards-and-market instrument.
source: UNESCO Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission — United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development
status_note: Application window closed in early 2026; endorsement decisions and resulting actions require separate project-level records.

document_title: Ocean Decade Call for Decade Actions No. 11/2026 — Global ONCE and GO-BC Endorsement Window
notes: The Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO launched Call for Decade Actions No. 11/2026 as a global process for submitting new Ocean Decade programmes, projects and resource contributions. The call lists thirty-one endorsed programmes, including Global Ocean Negative Carbon Emission (Global ONCE) and the Global Ocean Decade Programme for Blue Carbon (GO-BC), under which relevant proposals may seek endorsement. As of 6 August 2026, the project and contribution submission window remained open until 31 August 2026, while programme expressions of interest had already closed; resulting endorsement decisions are expected later and therefore no individual proposal is treated here as approved. This is an international scientific coordination and recognition procedure rather than a grant award, regulatory authorization or carbon-market mechanism. The call does not establish technical performance, environmental safety, additionality, permanence, monitoring rules or credit eligibility for any future marine carbon-removal action. Separate records should be created only after an identifiable action is endorsed or otherwise formally established, and its actual function should then be classified according to research, engineering, governance or market content rather than inferred from the programme under which it was submitted.
source: UNESCO Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission — United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development
status_note: Open project and contribution call through 31 August 2026; endorsement outcomes had not yet been finalized as of 6 August 2026.

country_or_region: Caribbean Sea and South Pacific Ocean
document_title: OceanWISE: Indigenous Knowledge Alliance
notes: OceanWISE is an endorsed Ocean Decade project led by the Asociación Centro para la Autonomía y Desarrollo de los Pueblos Indígenas in Nicaragua and operating across Indigenous coastal contexts associated with the Caribbean Sea and South Pacific Ocean. Running from 2024 through 2030, the alliance seeks to integrate Indigenous knowledge into territorial ocean management, strengthen Indigenous participation in decision-making and governance, safeguard cultural heritage and apply traditional methods relevant to carbon sequestration, ecosystem conservation and coastal-community resilience. Its policy significance lies in combining blue-carbon-related knowledge with rights, participation and locally grounded management rather than treating carbon as a stand-alone commodity. The official project description does not specify a quantified restoration area, a carbon baseline, a verified volume of removals, a permanence period, an approved methodology or issued credits. It also does not create binding national law or a general authorization for marine intervention. The project is therefore classified as a governance, knowledge and community-safeguard initiative with a substantive coastal blue-carbon component; any future engineering or crediting outcomes require separate evidence and should not be inferred from Ocean Decade endorsement alone.
source: Asociación Centro para la Autonomía y Desarrollo de los Pueblos Indígenas (CADPI) / Ocean Decade
status_note: Endorsed Ocean Decade project operating from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2030.

country_or_region: Indian Ocean, North Atlantic Ocean and South Atlantic Ocean
document_title: Marine Forest Restoration: A Coastal Gardening Plan
notes: This completed Ocean Decade project, led by Underwater Gardens International in Spain, ran from May 2022 through April 2025 and promoted an active-restoration model for marine forests. The initiative combined conservation and restoration, proposed a professional role for 'gardeners of the sea', applied ecoengineering across shallow, mesophotic and continental-shelf environments, involved citizens and local stakeholders, and described a novel carbon-sequestration approach alongside biodiversity and coastal-resilience objectives. It is included as an independent implementation-oriented project rather than as a general Ocean Decade programme entry. The official description confirms that the Decade Action has ended, but it does not publish a final quantified net-removal result, an independently verified carbon balance, a permanence or leakage framework, a registered methodology, or issued credits. The project page also does not establish legal authorization for replication in other jurisdictions. Accordingly, the record recognizes a substantive marine-forest restoration and carbon-sequestration demonstration while explicitly avoiding the assumption that restored biomass automatically represents durable atmospheric carbon removal or a marketable carbon asset.
source: Underwater Gardens International / Ocean Decade
status_note: Completed Ocean Decade project with an official implementation period from 1 May 2022 to 30 April 2025.

country_or_region: North Atlantic Ocean and Nordic Seas
document_title: Reconstructing the Biological Carbon Pump with Ancient Plankton DNA (BIOCAP)
notes: BIOCAP is an endorsed Ocean Decade research project led by NORCE in Norway and scheduled from 2024 through 2027. It develops ancient plankton DNA as a proxy for reconstructing changes in the biological carbon pump, combining sedimentary DNA observations with geochemical, climate and existing biodiversity data from surface sediments and three Late Quaternary sediment cores in the North Atlantic and Nordic Seas. The project aims to reconstruct biological-pump behaviour back to the Last Interglacial and improve understanding of whether future warming may weaken or strengthen ocean carbon transfer and storage. Its direct contribution to Global ONCE knowledge is the reconstruction of a core natural carbon-pump process and the evidence needed to evaluate climate feedbacks. BIOCAP is not a carbon-removal deployment project: it does not add nutrients, cultivate biomass, alter alkalinity, capture carbon directly or authorize any intervention. The official project page does not claim quantified anthropogenic removals, credits, a project baseline or an MRV methodology for commercial use. The record is therefore classified as theory, observation and modelling, with BCP used only as the researched mechanism rather than as evidence of engineered negative emissions.
source: NORCE / Ocean Decade
status_note: Active endorsed research project scheduled from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2027.

document_title: Ghana Ocean Climate Innovations Hub (GOCIB)
notes: The Ghana Ocean Climate Innovations Hub is an endorsed Ocean Decade project led by OceanRock Base together with Ghana's Land Use and Spatial Planning Authority, Western Region Directorate. Operating from 2024 through 2030, it seeks to organize a multi-stakeholder task force spanning public agencies, scientists, businesses, civil-society organizations, universities and coastal communities, and to compile, develop and implement nature- and ocean-based carbon-removal approaches for Ghana and wider West Africa. The project is policy-relevant because it combines technical innovation, stakeholder coordination, capacity development and regional diffusion rather than focusing on a single isolated experiment. The official action page does not identify a finalized intervention design, a defined restoration area, a quantified carbon baseline, a verified removal volume, permanence or leakage provisions, an approved MRV method, a project permit or issued credits. Its reference to implementing ocean carbon-removal techniques expresses the programme's intended direction, not evidence that a particular method has already delivered durable negative emissions. Separate records should be created for any later funded pilot, regulatory decision, methodology or crediting activity once sufficient official documentation exists.
source: OceanRock Base and Ghana Land Use and Spatial Planning Authority, Western Region Directorate / Ocean Decade
status_note: Endorsed Ocean Decade project scheduled from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2030.

document_title: Blue Economy Coalition for Ocean Climate Solutions
notes: The Blue Economy Coalition for Ocean Climate Solutions is an endorsed Ocean Decade project led by Mar y Comercio in Costa Rica and scheduled from October 2023 through December 2030. It brings together public, private and academic actors in Central America and the Caribbean to advance research, investment, collaboration, technology development and knowledge sharing around ocean resilience, carbon neutrality and effective carbon-removal strategies. The initiative functions primarily as a regional coalition and innovation-enabling platform: it seeks to mobilize partnerships and marine industries while connecting climate action with ecosystem protection and coastal-community development. The official project description does not specify a particular carbon-removal pathway, intervention location, environmental-assessment procedure, quantification protocol, permanence standard, credit registry or verified removal result. For that reason, no specific engineering pathway or carbon-pump label is inferred, even though negative-emissions development is a substantive objective. Ocean Decade endorsement does not supply legal authorization, public funding, methodology approval or credit issuance. Any later pilot, investment vehicle, technical standard or transaction should be entered separately and classified according to its actual documented function.
source: Mar y Comercio / Ocean Decade
status_note: Endorsed regional Ocean Decade project scheduled from 1 October 2023 to 31 December 2030.

document_title: Team CASPI Climate Innovation Hub
notes: Team CASPI Climate Innovation Hub is an endorsed Ocean Decade project led by the Caspian Environmental Consortium in Kazakhstan and scheduled from 2025 through 2030. The hub seeks to build youth and stakeholder capacity, promote scientific and technological innovation, support large-scale marine carbon-removal technologies and marine-ecosystem restoration, remediate coastal ecosystems to strengthen carbon-sequestration capacity, improve regional monitoring of industrial pollution and foster community entrepreneurship and coastal resilience. It is distinct from the separately recorded CaspianCDR technical project because this action is a broader regional innovation, partnership and capacity platform rather than a single defined carbon-removal process. The official description does not identify a selected technology, project site, quantified baseline, verified removal outcome, lifecycle assessment, permanence rule, environmental permit, approved methodology or issued carbon credits. References to large-scale technologies describe the hub's development ambition and cannot be treated as proof of deployment. The record therefore captures an active enabling and restoration-oriented initiative; any concrete demonstration, regulatory approval or crediting mechanism emerging from it requires a separate source-supported entry.
source: Caspian Environmental Consortium Ltd. / Ocean Decade
status_note: Endorsed Ocean Decade project scheduled from 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2030.

document_title: Belize Blue Cities and Beyond Project — Blue Economy Monitoring and Blue Carbon Readiness Support (P181064)
notes: The World Bank approved the Belize Blue Cities and Beyond Project (P181064) in January 2025, with PROBLUE support identifying a dedicated component for blue-economy monitoring and blue-carbon readiness through the project's closing date in 2029. The operation is intended to strengthen coastal and blue-economy management, geospatial planning and monitoring, improve institutional capacity and help Belize develop the regulatory, data and digital foundations needed for high-integrity blue-carbon finance and potential carbon-market transactions. It is recorded separately from the 2024 Belize readiness assessment because this is a financed implementation operation with a project identifier, procurement arrangements and a multi-year delivery period, rather than a completed diagnostic report. Board approval and financing do not mean that a blue-carbon crediting mechanism is already operational or that credits have been issued. The available official material does not establish verified project removals, permanence, additionality or final accounting rules. Market infrastructure, safeguards and transaction systems remain implementation objectives, and any future methodology approval, project registration or issuance event should be entered separately when formally documented.
source: World Bank / Government of Belize / PROBLUE
status_note: World Bank-financed operation approved in January 2025 and active through the planned 1 December 2029 closing date.

document_title: Groundwater Management for Healthy Blue Carbon Ecosystems and Coastal Resilience in the Pacific (P162938)
notes: The World Bank's official PROBLUE portfolio listed project P162938 as an activity supporting Pacific Island States in improving coastal resilience through groundwater management that protects water availability, water quality, groundwater recharge and the health of blue-carbon ecosystems. The intervention recognizes that hydrological conditions can determine the condition and carbon function of mangroves, tidal wetlands and other coastal ecosystems, linking source-to-sea water management with coastal carbon and adaptation outcomes. The project is entered independently because it has a distinct project number, regional scope, objective and closing date. The year recorded here is the year of the November 2025 official PROBLUE portfolio snapshot rather than an inferred original approval year, which the portfolio page does not state. The listed closing date was 30 June 2026, so the activity is treated as ended by August 2026 unless a later extension is formally published. The source does not report restoration hectares, quantified net removals, a carbon-accounting methodology, credit issuance or project-level permanence. The record therefore reflects enabling research and management support, not proof that groundwater interventions generated tradable or verified negative emissions.
source: World Bank / PROBLUE
status_note: Listed in the November 2025 PROBLUE portfolio with a 30 June 2026 closing date; no later extension was identified.

document_title: Blue Brazilian Amazon: Integrating Biodiversity, Gender, and Climate Resilience in Mangrove Management and Blue Finance (P504284/P511556)
notes: The World Bank's November 2025 PROBLUE portfolio listed projects P504284 and P511556 under the Blue Brazilian Amazon activity, designed to strengthen conservation and sustainable use of mangroves in the Brazilian Amazon while promoting gender equality and scaling blue-finance mechanisms. The grant links mangrove management, climate resilience, biodiversity, inclusive governance and financing rather than treating carbon as the sole ecosystem value. It is recorded as a distinct programme because the official portfolio provides a specific name, country, project identifiers, objective and closing date. The listed closing date was 31 May 2026, so the activity is classified as ended by August 2026 unless a formal extension is later documented. The portfolio entry does not state that a carbon-credit methodology was approved, a market platform was created, restoration acreage was completed or verified carbon units were issued. It also does not provide project-level additionality, permanence, leakage or a final net-removal balance. Blue finance is therefore classified as an enabling and scaling objective, not an accomplished crediting mechanism, and any subsequent fund, project registration or transaction should be documented separately.
source: World Bank / PROBLUE
status_note: Listed in the November 2025 PROBLUE portfolio with a 31 May 2026 closing date; financing and conservation outputs require project reporting.

document_title: Strategic Support for India's Blue Economy Policy Framework, Resilient Fisheries Transition and Blue Carbon Finance (P174798/P180932)
notes: The World Bank's November 2025 PROBLUE portfolio lists projects P174798 and P180932 as strategic support for India's Blue Economy Policy Framework, with priority reforms covering resilient marine fisheries, national marine-litter policy, port greening and decarbonization, and blue-carbon finance. The activity provides policy analysis, coordination and institutional support across several blue-economy pillars; blue carbon is a substantive finance and reform component but is not the sole subject of the grant. The project is entered separately because it has identifiable project numbers, a formal objective and a 30 June 2026 closing date. It is classified as ended by August 2026 unless an extension is later published. The official portfolio entry does not identify a particular blue-carbon ecosystem, approve a national carbon methodology, establish a registry, authorize an engineering project or report issued credits. For that reason, no engineering pathway or natural carbon-pump mechanism is inferred. The record captures policy and finance readiness only: later legislation, market rules, methodologies, restoration programmes or transactions must be supported by separate official instruments before being treated as implemented ONCE policy or engineering.
source: World Bank / PROBLUE
status_note: Listed in the November 2025 PROBLUE portfolio with a 30 June 2026 closing date; the support was advisory and reform-oriented.

document_title: HORIZON-MISS-2026-03-OCEAN-03 — By Fishers, for Fishers: Co-Management of Marine and Freshwater Ecosystems and Resources
notes: The European Commission opened HORIZON-MISS-2026-03-OCEAN-03 under the Restore our Ocean and Waters Mission to develop adaptive co-management approaches led with fishers and to reconcile viable fisheries with ecosystem recovery and local livelihoods. Expected outcomes include measurable improvements in critical marine or freshwater habitats, explicitly including blue-carbon sequestration capacity, through active and passive conservation and restoration; stronger ecosystem-based fisheries management; monitoring, data sharing and replication across multiple demonstration sites. The topic therefore provides a formal research and demonstration funding route for projects that may strengthen coastal carbon sinks, although blue carbon is one expected habitat outcome within a broader fisheries and biodiversity call. As of 6 August 2026 the call remained open, with no selected projects or sites confirmed. The topic does not itself restore an ecosystem, quantify removals, approve an accounting methodology, issue credits or authorize interventions under national law. Carbon outcomes, permanence, additionality and safeguards must be demonstrated by any awarded project, and only carbon-relevant awards should later be entered as separate ONCE project records.
source: European Commission — Horizon Europe Mission Restore our Ocean and Waters
status_note: Open 2026 Horizon Europe call; proposals and individual demonstration projects had not yet been selected as of 6 August 2026.

document_title: Accelerating Blue Finance: Instruments, Case Studies, and Pathways to Scale
notes: This World Bank and PROBLUE report reviews how blue-finance instruments can be designed and scaled to mobilize public and private capital for sustainable ocean and coastal outcomes. It examines instruments such as blue bonds, debt-for-nature swaps, insurance products, impact funds, outcome-based mechanisms, sustainability-linked finance and blue-carbon credits, together with enabling policy, institutional, data, metric, verification and inclusion requirements. The report uses case studies to identify implementation conditions, risks and pathways for moving from isolated pilots to coordinated finance systems, making it relevant to the standards, policy and market component of Global ONCE. It is a completed global assessment and practical guidance product, not a binding financial taxonomy, regulatory standard, approved blue-carbon methodology or investment commitment to any specific project. Discussion of blue-carbon credits does not establish that all coastal restoration generates eligible units, and the report does not issue credits, verify removals, set permanence rules or authorize engineering deployment. Individual financial facilities, methodologies, transactions and restoration projects mentioned or inspired by the report require separate records supported by their own formal decisions and project evidence.
source: World Bank / PROBLUE
status_note: Global analytical report published in June 2025; recommendations are non-binding and require separate implementation instruments.

document_title: Everlasting Swamp Blue Carbon Demonstration Project Literature Review and Gap Analysis
notes: This 190-page draft report assembles the scientific and management evidence needed to frame restoration choices for Everlasting Swamp, a heavily modified coastal floodplain wetland in the lower Clarence River system. It reviews the effects of drainage, levees and tide-limiting structures; acid sulfate soil exposure; water-quality deterioration; wetland vegetation and habitat change; hydrological connectivity; climate risks; and the potential for restored coastal wetland processes to rebuild blue-carbon functions and wider ecosystem services. The document also identifies evidence gaps that require field investigation, modelling, monitoring or consultation before a preferred intervention can be selected. Its role is diagnostic and preparatory: it supports the subsequent restoration-options assessment and project design process, but it does not choose an engineering option, approve tidal works, register an Australian Carbon Credit Unit project, establish a project baseline, or demonstrate additional, permanent and verified carbon removal.
source: New South Wales Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
status_note: Published on 11 December 2025 and labelled as a draft report supporting the continuing options-assessment process.

document_title: Everlasting Swamp Blue Carbon Demonstration Project — Project Update December 2025
notes: This official four-page project update translates the technical Wetland Restoration Options Assessment into a concise public account of the Everlasting Swamp investigation. It explains that historic drainage works, levees and tide-limiting structures altered wetland hydrology, reduced habitat quality, constrained fish movement and contributed to poor water quality and acid sulfate soil impacts. It presents the project as an investigation into wetland rehabilitation, climate resilience and the feasibility of blue-carbon restoration in New South Wales, and it was issued to support public exhibition of the draft options assessment. The update is an information and engagement document rather than a separate restoration decision. It does not identify a final preferred option, compel landholder participation, authorize construction or tidal reconnection, quantify an approved abatement volume, satisfy ACCU registration requirements, or create carbon credits. Any future implementation remains dependent on consultation, detailed design, environmental and cultural assessment, landholder engagement and project-specific approvals.
source: New South Wales Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
status_note: Published on 11 December 2025 as a completed public project update accompanying consultation on the draft options assessment.

document_title: Everlasting Swamp Blue Carbon Demonstration Project Frequently Asked Questions — December 2025
notes: This official fact sheet answers recurring questions about the purpose, scope and decision process of the Everlasting Swamp Blue Carbon Demonstration Project and directs readers to the December 2025 project update and the technical restoration-options assessment. It is designed to clarify why the department is examining hydrological rehabilitation, how blue-carbon benefits relate to wider wetland outcomes, what consultation means, and which matters remain unresolved. The document helps prevent an early-stage feasibility and options exercise from being interpreted as a predetermined construction programme. It is explanatory guidance only: it does not impose legal obligations, select a preferred hydrological option, provide a project permit, replace environmental or cultural heritage assessment, determine land-access arrangements, approve ACCU participation, or verify carbon sequestration. Statements concerning possible blue-carbon benefits describe project objectives and potential outcomes rather than measured additional removals or issued credits.
source: New South Wales Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
status_note: Published on 11 December 2025 as a current explanatory fact sheet for the continuing demonstration-project planning process.

document_title: Everlasting Swamp Blue Carbon Demonstration Project Wetland Restoration Options Assessment
notes: This 231-page draft assessment compares potential approaches for rehabilitating Everlasting Swamp and provides the principal technical basis for choosing whether and how hydrological restoration should proceed. The assessment considers the modified floodplain and tidal system, the location and scale of possible works, inundation behaviour, water quality, acid sulfate soils, vegetation and habitat responses, implementation constraints, environmental risks and the expected contribution of wetland recovery to blue-carbon sequestration and other ecosystem services. It is an options-comparison document issued for consultation, not a final engineering design or administrative approval. The department had not selected a preferred option when the assessment was published. Consequently, the document does not authorize earthworks, alteration of floodgates or levees, tidal reconnection, entry onto private land, ACCU project registration or credit issuance. Carbon outcomes remain prospective and would require a defined boundary, baseline, eligible method, monitoring plan and verification after any future project decision.
source: New South Wales Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
status_note: Published on 20 January 2026 as a draft options assessment; consultation closed, but a preferred restoration option had not yet been decided.

document_title: Addendum — Everlasting Swamp Options Assessment
notes: This official nine-page addendum supplements the Everlasting Swamp Wetland Restoration Options Assessment with a dedicated map series. The maps define the study area, show the indicative location of suggested works for each option and display modelled peak inundation depths under current tidal conditions. The addendum therefore provides spatial evidence needed to understand the physical footprint and hydrological implications of alternatives that could influence wetland recovery and blue-carbon habitat development. It must be read with the main draft assessment and does not function as a stand-alone project plan. Mapped works are suggestions for comparative assessment rather than approved construction locations, and modelled inundation is not a guarantee of ecological or carbon performance. The addendum does not select a preferred option, confer land access, satisfy environmental assessment, establish an ACCU project boundary, quantify verified removals or authorize credit issuance.
source: New South Wales Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
status_note: Published on 20 January 2026 as a mapping addendum to the draft restoration-options assessment; the underlying project decision remained pending.

document_title: Everlasting Swamp Blue Carbon Demonstration Project: What We Heard Report
notes: This consultation report records and organises community and stakeholder feedback received during the public exhibition of the Everlasting Swamp Wetland Restoration Options Assessment from 11 December 2025 to 31 January 2026. It summarises participation, identifies recurring themes and concerns, reports views on the proposed restoration alternatives and related matters, and explains the department’s responses and areas requiring further investigation or engagement. The report adds an accountability and social-safeguard layer to a potential blue-carbon restoration project by documenting how local knowledge, landholder interests, environmental concerns and implementation risks enter the decision process. It expressly does not represent a decision to proceed with any option. The project team was still working toward a preferred option, after which further landholder consultation, environmental impact assessment, cultural heritage work, mosquito and acid sulfate soil management and detailed design would be required. No carbon project, removal quantity or credit was approved by this report.
source: New South Wales Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
status_note: Published in June 2026 as the completed report on consultation held from December 2025 through January 2026; the preferred-option decision remained outstanding.

document_title: NI Blue Carbon Habitats
notes: This government-published spatial dataset consolidates the most recent monitored extents of selected blue-carbon habitats in Northern Ireland and organises features by waterbody and habitat type. It was developed in support of the Northern Ireland Blue Carbon Action Plan objective to identify and agree a mechanism for prioritising habitats for management, restoration and creation. The layer recognises a broad evidence domain that can include saltmarsh, seagrass, seabed sediments, biogenic reefs, kelp, maerl and other carbon-relevant marine features, while also reflecting biodiversity and wider ecosystem-service values. It is an active evidence and planning resource rather than a statutory designation, a complete record of every habitat or a carbon-stock inventory. The dataset contains the most recent mapped extent where monitoring evidence is available; absence from the layer may reflect missing surveys rather than confirmed habitat absence. It does not quantify additional removals, establish project baselines, prioritize sites by itself, approve restoration or issue carbon credits.
source: OpenDataNI / Northern Ireland Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs
status_note: Published as an active geospatial layer and last updated on 18 June 2026 under the Open Government Licence.

document_title: Transforming UK Offshore Marine Algae Biomass Production
notes: This government-supported innovation project, led by SeaGrown Limited under the Biomass Feedstocks Innovation Programme, developed and demonstrated an automated end-to-end system for offshore macroalgae farming. Building on SeaGrown’s offshore farm and the Phase 1 FATHOMS concept, the project addressed seeding, line deployment, cultivation and harvesting constraints that make conventional longline production labour-intensive, expensive and vulnerable in open-water conditions. Its policy relevance lies in expanding a domestic supply of marine biomass and testing whether larger and more reliable seaweed production can contribute to a UK blue-carbon capability and low-carbon products. The March 2025 final report documents the demonstration programme, but the project was principally a biomass-production innovation rather than a verified carbon-removal project. Cultivated seaweed uptake is not automatically equivalent to durable atmospheric removal: end use, decomposition, displacement effects, lifecycle emissions, export and storage pathways determine the net result. The award created no carbon-credit methodology, permanence rule or deployment entitlement outside applicable marine licensing.
source: UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero / Biomass Feedstocks Innovation Programme / SeaGrown Limited
status_note: Phase 2 demonstration completed and a redacted final report dated March 2025 was published through the UK government programme page.

document_title: Seagrass Protection and Recovery
notes: This Marine Management Organisation guidance resource explains the ecological, coastal-protection and blue-carbon functions of English seagrass meadows, describes major pressures and gives practical advice for avoiding damage and supporting recovery. It links carbon storage to plant biomass and long-term burial in sediments, while warning that loss of seagrass can remove sink capacity and expose stored carbon. The guidance recommends pressure removal before active restoration, including management of anchoring and recreation, advanced mooring systems, water-quality improvements, fisheries measures and mitigation of development impacts, and it outlines seed and transplant approaches used by local projects. It also situates action within the MMO’s responsibilities for marine non-licensable activities and protected-area conservation objectives. The publication is operational guidance rather than a universal restoration permit or carbon-accounting method. Local projects still require suitable ecological evidence, consents and monitoring, and restored area or plant growth cannot be treated as verified additional and permanent carbon removal without a separate methodology and assurance process.
source: UK Marine Management Organisation
status_note: Published as current government guidance on seagrass protection, pressure management and restoration support.

document_title: Exploring Shetland's Blue Carbon Habitats
notes: This UHI Shetland project produced a locally tailored baseline for sublittoral blue-carbon habitats in the Shetland Islands. The work reviewed existing spatial evidence, modelled potential habitat distributions and estimated the extent, carbon stocks, storage rates and production associated with seagrass, macroalgae, biogenic reefs and benthic sediments. Predictive MaxEnt modelling was used to address limitations in national-scale layers and to provide evidence that can inform regional marine planning, habitat management and future policy development. The project ran from April to July 2025 with UHI Net Zero funding and received endorsement as an Ocean Decade Activity. It was an evidence-building exercise rather than an on-the-ground restoration or carbon-market project. Modelled suitability does not confirm present habitat, measured carbon, additional sequestration or permanence at every mapped location, and the activity did not authorize marine works, establish a statutory inventory, certify a project baseline or issue credits. Its estimates should be applied with the report’s data and modelling limitations.
source: UHI Shetland / University of the Highlands and Islands
status_note: Implemented from April through July 2025 as a completed UHI Net Zero project endorsed as an Ocean Decade Activity.

document_title: Exploring Sublittoral Blue Carbon Habitat Suitability and Potential in the Shetland Islands
notes: This 64-page UHI Shetland report is the principal published output of the Shetland sublittoral blue-carbon project. It provides the first integrated assessment of habitat suitability and potential for seagrass, macroalgae, biogenic reefs and benthic sediments in the islands, combining available observations, spatial environmental variables, predictive modelling and literature-derived carbon information. The report creates a transparent evidence base for discussing where blue-carbon habitats may occur, their possible contribution to carbon storage and the priorities for improved mapping, sampling and marine planning. It is a scientific assessment rather than a legally adopted carbon account. Predicted habitat suitability and literature-based rates are not substitutes for site-specific stock measurements or repeated flux monitoring, and they do not establish additionality, permanence, leakage, ownership or an eligible crediting baseline. The report does not authorize conservation restrictions, aquaculture, restoration or seabed intervention; its value is to guide subsequent evidence collection and policy appraisal.
source: UHI Shetland / University of the Highlands and Islands
status_note: Published in 2025 as the completed technical report from the Shetland sublittoral blue-carbon assessment project.

document_title: CBESS Greenhouse Gas Fluxes in Saltmarsh and Mudflat Habitats
notes: This Environmental Information Data Centre dataset reports carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide flux measurements from paired saltmarsh and adjacent mudflat habitats at six intertidal sites in Morecambe Bay and Essex. Winter and summer sampling in 2013 used light and dark benthic-chamber incubations across a structured set of quadrats, creating direct evidence on greenhouse-gas exchange and the variability that must be considered when evaluating coastal wetland climate functions. The data were generated by the NERC- and BBSRC-supported Coastal Biodiversity and Ecosystem Service Sustainability programme and formally published as a reusable research dataset. It supports process understanding, inventory development and the assessment of restoration or managed-realignment claims, but it is not itself a national emission factor, an approved carbon-accounting method or an MRV standard. Measurements from six sites and two seasons cannot automatically be extrapolated to every UK wetland, and the dataset does not demonstrate project additionality, permanence, leakage, net abatement or eligibility for carbon-credit issuance.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Research data created in 2013 and formally published with a 2015 dataset reference date; the catalogue record remains available.

document_title: CBESS Total Organic Carbon in Mudflat and Saltmarsh Habitats
notes: This CBESS dataset quantifies organic carbon in the upper two centimetres of sediment at six intertidal sites in Essex and Morecambe Bay, with each site containing a saltmarsh and an adjacent mudflat. Replicate samples from a multi-scale quadrat design were analysed using loss on ignition, providing a structured comparison of surface-sediment carbon across habitats, regions and seasons. The data supply empirical evidence for understanding how intertidal habitat type and spatial heterogeneity affect measured carbon content and can support the design of inventories, field-sampling protocols and restoration assessments. The dataset is a research output, not a complete stock assessment: it represents shallow surface sediments rather than the full soil profile, and percentage organic carbon is not by itself a measure of total stock, burial rate or net atmospheric removal. It does not create an official emission factor, approve an accounting methodology, establish project boundaries or baselines, verify additionality and permanence, or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Research data created in 2013 and formally published with a 2015 dataset reference date; the catalogue record remains accessible.

document_title: Sediment-to-Atmosphere CO2 Flux and Soil Characteristics at Mangrove Sites in the Mekong Delta and Charlotte Harbor, 2022
notes: This cross-country dataset contains sediment grain size, sediment carbon content, stable-isotope measurements and sediment-to-atmosphere carbon dioxide flux observations from mangrove coastlines in the Mekong Delta of Viet Nam and Charlotte Harbor, Florida. Sampling was designed to test whether carbon properties and CO2 exchange differ between erosional and accretional geomorphic settings, an important limitation for assuming that all mangrove areas provide the same climate-mitigation performance. The metadata and citation were published in 2026, but the underlying files are embargoed until 31 December 2026. The record therefore establishes a forthcoming evidence product rather than an immediately reusable monitoring system. It does not provide a national mangrove inventory, an approved emission factor or a crediting baseline, and measured sediment carbon or short-period CO2 flux cannot alone demonstrate additional, durable net atmospheric removal. No restoration activity, project authorization, permanence obligation or carbon-credit issuance is created by publication of the dataset.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Metadata published in 2026; the data files were not yet released and were scheduled to remain embargoed until 31 December 2026.

document_title: Saltmarsh Carbon and Greenhouse Gas Flux Data for Northern Temperate Europe, Collated from Literature
notes: This Environment Agency-owned database, prepared by the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, synthesises published evidence on carbon accumulation, carbon stocks and carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide fluxes in natural and restored northern temperate saltmarshes. It was built through a systematic review of 8,974 papers and targeted searches of government and non-government sources, with the explicit aim of supporting potential greenhouse-gas inventory reporting and carbon accounting applicable to the United Kingdom. The inclusion of managed coastal realignment evidence is particularly relevant to evaluating restoration claims and identifying where default factors are too uncertain. The database is an evidence synthesis rather than an adopted inventory rule or project methodology. Variation in definitions, sites, measurement periods and methods must be considered before transferring values, and literature inclusion does not validate every result. The dataset does not set official emission factors, determine additionality or permanence, approve restoration, register projects or issue carbon credits.
source: UK Environment Agency / UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published on 17 September 2025 and made available through the government data catalogue, with files refreshed in July 2026.

document_title: Physical and Geochemical Properties of Saltmarsh Soils from UK Gouge Cores, 2018–2021
notes: This C-SIDE data product reports physical and biogeochemical measurements from 462 narrow-diameter gouge cores collected across 22 UK saltmarshes between 2018 and 2021. The sites were selected to represent contrasting sediment types, vegetation and sea-level histories, and the measurements provide dry bulk density and organic carbon evidence needed to calculate saltmarsh soil carbon stocks across different substrates and marsh settings. The dataset strengthens the empirical foundation for national mapping, sampling design and evaluation of managed-realignment or saltmarsh-creation projects. It is a completed scientific dataset rather than a government-approved carbon factor or project accounting method. The sampling network improves representativeness but does not eliminate spatial and depth uncertainty, and carbon contained in soils is not automatically additional atmospheric removal attributable to a project. The data do not define legal project boundaries, demonstrate permanence or leakage, authorize restoration, certify an inventory value or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library / C-SIDE
status_note: Formally published in July 2022 as a C-SIDE research dataset; the government catalogue record remains active.

document_title: Spatial Mapping of Surficial Soil Organic Carbon Storage and Stocks across Great British Saltmarshes
notes: This geospatial C-SIDE dataset maps organic-carbon density and stock in the upper ten centimetres of soil across 438 saltmarshes in Scotland, England and Wales. It covers approximately 451.65 square kilometres and combines C-SIDE and Marine Scotland measurements with existing national saltmarsh vegetation maps. The product converts field observations into spatially explicit evidence that can support natural-capital assessment, inventory development, identification of evidence gaps and the appraisal of restoration or disturbance risks. Its national coverage is valuable, but it represents surficial soil only and remains dependent on the quality, date and classification of input habitat maps and the modelling used between observations. Mapped existing stock is not the same as annual sequestration or additional project removal. The dataset is not a statutory inventory, an approved crediting baseline or proof of permanence, and it does not authorize habitat intervention, assign carbon ownership, verify project performance or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library / C-SIDE
status_note: Formally published on 7 July 2022 as a completed national-scale C-SIDE geospatial dataset; the catalogue remains available.

document_title: Dry Bulk Density, Loss on Ignition and Organic Carbon Content of Surficial Soils from Scottish Salt Marshes, 2018–2019
notes: This C-SIDE dataset contains 471 saltmarsh soil samples from 46 Scottish sites chosen to represent contrasting sediments, vegetation and sea-level histories. It records dry bulk density, soil texture, loss-on-ignition organic matter and elemental-analysis organic carbon in the upper ten centimetres. Citizen-science CarbonQuest samples were combined with structured C-SIDE coring, creating a broad empirical basis for characterising Scotland’s surface saltmarsh carbon storage and testing relationships between field methods and site conditions. The data can support mapping, inventory research and the design of monitoring for restoration, but they are not a complete profile of deep soil carbon or a direct measurement of annual net sequestration. Differences in collection method and spatial coverage require quality control before aggregation. The dataset does not establish official emission factors, additionality, permanence, leakage or ownership, and it does not authorize a restoration project, verify an offset or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library / C-SIDE / CarbonQuest
status_note: Formally published on 18 December 2020 as a completed Scottish saltmarsh carbon dataset; the catalogue remains active.

document_title: GPS Locations and Elevations of Soil Sampling Sites across UK Saltmarshes, 2018–2021
notes: This C-SIDE geospatial dataset records the coordinates and elevations of 1,323 soil-sampling locations distributed across UK saltmarshes. Sampling between 2018 and 2021 was designed to represent contrasting sediment, vegetation and relative sea-level settings and to support calculation of soil organic-carbon stocks and burial rates. The location and elevation information is essential for reproducibility, linkage to habitat and inundation variables, spatial modelling and future resampling, and therefore forms part of the measurement infrastructure required for credible blue-carbon evidence. The dataset does not itself contain a complete carbon account or prove sequestration; it must be combined with soil measurements, depth information, dating and appropriate spatial inference. Sampling locations are evidence points rather than legally defined project areas. Publication does not establish an official inventory, approve restoration, determine additionality, permanence or leakage, allocate carbon rights, register an offset project or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library / C-SIDE
status_note: Formally published in July 2022 as a completed C-SIDE geospatial sampling dataset; the catalogue record remains accessible.

document_title: Belowground Biomass and Carbon Content from Scottish Salt Marshes, 2021
notes: This C-SIDE dataset reports physical and biogeochemical measurements of belowground root biomass from four contrasting Scottish saltmarshes. Wide-gauge cores were processed to quantify root biomass and organic carbon through elemental analysis, and the measurements were combined to estimate belowground root carbon. The data address a component of saltmarsh carbon storage that can be missed when assessments focus only on aboveground vegetation or shallow bulk soil, and they can improve process understanding and the design of stock assessments. The four-site scope is intentionally focused and should not be treated as a national default factor without further analysis. Root carbon is a stock component rather than proof of annual net atmospheric removal, and its durability depends on decomposition, sediment dynamics and disturbance. The dataset does not create an approved carbon methodology, project baseline or permanence rule, and it does not authorize restoration, certify additionality, verify offsets or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library / C-SIDE
status_note: Formally published on 1 February 2022 as a completed Scottish C-SIDE research dataset; the catalogue remains available.

document_title: Bulk Elemental and Stable-Isotope Composition of Organic Matter from UK Terrestrial, Intertidal and Marine Environments, 2016–2021
notes: This C-SIDE dataset provides organic carbon, nitrogen and stable-isotope measurements for 491 samples collected from terrestrial, intertidal and marine materials across the United Kingdom. The sample set includes soils, peat and biomass; saltmarsh vegetation and roots, seagrass, mudflat material and faecal matter; and macroalgae, microalgae, zooplankton and aquaculture waste. The evidence was produced to constrain the origin of organic carbon when used with isotope-mixing models, helping distinguish terrestrial inputs from marine production in coastal carbon-stock assessments. Source attribution is important for avoiding the assumption that all carbon found in a wetland was newly fixed within the project boundary. The dataset is a scientific input, not a complete mixing model or national accounting rule. Isotopic similarity, end-member selection and transport introduce uncertainty, and the data do not demonstrate additionality, permanence or net removal. Publication does not authorize engineering, establish ownership, certify a project or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library / C-SIDE
status_note: Formally published on 5 April 2022 as a completed C-SIDE elemental and isotope dataset; the catalogue remains available.

document_title: Seagrass Potential Dataset
notes: This Environment Agency geospatial dataset identifies areas in English transitional and coastal waters that may be environmentally suitable for seagrass restoration. The analysis filters candidate polygons using ecological and physical criteria, removes existing saltmarsh and very small areas, considers conflicts such as ports and dredging, and assigns waterbody and river-basin information. A preferred-sites attribute distinguishes areas with fewer overlapping pressures, while additional areas can reflect expert consultation. The product is a restoration-screening and prioritisation aid, not confirmation that seagrass is currently present or that planting will succeed. Suitability layers must be followed by site surveys, pressure assessment, consent checks, stakeholder engagement and project design. The dataset does not approve restoration, create a statutory site allocation or quantify carbon stocks and sequestration. A mapped candidate area is not an eligible carbon-project boundary and does not demonstrate additionality, permanence, leakage, net climate benefit or credit entitlement.
source: Environment Agency / National Data Library
status_note: Dataset created and revised in July 2024 and maintained as an active government geospatial resource, with service files refreshed in April 2026.

document_title: National Seagrass Layer (England) — 2025 Revision
notes: The National Seagrass Layer collates current and historical polygon records for Ruppia and Zostera habitats in English waters from Natural England, the Environment Agency, Defra bodies and licensed third-party surveys. The 2025 revision provides an agreed current-extent layer based on the best available evidence, plus all-years data, confidence information and survey metadata. It supports marine protected-area assessment, Water Framework evidence, restoration planning and the mapping of a habitat recognised for biodiversity and carbon storage. The publication contains important caveats: seagrass is shown only where surveys exist; absence may mean no survey; point records are excluded; survey methods and accuracy differ; and some historical polygons indicate presence rather than reliable extent. It is therefore an evidence layer, not a complete national carbon inventory or a legal designation. It does not estimate verified carbon stocks or removals, approve restoration, define crediting baselines, demonstrate additionality or permanence, or issue credits.
source: Natural England / Environment Agency / National Data Library
status_note: Originally published in 2022 and formally revised in August–October 2025; the dataset is maintained on an annual basis.

document_title: St Austell Bay Acoustic Survey of the Seagrass Bed for the Cornwall Blue Carbon Mapping Project
notes: This survey dataset records the acoustic mapping undertaken by Cornwall Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority on behalf of Cornwall Wildlife Trust to delineate the seagrass bed in St Austell Bay. The work formed part of a Cornwall blue-carbon mapping initiative and provides site-scale spatial evidence that can support habitat extent assessment, conservation management, restoration planning and the design of later carbon-stock sampling. Acoustic mapping improves coverage compared with isolated observations, but the resulting habitat polygon is not a direct measurement of sediment carbon, annual sequestration or avoided emissions. Survey resolution, classification and ground-truthing affect the mapped extent, and the dataset represents conditions during the survey period rather than a guarantee of current condition. It does not establish an official carbon account, select or authorize a restoration intervention, determine additionality, permanence or leakage, register a crediting project, assign carbon ownership or issue credits.
source: Cornwall Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority / Cornwall Wildlife Trust / National Data Library
status_note: Survey conducted in 2022 and published as a reusable marine geospatial dataset supporting the Cornwall blue-carbon mapping project.

document_title: Gerrans Bay Acoustic Survey of the Seagrass Bed for the Cornwall Blue Carbon Mapping Project
notes: This Cornwall Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority dataset documents an acoustic survey commissioned for Cornwall Wildlife Trust to map the extent of the seagrass bed in Gerrans Bay as part of the county’s blue-carbon mapping work. The spatial output can be combined with habitat condition, sediment coring and repeated monitoring to improve estimates of where seagrass-associated carbon may be stored and where conservation or restoration could be considered. It is a mapping evidence product rather than a carbon inventory or intervention decision. Acoustic classification and ground validation determine accuracy, the survey represents a particular time, and mapped vegetation extent alone does not quantify soil-carbon depth, annual sequestration, displaced emissions or project additionality. The dataset does not create a protected-area rule, approve seagrass planting or mooring changes, define an eligible crediting boundary, prove permanence or leakage control, allocate carbon rights, verify removals or issue credits.
source: Cornwall Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority / Cornwall Wildlife Trust / National Data Library
status_note: Survey conducted in 2022 and published as a reusable marine geospatial dataset supporting the Cornwall blue-carbon mapping project.

subnational_area: Indo-Pacific development programme, including Fiji and Papua New Guinea
document_title: Nature-Based Solutions Evaluation — Evaluation Report
notes: This independent evaluation assesses three Australian international-development investments selected to test the effectiveness of nature-based solutions against climate, nature and development objectives: Climate Resilient by Nature, the Pacific Blue Carbon Program, and ReefCloud. The blue-carbon component is directly relevant to coastal carbon policy because it supports capacity to protect and restore mangroves, tidal wetlands and related ecosystems in Fiji and Papua New Guinea. The evaluation synthesises programme performance, implementation lessons and strategic principles and produces eighteen recommendations for future DFAT programming. It is an evidence and accountability document rather than a new funding decision, restoration permit or carbon-market rule. Inclusion of the Pacific Blue Carbon Program does not demonstrate that every supported site produced additional, permanent or independently verified atmospheric removals. The report does not establish a project baseline, leakage rule, durability obligation, registry, crediting methodology or transferable emission factor, and its recommendations require subsequent management and programme decisions before they become operational measures.
source: Australian Government — Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
status_note: Final independent evaluation published in March 2024 and retained as an active evidence source for DFAT programming.

document_title: Nature-Based Solutions Evaluation — Management Response
notes: DFAT's management response formally addresses the eighteen recommendations made by the independent Nature-Based Solutions Evaluation, which examined Climate Resilient by Nature, the Pacific Blue Carbon Program and ReefCloud. Its policy relevance lies in translating evaluation findings into departmental positions and intended management actions for future nature-based-solutions programming, including the design, governance, evidence base and partnership arrangements surrounding coastal blue-carbon capacity building in the Pacific. The response is recorded separately from the evaluation because it represents the responsible authority's disposition of the recommendations rather than the evaluators' findings. It does not itself create a new blue-carbon fund, approve a restoration site, establish a legal entitlement to undertake coastal works or adopt a carbon-credit methodology. Commitments in a management response remain subject to programme design, budgets, partner agreements and later implementation. The document does not quantify removals, certify additionality or permanence, allocate carbon rights, establish MRV requirements for a market, or issue credits.
source: Australian Government — Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
status_note: Published with the 2024 evaluation and used as DFAT’s formal response to its recommendations.

subnational_area: Tomago Wetlands, Hunter River, New South Wales
document_title: Accounting for Benefits from Coastal Restoration: A Case Study from the Hunter River
notes: This case study applies an early version of Australia's guide for measuring and accounting for the benefits of restoring coastal blue-carbon ecosystems to the previously restored Tomago Wetlands in the Hunter River. It uses existing site information to test project-level application of the United Nations System of Environmental-Economic Accounting Ecosystem Accounting framework and to organise evidence on ecosystem extent, condition and services associated with wetland restoration. The document is valuable as an applied accounting demonstration because it connects carbon storage and sequestration with other benefits such as habitat, water-quality improvement, coastal protection, fisheries, recreation and cultural values. It is not a new restoration approval and does not convert the historical project into a registered carbon-offset activity. Because the case study adapts methods to available retrospective data, its outputs should not be treated as a universal default factor or a complete prospective MRV plan. It does not independently establish additionality, leakage, permanence, ownership of carbon benefits, net climate abatement or eligibility for ACCUs or voluntary credits.
source: Australian Government — Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
status_note: Case study published with Version 1 of the national measurement and accounting guide in 2024.

document_title: Accounting for Benefits from Coastal Restoration: A Case Study from East Trinity Inlet
notes: This case study applies the draft national blue-carbon restoration accounting guide to the remediated East Trinity site near Cairns, where earlier works caused acid-sulfate-soil impacts and restoration subsequently improved wetland condition. The report uses the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting Ecosystem Accounting structure to assess changes in mangroves, saltmarsh and associated forests and to organise evidence on carbon sequestration and emissions, water purification, coastal protection, fish nursery and provisioning services, recreation and Indigenous cultural values. A cultural account was co-developed with the Mandingalbay Yidinji people. The study is an applied test of accounting methods using an existing restoration example, not a permit, crediting standard or new commitment to undertake works. Retrospective data availability required methodological adaptations, so reported tables should not be treated as universal factors or as a complete market-grade project baseline. The document does not independently prove additionality, permanence, leakage control, title to carbon, net atmospheric removal or eligibility for ACCUs or voluntary credits.
source: Australian Government — Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
status_note: Case study published with Version 1 of the national measurement and accounting guide in 2024.

document_title: Blue Heart Project: SEEA-EA Project-Level Blue Carbon Restoration Benefits — Case Study Summary Report
notes: This project-level ecosystem-accounting report evaluates benefits associated with reintroducing tidal flows at the 38.6-hectare Blue Carbon Pilot Project site within Queensland's Blue Heart area and places the findings in context using the restoring Yandina Creek Wetlands and the Coolum Creek Environment Reserve. It compiles SEEA Ecosystem Accounts covering ecosystem extent and condition, pressures, biodiversity, biomass and soil carbon stocks, atmospheric greenhouse-gas emissions and ecosystem-service supply. Monitoring before and after tidal reconnection documents early recovery signals while also identifying methane and nitrous-oxide risks under waterlogged, nutrient-rich conditions. The report demonstrates how carbon retention, sediment retention, water purification, nursery habitat and recreation can be expressed in biophysical and selected monetary terms. It is an official case-study output, not a national accounting rule or an approved offset methodology. The short post-restoration observation period and continuing ecological transition mean that early changes cannot be assumed to represent long-term additional and permanent removals. The report does not register a project, allocate carbon title or issue credits.
source: Australian Government — Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water / Griffith University
status_note: Final case-study report completed with monitoring through 2025 and released through DCCEEW in 2026.

document_title: Mungalla Station Blue Carbon Ecosystem Accounting — SEEA-EA Case Study
notes: This case study applies the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting Ecosystem Accounting framework to the Mungalla Station blue-carbon restoration context on Nywaigi Country. It examines current and expected flows of ecosystem services, benefits and disservices associated with restoring tidal wetland functions on former cattle-grazing land, with particular emphasis on cultural wellbeing, Traditional Owner priorities, biodiversity and climate regulation. Treating the report as a separate record from the original restoration grant preserves the distinction between undertaking restoration and subsequently producing an ecosystem account of its outcomes. The account can support transparent discussion of who receives benefits and how cultural and ecological values are represented, but it is not itself a carbon-credit methodology, legal determination of rights or consent, or project approval. The report does not automatically convert estimated carbon storage or climate-regulation services into saleable units. It does not independently demonstrate additionality, permanence, leakage management, net atmospheric removal, registry eligibility or credit issuance, and its cultural findings should be interpreted within the Nywaigi-led governance context.
source: Australian Government — Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water / Greening Australia / Nywaigi Traditional Owners
status_note: Final project-level ecosystem-accounting case study completed in 2025 and released through DCCEEW in 2026.

subnational_area: Richmond Park, Pitt Water–Orielton Lagoon, Tasmania
document_title: Accounting for Benefits from Coastal Saltmarsh Restoration: A Case Study from Richmond Park, Tasmania
notes: This official case study assesses the outcomes of temperate saltmarsh restoration at Richmond Park in Tasmania under the project Demonstrating Outcomes of Blue Carbon Ecosystem Restoration of Temperate Saltmarsh. It uses project-level ecosystem accounting to organise evidence on climate regulation, habitat and nursery functions, biodiversity, recreation and community benefits. The document is particularly useful for extending Australian blue-carbon accounting beyond tropical mangrove examples and for showing how a cool-climate tidal-marsh project can connect field observations with SEEA-style ecosystem extent, condition and service accounts. It is a reporting and learning product rather than a new restoration grant, statutory approval or carbon-credit standard. Accounted carbon stocks, retention or service values are not automatically equivalent to additional net removals and should not be transferred to other marshes without considering hydrology, sediment supply, vegetation, methane and nitrous-oxide fluxes and monitoring duration. The case study does not determine carbon ownership, prove permanence or leakage control, register an offset project or issue credits.
source: Australian Government — Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water / Blue Conservation Services
status_note: Version 1 dated 5 June 2025 and subsequently released as an official DCCEEW case study.

subnational_area: Upper Gulf St Vincent, South Australia
document_title: South Australian Blue Carbon Ecosystem Restoration Project — SEEA-EA Case Study
notes: This case-study report develops project-level ecosystem accounts for the South Australian Blue Carbon Ecosystem Restoration Project in the Upper Gulf St Vincent. The underlying restoration reconnects tidal processes to former coastal land, while the accounting work examines climate regulation, nursery and habitat functions, biodiversity, water purification and recreational benefits such as fishing, birdwatching and crabbing. The record is kept separate from the restoration grant because the document is a distinct formal assessment output that tests how SEEA Ecosystem Accounting can measure and attribute multiple restoration benefits. It can inform public investment and adaptive management, but it does not establish a nationally approved blue-carbon methodology or automatically convert ecosystem-service values into tradable credits. Site observations and account estimates remain dependent on boundaries, baselines, monitoring duration, hydrological response and treatment of non-CO2 gases. The report does not independently establish additionality, permanence, leakage, carbon title, registration or verified credit issuance, and it does not replace any environmental or cultural approvals required for works.
source: Australian Government — Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water / Flinders University
status_note: Final project-level ecosystem-accounting case study completed in 2025 and released through DCCEEW in 2026.

subnational_area: Australian coastline and Indigenous Sea Country
document_title: Blue Carbon in Australia: Understanding the Opportunity for Indigenous People
notes: This technical report examines where Australian blue-carbon and emerging nature-repair markets may create realistic opportunities for Indigenous people and where legal, methodological and commercial barriers remain. It distinguishes the presence of healthy mangroves, saltmarshes and seagrass from the narrower conditions required for a crediting project, including degradation or threat, an eligible activity, recognised rights, consent and a suitable method. The report reviews the existing ACCU Scheme tidal-restoration method, voluntary standards and developing biodiversity markets and maps Indigenous legal or consent rights along much of the coastline. It stresses that management responsibilities do not always equal rights recognised by a market and that strong rights often have limited overlap with the currently applicable blue-carbon method. The report supports Indigenous-led decision making, free prior and informed consent, capacity building and policy reform, but it does not grant project rights, provide legal advice for an individual claim or approve a methodology. Opportunity mapping does not prove financial viability, additionality, permanence or credit eligibility, and no quantified removal or credit issuance is certified by the report.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub / Indigenous Carbon Industry Network
status_note: Technical report published in 2024 as an output of NESP Project 3.20.

document_title: Reef Catchments Blue Carbon Case Study — Lessons Learned Report
notes: This lessons-learned report documents practical experience from the Reef Catchments blue-carbon case study under the Restore Blue initiative. It consolidates implementation observations relevant to assessing and planning coastal-wetland restoration, including the need to align ecological feasibility, landholder and stakeholder engagement, hydrological conditions, site information, monitoring expectations and the wider package of climate and non-carbon co-benefits. Recording the report separately from the underlying project avoids treating a learning product as a second restoration activity. Its value is primarily procedural: it helps future programmes understand barriers, sequencing and evidence needs before moving from opportunity identification to design and delivery. The document is not a statutory approval, funding award, ACCU method, voluntary-credit methodology or verification statement. Lessons from one regional case cannot be assumed to establish a national default baseline or carbon factor. The report does not certify additionality, quantify durable net atmospheric removal for sale, resolve carbon ownership, demonstrate leakage control, register a project or issue credits.
source: Great Barrier Reef Foundation / Reef Catchments / Restore Blue
status_note: Lessons-learned report dated March 2024; the documented case-study phase is complete.

document_title: Vegetation Composition Data from UK Saltmarshes, 2018–2021
notes: This C-SIDE dataset records percentage species cover, plant height, species richness and diversity from vegetation quadrats surveyed at 460 locations across 33 UK saltmarshes between 2018 and 2021. Sites represent contrasting sediment, vegetation and relative sea-level settings, allowing researchers to examine how plant-community composition relates to soil organic-carbon storage and to improve stratification for national or regional blue-carbon assessment. The data add an ecological-condition layer to soil measurements and can support repeat surveys, habitat mapping, restoration baselines and modelling of carbon variability. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in July 2022 as a completed C-SIDE dataset; the government catalogue record remains active.

document_title: Labile, Recalcitrant and Refractory Organic Matter in UK Saltmarsh Soils, 2018–2021
notes: This C-SIDE dataset quantifies labile, recalcitrant and refractory organic-matter pools in 1,211 down-core samples collected from UK saltmarshes between 2018 and 2021 and includes a carbon reactivity index. Separating organic matter by relative reactivity improves understanding of the likely stability and vulnerability of stored carbon compared with relying only on total organic-carbon concentration. The information can support durability research, process-based models, comparison of marsh types and the design of monitoring that distinguishes recently accumulated material from more resistant pools. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in July 2023 as a completed C-SIDE dataset; catalogue files remain available.

document_title: Radioisotope Concentrations in UK Saltmarsh Soil Samples, 2018–2021
notes: This C-SIDE dataset reports lead-210, lead-214, caesium-137 and americium-241 concentrations for 1,358 down-core soil samples from 19 UK saltmarshes. These radioisotopes support age-depth modelling, sediment accumulation analysis and estimation of carbon burial rates, which are essential for distinguishing a standing carbon stock from the rate at which new carbon is stored. The dataset can improve historical reconstruction and enable comparison of accretion and burial processes among marshes, while also making the underlying dating evidence reusable and auditable. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in July 2023 as a completed radioisotope dataset; the catalogue record remains accessible.

document_title: Dry Bulk Density, Loss on Ignition and Organic Carbon in English and Welsh Saltmarsh Surface Soils, 2019
notes: This CarbonQuest and C-SIDE dataset provides dry bulk density, soil texture, loss-on-ignition organic matter and elemental organic-carbon measurements for 212 surface-soil samples from 49 saltmarsh sites in England and Wales. Sampling to a depth of ten centimetres across contrasting habitat settings supports spatial estimation of surficial carbon density and helps test relationships among vegetation, sediment and carbon content. The citizen-science contribution also offers evidence on how broader sampling networks can supplement specialist field campaigns when quality controls are explicit. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in January 2022 as a completed England and Wales saltmarsh dataset; the catalogue remains active.

document_title: Sedimentological and Organic Carbon Data from the Kyle of Tongue Saltmarsh, Scotland, 2018
notes: This dataset contains physical and biogeochemical measurements from four hammer cores and 39 depth-interval samples collected at the Kyle of Tongue saltmarsh in northern Scotland.
