It reports dry bulk density, water content, porosity and organic-carbon content and was designed both to characterise an organic-rich loch-head marsh and to test coring approaches. The depth-resolved measurements can support evaluation of soil-carbon stocks, methodological comparability and the representation of northern marsh types that may be under-sampled in broader inventories. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in March 2021 as a completed site dataset; the government catalogue remains available.

document_title: Aboveground Biomass and Carbon Measurements from Ten UK Saltmarshes, 2019–2020
notes: This dataset reports aboveground vegetation biomass, organic-carbon concentration and calculated aboveground carbon for 144 samples from ten UK saltmarshes surveyed in 2019 and 2020. The sites were selected to represent contrasting sediment, vegetation and sea-level histories. The measurements complement soil and belowground datasets by quantifying the living aboveground carbon pool, supporting fuller ecosystem-stock assessments, vegetation-based stratification and evaluation of how plant-community change may affect carbon storage during conservation or restoration. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in May 2022 as a completed biomass dataset; the catalogue record remains active.

document_title: Physical and Geochemical Properties of Saltmarsh Soils from Wide-Diameter Cores in Essex, 2019
notes: This C-SIDE dataset contains physical and geochemical measurements from 19 wide-diameter gouge cores collected at eight Essex saltmarsh sites representing natural marsh, historic breaches and managed realignment. The design supports direct comparison of carbon-storage characteristics among marshes with different origins and management histories and helps test how corer diameter and site context affect stock estimates. It is particularly relevant to evaluating whether restored or realigned marshes converge toward natural reference conditions and to improving sampling protocols for project and inventory studies. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in July 2023 as a completed Essex C-SIDE dataset; the catalogue remains available.

document_title: Soil Profile Descriptions from Narrow-Diameter Cores in UK Saltmarshes, 2018–2021
notes: This C-SIDE dataset provides systematic soil-profile descriptions for narrow-diameter cores collected across UK saltmarshes between 2018 and 2021. Profile observations preserve contextual information on horizons, sediment characteristics and visible changes with depth that is not captured by a single carbon-concentration value. The descriptions can be linked with bulk-density, elemental-carbon, radioisotope and geospatial datasets to improve interpretation of stock calculations, identify depositional discontinuities and support transparent quality control when comparing natural and restored marshes. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in July 2023 as a completed C-SIDE profile-description dataset; the catalogue remains active.

document_title: Particle Size and Organic Carbon in Marine Sediments within the Trevose Box, April 2023
notes: This DEFRA-funded Fisheries Industry Science Partnership dataset reports particle-size distributions and organic-carbon content for marine sediment samples collected in the Trevose Box off southwest England in April 2023. Sampling was designed to investigate seabed sediment and carbon conditions in relation to mobile fishing activity, including scallop dredging and beam trawling. The data provide an evidence base for understanding how sediment type structures organic-carbon storage and for assessing disturbance-sensitive seabed carbon, a component that is often excluded from vegetated coastal blue-carbon inventories. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in 2024 as a completed marine-sediment dataset; the catalogue record remains active.

document_title: Saltmarsh Surface Elevation Change Data, United Kingdom, 2023–2024
notes: This dataset compiles sediment-surface elevation and accretion measurements from UK saltmarshes using internationally standardised rod Sediment Elevation Table and Marker Horizon methods. Instruments were deployed in 2023 in the Dornoch Firth, Solway Firth, Ribble, Wash, North Norfolk and Chichester Harbour and were resurveyed in spring 2024, with marker-horizon cores collected at selected locations. The observations provide a baseline for testing whether marsh surfaces are gaining elevation fast enough to maintain carbon-storing habitat under sea-level rise and for linking physical accretion to future carbon-burial estimates. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in August 2024 as a completed first-period elevation-change dataset; the catalogue remains active.

document_title: CBESS Sedimentation and Erosion Monitoring over Saltmarsh and Mudflat Habitats
notes: This CBESS dataset records surface-elevation change and sedimentation at paired saltmarsh and mudflat habitats across five UK intertidal sites in Morecambe Bay and Essex. Rod Sedimentation-Erosion Tables and associated marker horizons were deployed at different distances from the vegetated margin to quantify elevation dynamics and surface accretion. These measurements support analysis of habitat stability, sediment retention and the physical processes that underpin long-term carbon burial, and they provide a historical comparator for later national saltmarsh monitoring and restoration studies. The dataset is a reusable scientific evidence product rather than a binding inventory rule, a restoration approval or a carbon-credit methodology. Measurements and derived values must be interpreted with their sampling design, analytical methods, spatial coverage and uncertainty; they cannot automatically be transferred to every saltmarsh or marine sediment setting. Publication does not establish project additionality, permanence, leakage control or carbon ownership, and it does not register an offset, verify net atmospheric removal or issue credits.
source: UK Environmental Information Data Centre / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published in February 2016 as a completed CBESS monitoring dataset; the catalogue record remains available.

document_title: Enhancing Blue Carbon Considerations in the Marine Strategy Framework Directive
notes: This JPI Oceans policy brief identifies practical entry points for integrating blue carbon ecosystems into implementation of the EU Marine Strategy Framework Directive. It recommends using national marine strategies, monitoring programmes, environmental-status assessments and programmes of measures to better recognize carbon storage and sequestration, seabed disturbance, cumulative pressures and restoration opportunities. The brief supports stronger links with the Nature Restoration Regulation, regional sea conventions and marine protected-area planning. It is non-binding guidance and does not itself establish mandatory monitoring criteria, authorize restoration projects or quantify verified additional carbon removals.
source: JPI Oceans Blue Carbon Knowledge Hub
status_note: Published policy brief / active guidance

document_title: Pathways and Opportunities for Better Policy Integration of Blue Carbon Ecosystems under the EU LULUCF Regulation
notes: This JPI Oceans policy brief proposes pathways for integrating coastal and marine blue carbon ecosystems into EU and Member State implementation of the LULUCF Regulation. Recommendations include harmonized ecosystem definitions and spatial boundaries, stronger national datasets, progressive use of higher-tier greenhouse-gas inventory methods, better emission factors, EU and national blue carbon strategies, and alignment with compliance and certification systems. It also discusses capacity building, stakeholder participation and blended finance for restoration. The document is advisory: it does not amend the LULUCF Regulation, create a carbon-credit methodology, guarantee eligibility for compliance accounting or verify removals from individual projects.
source: JPI Oceans Blue Carbon Knowledge Hub
status_note: Published policy brief / active guidance

document_title: Strengthening Europe’s Ocean CO₂ Monitoring
notes: This JPI Oceans policy brief calls for a more resilient European surface-ocean CO₂ observing system. Its priority actions are to establish a European hub for certified seawater CO₂ reference materials, make fuller use of research and commercial vessels for observations, and introduce recurring audits of observation coverage, quality and data delivery. The proposed measures are intended to strengthen comparability, continuity, carbon-budget assessment and future evaluation of marine carbon dioxide removal. The brief is a call to action rather than an adopted monitoring obligation; it does not create the proposed hub, provide permanent funding or establish a binding MRV protocol for carbon-credit issuance.
source: JPI Oceans Knowledge Hub on Ocean Carbon Capacities
status_note: Published policy brief / proposed monitoring improvements

document_title: Roadmap for Securing the Supply of Reference Materials for the Seawater CO₂ System
notes: This roadmap provides an implementation concept for a European Ocean CO₂ Reference Materials Hub to reduce dependence on a single global supplier and improve continuity and comparability of seawater carbon measurements. It describes possible operating models, production and certification requirements, quality assurance, governance, phased implementation, budget considerations and links with European and international metrology initiatives. Reliable reference materials are presented as infrastructure for ocean-carbon observations and for evaluating marine carbon dioxide removal. The roadmap does not itself establish the hub, certify a particular product, commit governments to funding or create a legally binding technical standard.
source: JPI Oceans Knowledge Hub on Ocean Carbon Capacities
status_note: Published roadmap / proposed European reference-material hub

document_title: State of Europe’s Surface Ocean CO₂ Observations — Audit 2026
notes: This first JPI Oceans audit assesses Europe’s contribution to the surface-ocean CO₂ observation value chain at global, European, regional-sea and national levels. It documents uneven spatial coverage, declining participation by several countries, persistent gaps in the Mediterranean and Black Seas, reduced European observations in the Southern Ocean, and infrastructure vulnerability following closure of the European SOCAT hub. The audit recommends restoring sustained observations, strengthening data stewardship and repeating assessments to track progress. It is an evidence and accountability product, not a binding reporting rule, deployment authorization or project-level verification standard.
source: JPI Oceans Knowledge Hub on Ocean Carbon Capacities
status_note: Published audit / baseline for recurring assessment

document_title: Review of Marine Nature-Based Solutions
notes: This European Topic Centre report reviews 21 marine nature-based solutions across ecosystem protection, restoration, managed systems, artificial ecosystems, nature-inspired designs and geoengineering techniques. It compares implementation scales, maintenance needs, costs, environmental and socioeconomic benefits, trade-offs, stakeholder-engagement approaches and relevance to the Marine Strategy Framework Directive and Nature Restoration Regulation. The assessment includes blue carbon habitat restoration and selected carbon-removal interventions such as ocean fertilization, artificial upwelling and ocean alkalinity enhancement. It is a comparative evidence review and decision-support resource; it neither endorses every technique nor creates permission, funding, carbon credits or quantified removal claims.
source: European Topic Centre on Biodiversity and Ecosystems / European Environment Agency
status_note: Published technical review / decision-support evidence

document_title: The Coastal Carbon Library and Atlas: Open Source Soil Data and Tools Supporting Blue Carbon Research and Policy
notes: This USGS-listed publication establishes the Coastal Carbon Library and Atlas as open, standardized infrastructure for blue carbon evidence. Version 1.0.0 compiles 6,723 soil profiles from marshes, mangroves, tidal freshwater forests and seagrass systems, with tools for querying, mapping and downloading data and for supporting carbon-stock, burial-rate and soil-formation analyses. The publication recommends disaggregated data, documented provenance, standardized vocabularies and reusable templates. It strengthens monitoring and accounting capacity but is not an official carbon-credit methodology, national inventory rule, restoration programme or verification of additional removals from any specific project.
source: U.S. Geological Survey / Global Change Biology
status_note: Published open-data and methods resource

document_title: Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification of Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal: Exploring Scientific Consensus and Divergences Across Continents
notes: This global policy-bridge study synthesizes regional consultations on marine carbon dioxide removal MRV across Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Oceania and South America. It compares views on additionality, durability, environmental impacts, monitoring duration, governance, verification authority, data transparency and the relationship between project-level MRV and long-term global ocean observation. The study identifies areas of convergence while retaining regional differences relevant to legitimate governance of the ocean commons. It does not constitute a universally adopted MRV protocol, regulator-approved accounting methodology, carbon-credit standard or deployment authorization.
source: NOAA Institutional Repository / Elementa: Science of the Anthropocene
status_note: Published global policy-bridge assessment

document_title: Scaling Carbon Dioxide Removal in the Ocean: A US Federal Policy Roadmap
notes: This Carbon180 roadmap proposes a federal policy architecture for responsible expansion of marine carbon dioxide removal in the United States. It organizes recommendations around environmental impacts, efficacy and durability, social license, scaling and deployment, and responsible commercialization, with cross-cutting proposals on legislation, federal research, ocean observing, interagency coordination, permitting review, community engagement and infrastructure co-location. It explicitly covers ocean alkalinity enhancement, direct ocean capture and ocean fertilization. The roadmap is an NGO policy proposal rather than enacted federal policy; recommended bills, appropriations, programmes, permitting reforms and commercialization measures remain contingent on government action.
source: Carbon180
status_note: Published NGO federal-policy roadmap / recommendations not enacted

document_title: Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal Technologies: Hopes and Threats
notes: This Ocean & Climate Platform report synthesizes scientific knowledge on major marine carbon dioxide removal approaches, their proposed mechanisms, maturity, potential scale, costs, monitoring challenges and environmental and social risks. It is designed to inform public debate and policy at the ocean-climate-biodiversity interface and emphasizes that rapid emissions reductions remain the priority. The report finds that evidence remains insufficient for safe large-scale deployment and highlights uncertainty concerning efficacy, durability, additionality, ecological effects and governance. It is a knowledge-dissemination assessment, not a technology approval, carbon-credit methodology, quantified removal guarantee or authorization for field trials.
source: Ocean & Climate Platform
status_note: Published science-policy assessment

document_title: Navigating Hopes and Threats: How Precaution Should Guide Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal Research and Governance
notes: This Ocean & Climate Platform policy brief applies a precautionary approach to marine carbon dioxide removal research and governance. It recommends that any research be scientifically justified, transparent, environmentally protective and socially equitable, while preventing premature deployment and preserving emissions reduction as the primary climate response. The brief calls for stronger international coordination, translation of international commitments into national law, robust environmental assessment, public participation and safeguards for affected communities. It is non-binding advocacy and does not prohibit all research, authorize a field trial, create an enforcement mechanism or certify any mCDR approach as safe or scalable.
source: Ocean & Climate Platform
status_note: Published precautionary policy brief

document_title: Manx Blue Carbon Research Project Report
notes: This report presents the results of a four-year government-led research programme on carbon storage and ecosystem services in Manx waters. The programme mapped approximately 50,000 hectares of offshore muddy seabed, 196 hectares of seagrass and 7.4 hectares of saltmarsh, and estimated that the assessed habitats store about 500,000 tonnes of carbon, equivalent to roughly 1.8 million tonnes of CO₂. It provides an evidence base for marine management, fisheries decisions and the subsequent Blue Carbon Action Plan. The figures describe existing stocks and research estimates rather than verified additional removals, issued credits or authorization for restoration or carbon-market projects.
source: Isle of Man Department of Environment, Food and Agriculture
status_note: Final report published after four-year research programme

document_title: Blue Carbon Action Plan 2026–2030
notes: This Isle of Man action plan converts findings from the Manx Blue Carbon Research Project into a 2026–2030 programme for protecting carbon stores and strengthening marine ecosystem resilience. It organizes action around regulatory protection, continued monitoring and evidence, adaptive management, integration of blue carbon into climate and marine policy, and capacity building and partnerships. The plan supports informed conservation and restoration while linking blue carbon evidence to wider Net Zero and marine-management decisions. It does not establish a carbon-credit registry, guarantee quantified new removals, replace project-specific environmental assessment or automatically authorize restoration and fisheries-management interventions.
source: Isle of Man Department of Environment, Food and Agriculture
status_note: Active action plan for 2026–2030

document_title: Blue Carbon Projects Must Uphold the Land and Sea Rights of Coastal Peoples
notes: This Nature Climate Change policy brief argues that blue carbon projects must recognize the land and sea rights, authority and agency of Indigenous peoples, coastal communities and small-scale fishers. Its policy recommendations call for guidance co-developed with rightsholders, recognition of the full bundle of tenure rights, free, prior and informed consent or culturally legitimate decision processes, and community leadership and control over benefits. The brief treats these safeguards as legal and ethical duties rather than merely conditions for investment or project approval. It is scholarly policy guidance and does not create a binding global tenure regime, approve specific projects or establish a carbon-credit standard.
source: Nature Climate Change
status_note: Published scholarly policy brief

document_title: Explanation of Intended Effect: Improving Coastal Management and Supporting Blue Carbon and Ecosystem Restoration Projects
notes: The May 2026 explanation of intended effect proposes amendments to the New South Wales planning system to create clearer and more proportionate approval pathways for blue-carbon and broader ecosystem-restoration projects. It specifically addresses projects that restore tidal flows to previously drained land so that mangrove, saltmarsh and other tidal ecosystems can re-establish, while retaining environmental assessment, coastal-wetland protection and safeguards for potentially higher-impact proposals. The package also proposes clearer treatment of wetland migration pathways, minor mapping errors, routine vegetation management and coastal protection works. The document is a consultation-stage policy proposal rather than a final statutory amendment. It does not itself approve any restoration project, quantify additional carbon removals, establish a carbon-credit methodology, guarantee project eligibility under the Australian Carbon Credit Unit scheme, or replace project-specific development, biodiversity, water, cultural-heritage or environmental approvals.
source: New South Wales Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure
status_note: Consultation completed; proposed planning amendments remain under government consideration and are not yet final law.

document_title: Recommendations for Responsible Assessment of Engineered Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal Approaches
notes: This May 2026 civil-society consensus statement sets out precautionary recommendations for research, field experimentation, oversight and decision-making concerning engineered marine carbon dioxide removal. It calls for early and compensated participation by Indigenous Peoples, coastal communities and other knowledge holders; stage-gated experimentation; transparent environmental and social risk assessment; independent monitoring, reporting and verification; full life-cycle accounting of implementation emissions; durability assessment; open-access data; conflict-of-interest controls; and clear separation between research evidence and commercial claims. It also emphasizes that marine CDR must not substitute for rapid emissions reductions or divert climate finance from proven mitigation and adaptation measures. The statement is non-binding guidance and does not endorse any technology, authorize field trials, establish an internationally accepted MRV protocol, validate carbon credits, or demonstrate that any engineered approach currently achieves safe, durable and net-negative removal at climate-relevant scale.
source: Ocean Conservancy and participating environmental non-governmental organizations
status_note: Published as active non-binding civil-society guidance for responsible assessment of engineered marine CDR.

document_title: Means of Implementation for Ocean-based Climate Action
notes: This presentation prepared for the 2026 UNFCCC Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue explains how Global Environment Facility financing windows and enabling activities can support ocean-based climate action. It identifies conservation and restoration of high-impact blue-carbon ecosystems, blue-carbon accounting and transparency, coastal and wetland restoration, integrated coastal planning, monitoring frameworks, community livelihoods, Article 6 readiness, carbon-pricing frameworks, robust methodologies, verification, blue bonds, blended finance, guarantees and capacity development as interconnected means of implementation. The document is useful as an official UNFCCC-hosted overview of financing and policy pathways rather than a standalone funding decision. It does not award a grant, create a new carbon market, approve a project, establish a binding accounting methodology, certify a blue-carbon credit, or provide verified estimates of additional carbon removal. Access to finance remains dependent on the rules, priorities, safeguards and approval procedures of the relevant GEF programme and implementing entities.
source: Global Environment Facility presentation hosted by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
status_note: Presented during the 2026 Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue as an active policy and financing reference.

document_title: Our Coasts, Resiliency, and Carbon Dioxide Removal: A Practitioner-Informed Roadmap for Enhancing Coastal Resilience and CDR Potential Along the U.S. Coastline
notes: This practitioner-informed roadmap examines opportunities to integrate carbon dioxide removal into established U.S. coastal-resilience activities, including living shorelines, ecosystem restoration and stormwater-management infrastructure. It highlights the possibility of combining alkaline materials or other abiotic marine CDR components with projects already using sediment, rock, shell, drainage systems and long-term shoreline stewardship, while also recognizing natural carbon storage in tidal marshes and other vegetated habitats. The roadmap identifies enabling policy, permitting, procurement, monitoring and community-engagement conditions and stresses the need for robust life-cycle accounting and measurement before any carbon benefit is claimed. It is an exploratory implementation roadmap rather than federal or state regulatory guidance. It does not approve material placement, prescribe engineering specifications for a particular site, establish environmental safety thresholds, create a crediting methodology, verify net carbon removal, or conclude that adding alkalinity-enhancing materials will be appropriate in every coastal setting.
source: Carbon Removal Standards Initiative
status_note: Published as a current practitioner roadmap; implementation remains subject to site-specific research, permitting and monitoring.

document_title: Marine and Coastal Restoration Plan
notes: The Scottish Government's first dedicated Marine and Coastal Restoration Plan sets out a five-year framework for accelerating active restoration of marine and coastal habitats and species. It is organized around restoration opportunities and priorities, the regulatory environment, funding and finance, supply-chain and community enabling conditions, and evidence and monitoring. The plan explicitly recognizes that restored habitats such as seagrass meadows and saltmarsh can absorb and store carbon and contribute to climate mitigation and adaptation, while also providing biodiversity, fisheries, shoreline-resilience and community benefits. It supports better spatial prioritization, community-led activity, investment and improved coordination rather than prescribing a national restoration quota. The plan does not designate specific project sites, grant marine licences, create a blue-carbon crediting methodology, guarantee finance, or quantify additional and durable carbon removal. Individual projects remain subject to relevant environmental assessment, marine licensing, land rights, monitoring and other statutory requirements.
source: Scottish Government Marine Directorate
status_note: Published on 12 December 2025 and active as Scotland's first five-year marine and coastal restoration plan.

document_title: Marine and Coastal Restoration Plan: Strategic Environmental Assessment Post-Adoption Statement
notes: The post-adoption statement completes the Strategic Environmental Assessment process for Scotland's Marine and Coastal Restoration Plan. It explains how environmental considerations, the earlier environmental report, consultation responses, reasonable alternatives and monitoring requirements were taken into account when the final plan was adopted. The statement provides an auditable link between the draft assessment and the final policy across themes including restoration priorities, regulation, finance, communities, evidence and monitoring. Carbon-related relevance arises because the plan supports restoration of habitats capable of absorbing and storing carbon and the assessment considers climatic factors alongside biodiversity, water, soils, cultural heritage, landscape, population and material assets. This is an assessment and accountability document rather than a project authorization. It does not approve a restoration site, validate a carbon baseline, quantify net removals, establish a crediting method or remove the need for project-level environmental assessment and monitoring.
source: Scottish Government Marine Directorate
status_note: The statutory post-adoption assessment statement was published on 23 March 2026, completing this stage of the SEA process.

document_title: Draft Marine and Coastal Restoration Plan: Strategic Environmental Assessment Environmental Report
notes: The July 2025 environmental report provides the high-level Strategic Environmental Assessment of Scotland's draft Marine and Coastal Restoration Plan. It examines potential positive, negative and cumulative effects across biodiversity, soil, water, climatic factors, cultural heritage, landscape and seascape, population and human health, and material assets. The assessment recognizes potential climate benefits from restoring carbon-absorbing and carbon-storing habitats, but also records uncertainty, implementation-dependent outcomes, risks such as invasive non-native species and activity displacement, and the need to use existing indicators and monitoring programmes where proportionate. It was produced to support consultation and policy development, not to demonstrate verified carbon removal. The report does not authorize projects, identify guaranteed restoration sites, establish carbon-credit eligibility, determine additionality or permanence, or replace subsequent project-level environmental assessment. It has been superseded procedurally by the final plan and the 2026 post-adoption statement, but remains an independent evidence record.
source: Scottish Government Marine Directorate
status_note: Published for consultation on 29 July 2025; the assessment stage is complete and has been followed by the final plan and post-adoption statement.

document_title: Draft Marine and Coastal Restoration Plan: Consultation
notes: The consultation paper presented Scotland's proposed first Marine and Coastal Restoration Plan and sought views on actions under five themes: restoration opportunities and priorities, the regulatory environment, funding and finance, supply chains and communities, and evidence and monitoring. It explicitly included seagrass and saltmarsh restoration among possible active-restoration activities and recognized that habitats which absorb and store carbon can contribute to climate mitigation and adaptation. The consultation also explored protection mechanisms, monitoring requirements, financing barriers, community leadership and coordination with wider marine policy. It was a draft policy and public-engagement instrument, not the final plan. The consultation closed on 19 October 2025 and the final plan was subsequently published in December 2025. The document did not approve a project, create a restoration obligation, establish a carbon-credit methodology, quantify additional carbon removal or settle the precise design of future regulatory protections.
source: Scottish Government Marine Directorate
status_note: Consultation ran from 29 July to 19 October 2025 and was superseded by the adopted Marine and Coastal Restoration Plan.

subnational_area: UK Continental Shelf and territorial seas
document_title: Announcement of United Kingdom Carbon Dioxide Appraisal and Storage Licensing Round #2 — Version 2
notes: The updated public notice formally invited applications for Carbon Dioxide Appraisal and Storage Licences across fourteen offered areas in Scottish and English offshore waters. It explains the statutory basis of the licensing round, application boundaries, work-programme expectations, environmental and defence considerations, technical evaluation and the relationship between a carbon-storage licence and later approvals. A licence grants exclusive rights to explore and appraise a potential storage area, but actual injection and permanent storage require a separate storage permit, seabed rights and other regulatory consents. Applications closed on 24 March 2026 and are subject to evaluation, consultation and environmental review. The notice therefore opens an authorizing pathway but does not itself award a licence, approve drilling, authorize construction or injection, certify storage capacity, demonstrate containment, or establish verified carbon removals. Version 2 is recorded separately because it is a formally updated 2026 notice.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Version 2 was published on 6 February 2026; applications have closed and licence awards remain under evaluation.

document_title: 2nd Offshore Carbon Dioxide Storage Licensing Round Marine Conservation Zone Assessment
notes: This July 2026 assessment evaluates whether activities that could follow the second offshore carbon dioxide storage licensing round may affect designated Marine Conservation Zones and their protected features or supporting ecological and geomorphological processes. It screens applied-for areas, identifies relevant conservation sites, considers plausible exploration and appraisal activities, and determines where further assessment or mitigation may be needed. The assessment operates at licensing-plan level and is intended to inform regulatory decisions before any area is awarded. It does not provide project-specific engineering designs, approve seismic surveys or wells, grant a carbon-storage licence, authorize injection, or conclude that later development will have no environmental effects. Licensees would still need activity-specific environmental assessment, marine licences, well consents, storage permits and mitigation conditions. The document is therefore a precautionary safeguard and evidence record rather than evidence of achieved or permitted carbon storage.
source: United Kingdom Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
status_note: Published in July 2026 as a completed plan-level Marine Conservation Zone assessment for the licensing round.

document_title: Consent to Drill Carbon Storage Appraisal Well under Carbon Storage Licence CS006
notes: The North Sea Transition Authority granted consent for a carbon-storage appraisal well under licence CS006 in the Southern North Sea. The well is intended to acquire subsurface data for a possible expansion or build-out associated with the Endurance storage system, with drilling and a comprehensive data-acquisition and analysis programme scheduled to take approximately ninety days. The consent has a two-year term and represents a concrete regulatory authorization for appraisal activity. It does not authorize commercial carbon dioxide injection, approve a final storage development, certify storage capacity or containment, or demonstrate any completed carbon removal. Data generated by the well must still support site characterization, risk assessment and any later storage-permit application. Additional environmental, operational, well-integrity, health-and-safety and reporting requirements continue to apply under the relevant licence and consent framework.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Drilling consent was granted on 6 March 2026 for a two-year term; the appraisal programme is an active authorization, not an injection permit.

subnational_area: Endurance storage site, Southern North Sea
document_title: Endurance Carbon Storage Permit
notes: The North Sea Transition Authority awarded the United Kingdom's first offshore carbon-storage permit to the Endurance project in December 2024. The permit allows the operator to progress infrastructure installation and preparations for future injection at a site off Teesside, subject to the permit's operational, monitoring, containment, environmental and financial conditions. The announced permitted injection rate is up to four million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year and the indicative total is up to one hundred million tonnes over approximately twenty-five years. These figures describe authorized capacity and project plans, not verified storage already achieved. The permit followed assessment of leakage risk, storage-site suitability, environmental and human-health protection, technical competence and financial soundness. First injection remained prospective at the time of award, so this record must not be interpreted as evidence that carbon dioxide has already been injected, permanently contained or credited.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Storage permit awarded on 10 December 2024; infrastructure preparation is authorized and injection remains subject to permit conditions and project delivery.

subnational_area: Liverpool Bay and East Irish Sea
document_title: Three Carbon Storage Permits for Liverpool Bay CCS / HyNet
notes: The North Sea Transition Authority awarded three offshore carbon-storage permits to Liverpool Bay CCS Limited for the transportation and storage system serving the HyNet industrial cluster. The permits allow preparation of three stores in the East Irish Sea and are linked to a planned initial injection rate of approximately 4.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year, with an announced design total of about 109 million tonnes over twenty-five years. The project intends to use a combination of new and repurposed infrastructure and remains subject to the technical, environmental, monitoring, leakage-control and financial requirements embedded in the permits and wider regulatory framework. The stated volumes are permitted or planned capacity, not evidence of carbon dioxide already stored. At the time of award, initial injection was still targeted for a future date. The permits do not by themselves validate carbon credits or demonstrate permanent containment of any injected quantity.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Three storage permits were awarded on 24 April 2025; project preparation is authorized and future injection remains conditional on delivery and compliance.

subnational_area: Northern Territory and Commonwealth waters in the Joseph Bonaparte Gulf
document_title: Bonaparte Carbon Capture and Storage Project — EPBC 2026/10480
notes: The federal referral concerns a proposed large-scale carbon dioxide transport and geological-storage system extending from Middle Arm near Darwin to a saline aquifer approximately two kilometres below the seabed in Commonwealth waters of the Joseph Bonaparte Gulf. The concept includes an onshore inlet station, an offshore pipeline of roughly 260 kilometres, subsea power and communications infrastructure, manifolds and up to six injection wells, with phased capacity proposed for a multi-decade operating period. The EPBC portal status indicates that an assessment approach has been determined, meaning the proposal remains within environmental assessment rather than having received final approval. Project documents provide design aspirations and modelled storage potential, not verified capacity or removal. The referral does not authorize construction, injection, imported carbon dioxide, operation, carbon-credit issuance or permanent storage. Separate Northern Territory, Commonwealth offshore, pipeline, greenhouse-gas storage, cultural-heritage and other approvals remain relevant.
source: Australian Government EPBC Act Public Portal
status_note: Federal assessment approach determined; no final EPBC approval or authorization to construct and inject has been issued.

subnational_area: Browse Basin and Commonwealth waters off Western Australia
document_title: Browse Carbon Capture and Storage Project — EPBC 2026/10569
notes: The federal referral covers a proposed offshore carbon capture and storage system associated with the Browse gas development. The concept would separate reservoir carbon dioxide on floating production facilities, transport it through subsea flowlines and inject it into the Calliance Storage Formation in Commonwealth waters, with multiple injection wells and seismic or other monitoring of plume behaviour. Public project material describes expected injection rates and potential reductions in project Scope 1 emissions, but these are forecasts based on design assumptions rather than verified storage outcomes. The EPBC portal lists the project as awaiting a delegate decision. Accordingly, this record represents an environmental referral and proposed engineering pathway, not a final federal approval, storage permit or authorization to inject. It does not establish a carbon-credit methodology, prove additionality or permanence, or confirm that environmental and containment risks have been resolved.
source: Australian Government EPBC Act Public Portal
status_note: Referral lodged in 2026 and awaiting a delegate decision; no final EPBC approval or injection authorization is recorded.

document_title: Ichthys Carbon Capture and Storage Project — EPBC 2025/10366
notes: The federal referral concerns onshore carbon dioxide transport and tie-in infrastructure on the Middle Arm Peninsula. It proposes pipelines connecting the Ichthys LNG facility, a future Bonaparte CCS inlet station and the Darwin LNG boundary, together with tie-in stations, power and communications equipment and associated construction and pre-commissioning activities. The infrastructure is intended to enable future transfer of captured carbon dioxide to separately assessed offshore storage projects. The EPBC portal lists the proposal as awaiting a delegate decision. The referral is therefore not an approval of the onshore works and, importantly, is not an authorization for offshore injection or geological storage. It does not certify the performance of the linked Bonaparte or Bayu-Undan storage systems, establish carbon credits, or verify any removed or avoided quantity. Cumulative impacts and interfaces with the AGRU preparedness and offshore storage proposals require consideration through separate assessment processes.
source: Australian Government EPBC Act Public Portal
status_note: Federal referral remains awaiting a delegate decision; the proposal is enabling transport infrastructure rather than an offshore storage authorization.

document_title: Ichthys LNG Acid Gas Removal Unit Upgrade and CCS Preparedness Project — EPBC 2025/10273 Referral Decision
notes: The federal referral decision covers preparatory works at the existing Ichthys LNG facility, including upgrades to acid-gas removal units, carbon dioxide compression, dehydration, export metering, an in-plant export-pipeline section and associated power and control systems. The Commonwealth decision determined that the referred onshore preparatory action was not a controlled action under the EPBC Act. This decision is legally relevant to the specified scope but must not be treated as a general approval of the wider carbon capture and storage system. Hot commissioning, operational capture and export, connecting pipelines and offshore transport and geological storage are outside the referred action or subject to separate referrals and approvals. The decision does not authorize offshore injection, validate the containment performance of a storage formation, quantify net removal, or establish eligibility for carbon credits. Northern Territory environmental assessment and other statutory approvals continue independently.
source: Australian Government EPBC Act Public Portal
status_note: Referral decision made in 2025 for the limited onshore preparedness scope; connected operation and offshore storage remain separately regulated.

document_title: Approved Notice of Decision — Ichthys LNG AGRU Upgrades and CCS Preparedness Project
notes: The Northern Territory Environment Protection Authority's July 2026 notice approves the final terms of reference for an environmental impact statement for the Ichthys LNG acid-gas-removal upgrade and CCS-preparedness proposal. The decision follows public and government consultation and requires the environmental assessment to address cumulative interactions with the associated Ichthys and Bonaparte CCS proposals, planned and unplanned carbon dioxide releases, pipeline-rupture risks, human health, atmospheric processes, air quality, marine ecosystems and the relationship with continued LNG operations. This is a procedural environmental-assessment decision, not approval to construct, commission or operate the capture and export system. It does not authorize carbon dioxide transport or offshore injection, establish acceptable leakage levels, verify carbon removal, or approve the linked storage projects. A full environmental impact statement and subsequent statutory decisions are still required before the proposal may proceed beyond the assessed stages.
source: Northern Territory Environment Protection Authority
status_note: Final terms of reference approved on 3 July 2026; environmental impact assessment is continuing and no project approval has been issued.

document_title: Climate Technology Progress Report 2026 — Beyond the Blue Horizon: Scoping and Work Programme
notes: This April 2026 presentation sets out the scope and production work programme for the planned Climate Technology Progress Report 2026, provisionally titled Beyond the Blue Horizon. The proposed report will examine technologies for protecting and enhancing natural ocean carbon systems, strengthening ocean-carbon monitoring, intelligence and data infrastructure, and advancing emerging marine carbon dioxide removal approaches, with a dedicated regional focus on small island developing States. The work is intended to provide a scientifically credible and policy-relevant assessment for technology development and transfer under the UNFCCC Technology Mechanism. This document is a scoping presentation rather than the completed report. It contains the planned chapter structure, review milestones and launch timetable but does not provide final findings, rank technologies, authorize deployment, establish MRV or crediting rules, or conclude that any marine CDR approach is environmentally safe, durable, equitable or ready for scale.
source: UNFCCC Technology Executive Committee and UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre
status_note: Scoping and work programme presented in April 2026; the final report was scheduled for later in 2026 and was not yet contained in this document.

document_title: UKCS Well Applications and Consents Guide 2026
notes: The 2026 guide explains how operators apply through the Well Operations Notification System for North Sea Transition Authority consent to conduct well activities on the United Kingdom Continental Shelf, including wells under carbon dioxide appraisal and storage licences. It describes application timing, well categories, supporting information, consent conditions, completion reporting, abandonment and preparatory works. The guide makes clear that consent is required before specified activities begin and that consented operations must comply with licence and activity-specific conditions. For carbon storage, the procedural framework supports appraisal, site characterization and later monitoring, but the guidance itself is not a licence or well consent. It does not authorize a particular well, permit carbon dioxide injection, approve a storage development, validate capacity or containment, or replace environmental, health-and-safety and marine approvals. Its principal database function is to document the procedural and reporting standard applied to carbon-storage well operations.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Published as current 2026 procedural guidance; binding obligations arise through legislation, licences and individual consents.

document_title: Guidance on the Application for a Carbon Dioxide Appraisal and Storage Licence — December 2025
notes: The December 2025 guidance describes the process and technical marking scheme for applications for a Carbon Dioxide Appraisal and Storage Licence. It addresses eligible application areas, applicant competence and financial capability, exploration-operator arrangements, work programmes, site and storage-complex understanding, capacity and injectivity estimates, preliminary containment risks, data availability, environmental context, stakeholder and seabed-user considerations and net-zero planning. The document distinguishes a licence from a storage permit: a licence enables exclusive exploration and appraisal rights, whereas injection and permanent storage require a later storage permit and additional approvals. The guidance has no binding legal effect and does not guarantee that an application will be accepted. It does not grant acreage, authorize seismic acquisition or drilling, approve injection, certify a storage resource, demonstrate safe containment, or establish carbon-credit eligibility. It is nevertheless a formal regulatory standard for evaluating licence applications.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Updated guidance published in December 2025 and used for current carbon-storage licence application processes.

document_title: Guidance on Retention, Reporting and Disclosure of Carbon Storage Information and Samples
notes: This May 2026 guidance operationalizes the United Kingdom framework for retaining, reporting and potentially disclosing carbon-storage information and samples. It covers well engineering and geological information, physical samples, survey data, injection and production information, storage-resource estimates, computerized models, geotechnical material submitted with permit applications, storage-formation and site information, installations and monitoring information. It explains reporting routes, formats, timelines, minimum retention periods and protected periods under the Energy Act 2023 and the 2025 retention and disclosure regulations. The guidance supports regulatory oversight, long-term stewardship, transparency and reuse of subsurface evidence. It is not itself a storage licence, permit, monitoring approval or disclosure decision, and it does not verify a project's capacity, leakage performance or stored quantity. Although the guidance is non-binding, many underlying retention and reporting duties are legally binding through legislation and regulatory notices.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Published in May 2026 as active guidance supporting binding statutory retention, reporting and disclosure duties.

document_title: Guidance on Information and Samples Plans and Coordinators for Carbon Storage
notes: This May 2026 guidance explains the Energy Act 2023 requirements for information and samples plans and information and samples coordinators in connection with carbon dioxide appraisal and storage licences. It describes the licence events that trigger a plan, the allocation of responsibility, the retention, reporting, storage or transfer of information and samples, the process for agreeing and revising plans, and the coordinator's role in monitoring compliance and acting as the primary regulatory contact. The framework is designed to prevent loss of valuable well, survey, model, monitoring and storage-site evidence when licences are transferred, expire, are surrendered or otherwise change. The document provides regulatory expectations but is not a project approval, licence or storage permit. It does not authorize injection, determine disclosure of a specific dataset, certify MRV results, or validate carbon storage. Binding duties arise from the Energy Act and associated regulations rather than from the guidance alone.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Published in May 2026 as active implementation guidance for statutory information and samples planning duties.

document_title: Guidance for Carbon Storage Metering and Measurement Plans
notes: The July 2026 guidance sets out North Sea Transition Authority expectations for metering and measurement plans that may be required by an offshore carbon-storage permit before injection begins. It covers systems used to quantify carbon dioxide transported offshore and injected into individual wells, measurement methods, composition and phase behaviour, uncertainty, calibration and re-verification, continuous performance diagnostics, reconciliation of different meters, treatment of discrepancies and mismeasurement, data governance and emissions-related metering. The plan is intended to support regulatory stewardship and credible operational accounting throughout project development and operation. The guidance is deliberately non-prescriptive and has no binding legal effect by itself; the applicable storage permit determines whether a plan is required and what must be approved. The document does not certify any operator's meters, approve injection, establish a carbon-credit methodology, or verify a stored quantity.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Published in July 2026 as active operational guidance; project-specific obligations depend on storage-permit conditions.

document_title: Guidance for Carbon Storage Commissioning Plans
notes: The July 2026 guidance describes the expected content of a commissioning plan that may be required under an offshore carbon-storage permit before carbon dioxide injection starts. It addresses management and governance arrangements, contractor control, readiness and handover criteria, management of change, well commissioning, verification of well integrity and barriers, establishment of baseline conditions, injectivity testing, surface and subsea facilities, transport-network interfaces, carbon dioxide sources and composition, monitoring, emergency arrangements and consistency with the storage-site management and metering plans. The guidance is intended to reduce operational and containment risks during transition from construction to injection. It is non-binding and does not itself approve a commissioning programme, storage facility, well or injection start. Operators must still obtain all regulatory approvals and satisfy project-specific permit conditions. The document provides expectations for safe preparation, not evidence that commissioning, injection or permanent storage has occurred.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Published in July 2026 as active operational guidance; commissioning remains subject to project-specific storage permits and approvals.

document_title: Guidance on the Content of an Offshore Carbon Storage Site Management Plan
notes: The July 2026 guidance sets out expectations for an offshore storage-site management plan during the operational phase of a carbon dioxide appraisal and storage licence. It covers the integrated management of surface and injection facilities, wells and the storage unit; expected plume and pressure behaviour; key uncertainties and assumptions; operating envelopes; injection strategy; well integrity; monitoring and surveillance; significant irregularities and leakage prevention; risk registers; corrective action interfaces; data review; management of change; periodic updating and regulatory stewardship. The plan is intended to connect subsurface characterization, containment-risk assessment, facility design and operational decision-making. The guidance has no binding legal effect by itself and is not a substitute for legislation or permit conditions. It does not approve any site, determine that leakage risk is acceptable, authorize injection, verify permanence, or certify a stored quantity. A storage permit may require a project-specific plan acceptable to the regulator.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Published in July 2026 as active operational guidance; a binding project-specific plan may be required through a storage permit.

document_title: Carbon Storage Stewardship Expectations
notes: The North Sea Transition Authority's Carbon Storage Stewardship Expectations establish a structured best-practice framework for licence holders across five areas: containment-risk assessment, appraisal and subsurface characterization, data acquisition and use for appraisal and monitoring, technology development and deployment, and stakeholder engagement. Each expectation explains the regulatory purpose and provides a roadmap for demonstrating responsible performance across the licence lifecycle. The framework is designed to improve evidence quality, timely appraisal, containment assurance, technology planning, transparency and coordination with affected seabed users and communities. It does not replace legislation, licence clauses, environmental assessment, storage-permit requirements or individual regulatory decisions. Publication of the expectations does not approve a storage site, authorize drilling or injection, guarantee project progression, certify monitoring results or establish a carbon-credit standard. Compliance consequences depend on the underlying licence and statutory powers, while the expectations themselves primarily communicate regulator practice and good performance.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Published on 30 September 2025 as active stewardship guidance for carbon-storage licence holders.

document_title: The Oil and Gas Authority (Carbon Storage) (Retention of Information and Samples) Regulations 2025
notes: These regulations establish binding duties for relevant persons to retain specified carbon-storage information and samples generated or acquired under carbon dioxide appraisal and storage licences. Covered material includes well and wellbore information, geological and engineering samples, geophysical and other survey information, injection and production information, storage-resource estimates, computerized models, storage-formation and site information, installation information and monitoring evidence. The rules support regulatory continuity, future disclosure, independent scrutiny and safe long-term stewardship by preventing the loss or premature disposal of technically important records. They came into force in May 2025 and are implemented alongside Energy Act 2023 reporting powers and North Sea Transition Authority guidance. The regulations govern information custody rather than project authorization: they do not grant a licence or storage permit, approve injection, determine that a site is safe, verify stored carbon dioxide, or establish carbon-credit accounting.
source: United Kingdom Parliament / Secretary of State
status_note: Made in April 2025 and in force from 13 May 2025.

document_title: The Oil and Gas Authority (Carbon Storage and Offshore Petroleum) (Specified Periods for Disclosure of Protected Material) Regulations 2025
notes: These regulations specify when protected carbon-storage and offshore-petroleum information and samples may become eligible for disclosure by the North Sea Transition Authority. For carbon storage, the framework assigns immediate or delayed disclosure periods to categories such as surveys, wells, injection and production information, storage resources, computerized models, permit-application material, storage-formation and site information, installations, monitoring evidence and physical samples. The rules balance commercial confidentiality with the public-interest value of timely access to technical evidence and complement the Energy Act 2023 and the 2025 retention regulations. They were made in December 2025 and came into force in January 2026. The regulations do not require every item to be disclosed automatically at the first eligible date, and they do not approve projects, authorize injection, certify storage performance, validate MRV results or create carbon credits. Their function is governance of protected information rather than authorization of negative-emissions engineering.
source: United Kingdom Parliament / Secretary of State
status_note: Made on 19 December 2025 and in force from 9 January 2026.

subnational_area: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
document_title: UK Emissions Trading Scheme: Regulating Cross-Boundary CCS Pipelines
notes: This consultation examines how the United Kingdom Emissions Trading Scheme should regulate carbon dioxide pipelines that cross internal national, territorial-sea and continental-shelf regulatory boundaries before reaching an offshore geological store. It proposes alternatives for assigning a single lead regulator or jointly conferring functions, limiting the number of permits, locating the onshore-to-offshore transfer point, installing metering equipment and reporting transported carbon dioxide, venting, leakage and fugitive emissions. The purpose is to reduce administrative duplication without weakening emissions accounting or enforcement. The consultation closed on 4 June 2026 and the proposals remain policy options rather than final amendments to the UK ETS Order. It does not grant a pipeline permit, approve a route, authorize offshore injection, determine storage-site suitability or verify any carbon dioxide as permanently stored. Any resulting rule change would still operate alongside planning, marine, environmental, safety, economic-licensing and storage-permit requirements.
source: United Kingdom Emissions Trading Scheme Authority and Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
status_note: Consultation issued on 12 March 2026 and closed on 4 June 2026; final regulatory amendments had not been adopted in the source document.

document_title: The Carbon Dioxide Transport and Storage (Financing of Costs of Offshore Decommissioning) Regulations 2026
notes: These binding regulations require security for future decommissioning costs associated with covered offshore carbon dioxide transport and storage infrastructure. They establish independently constituted offshore decommissioning funds, rules for estimating liabilities, funding and investment strategies, monthly contributions, periodic reviews, reporting, governance, authorized withdrawals, transfers and fund closure. The structure is intended to protect decommissioning resources from the insolvency of a transport-and-storage licensee and reduce the risk that taxpayers or later operators inherit unfunded abandonment obligations. The instrument applies across the United Kingdom and came into force on 10 July 2026. It regulates financial security and stewardship rather than technical authorization of carbon storage. It does not award a storage licence or permit, approve a pipeline or installation, authorize injection, determine storage capacity, verify containment or create carbon credits. Operators remain subject to separate licensing, environmental, monitoring, abandonment-programme and health-and-safety requirements.
source: United Kingdom Parliament and Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero
status_note: Made on 11 June 2026 and in force from 10 July 2026 as UK Statutory Instrument 2026 No. 632.

document_title: Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage: Ensuring Fair Access to CO2 Infrastructure
notes: This consultation reviews the Storage of Carbon Dioxide (Access to Infrastructure) Regulations 2011 against the newer economic-licensing and regulated-asset-base framework for carbon dioxide transport and storage. It seeks evidence on transparent and non-discriminatory third-party access, capacity allocation, refusal grounds, dispute resolution, interaction with Ofgem licences, first-of-a-kind networks, future expansion and possible international users. The consultation is directly relevant to offshore geological storage because access rules affect pipelines and storage sites serving United Kingdom carbon capture and storage clusters. It closed on 20 February 2026 after an extension and does not itself amend the 2011 Regulations. It creates no entitlement to use a network, requires no owner to accept a specific connection and grants no storage, pipeline or injection authorization. Any future amendments would require a separate legal process and would continue to operate alongside technical compatibility, available capacity, environmental, safety, storage-permit and commercial requirements.
source: United Kingdom Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
status_note: Published on 28 November 2025, updated in January 2026 and closed on 20 February 2026; government conclusions were not contained in the consultation.

subnational_area: UK Continental Shelf and territorial seas
document_title: 2nd Offshore Carbon Dioxide Storage Licensing Round Habitats Regulations Assessment: Draft Appropriate Assessment
notes: This draft Appropriate Assessment evaluates the potential effects of awarding licences in the United Kingdom's second offshore carbon dioxide storage licensing round on protected habitats and species under the Habitats Regulations. It considers the six applications proceeding through assessment, plausible exploration and appraisal activities, relevant European sites, impact pathways, in-combination effects, mitigation and the conditions needed before licensing decisions. The document complements, but is independent from, the Marine Conservation Zone assessment already prepared for the licensing round. It is a plan-level safeguard and consultation document, not a project environmental impact assessment. Publication of the draft does not award acreage, authorize seismic surveys, approve wells, grant a storage permit or allow carbon dioxide injection. Licensees would still need activity-specific environmental assessments, marine and well consents, storage permits and mitigation measures. The assessment also does not quantify verified storage capacity, net removals or permanence.
source: United Kingdom Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
status_note: Draft Appropriate Assessment published for consultation in July 2026; final assessment and licensing decisions remained pending.

document_title: Report on Progress towards Reaching the Union-wide Target for CO2 Injection Capacity
notes: This European Commission report assesses progress toward the Net-Zero Industry Act target of at least fifty million tonnes of annual carbon dioxide injection capacity in the European Union by 2030. It consolidates Member State reporting, information from obligated oil and gas producers, announced storage projects, allocation of producer contributions, permitting status, cross-border infrastructure needs and risks to timely delivery. Because much anticipated capacity is offshore or beneath European seas, the report is directly relevant to marine geological carbon storage governance. It identifies implementation gaps and coordination needs but is not a storage-capacity certification or investment decision. Project announcements, producer contributions and modelled capacity remain subject to exploration results, permits, infrastructure construction, commercial demand and monitoring requirements. The report does not authorize an individual storage site, guarantee that the target will be met, verify injected quantities, determine permanence or establish carbon-credit eligibility.
source: European Commission
status_note: Commission report COM(2026) 252 final was issued on 28 May 2026 as the first formal progress assessment under the Union-wide injection-capacity framework.

document_title: Interim Information Sheet: Suggested Information in an MPRSA Research Permit Application
notes: This interim information sheet explains the information the United States Environmental Protection Agency generally expects in a complete research-permit application under the Marine Protection, Research, and Sanctuaries Act for projects involving placement of material in ocean waters. It covers applicant qualifications, research questions, sampling design, quality assurance and quality control, material characterization, quantities and placement methods, alternatives, environmental and navigational effects, monitoring, adaptive management, public-interest considerations and supporting technical evidence. The document is highly relevant to field research on ocean alkalinity enhancement, ocean fertilization and other marine carbon dioxide removal approaches that may involve ocean disposition. It is non-binding assistance and does not revise applicable regulations or predetermine the information needed for a particular proposal. It does not grant a research permit, authorize commercial deployment, establish a carbon-credit methodology, endorse a technology or confirm that a proposed experiment will be environmentally acceptable or net carbon-negative.
source: United States Environmental Protection Agency Marine Protection Permitting Program
status_note: Updated in March 2026 and active as interim applicant guidance; permit decisions continue to be made case by case under existing law.

document_title: Agreement between the Kingdom of Belgium and the Kingdom of Norway concerning the Transport of CO2 via Pipelines from Belgium to the Norwegian Continental Shelf
notes: This bilateral agreement creates a state-to-state framework for transporting captured carbon dioxide by pipeline from Belgium to storage sites on the Norwegian continental shelf. It addresses the cross-border legal and regulatory cooperation needed to connect Belgian capture and transport infrastructure with Norwegian offshore geological storage, including competent-authority coordination, applicable permitting and consistency with international and European carbon-storage rules. The agreement supports development of a transnational carbon dioxide network but is not a construction or operating permit for a specific pipeline or storage project. Signature does not by itself approve a route, guarantee capacity, authorize injection or establish that transported carbon dioxide has been permanently stored. Individual infrastructure components remain subject to domestic approvals, technical specifications, environmental assessment, metering, liability, storage-permit and commercial arrangements. The official treaty page records signature on 26 March 2026; entry into force and implementation depend on the procedures and notifications required by the agreement and the two states.
source: Governments of Belgium and Norway
status_note: Signed on 26 March 2026; the official source records signature but does not establish completed project authorization or verified transport and storage.

document_title: Consultation Note: Proposed Amendments to the Regulations on Transport and Storage of CO2 on the Continental Shelf
notes: This consultation note proposes technical and procedural amendments to Norway's regulations for transport and storage of carbon dioxide on the continental shelf. It seeks to modernize provisions developed before the current commercial-storage market, clarify licensing and operator obligations, improve alignment with the European Union CCS Directive, address project transfers and financial arrangements, and simplify selected administrative requirements while retaining safe-storage and environmental controls. The document also situates the amendments within Norway's expanding offshore storage sector and the start of injection by Northern Lights in 2025. The proposals were issued for consultation and are not themselves final regulations. They do not grant an exploration licence, approve a storage development, authorize pipeline construction or injection, determine site capacity, certify containment or establish carbon credits. Existing licences, pollution-control approvals, environmental assessments, monitoring plans and storage permits continue to govern projects unless and until legally adopted amendments take effect.
source: Norwegian Ministry of Energy
status_note: Consultation note issued in March 2026; proposed regulatory amendments remained subject to consultation and formal adoption.

document_title: Announcement of One Area Related to CO2 Storage
notes: This formal government announcement opened one North Sea area for applications for an exploration licence for offshore carbon dioxide storage. It defines the area made available, invites qualified companies with industrial storage plans to apply and initiates the licensing process under Norway's continental-shelf carbon-storage framework. The announcement is a distinct administrative step because it creates an opportunity to seek exclusive appraisal rights, but it does not itself grant those rights. The application stage was subsequently followed by a separate licence award in June 2025. The announcement did not approve seismic acquisition, drilling, development, pipeline construction or injection and did not certify storage capacity or containment. Any successful licensee remains responsible for an approved work programme, data acquisition, site characterization, environmental and pollution-control approvals, financial and technical competence, monitoring and a later exploitation or injection authorization. No verified carbon removal can be inferred from opening an area for applications.
source: Norwegian Ministry of Energy
status_note: Area announced on 5 March 2025; the application stage ended when the corresponding exploration licence was offered in June 2025.

document_title: Offer of One New Licence for CO2 Storage on the Norwegian Continental Shelf
notes: This government decision offered Equinor a new exploration licence for carbon dioxide storage in a North Sea area announced earlier in 2025. The licence provides exclusive appraisal rights and includes a binding work programme with milestones intended to develop knowledge of the geological formation and determine whether a commercially and environmentally acceptable storage project can be proposed. The award expands Norway's offshore storage-licensing portfolio and is a concrete authorization to conduct activities within the licence framework. It is not an exploitation licence or injection permit and does not approve a final development concept, pipeline, well programme or cross-border transport arrangement. Geological capacity and containment remain estimates until appraisal data and regulatory review support later decisions. The licensee must comply with environmental, technical, financial, data-reporting and safety obligations and obtain further approvals before injection. The award therefore represents an active appraisal-stage project, not evidence of carbon dioxide already stored or credited.
source: Norwegian Ministry of Energy
status_note: Licence offered on 13 June 2025 with an active work programme; development and injection require later regulatory approvals.

subnational_area: Jammerbugt, Inez and Lisa offshore coastal areas
document_title: Invitation to Apply for a Licence for Exploration and Use of the Subsoil for Geological CO2 Storage in Certain Offshore Coastal Areas (Fourth Tender Round)
notes: This Danish Energy Agency invitation launched the fourth tender round for licences to explore and potentially use the subsoil for geological carbon dioxide storage in the Jammerbugt, Inez and Lisa structures in nearshore North Sea areas. It specifies application timing, technical and financial competence, proposed work programmes, licence duration, selection criteria, model terms and restrictions relating to nature protection, defence and other marine uses. An exploration licence may provide up to six years for appraisal and a conditional route to seek an extension for storage operations, but the invitation itself awards no licence. The application window closed in March 2025. The document does not authorize surveys, wells, construction or injection, establish that any structure is suitable, guarantee storage capacity or verify permanent storage. Successful applicants would still require environmental assessment, marine and subsurface approvals, approved monitoring, financial security and a later storage authorization before operational injection.
source: Danish Energy Agency
status_note: Invitation published on 16 December 2024; applications were accepted from 9 January to 6 March 2025 and the tender window is closed.

document_title: Bonaparte Carbon Capture and Storage Project — Notice of Decision and Statement of Reasons for Assessment by EIS
notes: The Northern Territory Environment Protection Authority decided that the Bonaparte Carbon Capture and Storage Project requires assessment by environmental impact statement.
