status_note: Policy Brief No. 11 was launched in October 2023 as a completed science-policy assessment and remains a reference for subsequent European blue-carbon research and policy discussions.

document_title: Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage (Resource Management and Administration) Regulations 2025
notes: These Commonwealth regulations replace the 2011 resource management and administration regulations and provide a binding administrative, data, reporting and well-integrity framework under the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act 2006. For greenhouse gas storage titleholders, the regulations prescribe annual title assessment reporting, secure retention of information, collection and retention of cores and samples, well and survey reports, data submission, and specific monthly and annual greenhouse gas injection and accounting reports for injection licensees. They also establish the ability of the Titles Administrator to specify data formats and media and contain transition rules for activities and plans moving from the former regime. The regulations commenced on 31 March 2026 and are therefore part of the active legal architecture for offshore geological carbon dioxide storage in Australian Commonwealth waters. They do not themselves grant an assessment permit, declare a storage formation, issue an injection licence, approve a site plan, authorize a Sea Dumping Act disposal activity, or establish that injected carbon dioxide is permanently contained. Project proponents remain subject to the separate greenhouse gas injection and storage regulations, NOPSEMA environment and well-integrity requirements, EPBC Act assessment where applicable, Sea Dumping Act permits, title conditions and project-specific monitoring, risk-management and reporting obligations.
source: Australian Government, Federal Register of Legislation
status_note: Made in 2025 and commenced on 31 March 2026, replacing the 2011 RMA Regulations; the current Federal Register compilation is in force.

subnational_area: Commonwealth offshore petroleum and greenhouse gas titles
document_title: Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage (Approved Forms) Notifiable Instrument 2026
notes: This in-force notifiable instrument approves prescribed forms for title transactions under the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act 2006, including an instrument of transfer for greenhouse gas titles and a supplementary instrument accompanying an application for approval of a dealing involving greenhouse gas titles. The instrument is administrative rather than geological, but it is important to the governance of offshore carbon storage because legal control of an assessment permit, holding lease or injection licence determines which entity carries the titleholder's statutory obligations, financial responsibilities, reporting duties and compliance exposure. Standardized approved forms also improve the integrity and transparency of the Titles Register while allowing commercially sensitive details to be handled through the supplementary-instrument mechanism provided by the Act. The instrument does not itself approve a transfer, dealing or change of control; applicants must still submit the relevant transaction to the Titles Administrator and obtain the decision required under the Act. It does not authorize exploration, appraisal drilling, carbon dioxide transport or injection, declare a greenhouse gas storage formation, approve a site plan or verify permanent storage. Consequently, its ONCE relevance is to legal and institutional control of offshore storage titles rather than to carbon removal quantification. Technical, environmental, financial and monitoring obligations continue independently of the approved-form requirement.
source: Australian Government, Federal Register of Legislation
status_note: Registered as F2026N00148 on 27 February 2026 and currently in force, with approved forms covering greenhouse gas title transfers and supplementary dealing instruments.

document_title: Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage (Resource Management and Administration) Regulations 2025 — Specified Format and Medium for Data Instrument
notes: This Titles Administrator instrument operationalizes the 2025 Resource Management and Administration Regulations by specifying the format and medium in which titleholders must submit well and survey data. The remade regulations replaced detailed legacy schedules with provisions allowing NOPTA to keep technical submission requirements current as digital standards and technologies change. The instrument covers well-completion data, survey acquisition and processing data, interpretative survey information, reprocessed survey data and related outputs, and it applies to relevant well and survey activities commencing on or after 31 March 2026. For offshore greenhouse gas storage, consistent data formats support long-term regulatory access to subsurface evidence used for storage-formation characterization, monitoring design, title administration and later reassessment of storage performance. The instrument is a binding data-submission requirement within the regulatory system, but conformity with its file formats does not validate the scientific interpretation or prove containment. It does not authorize a survey or well, grant a greenhouse gas title, declare an identified storage formation, approve an injection licence or site plan, or verify carbon dioxide as permanently stored. Titleholders still need technically adequate acquisition and quality control, complete metadata, statutory reports and all project-specific environmental, safety, permitting and monitoring approvals. The instrument should therefore be treated as data-governance infrastructure supporting credible MRV and regulatory continuity.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: The instrument is effective from 31 March 2026 and applies to relevant well, survey and reprocessed-survey activities commencing on or after that date.

document_title: Offshore Greenhouse Gas Guideline for Declaration of Identified Greenhouse Gas Storage Formation
notes: This NOPTA guideline explains the application and decision process for declaration of an identified greenhouse gas storage formation under the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act 2006. A declaration is a critical technical and legal bridge between early appraisal and later access to a greenhouse gas holding lease or injection licence because the responsible Commonwealth decision-maker must be satisfied that the formation can permanently store a specified amount and kind of greenhouse gas substance, injected over specified periods and points, with a suitable sealing mechanism and defined spatial extent. The guideline helps applicants organize geological, reservoir, sealing, injectivity, containment and supporting evidence and understand the information NOPTA and the minister may require. It was revised in 2025 and remains current alongside the later 2026 RMA guidance updates. The guideline is non-binding explanatory material and a declaration itself is not a title and does not give a right to inject or store carbon dioxide. The document does not approve an assessment permit, holding lease, injection licence, site plan, environment plan or Sea Dumping Act permit, and it does not certify carbon credits or verified removals. Appraisal uncertainty can remain after declaration, and titleholders are expected to continue improving the geological model. Operational storage requires further technical, environmental, financial, monitoring and regulatory approvals.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Revised guideline published by NOPTA on 14 February 2025 and retained as current guidance for applications to declare identified GHG storage formations.

document_title: Offshore Greenhouse Gas Assessment Permits — Work-bid Guideline
notes: This NOPTA guideline explains the grant, administration and ongoing management of offshore work-bid greenhouse gas assessment permits under the Australian Commonwealth offshore storage regime. A work-bid permit gives a successful titleholder exclusive rights to explore the permit area for potential greenhouse gas storage formations and injection sites, subject to the committed work programme and other statutory conditions. The guideline addresses application content and assessment, title offer and grant, work-programme expectations, variations, suspensions and extensions, exemptions, surrender, expiry, cancellation and renewal-related processes. The March 2026 update aligns the guidance with the remade Resource Management and Administration Regulations and the current title-administration framework. The document is useful to ONCE because assessment permits are the legal entry point for subsurface characterization of potential offshore carbon dioxide stores, including seismic surveys, wells and other appraisal evidence. It is nevertheless non-binding guidance and does not itself award acreage or authorize every exploration activity. A permit holder may still need key greenhouse gas operation approval, NOPSEMA environment and well-integrity approvals and other project-specific permissions before undertaking field work. The guideline does not declare a storage formation, approve injection, establish storage capacity or permanence, or create carbon credits. Successful commercial storage remains conditional on later declaration, licensing, site-plan, environmental, Sea Dumping Act, monitoring and financial requirements.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Updated for the 31 March 2026 commencement of the remade RMA Regulations and active as current NOPTA guidance for work-bid GHG assessment permits.

document_title: Offshore Consolidated and Cross-boundary Greenhouse Gas Assessment Permits — Work-bid Guideline
notes: This NOPTA guideline addresses the specialized processes for consolidated work-bid greenhouse gas assessment permits and cross-boundary greenhouse gas assessment permits. These title types are important where geological storage prospects, appraisal programmes or title configurations cannot be managed efficiently as a single ordinary assessment permit, including situations involving adjoining areas and the statutory cross-boundary framework. The guideline explains the application, grant, administration and work-programme expectations for these permits and the mechanisms available during the life of the title, including changes to obligations and title status. Its March 2026 update brings the guidance into line with the remade Resource Management and Administration Regulations. From an ONCE governance perspective, the document supports coherent appraisal of potential offshore carbon dioxide storage formations across legal title boundaries and reduces uncertainty about how titleholders should structure applications and evidence. It is non-binding guidance and does not itself consolidate titles, grant a cross-boundary permit or authorize a survey, appraisal well or injection activity. It also does not establish that a geological structure is capable of permanent storage, approve an injection licence or site plan, reserve future storage capacity, or verify removal credits. Each project remains subject to ministerial or authority decisions, title conditions, key-operation approvals, environmental and well-integrity assessment, storage-formation declaration, monitoring requirements and later injection and disposal permissions before operational storage can occur.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Updated for 31 March 2026 and active as current NOPTA guidance on consolidated and cross-boundary offshore GHG assessment permits.

document_title: Offshore Greenhouse Gas Injection Licences Guideline
notes: This NOPTA guideline explains how offshore greenhouse gas injection licence applications are prepared, assessed, granted and managed under the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act 2006 and associated regulations. An injection licence is the principal title required before commercial geological injection and permanent storage can occur, and an approved site plan must be in force for the relevant storage formation. The guideline therefore sits at the transition from appraisal into operational storage and addresses matters such as applicant eligibility, declared storage formations, technical evidence, site plans, risk assessment, monitoring, interactions with other titles and post-grant administration. The March 2026 update aligns the guidance with the current RMA framework and related NOPTA materials. The guideline is non-binding and does not itself grant an injection licence, approve a site plan or confirm that an applicant has satisfied the statutory criteria. It also does not replace NOPSEMA environment plans, well operations management plans or safety requirements, the Sea Dumping Act permit needed for offshore disposal of carbon dioxide, or EPBC Act approvals where applicable. A granted injection licence is also not by itself evidence of verified climate removal: injected and stored quantities must be measured and reported, storage behaviour monitored, risks managed and permanence demonstrated under the applicable regulatory and accounting frameworks before any separate carbon-credit or removal claim can be substantiated.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Current NOPTA injection-licence guideline updated for 31 March 2026 and active under the remade RMA regulatory environment.

subnational_area: Commonwealth offshore petroleum and GHG title areas
document_title: Data Management Guideline — Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage
notes: NOPTA's Data Management Guideline provides the operational framework for information, reports, survey data, well data and physical samples that offshore petroleum and greenhouse gas titleholders must retain or submit under the 2025 Resource Management and Administration Regulations. The guideline explains the relationship between statutory reporting obligations, submission timeframes, repositories, data formats, confidentiality and eventual public release, and it directs titleholders to the accompanying specified-format instrument, fact sheets and reporting templates. For offshore geological carbon storage, high-quality data governance is essential because appraisal and injection decisions depend on a long-lived record of subsurface characterization, well information, seismic interpretation, injection history and monitoring evidence that may need to be reviewed after title transfers, closure or unexpected storage behaviour. The guideline is active from the commencement of the remade regulations on 31 March 2026. It is guidance rather than an independent authorization and does not validate the scientific quality of a dataset merely because it has been submitted. It does not grant a title, approve a well or survey, declare a storage formation, authorize injection or certify stored carbon dioxide. Titleholders remain responsible for obtaining technically defensible measurements, applying quality assurance and control, meeting project-specific monitoring plans and complying with environmental, safety, Sea Dumping Act and storage-licence conditions. The guideline therefore supports regulatory traceability and MRV but is not itself a carbon-crediting methodology.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Effective 31 March 2026 and published as current NOPTA guidance for information, report, data and sample management under the remade RMA Regulations.

document_title: NOPTA Forms Guidance — Greenhouse Gas
notes: NOPTA Forms Guidance — Greenhouse Gas is an application-navigation document that consolidates the forms, statutory provisions, supporting guidelines, fact sheets, fees and expected processing information relevant to greenhouse gas title applications. It covers processes such as applications associated with declarations of identified greenhouse gas storage formations and other title and administrative steps under Part 3.2 of the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act. By linking applicants to the correct forms and supporting evidence, the guidance helps reduce procedural inconsistency and improves the completeness of applications entering the offshore carbon storage regulatory system. The current version is effective in 2026 and operates alongside the remade RMA Regulations and the greenhouse gas injection and storage regulations. It is non-binding procedural guidance, not an approval or legal entitlement. Using the listed form does not mean the responsible Commonwealth Minister, Cross-boundary Authority or Titles Administrator must approve the application. The document does not declare a storage formation, award an assessment permit, grant a holding lease or injection licence, approve a site plan, authorize injection or establish permanent containment. It also does not quantify removals or create carbon credits. Applicants remain responsible for technical and financial evidence, environmental and well-integrity approvals, risk and monitoring plans, project-specific information requests, statutory fees and the separate Sea Dumping Act and EPBC Act processes where applicable.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Current greenhouse gas forms guidance is effective from 13 January 2026 and remains part of NOPTA's active application-support materials.

document_title: Developing a GHG Resource — GHG Injection Licence and Site Plan Applications Fact Sheet
notes: This NOPTA fact sheet explains the application and assessment pathway for a greenhouse gas injection licence and the accompanying site plan required before offshore operations to inject and permanently store a greenhouse gas substance can commence. It clarifies that applicants must hold an eligible precursor title, such as a greenhouse gas assessment permit or holding lease, and that the relevant storage formation must have progressed through the declaration process. It also emphasizes that offshore CCS projects operate under multiple legal frameworks, including the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act, the Environment Protection (Sea Dumping) Act and national environmental law, with responsibilities distributed among NOPTA, NOPSEMA, Sea Dumping regulators and the environmental assessment authority. The fact sheet is a concise procedural guide rather than a legal decision. It does not grant an injection licence, approve a site plan, determine that the storage formation will contain carbon dioxide permanently, or authorize a Sea Dumping Act disposal activity. It also does not replace the detailed injection-licence guideline, SROSAI, risk-assessment and monitoring-plan materials. A project cannot infer verified removal merely from application eligibility or licence grant: it must measure injection, maintain accounting records, monitor storage behaviour, manage leakage and other risks, satisfy environmental and well-integrity requirements and comply with all conditions imposed by the responsible authorities.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Version 1 was published in January 2025 and remains part of NOPTA's current greenhouse gas fact-sheet suite.

subnational_area: Commonwealth offshore greenhouse gas and petroleum title interactions
document_title: Significant Risk of Significant Adverse Impact (SROSAI) Fact Sheet
notes: This NOPTA fact sheet explains the statutory concept of a Significant Risk of a Significant Adverse Impact, or SROSAI, used when greenhouse gas storage and petroleum interests may affect each other under the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act. The framework is designed for coexistence between industries: when making specified decisions, the responsible Commonwealth Minister must consider whether a proposed greenhouse gas operation creates a legally significant risk of adverse impact on existing or potential petroleum exploration, recovery operations or commercial viability, and comparable rules can apply in the opposite direction. The fact sheet explains when the concept is relevant, the meaning of adverse impact and the information needed to support the decision. It is an important regulatory safeguard because storage formation use, pressure effects, wells and operational footprints can interact with other subsurface rights. The document is guidance and does not itself determine that a project has or has not passed the SROSAI test. It does not grant a greenhouse gas title, authorize injection, approve a site plan, assess all environmental or safety risks, or quantify permanent storage. SROSAI is also narrower than a complete storage-risk assessment: containment, leakage, engineering, marine environment, well integrity and climate-accounting issues are handled through other legal and technical processes. Passing a coexistence test therefore cannot be treated as proof of environmental acceptability or verified carbon removal.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Version 1 published in January 2025 and retained as active NOPTA guidance for decisions involving SROSAI under the offshore GHG title framework.

subnational_area: Commonwealth offshore GHG injection licence applications
document_title: Risk Assessment in Offshore Greenhouse Gas Injection Licences and Site Plans Fact Sheet
notes: This NOPTA fact sheet describes the risk-assessment information expected in greenhouse gas injection licence and site-plan applications. Its scope includes geological risks, risks to containment of injected greenhouse gas substances and risks created or modified by engineering enhancements, while making clear that infrastructure, safety and broader environmental risks are addressed through other regulatory processes. The fact sheet links the risk assessment to the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act, the Greenhouse Gas Injection and Storage Regulations, the injection-licence guideline, the identified-storage-formation guidance and NOPSEMA risk-management materials. This creates a structured bridge between the geological evidence developed during appraisal and the risk controls needed for operational storage. The document is non-binding guidance and cannot be treated as a regulator's acceptance of a particular project's risk model. It does not authorize injection, approve a storage site, specify a universal acceptable probability of leakage, or guarantee that modelled containment will occur. Risk assessment also does not substitute for monitoring: assumptions and predicted storage behaviour must be tested against operational data and revised where new information changes the risk profile. Separate environment plans, well-integrity controls, Sea Dumping Act assessment and other approvals remain necessary. The fact sheet does not verify carbon removal or create credits; permanence and accounting claims depend on measured injection, credible monitoring, corrective action and compliance over the storage lifecycle.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Version 1 published in January 2025 and active as NOPTA guidance for risk assessment within GHG injection licence and site-plan applications.

subnational_area: Commonwealth offshore GHG injection licence applications
document_title: Monitoring Plans in Offshore Greenhouse Gas Injection Licences and Site Plans Fact Sheet
notes: This NOPTA fact sheet explains how monitoring plans fit into greenhouse gas injection licence and site-plan applications under the Australian offshore storage framework. A draft site plan must accompany an injection-licence application and must satisfy criteria in the Greenhouse Gas Injection and Storage Regulations, while monitoring is linked closely to the geological and engineering risk assessment. The fact sheet situates the monitoring plan within the broader set of approvals administered by NOPTA, NOPSEMA, the Sea Dumping regulator and the national environmental authority and reminds proponents that information supplied across these processes should be consistent. For ONCE, the document is directly relevant to MRV because operational monitoring is how predicted carbon dioxide plume and pressure behaviour, containment performance and storage risks are tested after injection begins. The fact sheet is general guidance, not an approved monitoring plan for any site. It does not prescribe one universal technology suite or sampling frequency for all formations, and it does not grant an injection licence, site-plan approval or Sea Dumping Act permit. Monitoring results must be interpreted against project-specific baselines, risk models and performance expectations and can trigger revision or corrective action when behaviour differs from predictions. The document also does not create carbon credits or certify permanence; credible removal claims require measured injection and accounting data, ongoing storage surveillance, transparent uncertainty treatment and compliance with all licence and environmental conditions.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Version 1 published in January 2025 and retained as current NOPTA guidance on monitoring plans for offshore GHG injection licences and site plans.

subnational_area: Commonwealth offshore GHG injection licence areas
document_title: Greenhouse Gas Injection Licence Reporting Fact Sheet
notes: The Greenhouse Gas Injection Licence Reporting Fact Sheet translates the reporting obligations in the remade 2025 Resource Management and Administration Regulations into an operational schedule for offshore greenhouse gas injection licensees. Under the current framework, licensees must submit monthly greenhouse gas injection reports, monthly greenhouse gas accounting reports, annual injection reports and annual greenhouse gas accounting reports, using the relevant reporting templates and methods. These records create a recurring regulatory evidence stream for volumes injected, operational performance and carbon accounting and are therefore one of the clearest formal MRV components of Australia's offshore storage system. The fact sheet became effective with the new regulations on 31 March 2026 and should be read with the Data Management Guideline and current templates. It is guidance about compliance and does not independently establish the legal obligation beyond the regulations. Submitting a report does not mean the regulator has certified the data, storage permanence or climate benefit. The fact sheet does not approve injection, replace a site-plan monitoring programme, assess leakage or environmental effects, or create carbon credits. Licensees remain responsible for accurate measurements, quality assurance, corrections where required, retention and submission of supporting evidence and compliance with title, site-plan, environmental, well-integrity and Sea Dumping Act conditions. Any external carbon-removal claim requires additional accounting rules and verification beyond routine statutory reporting.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: Effective from 31 March 2026 as current reporting guidance accompanying the remade RMA Regulations and new GHG injection and accounting templates.

subnational_area: Commonwealth waters beyond three nautical miles
document_title: Offshore Carbon Capture and Storage Regulatory Approvals
notes: This March 2026 Australian Government guidance maps the principal Commonwealth regulatory approvals that an offshore carbon capture and storage project may need across the identify-and-assess, select, define, execute, operate, decommissioning and post-closure phases. It explains the interaction of the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act, the Environment Protection (Sea Dumping) Act and the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act and identifies the respective roles of NOPTA, NOPSEMA, the Sea Dumping regulator and the Nature Positive Regulation Division. The document is particularly useful because offshore CCS is not authorized through a single permit: assessment titles, key greenhouse gas operations, environment plans, well controls, storage-formation declaration, injection licence and site plan, Sea Dumping approval and other decisions must be sequenced or coordinated. The guidance explicitly states that each project is unique and may require additional approvals and that proponents remain responsible for satisfying all legal requirements. It is not a commitment by government to approve a project and does not cover every state or territory approval. It does not grant storage rights, authorize carbon dioxide injection, approve an environmental impact, certify a storage quantity or create carbon credits. Even when all project approvals are obtained, actual climate performance remains dependent on measured injection, containment, monitoring, reporting, corrective actions and applicable accounting rules.
source: Australian Government, Department of Industry, Science and Resources; DCCEEW; NOPSEMA
status_note: Published in March 2026 as current cross-regulator guidance on sequencing Commonwealth approvals for offshore CCS projects.

subnational_area: Commonwealth offshore petroleum and GHG regulatory system
document_title: 2025 Resource Management and Administration Regulations Guidance, Factsheets and Approved Forms Consultation
notes: This Department of Industry, Science and Resources consultation sought industry and stakeholder feedback on the guidance, fact sheets and approved forms prepared to implement the remade Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Resource Management and Administration Regulations 2025. The consultation covered material addressing annual title assessment reports and approved forms, field-development-plan requirements, data management and reporting, sample submission, technical information release timeframes and greenhouse gas reporting templates. It is independently relevant because it documents the participatory policy-development stage through which operational requirements were tested for clarity and usability before the new regulations commenced. The consultation opened in December 2025 and closed on 23 January 2026, allowing regulators to revise materials before the 31 March 2026 commencement date. The consultation itself was non-binding and did not bring the regulations into force or approve any individual guideline, title or project. Submitting comments did not grant greenhouse gas rights, authorize a survey, well or injection operation, or alter a storage formation. The process also did not establish carbon-credit eligibility or verify removals. Its function was governance quality assurance: improving how regulated entities understand and implement reporting, forms and data obligations. Final legal duties arise from the Act and regulations, while the published guidance and templates support compliance and can be updated independently as administrative practice evolves.
source: Australian Government, Department of Industry, Science and Resources
status_note: Consultation opened on 9 December 2025 and closed on 23 January 2026 ahead of the 31 March 2026 commencement of the remade RMA Regulations.

subnational_area: Commonwealth offshore title areas and National Offshore Petroleum Data and Core Repository
document_title: Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Sample Submission Standards
notes: These March 2026 NOPTA standards specify how physical samples collected from offshore wells and other operations are to be prepared, packaged, presented and submitted to the National Offshore Petroleum Data and Core Repository. The standards support compliance with the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act and the 2025 Resource Management and Administration Regulations and cover material such as drill cuttings, sidewall cores, fluid and gaseous samples, thin sections, submission addresses and practical handling requirements. Although many sample types originated in petroleum administration, the standards expressly apply within the petroleum and greenhouse gas storage data regime. For geological carbon storage, preserving cores and other physical evidence has long-term value for independent reassessment of reservoir and seal properties, well records, geochemistry and subsurface models after title transfers or as new analytical methods emerge. The standards are operational technical requirements but do not establish that a submitted sample is representative, scientifically sufficient or correctly interpreted. They do not authorize drilling, approve a greenhouse gas title or key operation, declare a storage formation, grant an injection licence or verify permanent containment. Titleholders still need valid sampling designs, chain of custody, laboratory quality control, metadata and regulatory reports. The document does not issue carbon credits or quantify storage; it strengthens the physical evidence archive that supports technical assurance and future regulatory scrutiny.
source: Australian Government, National Offshore Petroleum Titles Administrator
status_note: March 2026 standards, effective within the remade RMA reporting system from 31 March 2026 and currently used for physical sample submissions.

document_title: Environmental Improvement Plan: Annual Progress Report 2025 to 2026
notes: This statutory-style annual implementation report assesses England's progress during April 2025 to March 2026 against the 2025 Environmental Improvement Plan and Environment Act targets. For coastal carbon and ONCE-relevant ecosystem restoration, the report tracks the commitment to increase saltmarsh by 15 percent from the 2009 baseline and seagrass by 15 percent from the 2024 baseline by 2043, alongside oyster-reef recovery. It reports funding for sixteen coastal restoration projects expected to deliver approximately ninety-one hectares of saltmarsh and 2.65 hectares of seagrass, with annual project data collected through the Environment Agency's ReMeMaRe programme, reporting guidance and quality assurance by area project managers. It also records the Marine Enhancement Directory and a saltmarsh feasibility methodology as tools supporting scaled restoration. The report is valuable because it converts long-term habitat commitments into quantified implementation evidence and monitoring arrangements. However, funded or expected habitat area is not equivalent to verified carbon removal. The document does not provide a project-level carbon baseline, quantify net additional tonnes of carbon dioxide removed, establish permanence or leakage rules, issue credits, or automatically add the restored area to the national greenhouse gas inventory. Carbon outcomes depend on habitat establishment, long-term ecological condition, sediment and biomass carbon dynamics, disturbance, methane and other relevant greenhouse gases, and future accounting methodologies.
source: United Kingdom Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs
status_note: Published on 16 July 2026 and covers the completed statutory reporting period from April 2025 to March 2026; underlying EIP commitments continue.

document_title: Unlocking Benefits for People, Nature and Climate: Actions to Jointly Address Climate Change and Biodiversity Loss in England
notes: This cross-government policy paper sets out how England is integrating climate and biodiversity action across nature restoration, clean energy, rural land, seas and green finance. Its marine section explicitly identifies saltmarshes, mudflats and seagrass beds as long-term carbon sinks as well as coastal-defence and biodiversity assets, and notes that two of England's Highly Protected Marine Areas protect blue-carbon habitats. The paper also records continuing work through the UK Blue Carbon Evidence Partnership to address evidence gaps preventing saltmarsh from being incorporated into the United Kingdom Greenhouse Gas Inventory. This makes the publication important to ONCE because it links ecosystem protection and restoration with the national accounting problem rather than assuming that habitat conservation automatically produces reportable mitigation. The document is a policy synthesis and implementation narrative, not a new statute or carbon methodology. It does not establish emission factors, project boundaries, additionality, permanence, leakage rules or a date on which saltmarsh will enter the national inventory. It does not authorize restoration, create tradable blue-carbon credits or quantify verified removals from protected areas. Future accounting requires robust mapping, stock and flux measurements, uncertainty treatment and methodological decisions, while conservation actions remain subject to marine planning and site-specific governance. The paper therefore supports integrated policy direction and evidence development without converting ecological benefits into certified carbon claims.
source: United Kingdom Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs
status_note: Published on 14 July 2025 as an active cross-government policy paper describing integrated climate and biodiversity delivery in England.

document_title: State of Natural Resources Report 2025 — Marine Assessment
notes: Natural Resources Wales' State of Natural Resources Report 2025 Marine Assessment provides a national-scale evidence synthesis on the condition, pressures, resilience and economic and social services of Welsh marine ecosystems. The assessment explicitly identifies blue carbon as a service of Welsh seas and reports that Welsh marine habitats store more than 113 million tonnes of carbon while sequestering thousands of tonnes annually. It links these carbon functions to ecosystem condition, marine planning, restoration, climate change, pollution and emerging finance, and highlights case studies on estimating Welsh marine carbon-sink potential, seagrass restoration and saltmarsh recovery. It also identifies evidence gaps in habitat extent and condition, carbon sequestration, sediment processes and human pressures that limit robust management decisions. This is particularly relevant to ONCE theory and policy because it treats carbon storage as one ecosystem service within a broader sustainable-management framework rather than as an isolated credit commodity. The assessment is non-binding and does not itself create a blue-carbon market, establish a project methodology or approve restoration. The reported stock estimate is not a quantity of additional anthropogenic removal and should not be converted directly into credits. Quantitative policy or market use requires clear spatial boundaries, stock and burial measurements, uncertainty and counterfactual treatment, monitoring of disturbance and recovery, and decisions under greenhouse-gas inventory or crediting rules. The report's role is evidence synthesis and policy guidance.
source: Natural Resources Wales
status_note: Published as the Marine ecosystem assessment within SoNaRR 2025 and remains an official evidence base for Welsh sustainable natural-resource management.

subnational_area: Seychelles coral reefs and associated coastal and marine ecosystems
document_title: National Policy and Strategic Action Plan on Coral Reef Conservation and Management
notes: Seychelles' National Policy and Strategic Action Plan on Coral Reef Conservation and Management was designed to integrate coral-reef health into the wider national marine-conservation system during 2021–2025. The official implementation page frames Seychelles' coral reefs, seagrass and mangrove ecosystems within a broader blue-carbon context linked to the country's climate commitments, while the action plan itself focuses on effective governance, reduction of natural and anthropogenic stressors, management-oriented monitoring and research, financing and public awareness. Implementation measures include a representative steering committee, integration of reef concerns into marine spatial planning and protected-area management, coral propagation and restoration, a reef-quality scoring and mapping methodology and a standardized national monitoring and reporting system. The plan is relevant to ONCE primarily as a marine ecosystem governance and restoration framework, but coral reefs should not be treated mechanically as equivalent to mangrove, seagrass or saltmarsh carbon sinks because carbonate production and ecosystem carbon balances are scientifically complex. The policy does not establish a coral carbon-credit methodology, quantify additional net carbon dioxide removal, prove permanence, issue credits or create a national blue-carbon registry. Its 2021–2025 action period has ended, although institutions and monitoring practices developed under the plan may continue. Carbon claims for associated ecosystems require habitat-specific accounting, baselines, long-term monitoring and scientifically appropriate treatment of organic and inorganic carbon processes.
source: Seychelles Ministry of Fisheries, Agriculture and Blue Economy / SWIOFish3
status_note: The strategic action plan covered 2021–2025; its formal action period has ended, while several governance, monitoring and restoration mechanisms established under the programme may continue.

subnational_area: Dutch continental shelf — K14-FA and K14-FC storage formations
document_title: Kennisgeving besluit verlening CO2-opslagvergunning K14-FAFC, Ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat
notes: This official Dutch Government Gazette notice records the decision to grant Shell Exploration and Production (107) B.V. and Shell Gas & Power Developments B.V. a permit for the permanent geological storage of carbon dioxide in the K14-FA and K14-FC formations on the Dutch continental shelf. The formations are located in blocks K11 and K14 and form part of the wider Aramis carbon capture and storage system. The application was made under Article 25(1)(a) of the Mining Act and requested an injection period of up to 25 years; the State Secretary decided to grant the requested storage permit. This is therefore a binding project-specific authorization rather than a general policy statement or research programme. The notice establishes the legal storage right for the named formations but should not be interpreted as evidence that injection has already started, that the full requested capacity will be used, or that any amount of carbon dioxide has yet been permanently stored. Project construction, operation, monitoring, environmental compliance, financial-security obligations and other applicable approvals remain relevant throughout development and operation. The decision also does not create a carbon-credit methodology or certify climate-removal quantities.
source: Government of the Netherlands — Ministry of Climate Policy and Green Growth / Dutch Government Gazette
status_note: Storage permit granted and officially notified on 1 May 2026; the authorization is active, while actual injection and storage remain dependent on project delivery and compliance with permit conditions.

subnational_area: Geological CO2 storage sites regulated under Directive 2009/31/EC, including offshore storage
document_title: Guidance Document 1 — CO2 Storage Life Cycle and Risk Management Framework
notes: The European Commission's updated Guidance Document 1 provides the overarching life-cycle and risk-management framework for implementing Directive 2009/31/EC on the geological storage of carbon dioxide. The 2025 publication is part of the revised four-document CCS guidance set and is intended to improve understanding and support correct and more uniform implementation of the Directive by competent authorities, prospective storage operators and other stakeholders. It covers the progression of a geological storage project through major regulatory milestones and explains how risk assessment and risk management should be integrated across site selection, permitting, operation, closure and the period preceding transfer of responsibility. The guidance is directly relevant to offshore geological storage because the CCS Directive applies to qualifying storage in EU and EEA jurisdictions, including marine and continental-shelf settings. The Commission explicitly states that the guidance is not legally binding and does not represent an official interpretation that overrides EU law. It does not itself award storage acreage, grant a storage permit, authorize injection, approve a specific site, certify storage capacity or verify permanent containment. Project-specific decisions remain the responsibility of competent authorities under the binding Directive and national implementing law.
source: European Commission — Directorate-General for Climate Action
status_note: Updated CCS Directive guidance published in 2025 and currently used as non-binding implementation support for competent authorities and stakeholders.

subnational_area: Geological CO2 storage sites regulated under Directive 2009/31/EC, including offshore storage
document_title: Guidance Document 2 — Characterisation of the Storage Complex, CO2 Stream Composition, Monitoring and Corrective Measures
notes: The European Commission's 2025 update of Guidance Document 2 explains how key technical and environmental requirements of the CCS Directive should be applied to geological carbon dioxide storage. It addresses characterisation of the storage site and wider storage complex, the composition and acceptance of the carbon dioxide stream, monitoring design, interpretation of monitoring results and corrective measures where behaviour departs from expectations or leakage risks arise. These functions are central to offshore storage governance because a permit cannot be treated as sufficient evidence of safe long-term containment without site-specific characterisation, monitoring and the ability to respond to irregularities. The document is intended to support competent authorities and operators and to improve consistent implementation across the European Union. The Commission expressly identifies the guidance as non-binding: it does not amend Directive 2009/31/EC, replace national law or predetermine a competent authority's decision. It also does not grant a storage permit, approve any particular offshore reservoir, establish a verified amount of injected carbon dioxide or demonstrate permanence. Monitoring plans and corrective measures must still be approved and implemented for individual projects under the applicable legal framework.
source: European Commission — Directorate-General for Climate Action
status_note: Updated CCS Directive guidance released in August 2025 and active as non-binding implementation support.

subnational_area: Geological CO2 storage sites regulated under Directive 2009/31/EC, including offshore storage
document_title: Guidance Document 3 — Criteria for Transfer of Responsibility to the Competent Authority
notes: The European Commission's updated Guidance Document 3 addresses the conditions and evidence relevant to transferring long-term responsibility for a geological carbon dioxide storage site from the operator to the competent authority under the CCS Directive. It supports implementation of Article 18 by explaining how regulators and operators should assess whether available evidence demonstrates that stored carbon dioxide will remain completely and permanently contained and how monitoring, corrective-measure obligations, leakage-related allowance surrender and environmental-liability responsibilities interact before transfer. The guidance is particularly important for offshore storage because closure does not end regulatory responsibility automatically; long-term containment must be demonstrated and the statutory transfer criteria must be met. The 2025 revision forms part of the Commission's updated four-document CCS implementation package. It is non-binding and does not itself transfer responsibility for any site, shorten statutory periods, waive monitoring obligations or create a presumption that a closed project is safe. It also does not authorize injection or certify a quantity of permanent carbon dioxide removal. A project-specific transfer remains a formal decision by the relevant competent authority under EU and national law after the required evidence and financial arrangements have been satisfied.
source: European Commission — Directorate-General for Climate Action
status_note: Updated guidance published in 2025; it supports future transfer-of-responsibility decisions but does not itself transfer legal responsibility for any storage site.

subnational_area: Geological CO2 storage sites regulated under Directive 2009/31/EC, including offshore storage
document_title: Guidance Document 4 — Financial Security and Financial Contribution
notes: The European Commission's updated Guidance Document 4 is the financial-security component of the revised CCS Directive guidance package. It supports implementation of the Directive's requirements that storage operators provide adequate financial security before injection begins and make the required financial contribution before responsibility can ultimately be transferred to the competent authority. The guidance is designed to help authorities and operators interpret practical questions concerning the form, adequacy, timing and maintenance of financial arrangements across the storage life cycle, including the post-closure period. These requirements are material to offshore geological storage because long-lived monitoring, corrective measures, closure and post-transfer obligations can create costs well beyond the construction and injection phase. The Commission identifies the 2025 guidance package as a methodological aid for implementing the CCS Directive and notes that it is not legally binding. This document therefore does not provide project finance, subsidize a storage project, determine an operator's individual security amount, grant a permit, authorize injection or transfer responsibility. Project-specific financial security and contributions remain subject to competent-authority assessment under the binding CCS Directive and national implementing rules.
source: European Commission — Directorate-General for Climate Action
status_note: Updated guidance published as part of the 2025 CCS Directive implementation package; non-binding and currently applicable as regulatory support.

subnational_area: Denmark — geological CO2 storage permit applications, including offshore storage
document_title: Guidance on the Content of CO2 Storage Permit Applications in Denmark
notes: This Danish Energy Agency guidance sets out the expected content and administrative process for applications for a carbon dioxide storage permit under Section 23 d(2) of the Danish Subsoil Act. The official consultation page states that the guidance supplements existing guidance, standards, executive orders and legislation. It describes general application requirements, identifies plans and supporting material that must be included, explains the authority's approval process and expected duration, and addresses how the parallel environmental process can affect case handling. An appendix provides guidance for the project's environmental impact assessment. The document is highly relevant to offshore geological storage because Denmark's developing North Sea storage projects must move from exploration and appraisal into a separate storage-permit stage before operational injection can be authorized. The guidance was published for consultation on 28 November 2025, with the consultation closing on 9 January 2026, and the official portal lists an effective date of 10 April 2026. It remains non-binding guidance: it does not itself issue a storage permit, approve an individual reservoir, authorize injection, establish storage capacity, verify containment or create carbon credits. Applicants must still satisfy the statutory and project-specific technical, environmental, monitoring and financial requirements.
source: Danish Energy Agency
status_note: Published for consultation on 28 November 2025; the official consultation portal lists an effective date of 10 April 2026, after the consultation closed on 9 January 2026.

subnational_area: Danish maritime area and continental shelf
document_title: L 108 — Forslag til lov om ændring af lov om anvendelse af Danmarks undergrund og lov om kontinentalsoklen og visse aktiviteter på søterritoriet
notes: Bill L 108 proposed amendments to Denmark's Subsoil Act and legislation governing the continental shelf and certain activities in the territorial sea. The proposal sought clearer rules for decommissioning and reuse of installations, infrastructure, wells and other facilities previously used for subsurface activities and would have expanded the permit regime for transit pipelines in Danish maritime areas so that it could expressly cover new energy carriers, including carbon dioxide and hydrogen. The proposal was relevant to offshore carbon storage because reuse of existing North Sea infrastructure and the ability to transport carbon dioxide through offshore pipelines are important parts of developing geological storage chains in depleted reservoirs and other suitable formations. The bill would have created a more explicit authorization framework for such maritime infrastructure, but it did not itself grant a carbon dioxide storage licence or approve a specific pipeline or storage project. The Danish Parliament records the bill as lapsed after introduction on 4 February 2026 and first reading on 25 February 2026. Its proposed 1 July 2026 commencement therefore did not occur. This record represents a formal but unsuccessful legislative proposal and must not be treated as current binding law or evidence of project authorization.
source: Danish Parliament / Ministry of Climate, Energy and Utilities
status_note: Introduced on 4 February 2026 and considered at first reading on 25 February 2026; the bill lapsed before enactment and never entered into force.

subnational_area: United Kingdom offshore CO2 storage market
document_title: Evolution of Economic Regulation for CO2 Storage: Summary of Responses
notes: This Department for Energy Security and Net Zero outcome document summarizes 26 responses to the 2025 call for evidence on how economic regulation of carbon dioxide storage should evolve as the United Kingdom's storage market grows. Respondents generally viewed early storage networks as natural monopolies because of high capital costs, geographical constraints and cross-chain risks, while identifying scope for competition only as the market matures. The Regulated Asset Base model was widely considered important for early projects, but respondents also emphasized the need for an evidence-based transition, predictable regulation, transitional government support and risk-sharing mechanisms to maintain investor confidence. The government states that it and Ofgem will use the evidence to inform future policy decisions supporting continued growth of offshore carbon dioxide storage. The summary was published on 27 April 2026 and is distinct from the original 2025 call for evidence. It is an evidence and policy-development output rather than a new regulatory settlement. It does not amend storage licences, change permit conditions, guarantee a particular revenue model, allocate capacity, approve investment support or authorize injection. Any future economic-regulation changes require subsequent formal government or Ofgem decisions.
source: United Kingdom Department for Energy Security and Net Zero / Ofgem
status_note: Summary of 26 consultation responses published on 27 April 2026; it informs future economic-regulation policy but does not itself change the current regulatory model.

document_title: North Sea Transition Authority (Oil and Gas Authority) Review 2025
notes: This statutory review evaluates the effectiveness of the North Sea Transition Authority and the fitness and scope of its functions in relation to offshore petroleum and the storage of carbon dioxide. Published on 28 April 2026 under the Energy Act 2016 review requirement, the report provides an authoritative governance snapshot of the United Kingdom's offshore carbon storage regime. It records that the NSTA had issued four carbon storage permits, including Endurance and three HyNet permits, notes the wider portfolio of carbon dioxide appraisal and storage licences, describes the December 2025 launch of the second carbon storage licensing round, and explains that the licensing process is governed by the Storage of Carbon Dioxide (Licensing etc.) Regulations 2010. The review also discusses evolving storage-potential assessment methods, licensee work-programme obligations, updated licence and storage-permit guidance and Carbon Storage Stewardship Expectations. Its function is institutional assessment and policy assurance rather than project authorization. The review does not itself award a licence, grant a storage permit, approve injection, amend legal conditions, certify storage capacity or verify permanent containment. Project-specific rights and obligations continue to arise from legislation, licences, permits and related regulatory decisions.
source: United Kingdom Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
status_note: Statutory review published on 28 April 2026; it evaluates the NSTA and informs governance but does not itself grant or amend carbon-storage licences or permits.

document_title: UKCS Current Carbon Storage Licences (WGS84)
notes: This North Sea Transition Authority dataset is an authoritative spatial and administrative inventory of current carbon storage licences on the UK Continental Shelf. The WGS84 dataset was first added on 18 June 2026 and was updated on 26 July 2026. Available formats include geodatabases, GeoPackage, Excel, KML, GeoJSON, shapefile and CSV, supporting regulatory mapping and machine-readable analysis. The underlying attributes include licence reference and name, licence type and status, licensing-round or award process, licence start date, operator and partner organizations, links to licence documents and the public register, and fields indicating whether an injection permit has been approved and, where applicable, the permit start date and storage operator. This makes the dataset useful for distinguishing appraisal licences from projects that have progressed to a storage permit and for maintaining a current inventory of the offshore regulatory landscape. It is a monitoring and information product rather than a legal instrument that creates rights. Inclusion in the dataset does not itself grant a licence or permit, authorize drilling or injection, verify storage capacity, demonstrate containment or create carbon credits. Legal status must still be read from the underlying licence, permit and public-register documents.
source: North Sea Transition Authority / UK National Data Library
status_note: Current regulatory dataset created on 18 June 2026 and last updated on 26 July 2026; it inventories existing licences and permits rather than creating them.

document_title: Guidance on Applications for a Carbon Storage Permit — April 2025 Version 3
notes: The North Sea Transition Authority's April 2025 Version 3 guidance explains the process and evidence requirements associated with applications for a carbon storage permit and with notified changes to an existing or proposed storage operation. A storage permit is distinct from a Carbon Dioxide Appraisal and Storage Licence: licensees may appraise a licensed area, but they must obtain the permit before carbon dioxide can be injected for permanent storage on the UK Continental Shelf. The guidance addresses the project-development phases leading to an application, the content and review of permit-application documents, storage-site and storage-complex characterisation, development planning, containment risk, monitoring, corrective measures, provisional post-closure planning, financial security and operator competence. The 2025 update also explains how the NSTA may assess notified operational or operator changes and request further evidence. The guidance is explicitly non-binding and does not replace the Energy Act 2008 or Storage of Carbon Dioxide (Licensing etc.) Regulations 2010. It does not grant a permit, authorize injection, guarantee approval, certify storage capacity or demonstrate permanent containment. Each project remains subject to a project-specific NSTA decision and all applicable environmental, technical, financial and monitoring requirements.
source: North Sea Transition Authority
status_note: Version 3 published on 1 April 2025 and currently used to support UKCS carbon-storage permit applications and notified changes.

document_title: New Public Consultation — Proposed Changes to the Resource Management Regulations and the Regulations Relating to Documentation in Connection with Storage of CO2 on the Shelf
notes: The Norwegian Offshore Directorate opened a new round of public consultation on 2 July 2026 on proposed amendments to the Resource Management Regulations and the Regulations relating to documentation in connection with storage of carbon dioxide on the continental shelf. The new consultation follows a 2025 consultation and is expressly limited to provisions that were changed in response to comments received during that earlier process. It therefore represents a revised formal regulatory proposal rather than a duplicate publication of the first consultation. The changes concern resource-management and documentation rules that apply to offshore carbon dioxide storage activities, including the regulatory information and reporting framework used by the authorities. The Directorate proposes that the amendments take effect from 1 January 2027, while the deadline for comments is 1 October 2026. At the current stage the proposal remains under review and has no final binding effect. It does not grant a storage licence, approve an exploration programme, authorize drilling or injection, certify a storage formation or establish a carbon-credit mechanism. Existing binding legislation and licence conditions continue to apply unless and until final amendments are adopted and enter into force.
source: Norwegian Offshore Directorate
status_note: Revised consultation opened on 2 July 2026; comments are due by 1 October 2026 and the proposed amendments would take effect on 1 January 2027 if formally adopted.

document_title: Guidelines for the Regulations Relating to Documentation for CO2 Storage on the Shelf — Section 26 Status Reports
notes: The Norwegian Offshore Directorate issued new CCS guidelines on 3 November 2025 explaining how licensees should fulfil Section 26 of the Regulations relating to documentation in connection with storage of carbon dioxide on the Norwegian continental shelf. The purpose is to ensure that the authorities receive status-report information with the correct content and in the correct format when an exploration or exploitation licence is surrendered, lapses or expires. Under Section 26(1), the licensee must submit a status report to the Directorate within three months. The report must summarize collected data, studies and results, provide an overview of potential storage complexes in the licence area, and identify geotechnical material, where it is stored and the relevant storage format. This guidance strengthens the regulatory evidence base and continuity of subsurface information as licence areas change hands or return to the State. It is guidance rather than a new storage licence or deployment authorization. It does not approve a reservoir, authorize drilling or carbon dioxide injection, verify storage capacity or permanence, or create a crediting methodology. Binding duties derive from the underlying documentation regulations and licence framework; the guidance explains how those reporting duties should be met.
source: Norwegian Offshore Directorate
status_note: Guidelines issued on 3 November 2025 and active as implementation guidance for Section 26 status-report requirements.

subnational_area: Rotterdam Maasvlakte and Dutch North Sea — Aramis CO2 transport and offshore platform infrastructure
document_title: Projectbesluit Aramis
notes: The Aramis Project Decision is a binding Dutch spatial and project decision that enables the realization and operation of major carbon dioxide transport infrastructure connecting the Rotterdam Maasvlakte with offshore storage locations in depleted gas fields beneath the North Sea. Adopted under the Environment Act and Mining Act framework, the decision provides the spatial basis for the project and covers a carbon dioxide terminal and compression facilities on the Maasvlakte, a large offshore pipeline, connection points and North Sea platforms and associated infrastructure. The project is designed as open infrastructure that can serve multiple industrial carbon dioxide suppliers and multiple storage operators, with the offshore pipeline capable of supporting expansion as demand grows. The decision is directly relevant to marine geological storage because the network is constructed to deliver captured carbon dioxide to storage fields such as L04-A, K14-FA and L10-ALBE. However, the decision expressly distinguishes the Aramis infrastructure from the separate legal authorization of the geological storage formations themselves. It does not by itself grant the storage permits for each reservoir, prove that injection has begun, certify storage capacity or verify permanent containment. Individual storage operators remain subject to separate Mining Act permits, environmental requirements, monitoring, technical conditions and other implementing decisions.
source: Government of the Netherlands — Ministry of Climate Policy and Green Growth / Dutch Government Gazette
status_note: Project decision signed on 7 April 2025 and published on 25 April 2025; it provides the spatial authorization for Aramis infrastructure while separate storage permits remain necessary for individual reservoirs.

subnational_area: P18-2 storage formation, Dutch North Sea — Porthos project
document_title: Kennisgeving besluit wijziging CO2-opslagvergunning P18-2, Ministerie van Klimaat en Groene Groei
notes: This Dutch Government Gazette notice records a binding amendment to the P18-2 carbon dioxide storage permit used by the Porthos project in the Dutch North Sea. The permit holders, TAQA Offshore B.V. and EBN CCS B.V., applied to extend the permitted carbon dioxide injection period so that it may run through 31 December 2045 instead of 31 December 2041 and to change how the required financial security is expressed in the permit. The Minister of Climate Policy and Green Growth decided to amend the permit in accordance with the application and also made ex officio corrections, clarifications and additions. The P18-2 storage formation is located in block P18 and forms the geological storage component of Porthos. This record is therefore a project-specific regulatory modification, not a new general CCS policy. The decision changes the legal conditions of an existing offshore storage authorization but does not by itself show that the extended period will be fully used, quantify future stored volumes or certify permanent containment. It also does not establish a carbon-credit method. Injection, monitoring, financial security, closure and environmental obligations continue to be governed by the amended permit and the wider Dutch and European storage framework.
source: Government of the Netherlands — Ministry of Climate Policy and Green Growth / Dutch Government Gazette
status_note: Permit amendment published on 29 September 2025; the P18-2 authorization remains active with the amended injection period and financial-security provisions.

subnational_area: German exclusive economic zone and continental shelf; onshore storage only where enabled by individual Länder
document_title: Gesetz zur dauerhaften Speicherung und zum Transport von Kohlendioxid (Kohlendioxid-Speicherung-und-Transport-Gesetz — KSpTG), amended by the Act of 25 November 2025
notes: The 2025 amendment fundamentally expanded Germany's legal framework for carbon capture, carbon dioxide transport and permanent geological storage and renamed the statute as the Kohlendioxid-Speicherung-und-Transport-Gesetz (KSpTG). The consolidated law records the amendment of 25 November 2025 in Federal Law Gazette 2025 I No. 282, effective from 28 November 2025. It now regulates authorization and operation of carbon dioxide pipelines and permanent storage installations, including exploration, monitoring, closure and post-closure care. The law applies in Germany's exclusive economic zone and continental shelf and allows carbon dioxide stores located predominantly in those offshore areas, while injection in the territorial sea is excluded. It also creates an opt-in route under which individual Länder may allow permanent onshore geological storage within their territory. Construction, operation and substantial modification of a carbon dioxide store require prior plan approval, and offshore projects are subject to ecological siting restrictions, including protections relating to designated marine protected areas and sensitive marine uses. The framework requires site characterization, safety evidence, monitoring, corrective measures, carbon dioxide stream quality controls, financial security, closure and transfer-of-responsibility arrangements, public information and regulatory reporting. It also links German operators to EU-level carbon dioxide injection-capacity obligations under the Net-Zero Industry Act. The amendment creates a binding enabling and permitting framework for commercial-scale geological storage, but it does not itself approve any individual storage complex, certify a project-specific storage capacity, demonstrate that injection has started, or establish a carbon-crediting methodology. Each project remains subject to the relevant investigation, plan-approval, environmental, operating, monitoring and financial-security requirements.
source: Federal Republic of Germany — Federal Ministry of Justice / Federal Office of Justice (Gesetze im Internet)
status_note: The 25 November 2025 amendment entered into force on 28 November 2025; the amended KSpTG is the active federal CCS transport and storage framework.

subnational_area: German high seas jurisdiction, including the German exclusive economic zone, continental shelf and marine subsoil
document_title: Erstes Gesetz zur Änderung des Hohe-See-Einbringungsgesetzes
notes: The First Act Amending the High Seas Dumping Act was promulgated on 13 March 2026 as Federal Law Gazette 2026 I No. 70 and creates a substantially broader German legal framework for offshore carbon dioxide storage and marine geoengineering. The amendment adds carbon dioxide streams intended for permanent geological storage to the statutory exceptions from the general prohibition on introducing wastes or other substances into the high seas and provides that storage in the marine subsoil under German sovereignty, in the German exclusive economic zone and on the German continental shelf is governed by the authorization rules of the KSpTG rather than by a separate dumping permit under the High Seas Dumping Act. It also establishes a conditional legal route for exporting carbon dioxide streams to another state for offshore geological storage where the London Protocol Article 6 requirements are satisfied. At the same time, the amendment updates the statutory definition and regulation of marine geoengineering and replaces the annex with a list covering ocean fertilization, ocean alkalinization, biomass sinking, mineralization of carbon dioxide in basalt of the upper oceanic crust and technically assisted redistribution of seawater, including artificial upwelling. These listed marine-geoengineering activities are treated as exceptions only when carried out exclusively for scientific research and are subject to a precautionary environmental-protection regime, including requirements directed at marine protected areas, biodiversity, human health, water quality, waste prevention, scientific quality, independent review and the absence of economic motivation for research. The Act is therefore both enabling for offshore geological carbon dioxide storage and restrictive for experimental marine carbon-removal interventions. Crucially, promulgation did not make the amendment immediately operative: Article 2 provides that it enters into force only when at least one of the relevant London Protocol resolutions, LP.3(4) or LP.5(14), becomes effective for Germany, and the responsible federal ministry must announce that date in the Federal Law Gazette. As of the current database update, the official consolidated High Seas Dumping Act still reflects the pre-amendment text and the commencement date has not been announced. The Act therefore does not yet constitute an effective deployment authorization for the listed marine geoengineering techniques or a project-specific storage permit.
source: Federal Republic of Germany — German Bundestag / Federal Ministry for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety
status_note: Promulgated on 13 March 2026 as BGBl. 2026 I No. 70; entry into force remains conditional on LP.3(4) or LP.5(14) becoming effective for Germany and a federal commencement notice.

subnational_area: Germany; cross-border export of CO2 streams for offshore geological storage under the London Protocol
document_title: Gesetz zu den Entschließungen LP.3(4) vom 30. Oktober 2009 und LP.5(14) vom 11. Oktober 2019 über die Änderung des Artikels 6 des Protokolls vom 7. November 1996 zum Übereinkommen über die Verhütung der Meeresverschmutzung durch das Einbringen von Abfällen und anderen Stoffen von 1972 (Londoner Protokoll)
notes: This German treaty-approval law gives national legislative consent to London Protocol Resolution LP.3(4), which amends Article 6 to permit the export of carbon dioxide streams for disposal in sub-seabed geological formations under specified international arrangements, and to Resolution LP.5(14), which provides a mechanism for provisional application of that Article 6 amendment before it enters into force internationally. The law was promulgated on 13 March 2026 in Federal Law Gazette 2026 II No. 49 and entered into force on the day after promulgation. Its policy function is to create the constitutional and legal basis for Germany to accept the Article 6 amendment and, where the relevant international conditions are met, participate in cross-border carbon dioxide transport and offshore storage chains. The underlying London Protocol framework requires exporting and receiving states to conclude an agreement or arrangement allocating permitting responsibilities and ensuring protection of the marine environment. The measure is especially relevant to German emitters because offshore storage capacity may be accessed in Germany or in neighbouring storage jurisdictions through cross-border networks. However, the national approval law does not itself constitute an agreement with any particular receiving state, does not issue a transport or storage permit, does not approve an offshore storage formation, and does not demonstrate that any export or injection has commenced. The law also distinguishes its own domestic entry into force from the international effectiveness of LP.3(4) and LP.5(14) for Germany: the dates on which those resolutions become effective for Germany must be separately announced in the Federal Law Gazette. It should therefore be treated as an active international-governance enabling instrument rather than evidence that all cross-border operational prerequisites are already satisfied.
source: Federal Republic of Germany — German Bundestag / Federal Ministry for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety
status_note: Promulgated on 13 March 2026 as BGBl. 2026 II No. 49 and effective the following day; separate notice is required for the date on which LP.3(4) or LP.5(14) becomes effective for Germany.

subnational_area: France, including the continental shelf and exclusive economic zone under French jurisdiction
document_title: Loi n° 2026-403 du 26 mai 2026 de simplification de la vie économique — Article 43 amendments relevant to geological CO2 storage
notes: France's Law No. 2026-403 of 26 May 2026 on simplifying economic life includes, in Article 43, a package of amendments to the Mining Code and related environmental provisions that also affect the legal pathway for exploration and development of geological carbon dioxide storage. The amended Environment Code provision governing the search for underground formations suitable for geological CO2 storage requires an exclusive exploration permit and connects the permit holder to the development phase provided by the Mining Code. The revised framework also changes how conflicts are handled when proposed CO2-storage exploration overlaps with existing mining or underground-storage titles, allowing the minister responsible for mines to resolve the disagreement where the existing titleholder does not provide express consent within the regulatory period. Other Article 43 amendments simplify and reorganize procedures for mining and underground-storage titles, including concessions, extensions, environmental analysis and title administration. These changes are directly relevant to offshore carbon storage because France's geological CO2-storage regime applies not only on national territory but also on the continental shelf and in the exclusive economic zone under French jurisdiction. The law is an enabling procedural reform rather than a project approval: it does not select an offshore storage site, issue an exclusive exploration permit or storage concession, authorize carbon dioxide injection, quantify storage capacity, verify permanence, or establish carbon credits. Project-specific exploration, environmental authorization, concession and operating requirements remain necessary under the Environment Code and Mining Code. The law was promulgated on 26 May 2026 and the relevant amended Environment Code provisions are shown by Légifrance as in force from 28 May 2026; some broader Mining Code simplification provisions in Article 43 have separate commencement arrangements and may depend on implementing decrees.
source: French Republic — Légifrance / Ministry responsible for ecological transition and mining
status_note: Promulgated on 26 May 2026; relevant CO2-storage amendments are reflected in the Environment Code from 28 May 2026, while some associated mining-procedure provisions have separate commencement rules.

subnational_area: France, including maritime public domain, territorial waters, exclusive economic zone seabed and continental shelf
document_title: Décret n° 2025-851 du 27 août 2025 relatif aux titres miniers et aux titres de stockage souterrain
