status_note: Public consultation ran from 28 May to 12 June 2026; this draft was superseded by the final Liaoning 15th Five-Year Marine Economy Development Plan issued later in 2026.

document_title: 威海市人民政府办公室关于修改威海市蓝碳经济发展行动方案（2021—2025年）的通知
notes: This 2022 notice formally modified and reissued Weihai's 2021–2025 Blue Carbon Economy Development Action Plan, replacing the original 2021 notice. The amended plan continued the city's integrated programme for blue-carbon science, carbon-sink survey and evaluation, methodology and standards development, shellfish-algae carbon-sink research and marine negative-emissions technology demonstration. The document therefore provides the operative historical version for most of the plan period and shows how Weihai institutionalized blue carbon across research, engineering and market-governance functions. The plan period ended in 2025, and the notice itself did not create a site-specific deployment authorization, a stand-alone credit issuance rule or a verified quantity of marine carbon removals.
source: People's Government of Weihai Municipality
status_note: Modified and reissued in January 2022, superseding the 2021 version; the underlying 2021–2025 action-plan period has now ended.

document_title: 《威海市蓝碳经济发展行动方案（2021—2025年）》实施情况评估报告
notes: This official Weihai assessment reviews implementation of the city's 2021–2025 Blue Carbon Economy Development Action Plan after the end of its programme period. It reports on progress against the action plan's research, standards, institutional and blue-carbon development tasks and describes completion of the municipal blue-carbon policy and technical-system build-out. The report is useful evidence for distinguishing planned measures from activities that the city considers implemented or completed. It is retrospective assessment evidence rather than a new rule: it does not itself authorize a marine carbon-removal project, create a new crediting methodology, issue carbon units or extend the expired 2021–2025 action-plan period.
source: Weihai Municipal Marine Development Bureau / People's Government of Weihai Municipality
status_note: Official implementation assessment published in December 2025 after completion of the 2021–2025 action-plan period; it is a retrospective evaluation, not a successor policy.

document_title: 厦门经济特区海洋经济促进规定
notes: The Xiamen Special Economic Zone Provisions on Promoting the Marine Economy create a binding municipal legal basis for developing marine ecosystem-product value mechanisms and marine carbon-sink systems. The provisions direct the city to explore marine ecological-product trading rules and to build marine carbon-sink monitoring and accounting capacity through baseline surveys, observation plans, accounting standards and trading rules. They also support sink-enhancement pilots involving mariculture, coastal wetlands, mangroves and seagrass, connecting research and monitoring to practical ecosystem and aquaculture interventions. The law sets duties and policy direction but leaves detailed accounting formulas, project eligibility, credit issuance and individual ecological or sea-use approvals to subsequent implementing rules and project decisions.
source: Standing Committee of the Xiamen Municipal People's Congress
status_note: Adopted on 26 December 2023 and effective from 1 March 2024; active municipal legislation as of 7 August 2026.

document_title: 厦门市人民政府关于印发加快推进海洋经济高质量发展若干措施的通知（厦府规〔2025〕9号）
notes: Xiamen's 2025 measures for accelerating high-quality marine-economy development include a dedicated effort to deepen the city's marine carbon-sink trading infrastructure. The measures support the existing marine carbon-sink trading platform, conversion of monitoring and evaluation technologies, development of a methodology system, improved trading monitoring and verification, and expansion of cross-regional marine carbon-sink transactions. This makes the document a concrete municipal implementation policy for market and MRV capacity rather than a generic blue-economy statement. It does not itself validate a particular project, define every methodology formula, issue a carbon unit or authorize an ocean carbon-removal intervention; those functions remain with technical standards, project processes and market rules.
source: People's Government of Xiamen Municipality
status_note: Municipal normative policy issued in 2025 with a stated five-year validity period; active as of 7 August 2026.

document_title: 厦门市海洋环境保护若干规定（修订草案）
notes: The 2026 revision draft of Xiamen's marine environmental protection provisions contains a proposed blue-carbon governance clause. It would promote a marine carbon-sink trading mechanism, support research and standards for marine carbon sinks, and allow the purchase of marine carbon sinks or participation in marine carbon-sink projects to be considered in ecological-damage compensation arrangements. The draft therefore connects carbon-sink markets, technical standardization and environmental liability within a local legislative framework. Public consultation has ended, but the reviewed official material did not confirm final enactment of this revision; the draft should not be treated as binding current law, a crediting methodology, a project approval or evidence that compensation transactions have occurred.
source: Standing Committee of the Xiamen Municipal People's Congress
status_note: Public consultation opened on 17 March 2026 and closed on 18 April 2026; final enactment of the revision was not confirmed as of 7 August 2026.

document_title: 中华人民共和国国民经济和社会发展第十五个五年规划纲要
notes: China's national 15th Five-Year Plan Outline places marine carbon sinks within the country's broader ocean survey, ecological monitoring and carbon-accounting agenda. The outline calls for a new round of marine investigation, stronger ecological early-warning and monitoring capabilities, and exploration of marine carbon-sink accounting. This gives national strategic backing to the evidence and accounting infrastructure needed for later blue-carbon and marine carbon-sink policies. The wording is exploratory: the outline does not itself publish a marine accounting methodology, establish a marine crediting programme, quantify additional ocean removals, approve a project or authorize deployment of a marine carbon-removal technology.
source: National People's Congress of China / Government of the People's Republic of China
status_note: National 15th Five-Year development outline approved in 2026 and active for 2026–2030; marine carbon-sink accounting remains an explicitly exploratory implementation task.

document_title: “十五五”生态环境监测规划
notes: China's national 15th Five-Year ecological-environment monitoring plan explicitly advances a marine carbon-sink monitoring system. Official implementation material calls for establishing or improving monitoring and accounting work mechanisms for key coastal blue-carbon ecosystems including salt marshes, mangroves and seagrass beds. This is important evidence-building infrastructure for consistent inventories, long-term observation, accounting and later verification of marine sink outcomes. The plan is not a carbon-credit methodology or ecological restoration authorization and it does not claim quantified additional removals; its direct role is to strengthen monitoring, data and accounting capability across identified coastal ecosystems.
source: Ministry of Ecology and Environment / National Development and Reform Commission of China
status_note: National monitoring plan issued in July 2026 and active for the 15th Five-Year period; marine blue-carbon monitoring and accounting mechanisms are implementation tasks under development.

document_title: 国家应对气候变化“十五五”规划
notes: China's national 15th Five-Year climate-change plan includes ocean carbon-cycle research within a broader programme for climate science, ecosystem sinks and carbon-market governance. The plan calls for research on linkages between terrestrial and ocean carbon cycles and climate risks, while also strengthening ecosystem carbon-sink measurement, monitoring, accounting and carbon-stock surveys and improving the national voluntary greenhouse-gas reduction market's methodology and project-management system. The ocean-specific element is therefore primarily scientific and evidence-building rather than a deployment programme. The plan does not establish a dedicated ocean-removal methodology, authorize a marine geoengineering activity, quantify achieved marine removals or show that a specific ocean project has received credits.
source: Ministry of Ecology and Environment of the People's Republic of China
status_note: National climate-change plan issued in July 2026 and active for the 15th Five-Year period; the ocean-carbon component is a research and monitoring priority rather than a deployment authorization.

document_title: Niue NDC 3.0 — Carbon Storage Capacity and Marine Territory Preservation
notes: Niue's NDC 3.0 links its 2030 carbon-storage ambition with preservation of its extensive marine territory, placing ocean conservation within the country's mitigation and resilience narrative. The NDC commits to enhancing carbon-storage capacity through land and ecosystem initiatives and explicitly identifies preservation of the marine territory as part of that broader direction. The document does not provide a stand-alone quantified marine CO2-removal target, identify a mangrove or seagrass pathway, specify an ocean carbon accounting methodology, or establish a marine crediting mechanism. It is therefore recorded conservatively as a national climate commitment with marine carbon-storage relevance rather than as evidence of a deployed blue-carbon or marine CDR engineering project.
source: Government of Niue / UNFCCC
status_note: Active NDC 3.0 submitted on 17 July 2025; marine preservation is part of the national carbon-storage and climate commitment, without a separate quantified marine-removal programme.

document_title: 海南低碳岛建设方案
notes: Hainan's Low-Carbon Island Construction Plan creates a province-wide policy package for expanding both terrestrial and marine carbon sinks. Its marine component calls for stronger basic research on marine ecosystem carbon sinks, wider use of ecological carbon-sequestration and restoration technologies, systematic restoration of mangroves, coral reefs and seagrass beds, development of marine ranching and stronger fishery carbon-sink capacity. The plan sets an indicative 2030 mangrove-area objective of about 119,000 mu and a longer-term direction for a substantially larger blue-carbon contribution by 2045. These are strategic ecosystem and sink-enhancement objectives rather than verified additional removals: the plan does not provide a project-level baseline, a blue-carbon crediting methodology, a quantified tCO2e removal target for the marine package, or authorization for a named restoration or aquaculture project.
source: People's Government of Hainan Province
status_note: Provincial low-carbon island plan issued in 2025 and active; the marine blue-carbon actions are implementation and capacity-building objectives extending toward 2030 and 2045.

document_title: 2026年度省自然科学基金拟资助项目清单 — ONCE-relevant marine carbon research
notes: Zhejiang's 2026 provincial natural-science funding list contains several distinct projects directly relevant to Global ONCE research. The proposed portfolio includes continuous observation of how the biological carbon pump in the Yangtze Estuary responds to typhoons (QK26D060003, Second Institute of Oceanography), research on the evolution and controls of marine particulate organic-carbon burial in hypoxic coastal waters of Zhejiang (QK26D060007, Second Institute of Oceanography), and a continuing distinguished-young-scholar project on the carbon-sink efficiency and enhancement mechanisms of emerging blue-carbon macroalgal beds (RG26D060001, Zhejiang University). Together these projects strengthen observation, process understanding and sink-enhancement science across coastal carbon burial, BCP dynamics and macroalgal blue carbon. The source is a proposed-funding list, so it should not be interpreted as evidence of completed research outcomes, quantified anthropogenic removals, operational carbon-credit methodologies or deployment authorization.
source: Natural Science Foundation of Zhejiang Province / Zhejiang Provincial Department of Science and Technology
status_note: Included in the official list of projects proposed for 2026 provincial natural-science funding; project-level research results and any later deployment outcomes were not yet established by this funding list.

document_title: 福建省霞浦县自然资源局霞浦县盐田乡和长春镇红树林植被修复项目 — CCER Registration
notes: The Xiapu County mangrove vegetation restoration project in Yantian Township and Changchun Town completed registration in China's national voluntary greenhouse-gas reduction registration system in March 2026, becoming the country's first registered marine-sector CCER project. The project was developed through cooperation between Xiapu County and the Third Institute of Oceanography and is based on mangrove restoration work undertaken in local coastal waters. Official information states a 40-year crediting period and an expected total of 32,466 tonnes of CO2 reductions/removals over that period. Registration is a major market-access milestone but is not the same as final issuance: the projected 32,466 tonnes are ex-ante expectations, and actual CCER units require subsequent monitoring, verification and issuance under the national system. The registration also does not replace ecological restoration, sea-use or other legal approvals applicable to the underlying project activities.
source: Department of Natural Resources of Fujian Province / Xiapu County People's Government / Third Institute of Oceanography
status_note: National CCER project registration completed in March 2026; 40-year crediting period and 32,466 tCO2 expected total are project projections, with monitoring and issuance still required for realized credits.

document_title: 广州首个海洋碳汇项目首期减排量签发 — Nansha Mangrove GZCER
notes: Guangzhou's Ecology and Environment Bureau officially reported successful first-period issuance for the city's first marine carbon-sink project in Nansha Wetland. The issuance totals 1,251 tCO2e and corresponds exactly to the two previously publicized Phase I applications: 554 tCO2e from the mangrove afforestation component and 697 tCO2e from the mangrove restoration component. The projects used Guangzhou's 2025 trial mangrove carbon-inclusion methodology, clarified project carbon rights and underwent third-party verification before issuance. The official announcement states that the issued reductions are planned for transaction through the Guangzhou Emissions Exchange using negotiated or auction-based approaches, so issuance is confirmed while completion of a subsequent market sale should not be assumed from this document alone. Project revenues are intended to support continued mangrove establishment, restoration, monitoring, management and ecosystem improvement.
source: Guangzhou Municipal Ecology and Environment Bureau
status_note: First-period GZCER issuance confirmed in 2026 for a total of 1,251 tCO2e, split between 554 tCO2e afforestation and 697 tCO2e restoration; subsequent exchange trading was planned rather than confirmed completed in this source.

document_title: 人力资源社会保障部办公厅 生态环境部办公厅 国家林草局办公室关于颁布碳汇计量评估师国家职业标准的通知
notes: The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and the National Forestry and Grassland Administration jointly promulgated the national occupational standard for Carbon Sink Measurement Evaluators in April 2026. The standard professionalizes competency requirements for personnel engaged in carbon-sink investigation, monitoring, measurement, accounting, verification-related evaluation and technical assessment across ecosystem sink activities, providing a national workforce and quality-control foundation that is relevant to marine and coastal carbon-sink measurement as part of the broader carbon-sink profession. For the Global ONCE database, its principal significance is standardization and measurement capacity rather than authorization of a specific marine intervention. It does not establish a mangrove, seagrass, seaweed, ocean-alkalinity or geological-storage project methodology, does not issue carbon credits, does not quantify additional marine removals and does not itself approve deployment. Its practical effect is to standardize professional capabilities that can support more consistent carbon-sink data and assessment.
source: Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security / Ministry of Ecology and Environment / National Forestry and Grassland Administration, China
status_note: National occupational standard formally promulgated for implementation by joint ministerial notice dated 7 April 2026 and published in April 2026.

document_title: 令和8年版 環境・循環型社会・生物多様性白書
notes: Japan's 2026 Environment, Sound Material-Cycle Society and Biodiversity White Paper reports and sets out government measures for advancing blue-carbon action. It promotes conservation, restoration and creation of blue-carbon ecosystems including mangroves, salt marshes and tidal flats, seagrass meadows and seaweed beds, while also identifying offshore blue carbon as an emerging policy and research area. The white paper specifically discusses producing and growing seaweed to absorb greenhouse gases, storing or fixing the resulting carbon in the deep sea, and examining how such removals could be calculated and evaluated in light of ongoing IPCC work on carbon-dioxide-removal and CCUS inventory guidance. It calls for inter-ministerial and public-private coordination to examine these pathways. This is a significant policy-planning and evidence-building step, but the offshore and deep-sea concepts remain under study: the white paper does not itself authorize biomass sinking, establish a project baseline, issue credits, quantify verified removals or create a new permitting regime.
source: Ministry of the Environment, Japan
status_note: Cabinet-approved 2026 annual environment white paper published on 5 June 2026; reported measures are active while offshore blue-carbon accounting and deep-sea storage concepts remain under examination.

document_title: Belize NDC 3.0 Update
notes: Belize's NDC 3.0, submitted to the UNFCCC in June 2025, updates the country's medium-term climate commitments and maintains coastal and marine ecosystems as part of its mitigation and resilience strategy. The document strengthens actions for mangrove conservation and restoration and places coastal and marine resource preservation within the national climate framework, building on the previous commitment to enhance mangrove and seagrass carbon-sink capacity. The NDC links ecosystem protection and restoration with climate mitigation, coastal protection, biodiversity and sustainable development and provides the formal national commitment context for continued implementation through 2035. This record is kept separate from Belize's 2021 updated NDC because it is a new formal NDC version. The NDC is a national commitment rather than a project-level crediting methodology: it does not by itself certify individual mangrove removals, issue blue-carbon credits, establish additionality for a specific project or replace the detailed MRV and accounting rules needed for verified market issuance.
source: Government of Belize / UNFCCC
status_note: Active NDC 3.0 submitted to the UNFCCC on 14 June 2025, superseding the earlier 2021 updated NDC as Belize’s latest formal contribution.

document_title: Bahrain NDC 3.0
notes: Bahrain's NDC 3.0 converts the country's mangrove ambition into a quantified 2035 contribution with a defined reference indicator. It commits to planting 1.6 million mangrove seedlings by 2035, uses 2021 as the reference year with a zero-seedling reference point for this contribution, and identifies the Ministry of Municipalities Affairs and Agriculture and the Supreme Council for Environment among the relevant data providers. The NDC treats mangrove planting as an adaptation action with mitigation co-benefits, including coastal resilience, and states that implementation of the overall NDC is conditional on sufficient means of implementation and may draw on financing sources including carbon markets. This is a formal national climate commitment and a stronger reporting basis than a general mangrove policy statement. It does not, however, establish a blue-carbon crediting methodology, determine project-level additionality, quantify verified tonnes of CO2 removed by the seedlings, or guarantee that planting outcomes will generate tradable carbon units.
source: Kingdom of Bahrain / UNFCCC
status_note: Active NDC 3.0 submitted to the UNFCCC on 1 December 2025; mangrove contribution runs from 2022 to 2035 and is conditional on adequate means of implementation.

document_title: National Adaptation Investment Plan – Bahrain
notes: Bahrain's National Adaptation Investment Plan translates national adaptation priorities into a portfolio of investment concept notes and explicitly includes restoration of mangrove ecosystems for climate resilience. The mangrove concept combines stronger policy and institutional arrangements for mangrove management, restoration and sustainable management of mangrove ecosystems, and development of a blue-carbon market. The plan assigns an estimated investment envelope to the mangrove concept and identifies possible financing instruments that include grants, concessional finance, government resources and potential sales of blue-carbon credits. It therefore links ecosystem restoration with an intended market and finance architecture rather than treating mangroves solely as coastal protection. The plan also sets out project-management arrangements and responsible institutional roles. The market element is still an investment and implementation concept: this document does not itself create an operating blue-carbon registry, approve a crediting methodology, issue credits, establish verified baselines or demonstrate quantified additional removals from the proposed restoration activities.
source: Kingdom of Bahrain / UNFCCC
status_note: National adaptation investment plan published by the UNFCCC on 30 November 2025; the prioritized concept notes are implementation and financing plans rather than completed projects or an already operational blue-carbon market.

document_title: Bahrain. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1.
notes: Bahrain's first Biennial Transparency Report provides formal progress reporting on the national mangrove contribution and clarifies the status of several blue-carbon-related activities. It reports that Bahrain prioritized the Mangrove Transplantation Project, focused on Tubli Bay and Ras Sanad, with a target of planting 1.6 million mangrove seedlings by 2035 and implementation beginning in 2022. The report also records other strategies that had been under consideration, including an observatory in Tubli Bay, creation of a blue-carbon inventory consistent with international methodological guidance to estimate and document carbon pools and fluxes, and economic valuation of mangrove ecosystem services. The BTR is important because it distinguishes implemented restoration from proposed evidence and accounting measures. It does not indicate that the blue-carbon inventory or valuation system is already complete, and the transparency report itself does not establish a crediting mechanism, issue credits or provide project-level verified removal quantities for the mangrove transplantation programme.
source: Kingdom of Bahrain / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR submitted on 30 November 2025; mangrove transplantation is reported as in progress, while the Tubli Bay blue-carbon inventory and ecosystem-valuation concepts are described as strategies considered alongside the prioritized restoration project.

document_title: Seychelles. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1. National Communication (NC). NC4.
notes: Seychelles' first Biennial Transparency Report and fourth National Communication documents the country's first attempt to bring seagrass blue carbon directly into its national greenhouse-gas inventory. Using the national seagrass blue-carbon assessment and IPCC inventory software, the report finds that inclusion of seagrass materially changes the LULUCF sink and key-category analysis compared with the previous inventory. It states that the underlying carbon-estimation sampling followed the Coastal Blue Carbon manual and the IPCC coastal-wetlands accounting framework, while also documenting important data limitations and methodological assumptions. This makes the BTR a formal transparency and accounting milestone that complements, but is distinct from, the separate National Inventory Document already in the database. The report does not convert the estimated national sink into project credits, does not authorize seagrass restoration deployment, and does not establish project-specific additionality or permanence rules; its primary role is national reporting, methodological transparency and evidence building.
source: Government of Seychelles / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR and fourth National Communication submitted to the UNFCCC on 15 July 2025; seagrass inclusion is implemented in national reporting but remains constrained by data and methodological uncertainty.

document_title: Australia's first Biennial Transparency Report
notes: Australia's first Biennial Transparency Report provides a formal national progress account of the Blue Carbon Conservation, Restoration and Accounting Program. It reports Australian Government investment of AUD 9.5 million over four years from 2021–22 to 2024–25 for five on-ground projects restoring degraded mangrove, saltmarsh and seagrass ecosystems. The projects are intended to demonstrate, measure and account for climate, biodiversity, Indigenous and community benefits and to build a trusted approach capable of supporting greater private investment through carbon and environmental markets. The report states that four of the five restoration projects may be eligible to register under the ACCU Scheme blue-carbon method and that one project became the first registered project under that method on 5 June 2024. The BTR therefore documents both deployment and linkage to an operating national crediting framework, but registration is not the same as issuance: the report does not state that all five projects have generated credits or that their future removal quantities are guaranteed.
source: Australian Government / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR submitted for the 2024 transparency cycle; the four-year restoration and accounting programme ran through 2024–25, with one project reported as registered under the ACCU blue-carbon method on 5 June 2024.

document_title: Singapore's First Biennial Transparency Report 2024
notes: Singapore's first Biennial Transparency Report records completion of a dedicated Blue Carbon Policy and Finance Capacity Building Workshop under the Singapore–United Kingdom Third Country Training Programme. The workshop, held on 17–18 October 2023 and co-organized with the United Kingdom, the National University of Singapore Centre for Nature-based Climate Solutions and Conservation International, brought together 25 participants from ASEAN and AOSIS member States. It provided technical knowledge on policy and finance tools for conserving and restoring coastal blue-carbon ecosystems and strengthened participants' understanding of implementation potential for national mitigation and adaptation actions. The BTR therefore documents an implemented international capacity-building and policy-support activity directly relevant to blue-carbon governance and finance. It does not describe a Singapore blue-carbon removal project, quantify domestic removals, create a carbon-credit methodology or establish a regional market. Its ONCE value lies in formal reporting of completed cross-border knowledge, policy and finance capacity building.
source: Government of Singapore / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR submitted on 4 December 2024; the blue-carbon policy and finance workshop reported in the document was completed in October 2023.

document_title: Japan's First Biennial Transparency Report under the Paris Agreement
notes: Japan's first Biennial Transparency Report formally identifies blue-carbon initiatives as part of the policy package supporting implementation of Japan's NDC. The report states that initiatives related to blue carbon will be promoted alongside other carbon-sink measures and, in its detailed policy discussion, recognizes seaweed beds, seagrass beds and tidal flats as relevant blue-carbon ecosystems while noting that calculation methods are not yet fully established for all components. It reports continuing research aimed at establishing robust calculation approaches and contributing to future IPCC inventory guidance, together with conservation, creation and restoration activities. The document therefore links national mitigation policy, ecosystem restoration and methodological development within the Paris Agreement transparency system. It does not mean that every blue-carbon ecosystem is already counted in the national inventory, does not create a new J-Credit methodology by itself, and does not provide verified project-level removal quantities or authorize a specific deployment.
source: Government of Japan / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR for the 2024 transparency cycle; the UNFCCC-hosted report has a revised file dated 2025, while the underlying submission remains Japan’s first BTR under the Paris Agreement.

document_title: Bangladesh. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1.
notes: Bangladesh's first Biennial Transparency Report provides a formal greenhouse-gas inventory treatment of forest and other land uses that explicitly includes the Sundarbans mangrove forest and coastal plantations. The report describes use of IPCC inventory software, national land-cover mapping, national forest-inventory data, biomass and soil-organic-carbon factors, and a forest definition adapted to national mangrove conditions, including the low-stature Ceriops decandra areas of the Sundarbans. It reports that the Sundarbans mangrove resource is in good condition and that coastal plantations show an increasing trend while setting out the data and methodological basis used to estimate emissions and removals in the forest and land-use sector. This is directly relevant to coastal carbon accounting and MRV, but it is a national inventory report rather than a blue-carbon project methodology. It does not establish additionality, issue credits, authorize new mangrove planting or provide a stand-alone verified marine-removal quantity.
source: Government of Bangladesh / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR submitted to the UNFCCC on 31 December 2025 and published in January 2026; national mangrove and coastal-plantation data are incorporated into the land-use inventory framework.

document_title: The People's Republic of China First Biennial Transparency Report on Climate Change
notes: China's first Biennial Transparency Report records national policy implementation relevant to coastal blue carbon within the Paris Agreement transparency framework. The report states that guidance has been provided for social investment in blue-carbon protection and restoration projects covering mangroves, seagrass beds, coastal salt marshes, seaweed farms and other coastal zones. It places those activities alongside marine ecological-environment planning, integrated management of key sea areas and broader measures to improve climate resilience and ecosystem governance. The report therefore provides a formal national account that blue-carbon protection and restoration are being connected to policy guidance and investment rather than remaining solely a research topic. The BTR does not itself create a unified national blue-carbon crediting methodology, quantify a single national removal amount for the listed ecosystems, authorize individual restoration projects or demonstrate that all social-investment activities generate tradable credits. Its primary role is transparency reporting and policy implementation documentation.
source: Government of the People’s Republic of China / UNFCCC
status_note: China’s first BTR was submitted for the 2024 transparency cycle on 31 December 2024 and published by the UNFCCC in early 2025; the report documents active policy guidance and implementation measures.

subnational_area: United Kingdom and Crown Dependencies reported in the BTR
document_title: UK's first Biennial Transparency Report submitted to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, under the Paris Agreement
notes: The United Kingdom's first Biennial Transparency Report consolidates multiple blue-carbon policy, evidence and restoration activities across the UK and Crown Dependencies into a formal Paris Agreement progress report. It records Northern Ireland's development of a blue-carbon action plan, Scotland's Blue Economy Vision and Blue Carbon Forum evidence work, Jersey's prioritization of local blue-carbon sinks and seabed-carbon studies, Guernsey's blue-carbon assessment and marine spatial planning, Isle of Man blue-carbon mapping and management planning, and wider UK commitments to protect, restore and create blue-carbon habitats. It also reports coastal restoration programmes such as ReMeMaRe and the role of national adaptation planning. The report demonstrates that blue carbon has entered multi-jurisdictional policy planning, mapping and restoration practice, but it does not provide a single UK-wide verified removal total, create one uniform crediting methodology, or imply that every mapped seabed carbon stock is an additional anthropogenic removal eligible for carbon markets.
source: UK Government / Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
status_note: First UK BTR published and submitted on 27 December 2024; it reports a mixture of active restoration, evidence programmes and policy-development actions across UK jurisdictions.

document_title: Oman's First Biennial Transparency Report
notes: Oman's first Biennial Transparency Report documents active national mangrove restoration and its intended climate-mitigation contribution. The report describes cooperation with FAO on a comprehensive mangrove restoration programme designed to protect and enhance coastal mangrove ecosystems, use their carbon-sequestration potential in support of Oman's net-zero goal, involve fishing communities and improve restoration tracking through advanced monitoring systems such as FAO's SEPAL platform. The BTR also places mangrove activity within the country's broader climate-adaptation and mitigation implementation framework. This creates a formal transparency record linking coastal ecosystem restoration, carbon sequestration, community participation and monitoring. The report does not establish a project-level carbon-credit methodology, does not state that the restoration programme has generated issued credits, and does not provide a verified additional-removal total attributable to a specific mangrove project. Reported targets and expected mitigation benefits therefore should not be treated as certified carbon-market outcomes.
source: Sultanate of Oman / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR finalized and submitted in 2025; mangrove restoration cooperation is reported as active, with monitoring and programme implementation continuing.

subnational_area: International cooperation with Indonesia and Colombia
document_title: Norway's first Biennial Transparency Report under the Paris Agreement
notes: Norway's first Biennial Transparency Report documents international support for blue-carbon governance, markets and mangrove restoration through Norway's ocean-related development cooperation. It reports that Norway and Indonesia signed a cooperation framework running to 2028 that includes technical support to develop a robust and high-integrity national blue-carbon market, with intended outcomes including increased and verifiable carbon sequestration in coastal blue-carbon habitats and measurable financial and community benefits from blue-carbon projects. The BTR also reports support in Colombia for integrated mangrove management and mangrove restoration programmes. The record is therefore relevant to international market governance, MRV capacity, finance and ecosystem implementation rather than only general ocean cooperation. The reported Indonesian market is a development objective supported by technical assistance; the BTR does not state that a complete national blue-carbon crediting system was already operational at submission, and it does not issue credits or quantify verified project removals itself.
source: Government of Norway / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR submitted for the 2024 transparency cycle; Norway–Indonesia ocean cooperation is reported as running through 2028, while the blue-carbon market component remains a supported development and integrity-building process.

subnational_area: International support to SIDS and coastal developing countries
document_title: Canada's First Biennial Transparency Report
notes: Canada's first Biennial Transparency Report records climate-finance support for ocean and coastal nature-based solutions through the Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance. It reports a CAD 9 million contribution supporting Small Island Developing States and coastal developing countries in developing innovative finance and insurance solutions, including examples in which mangrove restoration may be financed through carbon credits. Under Canada's support, ORRAA selected locally led projects involving feasibility studies, pilot testing and implementation of financing solutions integrated with conservation and blue-carbon activities, capacity building, research, policy engagement and public-private partnerships. The report also describes support for scoping the Sea Change Impact Financing Facility, intended to mobilize large-scale private investment into coastal and ocean ecosystems. These are finance and market-enabling interventions rather than a Canadian blue-carbon credit standard: the BTR does not certify individual projects, guarantee carbon-credit issuance, quantify verified removals or establish additionality and permanence rules for the supported activities.
source: Government of Canada / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR for the 2024 transparency cycle; reported international blue-carbon and coastal-finance support was active through ORRAA and related financing-development activities.

document_title: Kenya's First Biennial Transparency Report
notes: Kenya's first Biennial Transparency Report places blue carbon explicitly within the country's adaptation and climate-policy implementation pipeline. The report lists a blue-carbon readiness assessment intended to support full integration of blue-carbon and ocean-climate actions into future NDC implementation, together with marine spatial planning, governance of coastal ecosystems, opportunities for nature-based enterprises such as seaweed farming and mangrove ecotourism, and implementation of the national mangrove management plan through national and county development planning. These measures show that Kenya is building the policy, evidence and institutional conditions for blue-carbon implementation rather than treating coastal ecosystems only as a biodiversity issue. The BTR does not itself establish a national blue-carbon registry or crediting methodology, does not certify seaweed or mangrove removals, and does not mean that every listed adaptation programme was fully implemented at the reporting date. The readiness assessment in particular is an evidence and integration step, not proof of quantified carbon removal.
source: Government of Kenya / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR submitted in December 2024; the report includes a mixture of planned and ongoing blue-carbon readiness, coastal planning, mangrove-management and nature-based enterprise actions.

document_title: Liberia. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1. National Communications (NC). NC3
notes: Liberia's first Biennial Transparency Report and third National Communication explicitly recognize coastal-zone protection through mangrove restoration as an adaptation action with mitigation co-benefits. The report identifies significant CO2 sequestration in coastal mangrove biomass and soils and notes that mangrove restoration can also reduce carbon losses associated with coastal erosion and soil disturbance. In parallel, the report identifies planned improvements to future reporting, including stronger integration of land-use activity data with the National Forest Monitoring System, improved uncertainty assessment, a dedicated greenhouse-gas inventory database integrated with the national MRV system and strengthened QA/QC. This makes the document relevant both to implementation of mangrove-based sink enhancement and to the accounting infrastructure needed to track such outcomes. The BTR does not create a project crediting methodology, issue carbon units or provide a separately verified blue-carbon removal total for mangrove restoration; its quantified and qualitative statements remain national transparency reporting.
source: Government of Liberia / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR and third National Communication submitted on 7 July 2026; mangrove restoration is reported as a mitigation-co-benefit action and inventory/MRV improvements are identified for subsequent reporting cycles.

document_title: Belize's First Biennial Transparency Report
notes: Belize's first Biennial Transparency Report provides a detailed formal progress account for the country's coastal and marine NDC actions. It reiterates the target to enhance the capacity of mangrove and seagrass ecosystems to act as carbon sinks by 2030 and reports the earlier commitment to remove a cumulative 381 ktCO2e between 2021 and 2030 through mangrove restoration. It documents implementation measures supporting marine spatial planning, governance, monitoring and enforcement of coastal resources and also records a planned National Seagrass Management Policy whose objectives include improved protection of seagrass ecosystems to maintain carbon-sink services. The report is unusually explicit about transparency limitations: it states that estimates of expected and achieved GHG reductions from the listed policies are not yet available and that additional reporting capacity is needed for BTR2. Accordingly, the BTR documents targets, governance and implementation status but does not verify that the 381 ktCO2e target has been achieved, issue credits or establish project-level additionality.
source: Government of Belize / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR originally submitted on 31 December 2024; the current UNFCCC-hosted file is a revised version dated 22 February 2026. The report notes that quantified achieved reductions for the coastal measures were not yet available.

document_title: Technical analysis of the first biennial update report of Seychelles submitted on 23 February 2024. Summary report by the team of technical experts
notes: This UNFCCC technical-analysis summary report records the independent review of Seychelles' first biennial update report and identifies specific capacity gaps that are directly relevant to coastal blue-carbon accounting. The team of technical experts highlighted the need to build national capacity to quantify greenhouse-gas sequestration by seagrass and mangrove forest ecosystems, strengthen the measurement, reporting and verification system for tracking mitigation actions and policies, and improve the use of international market mechanisms and voluntary cooperative approaches, including accounting for co-benefits from conservation of blue-carbon ecosystems. The findings therefore provide an official international assessment of the country's blue-carbon MRV, accounting and market-readiness needs rather than a new national deployment programme. The report does not establish a project-level carbon-credit methodology, issue internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, authorize mangrove or seagrass restoration, or quantify additional removals attributable to a new intervention. Its ONCE relevance lies in identifying concrete technical and institutional gaps that must be closed before robust blue-carbon sequestration accounting and market participation can be operationalized.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Team of Technical Experts
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical-analysis summary report published on 21 August 2025; it records assessment findings and capacity needs rather than creating a deployment authorization or crediting decision.

document_title: Technical analysis of the first biennial update report of the United Arab Emirates submitted on 25 June 2024. Summary report by the team of technical experts
notes: This UNFCCC technical-analysis summary report independently reviews the United Arab Emirates' first biennial update report and contains a direct finding on mangrove carbon accounting. The reviewed national inventory reported annual LULUCF emissions and removals for several inventory years and, for 2021, explicitly reported CO2 removals from mangroves. The technical experts also found that activity data for land uses and land-use transitions, including wetlands, were not clearly reported and recorded the Party's explanation that data availability, methodological alignment with the country's geographic and ecological conditions, and time constraints limited disaggregation and transparency. The review therefore documents both the existence of national mangrove-removal accounting and material gaps that need to be addressed in subsequent transparency reporting. It is an evidence and quality-assurance document, not a mangrove-restoration authorization. It does not create a carbon-crediting methodology, establish a new sequestration target, validate additionality, issue credits or approve any project. Its ONCE value is the formal international scrutiny of coastal sink inventory data and reporting quality.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Team of Technical Experts
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical-analysis summary report published on 3 September 2025; the review assesses UAE BUR information and reporting limitations but does not itself establish new national legal obligations.

document_title: United Arab Emirates. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1.
notes: The United Arab Emirates' first Biennial Transparency Report provides unusually detailed national reporting on coastal blue-carbon restoration, stock assessment and monitoring. It describes the 100 Million Mangrove Planting Initiative, launched in 2021 with a 2030 target, and states that expansion is expected to increase existing mangrove habitat from about 183 to 483 square kilometres. It also reports the National Carbon Sequestration Project, initiated in 2022 to increase carbon storage, and the National Blue Carbon Project, which assessed carbon storage across mangroves, salt marshes, seagrass meadows and algal mats. The report further describes mangrove carbon-sequestration monitoring, including soil or sediment accretion, and coastal restoration activity in Abu Dhabi, including a goal for 4,500 additional hectares of coastal areas under restoration by 2030. The BTR treats mangrove sequestration as a negative-emissions measure while also documenting the evidence base needed for national reporting. It does not itself issue carbon credits, approve a specific restoration permit or establish a project-level additionality and crediting methodology; its principal function is official transparency reporting on active measures and monitoring.
source: Government of the United Arab Emirates / UNFCCC
status_note: First UAE BTR submitted on 6 November 2025 and published by UNFCCC on 7 November 2025; it reports active national blue-carbon measures and monitoring rather than constituting a new project permit.

document_title: Costa Rica. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1.
notes: Costa Rica's first Biennial Transparency Report formally records implementation of the National Blue Carbon Strategy 2023–2030 as part of the country's climate-policy framework. The strategy is described as an integrated framework for the management, conservation, restoration and rehabilitation of blue-carbon ecosystems and wetlands with carbon-capture potential, while also emphasizing resilience and benefits for coastal communities. The BTR links these measures to broader climate action and highlights participation by communities, women and young people in the stewardship of coastal ecosystems. For the Global ONCE database, the report is important because it is an official UNFCCC transparency submission confirming that blue-carbon ecosystem management is embedded in an active national strategy rather than only discussed as a future concept. The report does not, in the cited blue-carbon material, provide a stand-alone quantified additional-removal volume, issue carbon credits, establish a new offset registry or authorize an individual restoration project. Its principal function is to document policy implementation and national progress, while the underlying strategy provides the operational planning framework for restoration and conservation.
source: Government of Costa Rica / UNFCCC
status_note: Costa Rica submitted and published its first BTR on 31 December 2024; the report records an active 2023–2030 national blue-carbon strategy and related implementation context.

document_title: Panama. Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1.
notes: Panama's first Biennial Transparency Report provides direct evidence that blue-carbon accounting and mangrove-restoration standards have moved from planning into formal national implementation. The report tracks an NDC target requiring national greenhouse-gas inventories to integrate blue carbon using chapter 4 of the 2013 IPCC Wetlands Supplement, with the indicator defined as the annual net emissions balance from coastal wetlands, specifically mangroves. It reports that, since 2022, the inventory has applied the Wetlands Supplement, forest land has been disaggregated to include mangroves and Panama has established an emission factor for carbon accumulated in mangrove ecosystems. The BTR also reports completion of the target to develop a manual of techniques for restoration of degraded mangrove areas, noting that the manual was approved and published in 2021. These are substantive MRV, accounting and technical-standard milestones. The BTR itself does not issue carbon credits, authorize a specific restoration site or claim a separate volume of additional removals; it is an official progress report documenting that the accounting and restoration-governance milestones have been achieved.
source: Government of Panama / UNFCCC
status_note: First Panama BTR published on 10 October 2024; it reports achieved blue-carbon inventory and mangrove-restoration-method milestones under the national NDC framework.

document_title: Colombia. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1.
notes: Colombia's first Biennial Transparency Report contains both direct blue-carbon policy tracking and an explicit accounting limitation that is important for interpreting national removal claims. The report identifies information and emission-factor gaps for marine and coastal blue-carbon ecosystems that prevent robust estimation of associated emissions and removals and explains that categories excluded from the NDC reference scenario are not counted in national NDC accounting until the required information is available. At the same time, it tracks coastal ecosystem actions, including a 2030 target for six climate-adaptation and risk-management initiatives supporting sustainable use of mangroves identified as a blue-carbon ecosystem, implementation of the national mangrove management and conservation programme, and coastal planning actions covering mangroves and seagrass. The BTR therefore combines evidence-building, accounting governance and ecosystem implementation. It does not claim that currently excluded blue-carbon removals are already credited toward the NDC, and it does not issue carbon credits or provide project-level deployment authorization. Its value is the transparent statement of both active ecosystem measures and remaining measurement constraints.
source: Government of Colombia / UNFCCC
status_note: Colombia submitted BTR1 on 31 December 2024; the UNFCCC document page was published in September 2025. The report records active blue-carbon actions while explicitly identifying unresolved national accounting gaps.

document_title: Report on the technical expert review of the first biennial transparency report of Panama
notes: This UNFCCC technical expert review independently evaluates Panama's first Biennial Transparency Report and provides a formal external confirmation of two ONCE-relevant implementation milestones. The review table records Panama's NDC indicator for the annual net balance of emissions from coastal wetlands, specifically mangroves, using the IPCC Wetlands Supplement and concludes that the target has been achieved because the national greenhouse-gas inventory has been prepared using chapter 4 of the Wetlands Supplement since 2022. It also reviews the target to develop a manual of techniques for restoration of degraded mangrove areas and confirms that the manual was approved and published in April 2021, again treating the target as achieved. This makes the review more than a simple repetition of the BTR: it is an independent transparency-framework assessment of reported implementation status. The report does not create a new mangrove methodology, issue credits, quantify project-level additional removals or grant a restoration permit. Its ONCE significance is external verification of national MRV and technical-governance progress under the Paris Agreement transparency system.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Expert Review Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical expert review report published on 11 April 2025; it independently confirms reported achievement of Panama coastal-wetland accounting and mangrove-restoration-manual targets.

document_title: Report on the technical expert review of the first biennial transparency report of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
notes: This UNFCCC technical expert review of the United Kingdom's first Biennial Transparency Report contains a distinct official assessment of blue-carbon measures reported across the country's marine and fisheries adaptation framework. The review records actions under the United Kingdom's Third National Adaptation Programme to protect, restore and create blue-carbon habitats and notes the ongoing Manx Blue Carbon Project, which maps and manages marine carbon stores for sequestration and ecosystem resilience. It also records Northern Ireland's Blue Carbon Action Plan, Scotland's wider blue-economy and marine-protection measures, and marine monitoring and policy frameworks relevant to climate-resilient fisheries and coastal ecosystems. The document is therefore an international technical assessment of reported policy implementation rather than a new domestic blue-carbon strategy. It does not set a separate national removal target, establish a carbon-credit methodology, issue credits or authorize an individual restoration activity. Its principal ONCE contribution is independent review evidence that blue-carbon habitat protection, mapping and restoration are embedded in ongoing UK and devolved marine-climate policy and are being tracked within the Paris Agreement transparency framework.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Expert Review Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical expert review report published on 17 October 2025 following the May 2025 review; it assesses reported blue-carbon and marine-resilience measures without creating new domestic authorization.

document_title: Report on the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference emission level and forest reference level of Samoa submitted in 2024
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment of Samoa's proposed forest reference emission level and forest reference level is directly relevant to coastal carbon accounting because the assessment team examined how mangroves are classified between forest land and wetlands. The review identified an apparent overlap, and Samoa clarified that mangroves meeting the national forest definition are classified as forest land while wetland areas with mangrove vegetation that do not meet that definition remain classified as wetlands. The assessment therefore addresses a concrete double-counting and land-classification issue that can affect the accuracy and consistency of mangrove carbon estimates. More broadly, the facilitative assessment modified Samoa's proposed 2013–2022 FREL from 316,245 to 278,590 tCO2e per year and its forest-carbon-stock enhancement FRL from –73,036 to –76,896 tCO2e per year and identified future improvements in activity data and geospatial information. The report does not issue REDD+ payments or blue-carbon credits, nor does it authorize mangrove restoration; it provides an official accounting-quality assessment and technical basis for future results-based reporting.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 8 July 2025; the facilitative process revised Samoa reference levels and clarified mangrove land classification for accounting consistency.

document_title: Pakistan. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1.
notes: Pakistan's first Biennial Transparency Report provides a formal national transparency record of mangrove carbon-sink action and forest-sector accounting. It reports the Ten Billion Tree Tsunami Programme's mangrove component, including a long-term objective of establishing or restoring about 350,000 ha of mangroves and implementation to date on approximately 75,000 ha. The report also presents an estimated carbon-sequestration potential of about 127 million tonnes for the reported mangrove-restoration activity and treats mangroves as a material forest carbon sink within national mitigation reporting. For ONCE purposes, the document is most important as an MRV, accounting and implementation-evidence source that links a coastal-wetland engineering pathway to national climate reporting. The sequestration figure is an estimate reported in the transparency document rather than an independently verified volume of additional removals delivered to a carbon-credit registry. The BTR does not itself issue blue-carbon credits, authorize a specific restoration project or establish a new carbon-market methodology.
source: Government of Pakistan / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR submitted on 31 December 2024 and published by UNFCCC in 2025; it reports active mangrove-restoration implementation and carbon-sink estimates, not a project-level crediting decision.

document_title: Sri Lanka. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1.
notes: Sri Lanka's first Biennial Transparency Report records the implementation context for national blue-carbon ecosystem protection and restoration. It links the National Policy on Conservation and Sustainable Utilization of Mangrove Ecosystems and the related Strategic Action Plan to mangrove and seagrass conservation, restoration and carbon-sequestration functions. The report describes restoration activity at sites including Anawilundawa and states that mangrove-restoration work is in progress, while also identifying future reforestation and restoration efforts that include mangroves. Because the BTR connects formal national policy, implementation activity and transparency reporting, it provides evidence for both coastal blue-carbon engineering and the monitoring/governance framework around that work. The document does not establish a blue-carbon registry or issue credits, and it does not provide a verified project-level quantity of additional carbon removal attributable solely to the reported mangrove or seagrass measures. Accordingly, the engineering tags reflect documented restoration action, while the primary ONCE type remains standards, policy and carbon trading because the BTR's formal function is transparency reporting.
source: Government of Sri Lanka / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR submitted on 31 December 2024 and published by UNFCCC on 3 January 2025; it reports active blue-carbon ecosystem policy and restoration measures rather than creating a new permit or crediting mechanism.

document_title: Papua New Guinea. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1.
notes: Papua New Guinea's first Biennial Transparency Report, formally submitted in January 2026 for the 2024 BTR cycle, provides national evidence on forest and coastal carbon-sink monitoring and mitigation action. The report treats mangroves as a distinct high-carbon ecosystem, reports national mangrove-area and carbon-stock information, and links ecosystem-based mitigation actions to restoration and reforestation. It also sits within Papua New Guinea's national forest monitoring and MRV architecture, making the document relevant to blue-carbon inventory quality as well as implementation tracking. The reported mangrove stock values represent ecosystem carbon stocks and inventory parameters, not automatically additional carbon removals from a new project. The BTR does not by itself create a blue-carbon credit, authorize a project, or demonstrate that the full reported stock is eligible for results-based finance. The record is therefore classified primarily as standards/policy and transparency, with secondary research and restoration-engineering content where mangrove reforestation is reported.
source: Government of Papua New Guinea / UNFCCC
status_note: First BTR submitted and published by UNFCCC on 5 January 2026; it documents mangrove carbon-stock information and implementation context but is not a project authorization or credit issuance.

document_title: Ghana. Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1
notes: Ghana's first Biennial Transparency Report provides a formal national transparency source for coastal-wetland carbon information. The report identifies mangroves as a distinct coastal forest resource and compiles area and carbon-stock evidence relevant to the national greenhouse-gas and land-sector evidence base. It also places coastal forest protection and REDD+ implementation within Ghana's wider climate-policy and forest-governance framework. For ONCE classification, its strongest function is evidence building, monitoring and carbon-accounting support rather than direct deployment of a new marine negative-emissions project. The carbon-stock figures describe stored carbon and accounting parameters; they should not be read as a quantified volume of additional removals generated by the BTR. The report does not itself establish a mangrove crediting methodology, issue credits or authorize a restoration project.
source: Government of Ghana / UNFCCC
status_note: First Ghana BTR published by UNFCCC on 30 December 2024; it contributes coastal-forest carbon evidence and transparency reporting rather than a new deployment authorization.

document_title: Indonesia. 2024 Biennial Transparency Report (BTR). BTR1.
notes: Indonesia's first Biennial Transparency Report records ongoing national mitigation and ecosystem-management measures that include mangrove protection and restoration. The report describes government institutions working on ecosystem protection, mangrove restoration and community-led conservation, and it places those activities within the national transparency framework for climate action. Indonesia's very large mangrove estate is therefore not merely background context: restoration and protection are reported as active measures within the institutional implementation system. For ONCE purposes, the BTR is primarily a policy, monitoring and transparency document, while the documented restoration activity supports a secondary ecological-restoration engineering classification. The BTR does not itself approve a particular mangrove project, create a blue-carbon methodology or issue carbon credits. Any national-scale forest or land-sector results reported elsewhere in the BTR should not be interpreted as mangrove-only removals unless explicitly disaggregated.
source: Government of Indonesia / UNFCCC
status_note: Indonesia submitted its first BTR for the 2024 transparency cycle; the UNFCCC document page was published in 2025. The report records active mangrove-restoration governance but does not itself create a project permit or credit.

document_title: Technical report on the technical analysis of the technical annex to the first biennial transparency report of Indonesia submitted in accordance with paragraph 14 of decision 18/CMA.1 on 24 December 2024
notes: This UNFCCC technical analysis evaluates Indonesia's voluntary REDD+ technical annex for results-based payments and therefore provides an independent review of forest-carbon accounting and reported mitigation results. Indonesia reported 2021–2023 REDD+ results of 68,980,679 tCO2e per year against the assessed forest reference level of 192,921,295 tCO2e per year. The underlying accounting framework explicitly addresses mangrove conversion and mangrove-related soil organic carbon within the national forest-reference and monitoring system, making the review directly relevant to coastal carbon MRV. The technical analysis found the submitted data partially transparent and partially consistent and identified areas for capacity-building and future technical improvement. The reported REDD+ result is national and is not a mangrove-only removal figure. The report does not issue a blue-carbon credit or authorize mangrove restoration; its role is technical verification and improvement of the results-based accounting framework.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC REDD+ technical-analysis report published on 18 March 2026; it reviews 2021–2023 national REDD+ results and the associated forest-carbon accounting framework.

document_title: Report on the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of Indonesia submitted in 2022
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment reviews Indonesia's national forest reference level for REDD+ results-based payments. The facilitative process reduced the assessed FRL from 267,705,902 to 192,921,295 tCO2e per year for the 2006–2020 reference period. The assessed methodology explicitly includes soil-organic-carbon emissions associated with peatlands and mangrove conversion and uses the 2013 IPCC Wetlands Supplement and country-specific information for mangrove-related emission factors. That treatment makes the report directly relevant to coastal-wetland carbon accounting, even though its formal scope is the national forest reference level rather than a standalone blue-carbon programme. The assessment identifies methodological improvements and consistency requirements; it does not create a restoration programme, issue REDD+ payments or authorize a mangrove project. Any national FRL value is an accounting benchmark and should not be treated as a quantified mangrove-removal outcome.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 3 January 2023; the assessed national FRL is 192,921,295 tCO2e per year and includes mangrove-related accounting elements.

document_title: Report on the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference emission level and forest reference level of Thailand submitted in 2021
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment treats mangrove forest as a distinct and highly material carbon-stock stratum within Thailand's FREL/FRL. Thailand calculated mangrove emission and removal factors using above-ground biomass measurements from 37 plots and applied stock-change methods across inventory cycles. The assessment team noted that mangrove forests accounted for a substantial share of the FREL and identified incomplete reconstructability of the mangrove estimates as an area for future technical improvement. The facilitative process modified the national FREL to 12,341,444 tCO2e per year and the FRL to -28,622,811 tCO2e per year. This is a formal MRV and accounting-quality review, not a mangrove restoration authorization or a credit issuance. The national reference levels also cover terrestrial forest classes, so they must not be interpreted as mangrove-only carbon-removal quantities.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 5 May 2022; it evaluates mangrove-specific emission/removal factors within Thailand's national forest reference accounting.

document_title: Report on the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of El Salvador submitted in 2021
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment reviews El Salvador's national forest reference level and the underlying land-classification and carbon-accounting methods used for REDD+ results-based payments. The submission treats mangrove forest as a distinct forest subclass and addresses its relationship with wetland and peatland accounting, making the review directly relevant to coastal carbon inventory consistency. The assessed FRL is 1,359,188 tonnes of CO2 per year for application during 2016–2025. The report's ONCE relevance lies in how it tests consistency, transparency and methodological treatment of coastal forest carbon within a national reference level. It does not establish a new mangrove restoration target, permit a project or issue a carbon credit. The national FRL is an accounting reference for multiple forest activities and should not be read as a mangrove-specific sequestration estimate.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 4 April 2022; it assesses El Salvador's national FRL and mangrove-related forest/wetland accounting treatment.

document_title: Report of the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of Suriname submitted in 2018
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment reviews Suriname's forest reference level for REDD+ and explicitly identifies mangrove forests within the national carbon-accounting evidence base. The assessment notes the use of a tier-1 above-ground carbon value for mangrove forest and discusses the need to improve country-specific information through the national forest inventory, including additional plots in mangrove strata. The facilitative assessment produced year-specific FREL values for 2016–2020 and identified monitoring and inventory improvements required for stronger carbon estimates. The document is therefore a formal evidence-building and MRV record for mangrove carbon rather than a direct restoration or deployment policy. It does not authorize mangrove projects, quantify additional blue-carbon removals from restoration or issue carbon credits. The FREL covers national forest emissions and is not a mangrove-only benchmark.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 23 November 2018; it identifies mangrove inventory data as part of Suriname's REDD+ reference-level improvement pathway.

document_title: Technical report on the technical analysis of the technical annex to the first biennial update report of Suriname submitted in accordance with decision 14/CP.19, paragraph 7, on 5 November 2022 (FCCC/SBI/ICA/2023/TATR.1/SUR)
notes: This UNFCCC technical report analyses Suriname's voluntary REDD+ results for 2016–2019 in the context of results-based payments. Suriname reported 9,178,978 tCO2e of results against the assessed year-specific forest reference emission levels. The technical analysis links those results to the national forest-monitoring and reference-level system and identifies expansion and improvement of national forest inventory sampling, including mangrove forests, as part of the future technical-improvement agenda. The report is relevant to blue-carbon governance because it tests the transparency and consistency of an accounting system that includes mangrove forest within the national forest estate. The reported REDD+ result is national and is not disaggregated as a mangrove-only removal outcome. The report does not itself issue results-based payments or blue-carbon credits.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — REDD+ Technical Analysis Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC REDD+ technical-analysis report published on 1 September 2023; it reviews Suriname's 2016–2019 results and identifies forest-inventory improvements relevant to mangrove accounting.

document_title: Technical report on the technical analysis of the technical annex to the first biennial update report of Suriname submitted in accordance with decision 14/CP.19, paragraph 7, on 5 November 2022 (FCCC/SBI/ICA/2023/TATR.2/SUR)
notes: This second UNFCCC technical-analysis report for Suriname evaluates a separate results period, covering REDD+ performance for 2020–2021. Suriname reported 8,936,741 tCO2e of results measured against the assessed forest reference emission levels for those two years. The analysis relies on the same national REDD+ monitoring and reference-level architecture in which mangrove forests are a recognized forest stratum and remain relevant to inventory improvement and uncertainty reduction. Its ONCE value is therefore primarily in MRV, accounting consistency and international technical review rather than direct engineering deployment. The reported result is national across covered forest activities and is not a mangrove-specific sequestration quantity. The report does not issue credits, make a project eligibility determination or authorize coastal restoration.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — REDD+ Technical Analysis Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC REDD+ technical-analysis report published on 6 September 2023; it assesses Suriname's 2020–2021 results under the national forest-monitoring framework.

document_title: Report on the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of Gabon submitted in 2021
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment is directly relevant to blue-carbon accounting because it records a specific methodological gap for mangrove forest. Gabon did not account for emissions from mangrove forest in the assessed FRL because robust data were not yet available, while an ongoing study was expected to provide the required evidence. The assessment also notes the use of Wetlands Supplement values for mangrove carbon gains in parts of the reference-level methodology and identifies country-specific mangrove data as an area for future improvement. The modified national FRL was -96,468,186 tonnes of CO2 per year, including an adjustment for national circumstances. That FRL is a national forest benchmark and does not quantify mangrove-only removals. The report neither authorizes mangrove restoration nor creates a carbon-credit mechanism; its significance is the formal identification of a coastal-carbon data and accounting gap.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 31 October 2021; it records that mangrove emissions were not fully accounted because of data limitations and identifies this as a future improvement area.

document_title: Technical report on the technical analysis of the technical annex to the first biennial update report of Gabon submitted in accordance with decision 14/CP.19, paragraph 7, on 29 December 2021
notes: This UNFCCC technical analysis evaluates Gabon's voluntary REDD+ results for 2010–2018 against the assessed national forest reference level. Gabon reported 187,104,289 tonnes of CO2 of results when measured against the adjusted FRL of -96,468,186 tonnes of CO2 per year. The analysis sits downstream of a reference-level methodology that explicitly treats mangrove forest as a distinct carbon-accounting issue and had identified data limitations for mangrove emissions. For ONCE purposes, the report is relevant as an international MRV and results-accounting review that carries those coastal-forest data-quality constraints into the results-based reporting system. The headline REDD+ result is national and must not be interpreted as mangrove-only removals. The technical report does not itself issue credits or payments and does not authorize mangrove engineering.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — REDD+ Technical Analysis Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC REDD+ technical-analysis report published on 7 October 2022; it reviews Gabon's 2010–2018 national REDD+ results against the assessed FRL.

document_title: Report on the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of Panama submitted in 2022
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment reviews Panama's national forest reference level and its carbon-accounting framework for all five REDD+ activities. The methodology uses a national sampling system in which mangroves form a specific forest stratum and applies wetland-related IPCC guidance where appropriate. The assessed FRL for the 2006–2015 reference period is -20,433,129.66 tCO2e per year. The report is important to ONCE because it places mangrove carbon within a formally assessed national monitoring, sampling and reference-level system used in the context of results-based payments. It does not establish a separate blue-carbon credit methodology or quantify the national FRL as mangrove-only removals. It also does not itself authorize restoration activity; its role is technical assessment of accounting quality and methodological consistency.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 25 August 2022; it assesses Panama's national FRL and the sampling/accounting system that includes mangrove forest.

document_title: Technical report on the technical analysis of the technical annex to the first biennial transparency report of Panama submitted in accordance with paragraph 14 of decision 18/CMA.1 on 30 June 2024
notes: This UNFCCC technical report analyses Panama's REDD+ technical annex to its first Biennial Transparency Report in the context of results-based payments. Panama reported annual results for 2016–2020 against its assessed FRL, with reported results ranging from 498,377 to 6,206,390 tCO2e by year. The technical analysis uses the national reference framework in which mangroves are one of the forest sampling strata, includes wetland-guideline treatment, and examines consistency of carbon pools, land conversions and enhancement activities. This creates a direct link between coastal-forest carbon accounting and the formal Paris Agreement transparency review process. The reported REDD+ results cover national forest activities and are not mangrove-only removals. The report does not issue credits or constitute a project permit; it verifies accounting consistency and identifies future capacity-building and technical improvements.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — REDD+ Technical Analysis Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC REDD+ technical-analysis report published on 16 May 2025; it reviews Panama's 2016–2020 national REDD+ results within a reference framework that includes mangrove forest.
