document_title: Report on the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference emission level of Honduras submitted in 2023
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment reviews Honduras's updated national forest reference emission level and the monitoring definitions used to estimate forest-sector emissions and removals. The assessed framework explicitly defines mangrove forest with tailored minimum-height and canopy-cover thresholds so that it can be operationalized consistently in national forest monitoring and future greenhouse-gas inventories. During the facilitative process the proposed FREL was modified from -17,347,363 to -5,545,227 tCO2e per year. The report is relevant to coastal carbon because the mangrove definition determines whether mangrove areas and their carbon changes enter the national accounting system consistently. The FREL remains a national forest benchmark rather than a mangrove-only removal estimate. The assessment does not create a restoration target, permit or carbon credit.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 6 March 2024; it evaluates an updated national FREL and formalizes mangrove-related forest-definition consistency for monitoring.

document_title: Technical report on the technical analysis of the technical annex to the second biennial update report of Honduras submitted in accordance with paragraph 7 of decision 14/CP.19 on 22 March 2024
notes: This UNFCCC technical report analyses Honduras's REDD+ results for 2021–2023 against the assessed national FREL of -5,545,227 tCO2e per year. Honduras reported results of 4,722,810 tCO2e for 2021, 259,211 tCO2e for 2022 and 6,796,176 tCO2e for 2023. The technical annex covers the same national forest-monitoring framework as the 2023 FREL submission, in which mangrove forest is explicitly defined and incorporated into operational forest monitoring. The report therefore extends mangrove-relevant accounting rules into the formal technical analysis of results-based reporting. The reported results are national and are not disaggregated as mangrove-only removals. The report does not issue credits, approve results-based payments or authorize a coastal restoration project.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — REDD+ Technical Analysis Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC REDD+ technical-analysis report published on 12 February 2025; it reviews Honduras's 2021–2023 national REDD+ results under the updated forest-monitoring framework.

document_title: Technical report on the technical analysis of the technical annex to the first biennial update report of Belize submitted in accordance with decision 14/CP.19, paragraph 7, on 30 August 2021
notes: This UNFCCC technical analysis evaluates Belize's voluntary REDD+ results for 2016–2018 and directly engages with mangrove carbon-stock monitoring. Belize's underlying system includes national estimates of mangrove carbon stocks, permanent forest plots and a forest definition that can capture low-stature mangrove formations. Belize reported REDD+ results of 81,794 tCO2e for 2016, 940,385 tCO2e for 2017 and 4,580,384 tCO2e for 2018 against the assessed national FRL. The review assesses transparency and consistency between the reported results and the national reference-level data, making it a substantive MRV and accounting record for a system that includes mangroves. The REDD+ results are national and should not be interpreted as mangrove-only removals. The report does not itself issue credits or authorize a mangrove restoration project.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — REDD+ Technical Analysis Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC REDD+ technical-analysis report published on 7 September 2022; it reviews Belize's 2016–2018 results under a national forest accounting system that includes mangrove carbon stocks.

document_title: Report on the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of Belize submitted in 2020
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment reviews Belize's forest reference level and contains specific methodological treatment of mangrove forest carbon. During the assessment Belize corrected a biomass equation used for mangrove forests and described disturbance and harvest-loss estimation across mature, secondary, mangrove and pine forest types. The assessment also links the reference-level work to national forestry and land-use policy review for REDD+ implementation. The assessed FRL provides year-specific reference values for 2016–2020 and is used for results-based reporting. The document is therefore directly relevant to mangrove carbon accounting, monitoring quality and technical-standard improvement. It does not quantify additional mangrove restoration removals, authorize a project or issue carbon credits.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 18 May 2021; it corrects and reviews mangrove biomass/accounting methods within Belize's national FRL.

document_title: Report on the technical expert review of the first biennial transparency report of Norway
notes: This UNFCCC technical expert review independently examines Norway's first Biennial Transparency Report and its reporting of international climate support. Among the reviewed support activities, Norway reports capacity-building and cooperation related to development of a national blue-carbon market in Indonesia and integrated mangrove management and restoration programmes in Colombia. The review therefore provides formal third-party confirmation that blue-carbon market readiness and mangrove-restoration support are part of Norway's reported international climate-finance and cooperation portfolio. Its primary ONCE function is transparency, international coordination and governance review, while the underlying supported programmes have secondary restoration-engineering relevance. The technical expert review does not itself establish Indonesia's blue-carbon market, authorize the Colombian restoration programmes or issue carbon credits. It should be treated as an official review record of reported support, not as the legal instrument governing those recipient-country activities.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Expert Review Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical expert review report published on 9 March 2026; it reviews Norway's reported international support, including blue-carbon market development and mangrove-restoration cooperation.

document_title: Honduras. Report of the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference emission level of Honduras submitted in 2017.
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment contains one of the clearest early examples of mangrove-specific carbon-accounting refinement in a REDD+ reference level. Honduras initially lacked reliable mangrove emission factors because national forest measurements covered only two plots, but during the assessment it revised the submission to treat mangrove forest as an independent stratum. Country and regional evidence was then used to derive above-ground, below-ground and other carbon-pool factors, including information from the Jeanette Kawas National Park. The assessment team considered the separate mangrove stratum an improvement in the accuracy and transparency of the FREL and identified more representative mangrove measurements as a future priority. The modified national FREL was 6,552,746.47 tCO2e per year. The document is an accounting and MRV assessment, not a restoration authorization or a mangrove-specific crediting decision.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 23 January 2018; the facilitative process introduced mangrove forest as an independent accounting stratum in Honduras's FREL.

document_title: Report on the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of Honduras submitted in 2020
notes: This later UNFCCC technical assessment expands Honduras's REDD+ reference-level coverage beyond deforestation to all five REDD+ activities and reviews the continuity of the national forest-monitoring framework. The system builds on the earlier technical work that established mangrove forest as a separate carbon-accounting stratum and therefore carries mangrove-specific monitoring into the broader FRL architecture. The assessed FRL is 8,142,121.66 tonnes of CO2 per year, covering different reference periods for deforestation and the other REDD+ activities. The assessment found the submission only partially transparent and complete and identified areas for future technical improvement. The FRL is a national forest accounting benchmark and cannot be read as a mangrove-only carbon result. The report does not issue credits, approve a restoration project or create a separate blue-carbon methodology.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 5 May 2021; it broadens Honduras's REDD+ reference-level framework while retaining the national monitoring architecture that includes mangrove forest.

document_title: Technical report on the technical analysis of the technical annex to the first biennial update report of Honduras submitted in accordance with decision 14/CP.19, paragraph 7, on 19 November 2020
notes: This UNFCCC technical analysis reviews Honduras's first reported REDD+ results for 2017–2018 against the assessed FREL of 6,552,746.47 tonnes of CO2 per year. Honduras reported 5,595,266.01 tonnes of CO2 of results for the two-year results period. The technical annex uses the same national forest area and reference-level system produced through the 2017 assessment, in which mangrove forest was introduced as an independent carbon-accounting stratum. The report therefore provides the results-based reporting counterpart to that mangrove-relevant MRV framework. The reported quantity is a national REDD+ result and is not a mangrove-only removal figure. The technical analysis does not itself issue credits or authorize mangrove restoration.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — REDD+ Technical Analysis Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC REDD+ technical-analysis report published on 26 August 2022; it assesses Honduras's 2017–2018 results against the FREL whose monitoring framework includes a distinct mangrove stratum.

document_title: Report of the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of Panama submitted in 2018
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment evaluates Panama's earlier national forest reference level and explicitly stratifies forest land by type, including mangrove forest. The methodology combines geospatial activity data, sampling information and emission/removal factors across forest strata, with mangroves treated separately from mature, secondary, disturbed and plantation forests. The facilitative process changed the assessed FRL from -56,991,334 to -27,735,675 tCO2e per year and extended the reference period to 2000–2015. The report provides a formal methodological baseline for later Panama REDD+ and BTR technical analyses that continued to include mangroves in national carbon accounting. The national FRL is not a mangrove-only sequestration estimate. The report does not authorize restoration or issue carbon credits; its function is technical assessment and improvement of forest-carbon accounting.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 15 April 2019; it assesses a national FRL in which mangrove forest is an explicit sampling and accounting stratum.

document_title: Report of the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference emission level of Madagascar submitted in 2018
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment is relevant to coastal carbon because it explicitly examines the treatment of mangrove forest in Madagascar's national FREL. The assessment records that mangroves were excluded from the FREL estimates and identifies the treatment of spiny forests and mangroves as an area for future technical improvement. The modified national FREL for the 2006–2015 reference period was 34,342,327 tCO2e per year. For ONCE purposes, the record is valuable as evidence of a formal accounting boundary and a recognized data/methodology gap for mangrove carbon rather than as evidence of quantified blue-carbon mitigation. No mangrove removals are claimed by this report because mangroves were outside the assessed FREL estimate. The document does not authorize restoration or create a mangrove crediting mechanism.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 10 December 2018; it explicitly identifies exclusion of mangroves from the FREL as a future technical-improvement issue.

document_title: Report on the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of Bangladesh submitted in 2019
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment directly addresses inclusion of low-stature mangrove forest in Bangladesh's REDD+ reference-level accounting. Bangladesh modified its operational forest definition so that Ceriops decandra-dominated mangrove areas in the Sundarbans could be included even where trees do not meet the usual five-metre height threshold. The assessment team commended that change as improving the comprehensiveness and accuracy of the FRL and identified the need to evaluate or derive more suitable species-specific biomass equations. The facilitative process modified the national FRL from 295,451 to 374,253 tCO2e per year. The report is therefore a substantive mangrove MRV and accounting-methodology record, not a restoration-project authorization. The FRL is a national forest benchmark and should not be interpreted as mangrove-only removals or issued blue-carbon credits.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 17 January 2020; it confirms an operational forest-definition change specifically designed to include Sundarbans mangrove forest in the FRL.

document_title: Report of the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of India submitted in 2018
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment examines India's national forest reference level and includes specific review of the treatment of mangrove areas. During the technical assessment India clarified that the national forest definition and treatment of mangroves were applied consistently across its FRL submission and other international forest reporting, with differences arising only from reclassification requirements. The report also reviews the underlying activity data, emission factors and carbon-stock information used to construct the national FRL of -49.70 MtCO2e per year for the 2000–2008 reference period. Its relevance to ONCE is methodological: it tests consistency and reproducibility of an accounting system that includes mangrove forest in national carbon-stock reporting. The report does not establish a mangrove restoration programme, quantify additional blue-carbon removals or create a crediting mechanism. The national FRL covers the wider forest sector and is not a mangrove-only benchmark.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 29 October 2018; it reviews the consistency of India's treatment of mangroves within national forest reference-level accounting.

document_title: Report of the technical assessment of the proposed forest reference level of Malaysia submitted in 2018
notes: This UNFCCC technical assessment explicitly includes mangrove forests in Malaysia's national forest reference-level methodology. Malaysia disaggregated forest-area data by categories that include mangrove forests, used the 2013 IPCC Wetlands Supplement, and applied mangrove-specific parameters such as a distinct root-to-shoot ratio derived from wetland guidance and literature. The assessed FRL for the 2000–2014 reference period is -213,053,000 tCO2e per year, covering sustainable forest management, conservation of forest carbon stocks and deforestation-related accounting elements. The review identifies methodological and carbon-pool improvements for future submissions and provides a formal technical basis for consistent mangrove-carbon treatment inside national forest MRV. The national FRL is not a mangrove-only removal quantity and the report does not establish a mangrove restoration target. It also does not issue carbon credits or authorize a specific project.
source: UNFCCC Secretariat — Technical Assessment Team
status_note: Official UNFCCC technical assessment report published on 7 March 2019; it assesses a national FRL that explicitly includes mangrove forest-area data and mangrove-specific carbon parameters.

subnational_area: Fujian Province — Fuzhou / Lianjiang and Fuqing
document_title: 全国首宗“沉积碳—惰性碳”海洋渔业碳汇交易签订
notes: An official Fujian government report records the signing on 11 April 2025 of what it describes as China's first marine fishery carbon-sink transaction combining sedimentary carbon and refractory or inert carbon. Approximately 326 tonnes of marine carbon sink were subscribed by parties involved in an illegal-fishing case as an alternative form of ecological restoration. The quantified product combines organic carbon deposited through submerged macroalgal processes with refractory dissolved organic carbon, and the accounting work was supported by a Jimei University team linked to the Ocean Negative Carbon Emissions programme. The report states that the transaction followed a macroalgae voluntary-emission-reduction methodology and referred to domestic CCER management and trading standards. It does not establish that the transacted units were nationally issued CCERs, and the transaction should therefore be treated as a local judicial/ecological-value realization mechanism rather than national credit issuance.
source: Fujian Provincial Development and Reform Commission
status_note: Completed local marine-carbon transaction reported by the provincial government; the source does not identify the units as nationally issued CCERs.

document_title: 赣榆区滨海盐沼司法蓝碳交易
notes: The Ganyu District government reports a completed judicial blue-carbon transaction involving 1,055 tCO2e from coastal salt-marsh restoration. The project links resource survey, monitoring, carbon-value accounting, market transaction and reinvestment of judicial ecological-restoration funds, and it is associated with approximately 151 hectares of restored coastal wetland. The official account presents the transaction as a local full-chain practice for converting salt-marsh restoration benefits into a tradable ecological product. It also states that the locality intends to continue developing projects that may later seek access to broader carbon markets. This record therefore captures the completed local judicial transaction and its supporting accounting process; it does not treat the 1,055 tCO2e as national CCER issuance.
source: People's Government of Ganyu District, Lianyungang
status_note: Completed judicial salt-marsh blue-carbon transaction; no national CCER issuance is established by the cited source.

document_title: 盐沼碳汇交易在条子泥湿地落地
notes: Dongtai's official government account records a completed transaction of 6,600 tonnes of salt-marsh carbon sink for CNY 1.5 million at Tiaozini Wetland. The underlying restoration programme rebuilt approximately 1,030 hectares of salt-marsh habitat through measures including conversion of former aquaculture areas, invasive-species control and recovery of native vegetation. Project carbon benefits were monitored and independently checked before the transaction, and the product was listed through a carbon-market platform. The purchase was used as an ecological-compensation mechanism connected with a coastal development project, with transaction proceeds directed back to wetland protection and management. The source describes a local blue-carbon ecological-product transaction rather than national CCER issuance.
source: Dongtai Municipal People's Government
status_note: Completed 2025 Tiaozini salt-marsh transaction; the official source describes a local ecological-compensation and blue-carbon market mechanism, not national CCER issuance.

document_title: 深圳市规划和自然资源局关于广东内伶仃岛-福田国家级自然保护区红树林保护碳汇交易公告（520吨司法替代修复标的，2025年3月）

The notice sets out the proposed quantity, transaction period and intended ecological-restoration use under the local mangrove carbon-sink framework. Because the cited document is a pre-transaction public notice rather than a transaction-result notice, it establishes that a transfer was formally offered but does not establish that the 520 tonnes were ultimately sold, cancelled or retired. The record is therefore classified as a completed consultation/public-notice stage, not as a completed credit transaction.

document_title: 嵊泗厚壳贻贝司法蓝碳认购协议
notes: An official Supreme People's Procuratorate source reports a judicial blue-carbon subscription involving 500 tonnes of carbon sink associated with thick-shelled mussel aquaculture in Shengsi, with a transaction value of CNY 50,000. The purchase was used to perform ecological-restoration liability arising from an illegal-fishing case. Carbon accounting was supported by a dedicated report prepared with scientific institutions including Zhejiang Ocean University and the Ningbo Ocean Research Institute, providing a quantified basis for the judicial subscription. The case demonstrates use of aquaculture carbon-sink value as substitute ecological restoration. It does not constitute evidence that the 500 tonnes were issued as national CCERs or admitted to the national compliance market.
source: Supreme People's Procuratorate of the People's Republic of China
status_note: Completed judicial subscription reported in June 2025; the source does not identify the units as national CCERs.

document_title: 嵊泗贻贝蓝碳交易协作框架协议
notes: A five-agency cooperation framework in Shengsi establishes an institutional basis for mussel blue-carbon transactions. The official procuratorate account describes coordinated responsibilities for aquaculture sea-area rights, carbon measurement and supervision, connection with transaction platforms, use of public-interest litigation or ecological-damage compensation funds to purchase mussel blue-carbon products, and a mechanism for feeding transaction income back into marine ecological protection. The agreement is a standing governance and coordination framework rather than an individual credit issuance decision. It supports market use of quantified mussel carbon-sink products but does not itself quantify a new removal amount or establish national CCER eligibility.
source: Zhejiang Provincial People's Procuratorate / Shengsi County authorities
status_note: Active inter-agency cooperation framework for mussel blue-carbon transactions; it does not itself issue carbon credits.

It is a governance instrument: it authorizes a substitute-restoration pathway under specified conditions but does not itself issue credits, quantify a new project or create national market eligibility.
source: Shengsi County People's Procuratorate and cooperating judicial/scientific institutions

document_title: 广东台山完成全国首次红树林保护碳汇公众认购
notes: The National Forestry and Grassland Administration reports a completed public subscription for 477 tonnes of mangrove-protection carbon sink in Taishan at CNY 336 per tonne. Revenue from the subscription is earmarked for mangrove tending, restoration, conservation management and public education, linking carbon value realization directly to continued ecosystem stewardship. The wider programme also reports substantial mangrove creation and restoration activity in the locality. The source discusses possible subsequent market listing and further development of mangrove carbon products, but the recorded event is a public subscription mechanism and is not evidence of national CCER issuance or compliance-market integration.
source: National Forestry and Grassland Administration
status_note: Completed 2025 public mangrove-carbon subscription; future market listing is described separately and was not established by this transaction.

document_title: 全国蓝碳交易联盟成立倡议

The official Shenzhen source reports broad institutional interest and continuing preparation or member recruitment, rather than establishment of a statutory national carbon market. The initiative is intended to support more standardized and scalable blue-carbon transactions and to connect project, research, finance and market actors. It does not itself create a regulated crediting methodology, issue credits, authorize individual projects or integrate blue carbon into China's national compliance market.
source: Shenzhen Municipal Planning and Natural Resources Bureau

document_title: 全国海洋标准化技术委员会海洋碳汇分技术委员会（TC283/SC8）
notes: The National Public Service Platform for Standards records the establishment in 2026 of the first-term Marine Carbon Sink Subcommittee (TC283/SC8) under the National Marine Standardization Technical Committee. Its formal scope covers general marine-carbon terminology and foundations, sequestration and sink enhancement, marine carbon storage, carbon-footprint-related marine fields, marine negative-emission activities and marine carbon-market mechanisms. The subcommittee creates a national institutional platform for developing and coordinating standards across these subjects. The registry page establishes the committee and its remit; it does not itself promulgate a particular accounting standard, authorize a marine CDR project or create tradable carbon units.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Standardization Administration of China
status_note: National marine-carbon standardization subcommittee established in 2026 and listed as the first active term on the official standards platform.

notes: Fujian's natural-resources authority issued this formal co-handling opinion in response to a provincial CPPCC proposal on developing blue-carbon trading. It summarizes implementation already undertaken in the province, including marine ecological-restoration programmes, coastal-wetland and mangrove restoration, work on carbon-sink fisheries and exploration of market mechanisms for marine carbon-sink value realization. The response reports cumulative restoration areas and explains how marine-carbon development is being connected with broader ecological-product value mechanisms. It is an official policy-response and implementation summary rather than a standalone carbon-credit methodology or trading platform. The portal marks the document as invalid or abolished, so its substantive value is primarily as a record of policy implementation and institutional position at the time of issuance.

The official account describes eligible case types, prerequisites for applying the mechanism, purchase and procedural requirements, judicial consequences and division of responsibilities among participating authorities. By the reporting date, the mechanism had been used in multiple marine-carbon judicial cases with a substantial aggregate quantity of subscribed carbon sink. The opinion creates procedural authorization and safeguards for the use of marine-carbon purchases in ecological restoration; it does not itself define a single engineering pathway, issue credits or establish national CCER eligibility.

The arrangement links ecological restoration, monitoring and carbon-value realization and is presented as a demonstration of a new financing route for seagrass conservation. The source describes an intended subscription, not a final quantified issuance or completed sale, so the project is classified as planned rather than completed.
source: National Forestry and Grassland Administration
status_note: Publicly announced seagrass blue-carbon subscription intention; the source does not establish final verified issuance or completion of the sale.

document_title: 江苏盐城滨海盐沼生态修复碳汇项目蓝碳生态系统碳汇交易签约
notes: In September 2023, a blue-carbon subscription agreement was signed for a coastal salt-marsh ecological-restoration project in Yancheng, Jiangsu, during the Global Coastal Forum period. Xiamen University documentation links the transaction to the dedicated Coastal Salt Marsh Ecological Restoration Project Carbon Sink Measurement and Monitoring Method developed by its blue-carbon team. The project therefore combines restoration of a defined salt-marsh ecosystem with project-specific baseline setting, monitoring and quantification of net carbon-sink change and a contractual mechanism for realizing ecological-product value. It is an important early Chinese salt-marsh market demonstration, but the transaction is not national CCER issuance and does not establish a generally applicable national offset methodology. The subscription agreement should also be distinguished from a regulatory approval for restoration construction. Carbon benefits remain dependent on the methodology's project boundary, baseline, monitored ecosystem response and treatment of greenhouse-gas sources. The record is kept separate from the methodology itself because one is a project transaction and the other is a technical accounting instrument. The relevant ecosystem pathway is salt-marsh/tidal-wetland restoration and the direct carbon-pump mechanism is BCP.
source: Xiamen University College of the Environment and Ecology / Yancheng project partners
status_note: Project-level blue-carbon subscription agreement signed in September 2023; transaction completed, with no evidence that it constitutes national CCER issuance.

document_title: 山东完成首批海草床碳汇交易
notes: The National Forestry and Grassland Administration reports Shandong's first batch of seagrass-bed carbon-sink transactions in Rongcheng. A verified quantity of 338.7 tonnes was registered and traded through Shandong's carbon-inclusive mechanism with six purchasing entities. The project is linked to seagrass restoration and expansion, and the official report describes accounting, verification and provincial carbon-inclusive registration before the market transaction. This is a subnational carbon-inclusive blue-carbon transaction, not national CCER issuance or compliance-market integration.
source: National Forestry and Grassland Administration / Shandong authorities
status_note: Completed provincial carbon-inclusive seagrass transaction; the source distinguishes it from the national CCER market.

document_title: 广州首宗红树林司法碳汇认购业务完成
notes: The National Forestry and Grassland Administration reports completion of Guangzhou's first judicial subscription for mangrove carbon sink. The transaction covered 554 tonnes and approximately CNY 105,000 and was used to perform substitute ecological-restoration responsibility in a judicial case. The purchased quantity came from a previously issued local mangrove afforestation carbon project, so this record represents the subsequent market use of already issued local units rather than a second issuance event. Transaction proceeds are directed toward mangrove protection and restoration. The record is therefore distinct from the earlier Guangzhou project issuance already present in the database.
source: National Forestry and Grassland Administration / Guangzhou authorities
status_note: Completed 2026 judicial purchase of 554 t from previously issued local mangrove units; this is a transaction event, not a duplicate issuance.

document_title: HY/T 0349-2022《海洋碳汇核算方法》
notes: HY/T 0349-2022 is China's recommended marine-industry standard for accounting marine carbon sinks. Issued by the Ministry of Natural Resources on 26 September 2022 and implemented from 1 January 2023, it provides standardized definitions, accounting boundaries and calculation approaches for marine carbon-sink capacity. The textbook notes that the standard covers multiple marine carbon carriers, including mangroves, salt marshes, seagrass beds, phytoplankton, large algae and bivalves, making it broader than the earlier HY/T 0305-2021 fisheries-carbon-sink method. Its principal policy function is measurement and accounting: it supplies a common technical language for surveys, scientific assessment, resource inventories and future project design. It does not itself create a carbon-credit registry, determine eligibility in the national CCER market, issue credits, authorize ecological restoration or engineered ocean CDR, or prove additional net atmospheric removal simply because a carbon stock is measured. Where individual ecosystem or aquaculture pathways are evaluated, additional project-specific methods may still be required for baselines, monitoring, additionality, permanence, leakage and transaction rules. The standard is therefore classified as an active MRV/accounting foundation rather than a trading mechanism.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Ministry of Natural Resources
status_note: Recommended marine-industry standard issued in 2022 and implemented from 1 January 2023; active as an accounting reference, not a national marine-carbon crediting mechanism.

document_title: DB4403/T 401—2023《海洋碳汇核算指南》
notes: DB4403/T 401—2023 is Shenzhen's recommended local guideline for marine carbon-sink accounting. It supplies a standardized local framework for quantifying marine carbon sinks and supports monitoring, inventory development and consistent carbon accounting in municipal marine management. The guideline is technical infrastructure rather than a tradable-credit methodology tied to a single project. It does not issue carbon units, authorize ecosystem restoration or establish national CCER eligibility.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Shenzhen Municipal Administration for Market Regulation
status_note: Recommended Shenzhen local standard issued in 2023 and effective from 1 January 2024.

document_title: DB13/T 5952-2024《海草床碳汇调查与评估技术规程》
notes: DB13/T 5952-2024 specifies technical procedures for surveying and assessing seagrass-bed carbon sinks in Hebei. It standardizes field investigation, carbon-stock or sink assessment and related monitoring steps needed to build comparable evidence for seagrass blue-carbon management. The document is an assessment standard and does not itself require restoration, approve a seagrass project or create tradable credits. Because the object is a seagrass carbon sink, the standard has a direct biological-carbon-pump relationship even though its primary function is MRV and accounting.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Hebei Provincial Administration for Market Regulation
status_note: Recommended Hebei local standard published in 2024 and effective from 24 July 2024.

document_title: DB37/T 4882.1—2025《海洋生态系统碳储量调查与评估技术规范 第1部分：海草床》
notes: Part 1 of Shandong's 2025 marine-ecosystem carbon-stock survey and assessment series standardizes investigation and evaluation for seagrass beds. It creates a common technical basis for carbon-stock inventories, monitoring and assessment of a core coastal blue-carbon ecosystem. The standard supports later policy, restoration evaluation and market work but does not itself mandate restoration, issue carbon credits or establish project additionality rules for a trading programme.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Shandong Provincial Administration for Market Regulation
status_note: Recommended Shandong local standard published on 29 July 2025 and effective from 29 August 2025.

document_title: DB37/T 4882.2—2025《海洋生态系统碳储量调查与评估技术规范 第2部分：盐沼湿地》
notes: Part 2 of Shandong's 2025 marine-ecosystem carbon-stock survey and assessment series standardizes investigation and evaluation for salt-marsh wetlands. It supports consistent measurement of salt-marsh carbon stocks, repeated monitoring and regional inventory development. Its function is evidence and methodology building; it does not itself create a restoration target, authorize a project or issue tradeable carbon units.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Shandong Provincial Administration for Market Regulation
status_note: Recommended Shandong local standard published on 29 July 2025 and effective from 29 August 2025.

document_title: DB37/T 4882.3—2025《海洋生态系统碳储量调查与评估技术规范 第3部分：海藻场》
notes: Part 3 of Shandong's 2025 marine-ecosystem carbon-stock survey and assessment series covers seaweed beds. The official national standards platform lists it as a current recommended local standard and records publication on 29 July 2025 and implementation from 29 August 2025. It standardizes survey and assessment of carbon stocks in natural marine macroalgal ecosystems, supporting inventory and monitoring work. Because the standard concerns assessment rather than aquaculture deployment, it is not classified as a macroalgae engineering programme and it does not create tradable credits.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Shandong Provincial Administration for Market Regulation
status_note: Recommended Shandong local standard published on 29 July 2025 and effective from 29 August 2025.

document_title: DB4403/T 488—2024《贝类养殖碳汇核算技术规范》
notes: DB4403/T 488—2024 establishes technical requirements for accounting carbon sinks from shellfish aquaculture in Shenzhen, including relevant local mariculture areas and cultivated shellfish such as oysters or scallops within its scope. It provides standardized quantification and monitoring support for fishery-carbon assessment and potential value realization. The standard does not itself authorize an aquaculture project, issue carbon credits or make quantified shellfish carbon eligible for the national CCER market.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Shenzhen Municipal Administration for Market Regulation
status_note: Recommended Shenzhen local standard in force from 2024.

document_title: QX/T 779—2025《碳储量估算和碳排放评估 红树林和盐沼湿地》
notes: QX/T 779—2025 provides technical requirements for estimating carbon stocks and assessing carbon emissions in mangrove and salt-marsh wetlands. The standard strengthens national technical capacity for consistent blue-carbon inventories and evaluation of two major coastal wetland systems. Its function is measurement and accounting; it does not prescribe a restoration project, create a carbon-crediting mechanism or authorize use of results in the national carbon market.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / China Meteorological Administration
status_note: Recommended meteorological-industry standard effective from 1 December 2025.

document_title: DB35/T 2238—2024《养殖海带碳汇评估技术规程》
notes: DB35/T 2238—2024 standardizes assessment of carbon sinks from cultivated kelp in Fujian. It supplies a technical basis for quantifying carbon-stock changes and sequestration associated with macroalgae aquaculture and therefore directly supports fishery-carbon accounting, monitoring and later ecological-value applications. The standard is an assessment method rather than an aquaculture deployment programme or carbon-credit registry, and it does not by itself establish national CCER eligibility.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Fujian Provincial Administration for Market Regulation
status_note: Recommended Fujian local standard published in 2024 and effective from 24 March 2025.

document_title: DB32/T 4544-2023《潮滩与盐沼生态系统碳储量调查技术规范》
notes: DB32/T 4544-2023 establishes survey requirements for carbon stocks in tidal-flat and salt-marsh ecosystems in Jiangsu. It provides standardized procedures for inventory development and field monitoring of coastal wetland carbon, creating a technical evidence base for restoration assessment and blue-carbon management. It does not itself establish a restoration obligation, crediting programme or transaction mechanism.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Jiangsu Provincial Administration for Market Regulation
status_note: Recommended Jiangsu local standard in force since 2023.

document_title: DB45/T 1230-2015《红树林湿地生态系统固碳能力评估技术规程》
notes: DB45/T 1230-2015 is a local technical specification for assessing carbon-sequestration capacity in mangrove wetland ecosystems. It standardizes a dedicated blue-carbon assessment process and provides an early formal technical basis for mangrove carbon-stock and sequestration evaluation in Guangxi. The standard is methodological and does not itself require mangrove restoration, issue tradable carbon credits or authorize a specific project.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region market-regulation authority
status_note: Recommended Guangxi local standard in force; the official standards platform lists the 2015 specification as a formal local standard.

document_title: DB44/T 2504—2024《滨海湿地生态系统固碳能力评估技术规程》
notes: DB44/T 2504—2024 standardizes assessment of carbon-sequestration capacity across coastal wetland ecosystems in Guangdong. Its scope covers multiple coastal wetland types and provides a common basis for monitoring, carbon accounting and comparative assessment. Because the scope is broader than a single engineering pathway and includes ecosystem types with different biogeochemical processes, no specific engineering pathway or carbon-pump label is inferred. The standard does not create credits, authorize restoration or establish a trading programme.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Guangdong Provincial Administration for Market Regulation
status_note: Recommended Guangdong local standard in force from 2024.

document_title: DB37/T 4935—2025《海岸带保护修复项目碳汇增量评估技术规范》
notes: DB37/T 4935—2025 establishes a technical specification for assessing incremental carbon-sink benefits generated by coastal protection and restoration projects in Shandong. Unlike a general carbon-stock inventory standard, it is explicitly linked to additional carbon benefits attributable to restoration activities and therefore provides an evaluation bridge between engineering implementation and carbon accounting. The document standardizes assessment but does not itself approve a restoration project, create a carbon-credit registry or guarantee market eligibility of assessed increments.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Shandong Provincial Administration for Market Regulation
status_note: Recommended Shandong local standard published on 9 October 2025 and effective from 9 November 2025.

document_title: DB3501/T 028—2024《滨海湿地生态系统服务功能评估技术规范》
notes: DB3501/T 028—2024 establishes a local technical framework for evaluating coastal-wetland ecosystem services in Fuzhou and explicitly includes carbon fixation as a regulating service to be quantified or valued alongside other ecosystem services. It supports systematic physical and economic assessment of coastal-wetland carbon benefits and can provide evidence for ecological-product value realization. It is broader than a dedicated carbon-crediting methodology and does not itself issue credits, set additionality rules or authorize restoration projects.
source: State Administration for Market Regulation / Fuzhou municipal standardization authority
status_note: Recommended Fuzhou local standard published in 2024 and effective from 20 March 2025.

document_title: 黄海金控集团三项碳汇金融创新工作入选2023年度江苏省绿色金融十大优秀案例
notes: An official Yancheng state-owned-assets report documents executed marine-carbon finance cases from 2023. These include Jiangsu's first 'marine blue-carbon loan—laver loan', which provided CNY 200 million to an intertidal laver project after assessment of approximately 361,300 tonnes of emission-reduction or sequestration potential over the loan period, and a separate marine-carbon-sink loan linked to a laver farm in Nantong using forward carbon-sink value assessment. The broader carbon-finance programme used forward carbon-sink pledge assessments to support substantial lending across wetland, forest and marine-aquaculture activities. The report demonstrates financial monetization of expected macroalgal carbon benefits, but it does not record issuance of verified national carbon credits and the assessed forward quantities should not be interpreted as realized removals.
source: Yancheng Municipal State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission
status_note: Official 2024 summary of executed 2023 green-finance cases; individual loan maturities and realized carbon removals are not specified.

document_title: 青岛市美丽城市建设实施方案（2025-2027年）
notes: Qingdao's 2025–2027 Beautiful City implementation plan assigns municipal agencies to improve the marine carbon-sink monitoring system, conduct a citywide survey of the distribution of marine-ecosystem carbon sinks and establish a blue-carbon database. These are explicit implementation tasks with responsible agencies, not general references to ocean protection. The plan therefore creates a formal municipal monitoring, mapping and data-building programme for marine carbon sinks. It does not quantify removal targets, authorize restoration deployment or create a carbon-crediting mechanism.
source: Qingdao Municipal People's Government General Office
status_note: Adopted municipal implementation plan covering 2025–2027 with assigned marine-carbon monitoring, survey and database tasks.

document_title: 威海完成全省首单牡蛎碳汇交易
notes: Weihai's municipal government reports completion on 12 August 2025 of Shandong's first oyster carbon-sink transaction through the city's Green e-Finance platform. Five participating purchasers acquired a combined 1,500 tonnes of oyster carbon sink, and transaction certificates were issued at the event. The transaction was supported by a bivalve-aquaculture carbon-sink methodology developed with the Yellow Sea Fisheries Research Institute, providing a quantified technical basis for oyster-carbon accounting. The official report describes a local marketization experiment and future plans for insurance, loans and a full accounting–trading–finance service chain. It does not identify the 1,500 tonnes as national CCER issuance.
source: Weihai Municipal People's Government / Rushan municipal authorities
status_note: Completed local oyster carbon-sink transaction of 1,500 t on 12 August 2025; not identified as national CCER issuance.

document_title: 第144336号：关于“建设零碳海岛科学监测体系”的提案答复
notes: Yantai's formal 2025 proposal response documents implementation of the city's marine-carbon programme rather than merely discussing a future idea. It states that the Yantai Marine Carbon Sink Work Implementation Plan had passed review by the 76th municipal government executive meeting and had been jointly issued by 12 municipal departments and units. The response also records creation of a blue-carbon project reserve with 29 projects across five categories, pilot marine-carbon stock and flux surveys, monitoring and assessment of seagrass beds and seaweed beds around Changdao, and continued work on marine-carbon technology and value realization. The response does not itself replace the underlying implementation plan or constitute a carbon-credit issuance decision, but it is a formal official record of active municipal implementation.
source: Yantai Municipal People's Government / Yantai marine authorities
status_note: Formal 2025 implementation response documenting that the municipal marine-carbon work plan had been approved and jointly issued, with monitoring and project-reserve work underway.

document_title: 射阳县国民经济和社会发展第十五个五年规划纲要
notes: Sheyang County's 15th Five-Year Plan creates a detailed local ecological-carbon value programme that expressly includes marine carbon sinks. It calls for research, monitoring, measurement and accounting of marine, forest and wetland carbon resources; establishment of a county ecological-product catalogue and carbon-sink database; accelerated project filing and verification for carbon-sink products; and exploration of a mechanism in which wind-power enterprises purchase blue carbon to offset emissions. The plan also seeks to strengthen the county carbon-sink trading centre and develop carbon-finance products such as loans and insurance. These are formal planning commitments, but the plan does not establish that a specific marine credit has already been verified or admitted to the national CCER market.
source: Sheyang County People's Government
status_note: Adopted county 15th Five-Year Plan with active planning commitments for marine-carbon MRV, databases, product verification, trading and finance.

document_title: 山东省人民政府关于印发“十大创新”“十强产业”“十大扩需求”行动计划（2024—2025年）的通知
notes: Shandong's 2024–2025 action-plan package assigns the provincial marine and environmental authorities to conduct a province-wide survey and assessment of marine carbon-sink resources, carbon stocks, current sink quantities and additional sequestration potential. The task is framed as a concrete implementation measure for developing Shandong's blue-carbon industry and is accompanied by responsible agencies. It therefore qualifies as a formal mapping, inventory and assessment programme rather than a generic marine-development policy. The action plan does not itself create tradable credits, specify a project-level methodology or authorize a particular restoration project.
source: Shandong Provincial People's Government (official government repost)
status_note: Adopted provincial action plan for 2024–2025 with an explicit marine-carbon resource, stock, sink and potential assessment task.

document_title: 国家碳达峰试点（广州）实施方案
notes: The National Carbon-Peaking Pilot (Guangzhou) Implementation Plan gives substantive research and demonstration support to blue-carbon science and technology, marine biological carbon-fixation mechanisms and satellite remote-sensing time-series monitoring. It calls for major basic research in these fields and for low- and zero-carbon technology demonstrations. The marine component is primarily research, monitoring and technology-development support rather than deployment of a quantified blue-carbon removal project. The plan does not establish a marine crediting methodology or authorize a specific carbon-sink transaction.
source: National Development and Reform Commission / Guangzhou Municipal People's Government
status_note: Adopted national carbon-peaking pilot implementation plan for Guangzhou with active blue-carbon research and monitoring tasks.

document_title: 烟台市人民政府关于印发烟台市碳达峰工作方案的通知
notes: Yantai's municipal carbon-peaking work plan formally assigns preparation of a dedicated Marine Carbon Sink Work Implementation Plan to the municipal marine development and fisheries authority, with a specified completion timetable. This is a concrete governance commitment that placed marine carbon sinks inside the city's carbon-peaking policy architecture and required a specialized follow-on plan rather than merely mentioning blue carbon as a concept. The 2023 document does not itself contain the full marine-carbon methodology, project portfolio or quantified removal target; those functions were delegated to the subsequent dedicated implementation plan.
source: Yantai Municipal People's Government
status_note: Adopted municipal carbon-peaking plan; its marine-carbon task was subsequently implemented through a dedicated city work plan.

document_title: 烟台市湾长制办公室关于印发《2024年湾长制工作要点》的通知
notes: Yantai's 2024 Bay Chief System work priorities require completion of the city's Marine Carbon Sink Work Implementation Plan and explicitly support research and application of a marine-carbon CCER methodology, including efforts to submit or obtain recognition of such a methodology at national level. The document also assigns continued marine ecological monitoring responsibilities. These are formal annual implementation tasks with named responsible agencies. The measure supports methodology development and monitoring but does not establish that a marine methodology had already been approved nationally or that any project had received CCER issuance.
source: Yantai Bay Chief System Office / Yantai Municipal People's Government
status_note: 2024 annual work programme completed its policy period; it required marine-carbon plan completion, methodology research and monitoring work.

document_title: 国家碳达峰试点（烟台）实施方案
notes: The National Carbon-Peaking Pilot (Yantai) Implementation Plan contains a dedicated marine-carbon technology research programme. It calls for development of marine carbon-sink project methodologies to support voluntary transactions; research on rapid monitoring of marine carbon stocks and fluxes; and technology work on ecosystem sequestration and enhancement, subseabed geological CO2 storage, seagrass-bed and seaweed-bed restoration, salt-marsh carbon enhancement, cross-ecosystem carbon-flux observations and other marine carbon-storage measures. The plan establishes research and demonstration priorities rather than deployment authorization. No quantified removal is credited by the plan itself and no individual marine CCER methodology is approved through this document.
source: Yantai Municipal People's Government / National Development and Reform Commission pilot programme
status_note: Adopted national carbon-peaking pilot plan with an active marine-carbon technology research and methodology-development programme.

document_title: 第143255号：关于“关于加快推进我市海洋碳汇研究”提案的答复
notes: Yantai's formal 2024 proposal response records concrete preparatory implementation of the city's marine-carbon programme. It states that a dedicated Marine Carbon Sink Work Implementation Plan had been drafted and submitted for municipal executive review, covering scientific research, ecological protection and restoration, integration with marine industries, diversified carbon-value realization and pilot projects. It also records preparation of a Shandong seagrass-bed carbon-inclusive methodology, drafting of seagrass-bed and seaweed-bed carbon-stock survey standards, establishment of a 29-project blue-carbon reserve, and monitoring and assessment work around Changdao. Because the response predates final issuance of the dedicated plan, it documents an under-review planning stage rather than final legal authorization.
source: Yantai Municipal People's Government / Yantai marine authorities
status_note: Formal 2024 response documenting a marine-carbon work plan under municipal review and associated methodology, standards, project-reserve and monitoring work.

document_title: Ocean Climate Action Plan
notes: The Ocean Climate Action Plan is a U.S. federal interagency roadmap developed by the Ocean Policy Committee to coordinate ocean, coastal and Great Lakes climate mitigation and adaptation actions. For marine carbon dioxide removal, it sets a 2030 objective to build sufficient knowledge about the efficacy and trade-offs of different mCDR methods to guide deployment decisions and calls for a robust regulatory framework for research and possible later deployment that protects human health, the marine environment and affected communities. The plan also includes dedicated sections on sequestration of captured CO2 in sub-seabed geologic formations and on blue carbon and nature-based solutions. It coordinates research, governance, regulatory-development and restoration priorities but is not itself a statute, permit or carbon-credit methodology. The plan does not appropriate a single dedicated USD 6 billion mCDR budget; funding discussed around OCAP implementation comes from multiple federal programmes and broader infrastructure and climate legislation. Current federal NOAA and ocean-policy resources continue to list the 2023 plan as an official strategic document, although implementation priorities can change across administrations.
source: Ocean Policy Committee, Executive Office of the President / NOAA
status_note: Published in March 2023; still listed in current federal ocean-policy and NOAA strategic-plan resources

document_title: NOAA/NOPP Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal Research Partnership — USD 24.3 Million Awards
notes: In September 2023, NOAA's Ocean Acidification Program, acting on behalf of the National Oceanographic Partnership Program, announced USD 24.3 million for 17 marine carbon dioxide removal research projects involving partners from 47 institutions. NOAA reported that USD 14.36 million from the Inflation Reduction Act supported ten projects, while an additional USD 10 million came from NOAA programmes and appropriations together with the Department of Energy, Office of Naval Research, National Science Foundation and ClimateWorks Foundation for seven more projects. The portfolio covers macroalgal cultivation, ocean alkalinity enhancement, enhanced weathering, electrochemical approaches, iron fertilization, field trials, modeling, monitoring, community engagement and ecological-risk research. Its purpose is to reduce uncertainty about efficacy, co-benefits, risks and the science needed for future regulatory frameworks. These are research awards and controlled studies, not a general authorization for commercial mCDR deployment and not a carbon-crediting mechanism. Later Ocean Climate Action Plan progress materials in 2024 highlighted these awards, which can make secondary summaries appear to date the portfolio to 2024; the official NOAA award announcement itself is dated 7 September 2023, so the database year remains 2023 and no duplicate 2024 USD 24 million funding round is created.
source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) / National Oceanographic Partnership Program (NOPP)
status_note: USD 24.3 million portfolio announced 7 September 2023; 17 mCDR research projects, with programme activity continuing after award

document_title: Carbon to Sea Initiative — Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement Research and Development Programme
notes: Carbon to Sea launched in June 2023 as a philanthropic non-profit research and development initiative focused on ocean alkalinity enhancement. At launch it reported raising more than USD 50 million from philanthropic funders and committing USD 23 million in grants to a network of researchers. The programme evaluates multiple OAE pathways, funds laboratory and field research, supports locally operated research sites, develops measurement and verification capabilities, investigates environmental safety and scalability, and seeks to help develop responsible regulatory frameworks and expand the scientific community working on OAE. It is a non-state research-funding programme rather than a U.S. government policy, statutory authorization, carbon-credit standard or blanket permission for ocean deployment. Its inclusion in this database reflects its formal, well-funded Global ONCE research and governance role, not governmental legal force.
source: Carbon to Sea Initiative
status_note: Non-profit initiative launched 7 June 2023 with more than USD 50 million raised; programme remains active

document_title: Transforming Climate Action: Addressing the Missing Ocean
notes: Transforming Climate Action: Addressing the Missing Ocean is a major Canada First Research Excellence Fund research initiative led by Dalhousie University with Memorial University of Newfoundland, Université du Québec à Rimouski and Université Laval. The federal CFREF award is CAD 154,414,655, and Dalhousie reported that the grant helps activate a broader research programme approaching CAD 400 million with partner contributions. The initiative focuses on reducing uncertainty in the North Atlantic carbon sink and ocean carbon pump, improving observations and climate prediction, co-designing and evaluating novel ocean-based climate-mitigation approaches, advancing the science and technology of ocean-based carbon dioxide removal, and integrating Indigenous knowledge, justice, equity and community participation into adaptation and governance research. It is a multi-year research and innovation programme, not a deployment permit, carbon-crediting methodology or finding that any specific ocean CDR pathway is ready for commercial scale.
source: Government of Canada — Canada First Research Excellence Fund / Dalhousie University
status_note: CFREF award announced in 2023 at CAD 154,414,655; multi-year programme remains active

document_title: Convention on the Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes and Other Matter (London Convention)
notes: The 1972 London Convention establishes the foundational international regime for controlling deliberate dumping of wastes and other matter at sea. Röschel and Neumann classify the London Convention together with the London Protocol as the only international treaty framework that directly and explicitly governs ocean-based negative-emissions activities when those activities fall within the legal concept of dumping. The Convention requires Contracting Parties to prevent marine pollution caused by dumping, prohibits or tightly controls specified categories of material, and relies on national permitting systems for activities that fall within its scope. In the marine CDR context, the paper explains that the framework can become relevant where a technique involves deliberate placement of substances or material into the ocean; later LC/LP decisions expressly brought ocean fertilization within this governance system. The Convention itself does not name modern mCDR technologies, does not authorize ocean fertilization or ocean alkalinity enhancement, does not establish carbon-removal accounting, and does not create carbon credits. Its ONCE relevance is therefore regulatory and precautionary: it supplies binding anti-pollution obligations and a legal basis on which later marine-geoengineering decisions and assessment procedures were built.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Convention
status_note: London Convention adopted in 1972 and in force internationally since 30 August 1975.

document_title: 1996 Protocol to the Convention on the Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes and Other Matter (London Protocol)
notes: The 1996 London Protocol modernizes the international dumping regime by replacing the older list-based approach with a more precautionary system in which dumping is generally prohibited unless a material appears on the permitted reverse list and the activity satisfies assessment and permitting requirements. Röschel and Neumann identify the Protocol, together with the London Convention, as the core direct international legal framework for ocean-based negative-emissions technologies that involve the placement or disposal of matter at sea. The Protocol is especially important because later resolutions under it created dedicated rules for ocean fertilization and a 2013 amendment designed to regulate marine geoengineering through a positive list, environmental assessment and permit system. The original 1996 Protocol does not itself endorse marine CDR, quantify climate benefits, establish a carbon-credit methodology, or make every ocean intervention subject to its jurisdiction. Its relevance depends on whether a proposed activity falls within the Protocol's dumping or placement rules and on the additional decisions and amendments adopted by Parties. It therefore functions primarily as a binding environmental safeguard and permitting framework rather than as a deployment-support instrument.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Protocol
status_note: Adopted on 7 November 1996 and in force since 24 March 2006.

document_title: Convention on Biological Diversity
notes: The Convention on Biological Diversity is a binding global treaty for the conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources. Röschel and Neumann place the CBD within the implicit governance framework for ocean-based negative-emissions technologies because marine CDR can alter biodiversity, ecosystem structure and ecosystem services even when the Convention does not expressly regulate a particular CDR technique. The treaty requires Parties to identify and monitor important components of biodiversity, develop national conservation strategies, establish protected-area and in-situ conservation measures, and use environmental impact assessment for projects likely to have significant adverse effects on biodiversity. Those general obligations create a biodiversity-safeguard layer that can become relevant to ocean fertilization, alkalinity enhancement, artificial circulation, biomass interventions and coastal ecosystem projects. The Convention itself does not authorize or prohibit marine CDR as a class, does not define carbon-removal accounting rules, and does not issue carbon credits. More specific CBD COP decisions adopted later provide the explicit precautionary positions on ocean fertilization and climate-related geoengineering.
source: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
status_note: Adopted in 1992 and in force since 29 December 1993.

document_title: CBD COP 15 Decision 15/4 — Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework
notes: CBD COP 15 Decision 15/4 adopts the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, including global goals and 2030 targets for biodiversity conservation, restoration, sustainable use and the reduction of biodiversity loss. Röschel and Neumann identify Targets 8 and 11 as relevant to the governance of ocean-based negative-emissions technologies. Target 8 calls for minimizing the impacts of climate change and ocean acidification on biodiversity and increasing resilience through mitigation, adaptation, disaster-risk reduction and nature-based or ecosystem-based approaches while minimizing negative and fostering positive impacts of climate action on biodiversity. Target 11 calls for restoring, maintaining and enhancing nature's contributions to people, including ecosystem functions and services. The paper interprets these provisions as implicit support for coastal blue-carbon ecosystems and potentially other climate actions that provide ecosystem benefits, while simultaneously creating a biodiversity safeguard against harmful climate interventions. The framework is non-binding and does not specifically approve ocean CDR, identify a marine CDR engineering pathway, create a permit, quantify removals, or establish a carbon-credit method. Its relevance is strategic and conditional rather than a deployment authorization.
source: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
status_note: Adopted by CBD COP 15 in December 2022 as the global biodiversity framework for the period to 2030 and beyond.

document_title: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
notes: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) is the overarching binding legal framework for ocean uses and protection of the marine environment. Röschel and Neumann classify UNCLOS as an implicit governance framework for ocean-based negative-emissions technologies because it does not expressly regulate marine CDR but establishes duties that can apply to activities capable of altering or polluting the ocean. The paper highlights Article 192's general obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment, Article 196 on pollution and harmful or significant changes arising from technologies under national jurisdiction or control, Article 204 on monitoring the risks or effects of pollution, Article 206 on assessment of activities that may cause substantial pollution or significant harmful changes, and Article 208 on pollution from seabed activities. These obligations can shape national authorization, environmental assessment and monitoring of future ONET activity. UNCLOS does not constitute a blanket permit or prohibition for marine CDR, does not establish carbon-removal accounting or crediting, and many questions about how its provisions apply to specific emerging technologies remain untested in practice. Its ONCE role is therefore a binding environmental and jurisdictional safeguard framework.
source: United Nations
status_note: Adopted on 10 December 1982 and in force since 16 November 1994.

document_title: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
notes: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) establishes the binding institutional framework for international climate cooperation and explicitly treats sinks and reservoirs of greenhouse gases as part of mitigation policy. Article 4.1(d) calls on Parties to promote sustainable management and cooperate in the conservation and enhancement, as appropriate, of sinks and reservoirs including biomass, forests and oceans as well as terrestrial, coastal and marine ecosystems. Röschel and Neumann therefore classify the Convention as an implicit governance framework for ocean-based negative-emissions technologies: ONETs seek to increase atmospheric CO2 removal or storage through changes in the ocean, while the Convention supplies the broader climate purpose, reporting system and international process within which such activities may be discussed. The paper also stresses that, at the time of its review, formal UNFCCC negotiations had not explicitly adopted a general governance regime for geoengineering or marine CDR. The Convention does not authorize a specific ONET, does not establish a marine CDR permit or project crediting methodology, and does not by itself prove additionality or permanence of ocean carbon storage.
source: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)
status_note: Adopted in 1992 and in force since 21 March 1994.

document_title: Paris Agreement
notes: The Paris Agreement establishes the international climate framework for holding the increase in global average temperature to well below 2°C and pursuing efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C, with progressively updated nationally determined contributions and a long-term balance between anthropogenic emissions and removals by sinks. Röschel and Neumann use the Paris temperature objective as the policy context in which carbon dioxide removal has become relevant to net-zero pathways and therefore to research and governance of ocean-based negative-emissions technologies. The Agreement also recognizes conservation and enhancement of sinks and reservoirs and provides transparency, accounting and cooperative mechanisms that can influence how Parties frame removal activities in national climate policy. However, the Agreement does not specifically endorse marine CDR, does not define an ocean-based removal methodology, does not issue project permits, and does not establish that an ONET is eligible for Article 6 crediting. Any marine CDR activity would still require separate scientific evidence, environmental governance, national authorization and applicable accounting rules. The record therefore treats the Agreement as enabling climate-policy context rather than as a direct deployment instrument.
source: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)
status_note: Adopted on 12 December 2015 and in force since 4 November 2016.

document_title: Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue 2022
notes: The 2022 UNFCCC Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue was convened under the UN climate process following the COP26 mandate to strengthen ocean-based climate action. Röschel and Neumann cite the dialogue as evidence that the UNFCCC process was increasingly integrating the ocean into climate solutions and specifically note support for incorporating coastal blue-carbon ecosystems into UNFCCC processes such as nationally determined contributions. The dialogue brought together Parties, experts and stakeholders around mitigation, adaptation, ocean science, finance and implementation, helping connect marine ecosystem management with national and international climate planning. For Global ONCE purposes, its most direct relevance is the policy mainstreaming of mangroves, tidal marshes and seagrass as climate-relevant coastal ecosystems rather than authorization of high-intervention marine geoengineering. The dialogue was a coordination and policy-development process, not a binding treaty decision, project permit, carbon-credit methodology or quantified deployment programme. It does not establish that restoration produces a particular amount of additional removals and does not create a general legal pathway for ocean alkalinity enhancement, ocean fertilization or other mCDR techniques.
source: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)
status_note: The 2022 dialogue was completed within the UNFCCC process; its conclusions informed continuing ocean-and-climate dialogue and policy integration.

document_title: Convention on Wetlands of International Importance Especially as Waterfowl Habitat (Ramsar Convention)
notes: The Ramsar Convention is a binding global treaty for the conservation and wise use of wetlands through national action and international cooperation. Röschel and Neumann include the Ramsar system in the indirect governance framework for ocean-based negative-emissions technologies because wetlands and their ecosystem services can be affected by marine climate interventions, while coastal wetlands themselves are important blue-carbon ecosystems. The treaty requires Parties to designate Wetlands of International Importance, promote conservation of listed sites and pursue the wise use of wetlands in their territories. The Convention text predates modern blue-carbon policy and does not itself establish a carbon-removal objective or carbon market. Its specific Global ONCE relevance is strengthened by later Ramsar instruments, especially Resolution XIII.14 on conservation, restoration and sustainable management of coastal blue-carbon ecosystems. The foundational Convention therefore supplies a binding conservation framework and institutional platform, but it does not authorize restoration projects, quantify carbon removals, establish additionality or permanence rules, or issue carbon credits. Any blue-carbon project remains subject to separate national law, scientific accounting and project-specific safeguards.
source: Convention on Wetlands (Ramsar Convention)
status_note: Adopted on 2 February 1971 and in force since 21 December 1975.

document_title: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals
notes: The Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS, or Bonn Convention) is a binding treaty for conserving migratory species and the habitats on which they depend. Röschel and Neumann include CMS in the indirect governance landscape for ocean-based negative-emissions technologies because large-scale interventions such as artificial upwelling, artificial downwelling, ocean fertilization or other changes to ocean temperature, chemistry, productivity and habitat could affect migratory marine species. The paper highlights the Convention's requirements concerning endangered migratory species, including measures to conserve or restore habitats and to prevent, remove, compensate for or minimize adverse effects of activities or obstacles that seriously impede migration, as well as control factors that endanger listed species. CMS does not specifically regulate marine CDR, create a carbon-removal permit, establish a moratorium on ONETs, or provide a carbon-accounting methodology. Its Global ONCE relevance is therefore as a binding biodiversity and species-protection safeguard that decision-makers may need to consider when evaluating environmental effects of proposed marine interventions, especially where impacts are transboundary or affect listed migratory species.
source: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS)
status_note: Concluded in 1979 and in force since 1 November 1983.

document_title: Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage
notes: The 1972 World Heritage Convention creates a binding international framework for identifying, protecting, conserving, presenting and transmitting cultural and natural heritage of outstanding universal value. Röschel and Neumann treat the Convention as part of the indirect governance framework for ocean-based negative-emissions technologies because marine and coastal interventions can affect the ecological condition, cultural values and ecosystem services of natural World Heritage properties. The paper specifically points to Article 6, under which Parties should not take deliberate measures that might directly or indirectly damage cultural and natural heritage situated in the territory of other States Parties, and notes that marine World Heritage sites include important coastal blue-carbon ecosystems. UNESCO's later blue-carbon assessment further documents the carbon assets of mangrove, tidal-marsh and seagrass ecosystems in these sites. The Convention itself does not create a marine CDR policy, a carbon-credit methodology or a project permit. Its ONCE relevance is a binding heritage-protection constraint and conservation objective that may need to be integrated into environmental assessment and siting decisions for interventions capable of affecting World Heritage properties.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
status_note: Adopted on 16 November 1972 and in force since 17 December 1975.

document_title: Agreement for the Implementation of the Provisions of UNCLOS Relating to the Conservation and Management of Straddling Fish Stocks and Highly Migratory Fish Stocks
notes: The 1995 UN Fish Stocks Agreement implements UNCLOS principles for the conservation and management of straddling fish stocks and highly migratory fish stocks. Röschel and Neumann include it in the indirect governance framework for ocean-based negative-emissions technologies because ONETs can alter productivity, food webs, oxygen conditions, habitat and other ecosystem services that support fisheries. The Agreement applies precautionary and science-based conservation principles, requires measures to maintain or restore stocks at sustainable levels, calls for protection of biodiversity in the marine environment, and promotes scientific research and development of appropriate technologies in support of fisheries conservation and management. The paper notes that positive or negative changes in fish populations arising from ocean interventions could therefore interact with obligations under this fisheries regime. The Agreement does not authorize ocean fertilization as a fisheries-enhancement technology, does not make artificial upwelling or other ONETs a conservation measure by default, and does not establish carbon-removal accounting or credits. Its ONCE function is a binding fisheries and biodiversity safeguard that must be considered where a proposed marine intervention could affect managed stocks or associated ecosystems.
source: United Nations — Division for Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea
status_note: Adopted on 4 August 1995 and in force since 11 December 2001.

document_title: Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (A/RES/70/1)
notes: UN General Assembly Resolution A/RES/70/1 adopts the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its 17 Sustainable Development Goals. Röschel and Neumann use the Agenda as a cross-sector governance principle for ocean-based negative-emissions technologies, emphasizing that climate action under SDG 13 and conservation and sustainable use of the ocean under SDG 14 are part of an integrated set of goals rather than objectives to be pursued in isolation. The paper argues that ONET governance should assess synergies and trade-offs with food security, livelihoods, biodiversity, equity and marine environmental protection instead of treating atmospheric CO2 removal as the only policy objective. The Agenda is therefore relevant as a high-level policy-coherence framework for decisions on marine CDR, including distributional and sustainable-development considerations.
