It does not specifically authorize or prohibit any ONET, establish environmental-assessment procedures for marine geoengineering, quantify carbon removals, or create carbon credits. Its role in the database is strategic and normative: it provides internationally agreed goals and a policy-planning framework against which climate and ocean interventions can be assessed.
source: United Nations General Assembly
status_note: Adopted by the UN General Assembly on 25 September 2015; the Agenda and SDGs guide international policy through 2030.

document_title: Agreement under UNCLOS on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement)
notes: The BBNJ Agreement establishes a binding UNCLOS implementing framework for the conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction. The 2023 Röschel and Neumann paper discussed the then-draft agreement as a potentially important way to close governance gaps on the high seas, especially through environmental impact assessment, benefit sharing and coordination with other international processes. The final Agreement covers marine genetic resources and benefit sharing, area-based management tools including marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments, and capacity-building and transfer of marine technology. These elements can become relevant to future ocean-based negative-emissions activities conducted in or affecting areas beyond national jurisdiction, particularly where an intervention may have more than minor or transitory effects or interacts with protected areas and biodiversity objectives. The Agreement does not specifically authorize marine CDR, list an approved ONET, create carbon credits, or replace the London Convention/London Protocol regime. Its relevance is procedural and environmental: it adds binding high-seas governance, assessment, consultation and biodiversity safeguards that may apply alongside sectoral rules.
source: United Nations — BBNJ Agreement
status_note: Adopted on 19 June 2023; the Agreement entered into force on 17 January 2026.

document_title: Scientific Synthesis of the Impacts of Ocean Fertilization on Marine Biodiversity (CBD Technical Series No. 45)
notes: CBD Technical Series No. 45 provides an official scientific synthesis of the potential effects of deliberate ocean fertilization on marine biodiversity and ecosystem processes. Prepared by the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity after the international policy response to proposed ocean-fertilization activities, it reviews the scientific rationale for nutrient addition, the expected stimulation of phytoplankton production, the uncertain fraction of carbon exported and retained at depth, possible changes in food webs and species composition, oxygen and nutrient effects, biogeochemical feedbacks, and the limitations of current knowledge. The Röschel and Neumann paper uses this CBD assessment as part of the evidence base for understanding ocean-fertilization impacts and the precautionary governance response. The report is evidence-building rather than authorization: it does not approve field deployment, establish a carbon-credit methodology, demonstrate durable net atmospheric CO2 removal, or supersede the London Convention/London Protocol assessment system. Its policy significance lies in informing biodiversity safeguards and the CBD COP decisions that restrict climate-related geoengineering in the absence of adequate scientific and governance foundations.
source: Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity
status_note: Published in 2009 as CBD Technical Series No. 45; official scientific assessment supporting subsequent CBD ocean-fertilization and geoengineering governance.

document_title: Making a Short-Term EU Purchasing Programme Work for Permanent CDR
notes: This Negative Emissions Platform (NEP) discussion paper proposes a near-term European Union purchasing programme for permanent carbon dioxide removal before any long-term integration of removals into the EU Emissions Trading System is settled. Its recommended design combines buyer aggregation through an EU Buyers' Club, results-based per-tonne public support paid after Carbon Removals and Carbon Farming (CRCF)-verified delivery, private and Member State co-purchasing, recurring procurement rounds, and a pathway to larger-scale support associated with the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank. The paper recommends beginning with a EUR 1 billion pilot in 2026 and argues for a diversified portfolio of durable CDR pathways. Its proposed eligibility discussion expressly includes direct ocean capture among the methods that could participate once an applicable certification methodology and other eligibility conditions exist, making the paper directly relevant to marine CDR policy and finance. The EUR 1 billion figure, however, is an NEP policy recommendation rather than an adopted EU budget appropriation or a binding European Commission procurement commitment. The distinction is especially important because the official EU CRCF Buyers' Club has subsequently become a real voluntary market platform, but the Commission states that, as of April 2026, its approved permanent-removal methodologies cover DACCS, BioCCS and biochar carbon removal; marine pathways such as ocean alkalinity enhancement and direct ocean capture are not part of that initial approved-methodology set. This record therefore captures a substantive quasi-formal policy proposal that could shape future marine CDR demand, not an existing authorization or guaranteed public purchase of ocean removals.
source: Negative Emissions Platform (NEP)
status_note: Published discussion paper dated December 2025 and promoted by NEP in January 2026; the proposed EUR 1 billion 2026 pilot is a recommendation, not an adopted EU appropriation or procurement award.

document_title: 国家重点研发计划“全球变化及应对”重点专项项目“近海生态系统碳汇过程、调控机制及增汇模式”（2016YFA0601400）
notes: The project 'Processes and Approaches of Coastal Ecosystem Carbon Sequestration' (PACECS; project 2016YFA0601400) was funded under China's National Key Research and Development Program and led by Xiamen University. The official project profile lists a 2016-2021 duration and a budget of RMB 25 million. It targeted fundamental processes, regulatory mechanisms and engineered approaches for strengthening carbon sequestration in China's coastal and marginal-sea ecosystems, with particular attention to particulate organic carbon burial, microbially mediated refractory dissolved organic carbon production, carbon-sink indicators and measurement protocols, and demonstrations of ocean carbon-sink enhancement. Xiamen University's 2021 performance review reports 65 cruises or field-observation activities, 23 independently organized field investigations, four artificial-upwelling sea trials, 91 first-acknowledgement SCI papers, 31 authorized patents and 20 draft carbon-sink indicator standards. The project also supported the development of China's first artificial-upwelling carbon-sink enhancement demonstration area in Aoshan Bay. These outputs make PACECS a major national research-and-demonstration programme directly relevant to ONCE science and engineering. The project nevertheless remained an R&D programme: draft indicators and measurement protocols were research outputs rather than automatically binding national standards, and the programme did not itself create a carbon-credit registry, authorize commercial-scale marine geoengineering, or establish a national compliance methodology for monetizing its experimental carbon-sink results. Its strongest policy function was to build the scientific, technical and measurement foundation for subsequent planning, standards and potential carbon-market applications.
source: Ministry of Science and Technology National Key R&D Programme / Xiamen University
status_note: National Key R&D project implemented during 2016-2021 and completed its project/task performance-review process in 2021; its draft standards and demonstrations were R&D outputs, not general deployment authorization.

document_title: 国家级人工上升流增汇示范工程（山东鳌山湾）
notes: This national-level artificial-upwelling carbon-sink enhancement demonstration was developed in Aoshan Bay, Shandong, by a Zhejiang University team under the National Key R&D subproject on coastal blue-carbon sink enhancement. Zhejiang University reports that work began in 2017 and that all sea trials were completed by March 2020, making it China's first completed artificial-upwelling sink-enhancement demonstration project. The approximately 500-mu demonstration area integrated a marine-energy in-situ power platform, a data and automated-control centre, an ocean-environment and carbon-sink monitoring system, artificial-upwelling equipment and a large-scale macroalgae cultivation system. The artificial upwelling was designed to transport nutrient-rich bottom water to the euphotic layer, stimulate phytoplankton and macroalgal production and thereby enhance biological carbon uptake; the macroalgae component was intended to combine enhanced primary production with harvest-based removal of biomass. The project is important as an actual field demonstration rather than a purely theoretical study, and it generated operational experience on engineering, environmental monitoring and integrated aquaculture. At the same time, the demonstration should not be interpreted as a general legal permission for large-scale artificial upwelling in Chinese waters, as proof of durable net atmospheric CO2 removal at commercial scale, or as an approved carbon-credit methodology. Its function was experimental validation under a national R&D programme, with environmental performance, permanence, full lifecycle emissions and ecological effects requiring further evaluation before broader deployment.
source: Zhejiang University Ocean College / Ministry of Science and Technology National Key R&D Programme
status_note: Field demonstration initiated under a National Key R&D subproject in 2017; Zhejiang University reported completion of all sea-trial tasks by March 2020. It was an R&D demonstration, not a general deployment permit.

document_title: Ocean Finance for the Sustainable Ocean Economy
notes: This Ocean Panel-commissioned working paper, launched on 6 June 2025, assesses the global ocean-finance gap and sets out a high-level roadmap for governments, development-finance institutions, philanthropies and private investors. It estimates that roughly USD 550 billion per year is required to meet global ocean-sustainability goals while less than one percent of official development assistance and philanthropic finance is directed to ocean-related sustainability, and it examines blended finance, guarantees, debt instruments, carbon and biodiversity credits, payments for ecosystem services, matchmaking platforms and other mechanisms intended to move capital toward a sustainable ocean economy. For ONCE purposes, the paper contains a dedicated discussion of blue-carbon credits and uses Kenya's Mikoko Pamoja mangrove project to illustrate how verified carbon revenue can finance restoration and community benefits when credible baselines and ecological and social safeguards are present. It also discusses the Mangrove Breakthrough's blue-carbon finance roadmap and ocean-finance vehicles such as the Global Fund for Coral Reefs, the Sea Change Impact Financing Facility and the Octopus Desk, whose initial focus includes blue-carbon investment and sustainable seaweed aquaculture. The paper therefore provides substantive policy and finance guidance relevant to marine carbon sinks, but it is not a treaty, regulation, carbon-credit standard or funding appropriation. It was commissioned by the Ocean Panel as a working paper, and its analytical findings, examples and recommended actions should not be treated as binding commitments by every Ocean Panel member government or as guarantees that the finance targets and investment ambitions described in the report have already been capitalized or disbursed.
source: High Level Panel for a Sustainable Ocean Economy / World Resources Institute
status_note: Working paper launched on 6 June 2025 and currently used as analytical guidance; it is a commissioned expert paper rather than a binding Ocean Panel member-government commitment or direct funding authority.

document_title: Global Fund for Coral Reefs (GFCR)
notes: The Global Fund for Coral Reefs (GFCR), established and launched in 2020, is a United Nations-linked public-private blended-finance mechanism dedicated to coral reefs and associated coastal ecosystems. Its architecture combines a UN Fund that provides grants, technical assistance and concessional finance with a private-sector equity fund that invests in commercial reef-positive businesses and projects. Current GFCR materials describe a coalition of more than 60 nations, UN agencies, financial institutions, philanthropies, investors and conservation organizations and a portfolio operating across more than 20 developing nations. The programme's financing model is directly relevant to ONCE because GFCR explicitly develops sustainable finance mechanisms that can include payments for ecosystem services such as blue carbon, alongside biodiversity credits, reef insurance, debt conversion, bonds, conservation trust funds and sustainable financing for marine protected areas. The 2025 Ocean Panel finance paper similarly identifies blue-carbon and biodiversity credits among GFCR's possible financial mechanisms and describes an ambition to leverage USD 2-3 billion in public and private finance. These are portfolio and leverage ambitions rather than guaranteed disbursements to blue-carbon projects. GFCR is broader than carbon removal: coral resilience, sustainable businesses, fisheries, aquaculture, tourism, pollution reduction and community adaptation are major parts of the mandate, and not every GFCR-supported activity generates a carbon sink. The fund does not itself make every supported project a verified carbon-removal project, and any blue-carbon credits still require an applicable project methodology, credible baselines, monitoring, permanence and safeguards under the relevant standard and jurisdiction.
source: Global Fund for Coral Reefs / United Nations Multi-Partner Trust Fund partners
status_note: Active blended-finance mechanism established in 2020; blue carbon is one eligible finance pathway within a broader reef-resilience portfolio, not the sole purpose of the fund and not an automatic carbon-credit certification.

country_or_region: Global South and Small Island Developing States
document_title: Sea Change Impact Financing Facility (SCIFF)
notes: The Sea Change Impact Financing Facility (SCIFF) is an Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance (ORRAA) initiative whose concept was launched at the One Ocean Summit in 2022 to create an open financing architecture for coastal and ocean ecosystems, particularly in the Global South and Small Island Developing States. ORRAA states that SCIFF is designed to drive at least USD 1 billion of private investment into coastal and ocean ecosystems by 2030 and to provide a springboard for mobilizing at least USD 2.5 billion in broader finance. Its architecture is intended to bridge grants and investment capital, de-risk projects, develop market infrastructure and integrate sustainable blue finance into wider climate and biodiversity finance. SCIFF's stated ocean-conservation sector explicitly includes payments for ecosystem services and blue carbon, while the broader facility supports a mix of ocean conservation, sustainable seafood, blue technology, infrastructure, renewable energy and ridge-to-reef activities. The blue-carbon component makes SCIFF relevant to marine carbon-sink finance, but the headline USD 1 billion and USD 2.5 billion figures are mobilization objectives rather than evidence that those amounts have already been committed to or spent on carbon removal. The facility does not itself issue carbon credits, prescribe a universal blue-carbon methodology or authorize restoration projects. Instead, its policy role is to create finance vehicles, coordination mechanisms and enabling market infrastructure through which qualifying coastal and ocean projects can obtain grants, investment, guarantees or other forms of support subject to project-level due diligence, impact measurement, community safeguards and the requirements of any applicable carbon standard.
source: Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance (ORRAA)
status_note: Active ocean-finance architecture originating from a 2022 concept and subsequently developed into multiple finance instruments; its USD 1 billion and USD 2.5 billion figures are mobilization ambitions, not fully disbursed blue-carbon funds.

document_title: The Octopus Desk — A Financial Marketplace for a Regenerative and Sustainable Blue Economy
notes: The Octopus Desk is a blue-finance marketplace initiative developed by ORRAA with Investable Oceans as part of the wider Sea Change Impact Financing Facility. Its stated purpose is to connect project developers, donors, investors and advisers, reduce fragmentation in the sustainable ocean investment market and improve deal flow for projects in the Global South. ORRAA's 2024 project materials describe a 'high-tech, high-touch' platform intended to match investors with investable opportunities, provide market information on financial performance, impact and resilience, and support greater consistency in impact measurement, key performance indicators, monitoring and reporting. The same materials identify blue-carbon investments for climate mitigation, resilience, adaptation and biodiversity regeneration, together with sustainable seaweed aquaculture, as initial platform focus areas. The 2025 Ocean Panel working paper repeats those focus areas and notes an intention to facilitate investment into smaller ocean-economy enterprises, including transactions beginning around USD 50,000, while standardizing aspects of impact reporting. This makes the platform relevant to both coastal blue-carbon finance and macroalgae-related ocean investment. The Octopus Desk should nevertheless be classified as enabling market infrastructure rather than as a carbon registry or certification system. It does not itself verify tonnes of CO2, guarantee that listed projects receive capital, create a compliance carbon market or authorize marine activities. Any blue-carbon or seaweed project matched through the platform remains subject to its own accounting methodology, environmental and social safeguards, legal approvals and investor due diligence.
source: Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance (ORRAA) / Investable Oceans
status_note: Active ORRAA/Investable Oceans market-building initiative; 2024 materials described the platform as being in establishment and development, with blue carbon and sustainable seaweed aquaculture among its initial focus areas.

document_title: Negative Emissions Technologies and Reliable Sequestration: A Research Agenda
notes: This National Academies consensus study provides a U.S. research agenda for negative-emissions technologies and gives coastal blue carbon a dedicated assessment. It defines coastal blue carbon as land-use and management practices that increase carbon stored in living biomass and sediments in mangroves, tidal marshes, seagrass beds and other tidal or salt-water wetlands. The report treats restoration, creation, managed transgression and nature-based coastal adaptation as potential carbon-removal pathways, while distinguishing true atmospheric removal from storage of externally supplied carbon-rich material. It recommends a substantial national research initiative and specifies research needs for basic science, mapping, long-term field networks, project deployment, monitoring and verification, permanence, environmental constraints, social incentives and permitting. The synthesis includes illustrative annual research-budget estimates for coastal blue-carbon work, but these figures are committee recommendations rather than congressional appropriations or awarded grants. The report also discusses regulatory barriers and the need to accelerate appropriate permitting without weakening safeguards. It is an evidence-building research strategy: it does not itself authorize coastal projects, issue carbon credits, establish a mandatory accounting methodology, or prove that any particular restoration project produces additional and permanent net removals.
source: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM)
status_note: Consensus study published in 2019; the study is complete, while its research recommendations remain a reference rather than an appropriation or deployment authorization.

document_title: IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate (SROCC)
notes: The IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate assesses climate-change responses involving marine and coastal systems and is directly relevant to the evidentiary basis for ocean negative-emission governance. Its assessment covers coastal blue-carbon ecosystems and discusses proposed open-ocean interventions including ocean fertilization, artificial upwelling and ocean alkalinization. The report recognizes that protection and restoration of vegetated coastal ecosystems can contribute to mitigation and provide adaptation and ecosystem co-benefits, while emphasizing limits on the globally scalable mitigation contribution and the need for reliable accounting. For more interventionist marine carbon-removal approaches, it highlights scientific uncertainty, reversibility, ecological side effects, monitoring and attribution difficulties, governance constraints and social acceptability. The textbook specifically cites SROCC when discussing artificial upwelling as an emerging ocean-engineering approach. SROCC is an assessment report rather than a regulatory instrument: it neither permits marine geoengineering nor establishes a carbon-crediting programme. Its policy significance is evidence-building, risk assessment and synthesis for governments, and its treatment of the technologies should not be read as endorsement of deployment or as a quantified authorization of net carbon removal.
source: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)
status_note: IPCC assessment finalized in 2019; the report remains an authoritative scientific reference but is not a deployment permit or operating carbon-credit standard.

document_title: 国务院关于印发《全国海洋经济发展“十二五”规划》的通知（国发〔2012〕50号）
notes: The State Council's Twelfth Five-Year Plan for national marine economic development is an early national planning document that explicitly links marine economic policy with the carbon-sink function of coastal and marine ecosystems. In the book, it is identified as one of the first Chinese national policy documents to introduce the marine-carbon-sink concept and to connect that concept with ecological restoration. The plan promotes greener marine development and, in relevant coastal-development provisions, calls for use and protection of coastal ecological functions, including the blue-carbon-sink function associated with wetlands, deltas, islands and other marine ecosystems. Its practical role was broad policy planning rather than creation of a carbon market or a project-level methodology. It did not establish a national marine-carbon credit registry, define additionality or permanence rules, or authorize engineered ocean carbon dioxide removal. Because it belonged to the 2011–2015 Twelfth Five-Year Plan period, the implementation period has ended. It remains historically important as an early national policy basis for later Chinese blue-carbon, ecological-restoration, monitoring and market-development initiatives.
source: State Council of the People's Republic of China
status_note: Adopted in 2012 for the 2011–2015 Twelfth Five-Year Plan period; the planning period has ended.

document_title: 《生态文明体制改革总体方案》
notes: The Overall Plan for Reforming the System for Developing an Ecological Civilization is a national institutional-reform blueprint jointly issued by the CPC Central Committee and the State Council. It is directly relevant to the marine-carbon-sink database because the official text calls for establishing effective mechanisms to increase carbon sinks in forests, grasslands, wetlands and the ocean while strengthening international cooperation on climate change. The measure is therefore broader than a marine policy but explicitly places ocean carbon sinks inside China's national ecological-civilization and climate-governance architecture. Its policy function is enabling and institutional: it directs development of mechanisms and governance systems rather than prescribing a specific marine-engineering pathway, an accounting formula or a tradable marine-carbon unit. The book identifies this document as an important step in the domestic policy history of marine carbon sinks. The plan's stated reform horizon focused on establishing major institutional systems by around 2020, so the original implementation horizon is treated as completed, although many institutions and later policies developed from it continue. It should not be interpreted as establishing a marine CCER methodology or as authorizing ocean-engineering deployment.
source: Central Committee of the Communist Party of China; State Council of the People's Republic of China
status_note: Issued in 2015 with a major institutional-reform horizon centered on 2020; the original implementation horizon is complete, although its policy influence continues.

document_title: 《中华人民共和国气候变化第一次两年更新报告》
notes: China's First Biennial Update Report under the UNFCCC is an official national transparency submission dated December 2016 and submitted to the UNFCCC secretariat on 12 January 2017. The textbook identifies Chapter 5 of this report as an important point at which marine carbon sinks entered China's formal climate-reporting and policy narrative. As a biennial update report, the document reports national circumstances, greenhouse-gas information, mitigation policies and actions, institutional arrangements, support needs and other implementation information under the Convention. Its marine-carbon relevance is evidentiary and policy-coordination oriented rather than a stand-alone project mandate. The report helped place marine sinks within the country's climate-governance and international-reporting context, but it did not create a national marine-carbon crediting mechanism, approve an engineered marine CDR project, or provide a project-level MRV methodology for additional carbon removal. The reporting cycle has been superseded by later biennial update and transparency reports. Accordingly, this record is classified as a completed official report whose historical importance lies in formal reporting, evidence building and international coordination.
source: Government of the People's Republic of China / National Development and Reform Commission
status_note: Report dated December 2016 and submitted to the UNFCCC on 12 January 2017; superseded by later national transparency submissions.

document_title: 《中共中央 国务院关于完善主体功能区战略和制度的若干意见》（中发〔2017〕27号）
notes: The 2017 Opinions on improving the major functional-zone strategy and system are a national spatial-governance policy with a specific blue-carbon provision. As summarized in the textbook and contemporaneous official policy reporting, the Opinions call for exploring the establishment of a blue-carbon standards system and a trading mechanism. This language is important because it moves beyond general recognition of marine carbon sinks and explicitly identifies standardization and market design as areas for policy development. The clause is exploratory: it does not itself create a national blue-carbon market, approve a marine project, define a crediting methodology, or make marine carbon sinks eligible for the national CCER system. The document's overall purpose is broader spatial and ecological governance, including differentiated functional-zone management and protection of ecological space. For the ONCE database its relevant function is therefore policy planning for standards and trading rather than direct negative-emissions engineering. Later national and local methodologies, pilot transactions and monitoring programmes should be recorded separately rather than treated as implementation automatically created by this 2017 Opinion.
source: Central Committee of the Communist Party of China; State Council of the People's Republic of China
status_note: Adopted in 2017; the blue-carbon provision is an exploratory policy direction and does not itself establish an operating crediting or trading system.

document_title: 《中共中央 国务院关于完整准确全面贯彻新发展理念做好碳达峰碳中和工作的意见》
notes: This central policy document provides China's high-level national framework for carbon peaking and carbon neutrality. It explicitly requires consolidation and enhancement of ecosystem carbon sinks and, within that task, calls for integrated protection and restoration of marine ecosystems and improvement of the carbon-sequestration capacity of mangroves, seagrass beds and salt marshes. The measure is therefore directly relevant to coastal blue-carbon restoration and sink enhancement, while remaining a national strategic policy rather than a project-level implementation standard. It provides an enabling mandate for ecological protection and restoration, supports later planning and monitoring work, and places marine blue carbon within the broader national '1+N' carbon-neutrality policy system. The document does not quantify an authorized amount of additional marine CO2 removal, establish a marine-carbon credit registry, prescribe project additionality or permanence rules, or authorize engineered marine CDR such as alkalinity enhancement or ocean fertilization. Its relevant engineering pathways are limited to the specific coastal ecosystems named in the policy, and its carbon-pump tag is therefore BCP rather than a generalized multi-pump assignment.
source: Central Committee of the Communist Party of China; State Council of the People's Republic of China
status_note: National carbon-peaking and carbon-neutrality framework adopted in 2021 and still relevant to implementation through the 2030/2060 policy horizons.

document_title: 《“十四五”海洋生态环境保护规划》
notes: The Fourteenth Five-Year Plan for Marine Ecological and Environmental Protection was jointly issued by six central agencies and coordinated national marine environmental policy for the 2021–2025 planning period. It links marine environmental protection with climate policy by calling for monitoring and assessment of marine carbon sources and sinks, climate-response monitoring, restoration of typical marine ecosystems and measures to improve the ocean's carbon-sequestration role and climate resilience. The plan also strengthens ecological monitoring, risk prevention, integrated land-sea governance, institutional capacity, investment safeguards and international cooperation. For this database its most direct ONCE functions are evidence building through carbon-source/sink monitoring and enabling ecological restoration of coastal blue-carbon systems. It does not establish a tradable national marine-carbon unit, a CCER methodology, or authorization for engineered ocean CDR. The plan period ended in 2025, so the formal Five-Year Plan is classified as ended as of 2026 even though programmes, datasets, restoration projects and successor policies may continue. Subsequent monitoring standards and local transactions remain separate records.
source: Ministry of Ecology and Environment; National Development and Reform Commission; Ministry of Natural Resources; Ministry of Transport; Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs; China Coast Guard
status_note: Implemented for the 2021–2025 Fourteenth Five-Year Plan period; that formal planning period ended in 2025.

document_title: 《山东省碳达峰实施方案》
notes: Shandong's provincial carbon-peaking implementation plan contains an unusually explicit marine-carbon-sink workstream. It requires development of a marine-carbon-sink standards system, a province-wide baseline survey of the distribution of marine ecosystem carbon sinks, improvement of marine-carbon monitoring, marine ecological protection and restoration, continued coastal-restoration programmes, exploration of pathways for enhancing and utilizing marine carbon sinks, and construction of research and innovation platforms for marine sinks and ocean negative emissions. These measures make the plan more than a generic provincial decarbonization strategy. Its main function is to coordinate research, monitoring, standards development, restoration and future utilization through the province's 2030 carbon-peaking horizon. The policy remains enabling and preparatory: it does not by itself issue blue-carbon credits, define an approved offset methodology, guarantee additional carbon removal, or authorize engineered marine CDR deployment. Because the official language covers marine ecosystems broadly rather than one specific habitat, no narrower engineering pathway or carbon-pump mechanism is inferred beyond the evidence in the document.
source: Shandong Provincial People's Government
status_note: Issued in December 2022 with implementation directed toward Shandong's pre-2030 carbon-peaking objective.

document_title: HY/T 0305-2021《养殖大型藻类和双壳贝类碳汇计量方法 碳储量变化法》
notes: HY/T 0305-2021 is a recommended Chinese marine-industry standard issued by the Ministry of Natural Resources for estimating carbon sinks from maricultural macroalgae and bivalves using the carbon-stock-variation method. It was issued on 9 February 2021 and entered into implementation on 1 June 2021. The standard defines a technical calculation framework applicable to marine-cultured large algae and bivalves and is identified in the textbook as China's first fisheries-carbon-sink accounting method. Its policy function is measurement and accounting: it creates a common technical basis for quantifying relevant changes in carbon stock and supports research, project assessment and possible later market applications. It does not itself create a carbon-credit registry, determine whether a project is additional, establish permanence or leakage rules for an offset programme, or make quantified aquaculture carbon automatically eligible for national CCER compliance or voluntary trading. Macroalgal aquaculture is tagged BCP, while bivalve shell formation is tagged CCP, reflecting the most direct pathway-specific carbon-pump relationships rather than treating all aquaculture as a single undifferentiated mechanism.
source: Ministry of Natural Resources of the People's Republic of China
status_note: Recommended marine-industry standard issued 9 February 2021 and implemented from 1 June 2021.

document_title: Priority Agenda: Enhancing the Climate Resilience of America's Natural Resources
notes: The 2014 Climate and Natural Resources Priority Agenda was developed by the U.S. Council on Climate Preparedness and Resilience as a cross-federal framework for strengthening the resilience of natural resources under climate change. The textbook highlights the Agenda because it recognizes the role of coastal habitats in climate mitigation and calls for stronger protection and restoration that can preserve or increase blue-carbon storage. The federal framework links resilience planning with the capacity of natural systems, including wetlands and coastal areas, to absorb and store carbon, and it sought to align federal investments, programmes, information and management practices around climate-resilient natural-resource stewardship. For the marine-carbon database, its effect is enabling rather than transactional: it supports coastal habitat conservation, restoration, monitoring and climate-resilience policy but does not establish a blue-carbon offset methodology, issue credits, create a national marine-carbon market, or authorize an engineered ocean CDR project. It was an Obama Administration priority agenda rather than a permanent statute; its specific administration-wide programme has ended, although related federal coastal-resilience and blue-carbon work continued through later policies.
source: U.S. Council on Climate Preparedness and Resilience / Executive Office of the President
status_note: Federal cross-agency priority agenda issued in 2014; the administration-specific framework has ended, although related coastal-resilience programmes continued.

document_title: Strategic Plan to Protect California's Coast and Ocean 2020–2025
notes: The California Ocean Protection Council's 2020–2025 strategic plan established statewide priorities for protecting and managing the coast and ocean over a five-year period. Its climate work includes protection, restoration and where appropriate recreation of coastal wetlands and other nature-based coastal systems that store carbon while also supporting biodiversity, shoreline resilience and adaptation. The textbook cites the plan as a U.S. subnational example that integrates blue-carbon protection, marine ecological restoration and climate adaptation into coastal policy. The plan's role was to guide state coordination, investment and implementation rather than to create a stand-alone carbon-crediting programme. It did not declare all protected wetland carbon to be additional atmospheric removal, prescribe a single offset methodology, or authorize engineered marine CDR. The 2020–2025 planning period has ended and California subsequently moved to a new strategic planning cycle, so the record is classified as ended/superseded. Project-level restoration decisions, permits and any later blue-carbon demonstration legislation should be maintained as separate records rather than inferred from this plan.
source: California Ocean Protection Council
status_note: Strategic plan covered 2020–2025 and has been superseded by the next Ocean Protection Council planning cycle.

document_title: Green Growth Strategy Through Achieving Carbon Neutrality in 2050
notes: Japan's Green Growth Strategy is an industrial and climate-policy roadmap for achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. The revised strategy gives coastal and marine carbon a concrete policy role by promoting creation, restoration and conservation of seaweed and seagrass beds and tidal flats, development of methods to measure the CO2 absorbed and stored by these ecosystems, cooperation among industry, government and academia, and development of technologies and business models that can expand blue-carbon benefits. It also links seaweed and other marine biomass to innovation pathways within a circular and low-carbon economy. The strategy therefore combines research, standardization, ecosystem enhancement and industrial policy rather than functioning as a single carbon-market rule. It supports the evidence base that later underpins Japanese blue-carbon crediting initiatives, but it does not itself issue J-Blue Credits, certify a particular project or make all seaweed cultivation an approved carbon-removal activity. The record uses the revised 2021 strategy because that version contains the operational blue-carbon measurement and ecosystem-restoration direction; subsequent J-Blue credit rules and certificates remain separate database records.
source: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI), Japan
status_note: Revised Green Growth Strategy released in 2021 as a policy roadmap toward Japan's 2050 carbon-neutrality objective.

document_title: 《滨海盐沼生态修复项目碳汇计量与监测方法》
notes: This methodology was developed by Xiamen University's coastal blue-carbon research team for quantifying and monitoring carbon sinks generated by coastal salt-marsh ecological-restoration projects. It was reviewed by competent-sector and industry experts in September 2023 and was subsequently used to support early Chinese salt-marsh blue-carbon project development, including the Yancheng transaction described separately in the database. The method addresses project-boundary setting, baseline and project scenarios, carbon pools and greenhouse-gas sources, monitoring and calculation of net carbon-sink change attributable to restoration. Its principal function is MRV and accounting for a specific ecological-restoration pathway rather than establishment of a general emissions-trading system. The methodology is important because it provides a project-oriented technical bridge between salt-marsh restoration and marketable environmental value, but the expert review does not make it a national CCER methodology or a mandatory national standard. It does not itself issue credits, approve restoration construction, or guarantee additionality, permanence or market acceptance outside the programmes and transactions that choose to apply it.
source: Xiamen University / coastal blue-carbon methodology development and expert-review process
status_note: Methodology completed and expert-reviewed in September 2023; usable as project guidance but not established as a national CCER methodology.

subnational_area: Guangdong Province — Daya Bay / Pearl River Mouth Basin
document_title: 《在中国大亚湾地区开发和运营碳捕集、利用与封存（CCS/CCUS）项目联合研究协议》
notes: On 17 January 2023, CNOOC, the Guangdong Provincial Development and Reform Commission, Shell and ExxonMobil signed a joint study agreement concerning development and operation of a large-scale CCS/CCUS project in the Daya Bay area. The textbook describes the agreement as the start of work toward China's first offshore ten-million-ton-scale CCS/CCUS cluster concept. The study connects concentrated industrial CO2 sources in the Daya Bay and Huizhou area with potential transport and geological storage in offshore formations of the Pearl River Mouth Basin. Its immediate policy and programme function is collaborative research, source-sink matching, site evaluation, technical assessment and preparation for possible future infrastructure and investment. The agreement is not equivalent to a full construction permit, injection authorization or proof that the proposed cluster has reached commercial-scale storage. It also does not represent atmospheric carbon dioxide removal unless the captured CO2 source and life-cycle accounting separately satisfy removal criteria. The ONCE relevance here is marine geological CO2 storage and the governance, monitoring and environmental-risk evidence needed before deployment.
source: China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC); Guangdong Provincial Development and Reform Commission; Shell; ExxonMobil
status_note: Joint study agreement signed in January 2023; it initiates collaborative assessment and cluster development work rather than constituting a full-scale offshore injection permit.

document_title: 《红树林保护修复专项行动计划（2020—2025年）》
notes: The National Mangrove Protection and Restoration Special Action Plan for 2020–2025 was jointly issued by the Ministry of Natural Resources and the National Forestry and Grassland Administration. It explicitly recognizes mangrove ecosystems as important for carbon sequestration and storage and sets a national programme for strict protection, scientifically planned restoration, new mangrove establishment and improved ecosystem quality. The plan assigned implementation responsibilities to coastal provinces, required monitoring and assessment, encouraged local fiscal support and provided a land-use planning incentive linked to qualified new mangrove area. It also called for market-oriented restoration, encouraged social capital, and specifically proposed research and development of mangrove carbon-sink projects and exploration of ecological-product value-realization pathways. The policy therefore combines a direct restoration programme with governance, financing and future carbon-market exploration. The 2020–2025 action period has ended, so the plan itself is classified as ended, while restoration sites and carbon projects created under or alongside it may remain active. The plan did not create a national mangrove crediting standard or automatically certify restored hectares as additional carbon removals.
source: Ministry of Natural Resources; National Forestry and Grassland Administration
status_note: National special action plan implemented for 2020–2025; the formal plan period ended in 2025.

document_title: 湛江红树林造林项目（VCS/CCB注册及首笔碳减排量转让）
notes: The Zhanjiang Mangrove Afforestation Project is a long-duration blue-carbon restoration and carbon-finance project built on mangrove planting and restoration in Zhanjiang, Guangdong. The textbook reports that approximately 380 hectares of restored mangrove were developed under the Verified Carbon Standard and Climate, Community & Biodiversity standards, with an estimated 160,000 tonnes of CO2 reductions/removals over the 2015–2055 project period and an average of about 4,000 tonnes per year. On 8 June 2021, an initial transfer agreement covering 5,880 tonnes was signed, widely described as an early landmark Chinese blue-carbon transaction. The project combines ecological restoration, project-level carbon accounting, third-party standard requirements and market transfer, with revenues and co-benefits intended to support continued mangrove protection, restoration and local communities. The project uses external VCS/CCB standards; it did not create a Chinese national crediting system and its credits should not be treated as national CCER units. Quantified climate benefits remain subject to the applicable project baseline, monitoring, verification, permanence and leakage rules rather than being inferred simply from protected mangrove area.
source: Zhanjiang municipal authorities / Zhanjiang mangrove project participants
status_note: Project period runs from 2015 to 2055; first 5,880-tonne carbon-reduction transfer agreement was signed on 8 June 2021.

document_title: 象山县西沪港养殖藻类蓝色碳汇拍卖交易
notes: On 28 February 2023, Xiangshan County in Ningbo organized an auction-form transaction for quantified blue-carbon benefits from marine aquaculture in Xihugang. Official local reporting describes approximately 2,340.1 tonnes of carbon sink for a one-year accounting period associated with cultured macroalgae such as kelp, laver and Ulva; the auction began at RMB 30 per tonne and concluded at RMB 106 per tonne. The textbook cites the transaction as China's first auction-style blue-carbon deal and uses it to illustrate emerging local market experimentation before marine carbon sinks have been incorporated into the national CCER market. Its policy significance is therefore a project-level market demonstration and ecological-value transaction, not creation of a nationally fungible carbon credit. The transaction does not establish a national methodology, compliance-market eligibility or a permanent registry, and the quantified amount should be understood within the local calculation and transaction framework. Because the transaction concerned macroalgal aquaculture, the engineering pathway is fishery carbon sink through macroalgae and the directly associated carbon-pump mechanism is BCP.
source: Xiangshan County People's Government / local marine-carbon transaction organizers
status_note: Auction transaction completed on 28 February 2023; it is a completed local market demonstration rather than an ongoing national crediting programme.

document_title: 连江县首张“蓝色碳票”发行与海洋渔业碳汇备案
notes: On 3 June 2023, Lianjiang County in Fuzhou issued what official provincial reporting described as China's first Blue Carbon Ticket filed and confirmed by a marine and fisheries authority. The certificate covered 171.7966 hectares of marine area and represented approximately 27,456 tonnes of quantified carbon reduction/sink benefits associated with marine aquaculture, with an estimated value above RMB 550,000. The ticket was designed as a local ecological-product and benefit-right instrument that could support financing, transfer and market recognition of marine carbon-sink value. It sits within Lianjiang's local marine-carbon management and service-platform experimentation and is therefore relevant to crediting, registration and economic-value realization. The instrument is not a national CCER unit, does not by itself establish compliance eligibility under China's national emissions trading system, and should not be treated as equivalent to a nationally standardized offset. Carbon benefits remain dependent on the local accounting, filing and project-boundary rules. The associated aquaculture portfolio is tagged to fishery carbon-sink engineering, with macroalgal and bivalve pathways where applicable.
source: Lianjiang County / Fujian marine and fisheries authorities
status_note: First local Blue Carbon Ticket was issued and filed on 3 June 2023; the local certificate mechanism is distinct from the national CCER system.

document_title: 深圳市福田红树林自然保护区红树林保护碳汇拍卖（深碳交告〔2023〕1号）
notes: Shenzhen's 2023 Futian Mangrove Nature Reserve auction was a formal public transaction of quantified mangrove-protection carbon-sink value. The auction notice stated that a third party had verified 38,745.44 tonnes of carbon sink associated with protection activities over approximately 126 hectares during the first monitoring period from 1 January 2010 to 1 January 2020. Roughly one tenth of the total verified quantity was offered in the first auction. The starting price was RMB 183 per tonne and the winning price on 26 September 2023 was RMB 485 per tonne; official follow-up stated that proceeds would be remitted to municipal finance and used to support mangrove protection and restoration. The transaction is important as a local ecological-product value-realization mechanism and as an example of monitored blue-carbon trading. It is not national CCER issuance and does not establish a generally applicable national credit methodology. Because the underlying activity is protection of an existing mangrove system, the verified quantity should not automatically be interpreted as newly additional atmospheric removal without examining the project baseline and accounting rules used for the transaction.
source: Shenzhen Planning and Natural Resources Bureau / Shenzhen Public Resources Trading Center
status_note: First auction concluded on 26 September 2023; the transaction is complete, while later Shenzhen mangrove-carbon transactions are recorded separately.

subnational_area: Guangdong Province — Pearl River Mouth Basin / Enping 15-1
document_title: 恩平15-1海上二氧化碳地质封存示范工程
notes: The Enping 15-1 offshore CO2 geological-storage demonstration project is operated by CNOOC in the Enping Sag of the Pearl River Mouth Basin, roughly 200 km from Shenzhen in about 90 metres of water. The textbook records formal project establishment in December 2020, construction beginning in November 2021 and offshore CO2 injection starting in June 2023. The project is designed to separate high-concentration associated CO2 from offshore oil-field production and reinject it into a subsea saline formation, with an expected storage rate of about 300,000 tonnes per year and cumulative storage of about 1.5 million tonnes. It is widely described by CNOOC as China's first offshore CO2 storage demonstration project and has generated operational evidence for injection, reservoir selection and monitoring. The project demonstrates marine geological CO2 storage, but storage of industrial associated CO2 is not automatically atmospheric carbon dioxide removal; life-cycle source accounting must be treated separately. This record therefore captures the offshore storage engineering and monitoring programme without claiming a negative-emission quantity beyond what the project documents.
source: China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC)
status_note: Project established in December 2020, construction began in 2021 and offshore CO2 injection started in June 2023; project remains operational.

document_title: 《福州市连江县海洋碳汇管理暂行办法》
notes: Lianjiang County's Interim Measures for Marine Carbon Sink Management provide the local policy framework behind the county's early marine-carbon-sink development, filing, transaction and financial experimentation. Official government reporting on the county's blue-carbon work links the measures with resource surveys, carbon-sink assessment, a marine-carbon service platform, local transaction mechanisms and the issuance of Blue Carbon Tickets representing verified or filed marine-carbon benefits. The measures are relevant to macroalgae and shellfish aquaculture because these activities are central to Lianjiang's marine-carbon resource base. Their function is local governance and market infrastructure rather than national credit certification. The measures do not make Lianjiang certificates equivalent to China Certified Emission Reductions, do not create compliance-market eligibility, and should not be interpreted as a national marine-carbon accounting standard. The separate 2023 Blue Carbon Ticket is recorded as a project-level implementation outcome. This policy record is included because verification of the textbook's ticket example identified the formal local management measure that organized the underlying marine-carbon administration and transaction framework.
source: Lianjiang County People's Government
status_note: Local interim management measure in force during Lianjiang's marine-carbon pilot development; national CCER equivalence is not established by the measure.

document_title: 全国二氧化碳地质储存潜力评价与示范工程
notes: From 2010 to 2012, the China Geological Survey implemented the national CO2 geological-storage potential evaluation and demonstration programme to establish a national technical basis for geological carbon storage. The programme developed evaluation indicators and methods for storage potential and suitability, compiled national and basin-scale mapping, identified candidate storage targets, and developed site-selection, investigation and assessment methods for deep saline formations. Although the programme was not exclusively marine and its principal demonstration injection was onshore in the Ordos region, its mapping and basin-evaluation work explicitly included major coastal and offshore sedimentary basins such as the Bohai Bay and Pearl River Mouth basins; later China Geological Survey work extended this evidence base to China's adjacent seas. The textbook cites the programme in the chapter on China's marine geological CO2 storage as an institutional precursor to systematic offshore storage evaluation. It is therefore included as research and evidence-building relevant to marine geological storage. The original 2010–2012 programme has ended and did not itself authorize offshore injection or establish a marine carbon-crediting mechanism.
source: China Geological Survey
status_note: National geological-storage evaluation and demonstration programme operated from 2010 to 2012; the original programme is complete, with later offshore assessment building on its methods.

document_title: COM(2022) 672 final — Proposal for a Regulation establishing a Union certification framework for carbon removals
notes: The European Commission's 2022 proposal for a Union certification framework for carbon removals was the formal legislative precursor to Regulation (EU) 2024/3012. The proposal defined carbon removal broadly enough to include storage of atmospheric or biogenic carbon in the marine environment and proposed an EU-wide voluntary system built around quantification, additionality, long-term storage, sustainability, third-party verification, certification schemes and registries. The textbook discusses the Commission's 2022 carbon-removal policy initiative in connection with stronger investment in coastal ecosystems, biodiversity and sustainable carbon storage. This record is retained separately from the 2024 final Regulation because the database rules treat a formally published draft/proposal and the later adopted legal act as distinct versions. The proposal was not itself binding law and did not create an immediately usable marine-carbon methodology or authorize engineered marine CDR. The legislative procedure was completed when the final CRCF Regulation was adopted in 2024. Subsequent EU methodology work, including later exploration of tidal-marsh and seagrass certification, should not be backdated into the 2022 proposal.
source: European Commission
status_note: Commission proposal published 30 November 2022; legislative procedure completed with adoption of Regulation (EU) 2024/3012 in 2024.

document_title: 国家自然科学基金委员会基础科学中心项目“海洋碳汇与生物地球化学过程”
notes: The National Natural Science Foundation of China approved the Basic Science Center project 'Marine Carbon Sink and Biogeochemical Processes' in 2021, with the research centre operating from 2022 through 2026 under project number 42188102. The textbook preface identifies it as China's first National Natural Science Foundation Basic Science Center in the marine field and as a major institutional investment in marine-carbon science. Led by Xiamen University with collaborators from Tongji University and the South China Sea Institute of Oceanology, the centre focuses on the formation, regulation and environmental effects of marine carbon sinks and their feedbacks with climate change. The microbial carbon pump is an explicit cross-disciplinary theoretical core, while the programme integrates biological, chemical and geological research to develop deeper understanding and potential methods for marine sink enhancement. Its policy function is national research funding, scientific coordination, talent and platform building rather than engineering deployment. The approval does not authorize ocean intervention, issue carbon credits or establish a regulatory standard. Research outputs may inform later technologies and policy, but any deployment or trading mechanism requires separate evidence, methodology and authorization.
source: National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) / Xiamen University
status_note: Approved by NSFC in 2021; project period runs from January 2022 through December 2026 and is active as of August 2026.
